entry.title: Relearning English
entry.content:
Over the past few days, I have started learning English again. By accident, I discovered that thinking in English is quite a good way to stop my mind running in circles.

Perhaps my vocabulary is simply not large enough to let my thoughts roam freely. In Chinese, one small event can recurse through emotions, the past, and the future; in English, all that remains in my head is: who did what, and why?

As I continued, English also began to seem less difficult than I had imagined. Language is, after all, a tool for stating facts and expressing relationships. Grammar provides the structures shared by sentences; vocabulary fills those structures with whatever we actually want to say; and other words establish cause, contrast, and condition between the parts. Taking the process apart slowly—watching one sentence grow and several sentences join into a complete thought—is surprisingly satisfying.

Learning a language again from the beginning really does feel like retraining expression. Many things that I once said by intuition now require me to see the subject, verb, and object clearly, and to identify exactly where the premise of a judgement lies. In this respect, at least, English has forced me to become a little more rigorous.

Of course, the side effect of training my expression this way is also obvious: I already talked like I was writing a paper, and now I sound even more like one. How to learn to speak like a normal human being can wait until later.

For now, here is the core outline of English grammar that I have put together.

I. The Skeleton of a Sentence

The subject, verb, and object or complement form the main skeleton of a sentence. Modifiers and adverbials expand it outwards, while clauses place an entire proposition inside one of its grammatical positions.

The most basic English sentence structures can be divided into five patterns:

Pattern Structure Example
SV Subject + Verb Birds fly.
SVO Subject + Verb + Object I like music.
SVC Subject + Linking Verb + Subject Complement She is happy.
SVOO Subject + Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object I gave him a book.
SVOC Subject + Verb + Object + Object Complement I found the book useful.

These five patterns provide the skeleton. One particularly important addition here is the subject complement. In She is happy., happy is not an object. It describes the state of the subject, She, so it is a subject complement, also called a predicative complement.

II. What Can Occupy the Subject and Object Positions?

The subject, object, and complement positions can contain more than a single noun. They can gradually be filled by increasingly complex structures:

For example:

English can treat an action, or even a whole proposition, as a “thing” and place it inside a sentence. Once this becomes clear, noun clauses cease to look quite so mysterious.

III. Modifiers: Expanding Nouns

A modifier of a noun answers two questions: Which one? What kind of one?

These forms look different, but they all do the same job: they add information to a noun.

IV. Adverbials: Expanding an Action or a Whole Sentence

An adverbial answers questions such as: When? Where? Why? How? Under what condition? For what purpose?

Logical relations such as cause, condition, concession, time, and purpose mostly appear here.

V. Complements: Completing the Meaning

With some verbs, a noun alone is not enough. Something else must explain what the subject or object is, what state it is in, or what it does.

This is where linking verbs, subject complements, object complements, infinitives, and participles appear. Before memorising the terminology, I can ask a simpler question: Whom does this part describe, or whose state does it complete?

VI. The Verb System

Many changes in an English sentence are controlled by the verb. Instead of memorising the so-called twelve or sixteen tenses as separate tables, it is more useful to begin with four dimensions:

  • Tense: whether an event is located in the past or the present.
  • Aspect: whether the event is viewed as ongoing, completed, or in a general state.
  • Voice: who performs the action and who undergoes it.
  • Modality: attitudes such as ability, obligation, necessity, and possibility.

These are not several unrelated tables. They are different ways of describing the same action from different positions in time, state, and attitude.

VII. Non-finite Verbs: Turning Actions into Sentence Components

Infinitives, gerunds, and participles all derive from verbs, but they no longer function independently as the finite verb of a clause. They can instead act as nouns, modifiers, adverbials, or complements:

Non-finite forms should therefore not be memorised only as fixed patterns. The more important question remains: What grammatical function is this form performing here?

VIII. Three Types of Subordinate Clause

The three main types of subordinate clause simply hand an entire clause the work that would otherwise be performed by a word or phrase.

Clause Function in the larger sentence Example
Noun clause Subject, object, or subject complement I think that he is right.
Relative clause Modifier of a noun The man who came yesterday is my teacher.
Adverbial clause Adverbial of cause, condition, time, concession, and so on I stayed home because it was raining.

IX. Logic between Sentences

Only when connecting words join several propositions together do we move from “making sentences” to expressing a complete line of reasoning.

Logical relation Common expressions
Cause and effect because / so / therefore
Contrast and concession but / however / although
Condition if / unless
Purpose to / in order to / so that
Addition and progression and / also / moreover / not only…but also
Comparison than / as…as / compared with
Example for example / such as
Explanation and reformulation in other words / that is / which means
Inference therefore / thus / as a result

For a beginner, mastering cause and effect, contrast, condition, and purpose is already enough to express many complete ideas. Two common Chinese-influenced structures also deserve attention: English does not normally use because...so... together, nor does it normally use although...but... together. One side of the connection is enough.

X. The Order of Study

The whole system of grammar can first be compressed into one line:

More specifically:

For example:

The student who is sitting by the window studies English because he wants to study abroad.

Remove the two bold sections, and only this remains:

The student studies English.

This is an ordinary SVO sentence. The first bold section is a relative clause; the second is an adverbial clause of reason. What we call a difficult long sentence often begins as something very simple, then grows layer by layer.

XI. Points Not Yet Developed

The outline above explains the core architecture of English grammar: what skeleton a sentence has, how information is added, how clauses expand it, and how several propositions form a line of reasoning. It does not, however, cover every point of grammar. The following topics still belong on the map, but have not yet been developed one by one.

Area Points not yet developed
Noun system Count and non-count nouns, singular and plural, possession, articles, determiners, quantifiers, and pronouns
Adjectives and adverbs Position in the sentence, comparatives, superlatives, degree modification, and as...as
Preposition system Temporal, spatial, and abstract relations, together with prepositional collocations
Verb system Transitive and intransitive verbs, verb valency, auxiliary verbs, phrasal verbs, and subject–verb agreement
Tense, aspect, and voice The precise meanings of different tense–aspect combinations, the uses and limits of the passive, and sequence of tenses
Modality Differences among can/could/may/might/must/should when expressing ability, possibility, inference, obligation, and shades of attitude
Sentence transformations Negatives, yes–no questions, wh-questions, imperatives, and exclamatives
Special constructions Existential there, anticipatory and dummy it, cleft sentences, inversion, ellipsis, and substitution
Details of non-finite verbs Choosing between to do and doing, present and past participles, absolute constructions, and dangling modifiers
Details of clauses Differences among that/whether/what, restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses, relative pronouns, and relative adverbs
Conditionals and the subjunctive Real and unreal conditions, the subjunctive, and mixed conditionals
Reported speech Direct and indirect speech, together with changes in person, tense, time, and place during conversion
Organisation between sentences Coordination, parallelism, reference, ellipsis, substitution, punctuation, and information cohesion
Actual use Collocation, register, politeness, stress, intonation, and information focus

Some of these topics belong to grammar in the narrow sense, while others approach vocabulary, pragmatics, and discourse organisation. I have placed them together for the moment because, when English is actually used, they do not appear in separate textbook chapters.

Once I had sorted out this grammatical framework, I went back to scrolling through some videos. I automatically began analysing the structure of the sentences and the logic of the way their authors wrote, only to discover how much of the dialogue said almost nothing and how thin its content was. But that, too, can wait for another time.

entry.title: Building a Custom Huawei Tablet Theme from Scratch: HWT Dynamic Lock Screen and Home-Screen Wallpaper
entry.content:
MatePad Air · HarmonyOS 4.2 · 2800 × 1840
Beginning with an illustration I liked, I produced a native .hwt theme that Huawei’s Themes app could recognise, install, and use normally.

PDF Tutorial

  • Download the PDF

  • Download the Theme Used in This Tutorial

0. Why I Made a Huawei Theme Myself

The reason was simple:

Themes in Huawei’s store are far too expensive, and I found very few that genuinely appealed to me.

Many themes are essentially new arrangements of wallpapers, icons, fonts, and lock-screen layouts, yet they are not cheap. Worse, even after paying, I would often have to accept elements I did not want: enormous type, gaudy icons, peculiar lock-screen layouts, or wallpaper compositions unsuited to a tablet in landscape orientation.

In that case—

why not simply make one myself?

My requirements were clear:

  • Use a two-character illustration I liked on the home screen;
  • Place one character on each side and reserve the centre for icons and widgets;
  • Compose the lock screen separately instead of forcing it to share the home-screen image;
  • Put the time in the empty central region;
  • Preserve Huawei’s native lock screen, notifications, password, fingerprint, and unlocking logic;
  • Package the result as a real .hwt theme rather than installing a third-party “fake lock screen” app.

That decision led to this project.

The final result was:

Quiet Pair · Clear Clock v5

The home screen uses what I consider the strongest v3 composition, while the lock screen uses v2, whose characters are positioned more naturally. Both were adapted to the native 2800 × 1840 landscape and 1840 × 2800 portrait resolutions of my MatePad Air.

The most interesting part was not merely changing a wallpaper. It was gradually discovering how an HWT theme actually works under HarmonyOS 4.x.

1. Final Result

The final configuration:

  • Device: HUAWEI MatePad Air (DBY2-W00)
  • System: HarmonyOS 4.2
  • Landscape resolution: 2800 × 1840
  • Portrait resolution: 1840 × 2800
  • Home-screen wallpaper: v3
  • Lock-screen wallpaper: v2
  • Lock-screen clock: rendered in real time by the system DateTime component
  • Theme format: .hwt
  • Final version: v5 VectorClock

For the home screen, I moved the two characters towards the left and right, deliberately leaving a broad central region. Folders, icons, and widgets can therefore occupy the centre without covering either character.

The lock screen did not continue with the v3 home-screen composition, but returned to v2.

The reason is straightforward:

The home screen and lock screen perform entirely different visual tasks.

The home screen must remain usable, so the centre must accommodate objects. A lock screen is closer to a complete illustration and needs only to avoid the clock, date, and notifications.

I therefore stopped insisting that one image should serve every purpose:

Use the image best suited to the home screen there, and the image best suited to the lock screen on the lock screen.

The result immediately looked more natural.

2. Why I Did Not Use a Third-Party Lock-Screen App

At first, I considered finding a third-party application.

Such software, however, generally places another interface over the system lock screen, producing:

Attractive third-party lock screen
↓
Swipe
↓
Huawei system lock screen
↓
Unlock again

The classic double lock screen.

A third-party application cannot truly replace HarmonyOS password, fingerprint, or security authentication either.

I therefore chose the native Huawei HWT theme route.

HWT determines only how the lock screen looks. HarmonyOS continues to handle security, notifications, and unlocking.

That division of responsibility is precisely what makes this route comfortable.

3. Sources I Consulted

I mainly consulted Huawei’s official documentation and compared it with an HWT package already recognised by my tablet:

  1. Huawei Theme Studio
  2. Tablet theme specifications for HarmonyOS 4.x and earlier
  3. Huawei Themes Engine and lock-screen application documentation
  4. Documentation for the Time component
  5. Documentation for the DateTime component
  6. Huawei’s dynamic-theme Codelab
  7. An HWT already loading correctly on my MatePad Air

The official documents answered:

What does the engine theoretically support?

The working HWT and tests on the device answered:

Why does a theoretically valid package remain invisible to the tablet?

That distinction mattered throughout. Some behaviour is officially specified; other behaviour is merely compatibility experience obtained on HarmonyOS 4.2 + MatePad Air. I will keep the two apart.

4. What Is an HWT?

Once this point is understood, the production process becomes much simpler.

An .hwt is not a mysterious binary format. It is essentially:

Theme resources arranged according to Huawei’s directory rules, plus XML configuration files, compressed as a ZIP and renamed with the .hwt extension.

The workflow is:

My final directory looked roughly like this:

Four sections matter most:

description.xml

The metadata of the theme: its name, author, version, and so forth.

unlock/

The part that controls the dynamic lock screen. Its XML specifies:

  • The background image;
  • The position of the clock;
  • The position of the date;
  • The unlocking region;
  • Separate landscape and portrait layouts.

wallpaper/

The home-screen and static lock-screen wallpapers.

preview/

The cover and preview images displayed by the Themes app.

I later discovered that “the lock-screen XML can run” and “the Themes app is willing to recognise the HWT” are separate questions. The latter also depends on metadata, previews, directory structure, and even caching.

More on that trap later.

5. Complete Production Procedure

The following steps are the reusable part of the process. Changing the wallpaper later should require little more than repeating them.

Step 1: Confirm the Device Parameters

Open:

Record:

  • The exact model;
  • HarmonyOS version;
  • Screen resolution;
  • Main orientation.

My device:

I mainly use landscape orientation, so I prepared:

If the device already contains a third-party .hwt that it recognises, back it up. It becomes a valuable reference implementation.

Step 2: Design the Composition before Producing the Wallpaper

Do not merely find an image, scale it to 2800 × 1840, and declare the job finished.

The home and lock screens should be designed separately.

My home-screen principle was:

Thus, in v3:

  • Asuka moved left;
  • Rei Ayanami moved right;
  • A broad empty region appeared in the centre.

For the lock screen, I used v2:

  • The distance between the characters felt more natural;
  • The centre remained available for the clock;
  • The clock moved down by roughly 90–100 px from its original position.

Do not force a landscape image into a portrait canvas either. Perform a new centre crop and inspect the faces, clock area, status bar, and notification area.

Step 3: Prepare the Wallpapers

My final resource sizes were:

Recommendations:

  • JPG;
  • sRGB;
  • JPEG quality around 90–94;
  • Avoid repeated recompression;
  • Do not put numerous nearly identical large images in one HWT.

This preserves quality while controlling package size.

6. Writing description.xml

For example:

I retained the values already verified on the device in the reference HWT:

I did not continue inventing fields. This became an important lesson:

When an HWT is not recognised, do not speculate about metadata. Match a theme already verified on the same device as closely as possible.

7. Writing unlock/theme.xml

Example:

The most important line is:

It tells the engine that the true dynamic lock-screen configuration lies under unlock/lockscreen/.

8. Producing the Actual Lock-Screen Manifest

A simplified example:

Pay particular attention to:

and:

These anchor the time to the centre of the screen. Moving it vertically then requires changing only:

9. An Important Trap: Should the Clock Use PNG, SVG, or Text?

This was one of the more interesting changes in direction.

The first clock used:

with files such as:

The advantage is complete control over the font, including numbers pre-rendered in an attractive serif face.

The drawback is equally obvious: they blur when enlarged, particularly on a 2800 × 1840 tablet.

My first thought was to replace the digits with SVG. Huawei’s Time documentation, however, still centres on PNG digit resources and gives no clear method for replacing the set directly with SVG.

I therefore did not force SVG into the design. I changed to:

HarmonyOS renders the text in real time.

Advantages:

  • Extremely clear time;
  • No PNG resolution limit;
  • Sharp edges after enlargement.

Disadvantages:

  • Less freedom to select a custom font;
  • Difficult to reproduce the earlier serif digits exactly.

I chose clarity. The version became v5 VectorClock / Clear Clock. Strictly speaking, it is not an SVG clock, but a system DateTime text-rendering solution.

10. Prefer Separate Landscape and Portrait Manifests

The theme retained:

and added device-specific files:

Huawei’s standard resource sizes and native-resolution optimisation for the MatePad Air are not mutually exclusive. The engine supports virtual coordinates and scaling. For one device, however, I prefer native backgrounds at:

This reduces secondary scaling, blur, unnecessary centre cropping, and shifts in character placement.

11. Why the First Theme Did Not Appear at All

This was the worst trap in the project.

My first, very clean package contained:

It theoretically included every dynamic lock-screen resource. After copying it to:

the Themes app could not see it.

By dismantling a working HWT for comparison, I gradually added:

I also removed unverified metadata and used a new file and theme name. The theme then appeared.

No official document I found states that HarmonyOS 4.2 must reject a lockscreen-only HWT, so this should not be presented as an official rule.

What can be stated is:

On my MatePad Air running HarmonyOS 4.2, the first minimal lock-screen package was not recognised; after a complete theme shell was added by reference to a working HWT, it was recognised.

This is device-tested compatibility experience, not a formal specification.

12. Packaging a Real HWT

Suppose the directory is:

Enter MyTheme and compress its contents:

Do not produce:

The correct result is:

Opening the HWT should reveal description.xml immediately at its first level.

13. Inspect the Package before Installation

Run:

to verify that the ZIP is intact, then:

to inspect its structure.

Confirm:

The last point is particularly important on Windows. With extensions hidden, a file displayed as:

may actually be:

HarmonyOS will not recognise it.

14. Installing the Theme on a Huawei Tablet

Copy:

to:

Move old test versions elsewhere first. Then navigate through:

and, if necessary:

Reopen:

The new theme should appear. To apply only one section, use:

and choose the wallpaper, lock screen, icons, font, or another element. Names vary slightly among HarmonyOS versions.

15. If the Theme Still Does Not Appear

Check in this order.

1. Path

Is it:

2. Extension

Is it:

rather than:

3. Package Structure

Does the first level contain:

4. Metadata

Use an HWT already recognised by the same device as a reference.

5. preview / wallpaper

For a minimal unlock-only package, try adding the complete theme structure.

6. Cache

Clear the Themes app cache and force-stop it.

7. File Name

Do not repeatedly overwrite:

Use:

and change the theme title. This reduces cache interference.

16. Other Common Problems

The Time Is Blurry

When using:

first inspect the source dimensions of the PNG digits, or replace them with:

The Time Is in the Wrong Position

Change:

and tune landscape and portrait separately. One coordinate set will not automatically fit both.

A Character Is Cropped

Do not blame the XML first. Suspect the wallpaper composition. If center_crop never looks right, produce a new wallpaper at the target aspect ratio.

The Home Screen Looks Good but the Lock Screen Looks Strange

Stop forcing both scenes to use one image. My solution was:

Applying the Theme Changes the Icons

The reference HWT may contain its own icon mappings. Use an empty compatibility placeholder, or apply only the lock screen and wallpaper through theme mixing.

17. How the Theme Developed

The project passed through several versions.

v1

First dynamic-lock-screen attempt. The clock was too high, the package used a minimal lockscreen-only structure, and the MatePad Air did not recognise it.

v2

I dismantled a working HWT and used it as a reference, adding description, preview, wallpaper, unlock, and icons/launcher shells while moving the time down.

The theme was finally recognised. I continued to like the character placement in this lock screen.

v3

I recomposed the source artwork, moving Asuka left and Rei Ayanami right to create more central space.

The home screen became clearly better than v2, although the lock screen felt less natural.

v4 Hybrid

I therefore used:

and added native-resolution resources:

The visual plan was now settled.

v5 VectorClock

Finally, I solved the blurry-clock problem by changing:

to:

HarmonyOS now renders the time. The result is Quiet Pair · Clear Clock v5.

18. What I Actually Learned

In retrospect, the project was much more interesting than changing a wallpaper. At least five things became clear.

First, Rendering and Recognition by the Themes App Are Different

Correct lock-screen XML does not guarantee that HarmonyOS will regard the .hwt as a complete theme.

Second, Adaptation Is Not Merely Changing Image Resolution

Real adaptation means treating all four situations separately:

It is not a matter of using one image everywhere. Whether an image looks good depends upon its use.

Third, Let the System Render Whatever It Can

Beautiful PNG digits still face resolution limits on a large screen. By contrast,

lets the system generate the text in real time.

Fourth, an HWT Already Working on the Device Is Extremely Valuable

Official documentation says what the correct theoretical structure is. A working theme says what this particular machine actually accepts. Combining the two is far more efficient than guessing.

Fifth, Change Only One Variable in Each Test

The Themes app has a cache. If wallpaper, XML, metadata, and directories all change before a test, a success or failure reveals nothing about its cause.

Version the work:

This is why the second half of the project became much more efficient.

19. Minimal Reproduction Procedure

Once the principles are understood, rebuilding a theme requires:

Changing the style later requires only:

followed by repackaging.

20. One-Page Checklist

  • Device model, system version, and resolution confirmed
  • Home and lock screens composed separately
  • Landscape and portrait wallpaper dimensions correct
  • description.xml encoded as UTF-8
  • unlock/theme.xml points to lockscreen
  • Every src in the manifest exists
  • Clock component deliberately chosen as Time or DateTime
  • preview/ exists
  • wallpaper/ exists
  • unlock/ exists
  • No extra directory level in the archive
  • File is not .hwt.zip
  • unzip -t passes
  • New version uses a new file name
  • Themes app cache cleared
  • Landscape checked
  • Portrait checked
  • Notifications checked
  • Charging state checked
  • Swipe-to-unlock checked

21. References

The principal sources were:

  • Huawei Theme Studio
    https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/en/huawei-theme-studio/
  • Huawei tablet theme specifications for HarmonyOS 4.x and earlier
    https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/cn/doc/tablet-themes-specification-0000001078779076
  • Lock-screen application / Themes Engine
    https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/cn/doc/unlock-application-0000001305921217
  • Time component
    https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/cn/doc/content/time-0000001074625954
  • DateTime component
    https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/cn/doc/content/datetime-0000001073760045
  • Dynamic Theme Codelab
    https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/en/codelab/theme-particle/index.html
  • Huawei theme mixing / DIY
    https://consumer.huawei.com/cn/support/content/zh-cn16028416/

Conclusion

It began because the theme store was expensive and offered almost nothing I genuinely liked.

From changing a wallpaper, I moved into HWT directories, the HarmonyOS Theme Engine, dynamic lock-screen XML, landscape and portrait adaptation, PNG clocks, and DateTime text rendering.

Having made the entire route work, however, new themes will be much easier.

The project left behind not only the Quiet Pair · Clear Clock theme, but also a reusable process:

Consult official documentation to determine capability boundaries; examine an HWT verified on the actual device to confirm compatibility; adjust composition and coordinates through screenshots; finally, test through explicit versions.

Changing the wallpaper, characters, clock, date format, or entire visual style no longer requires starting from zero.

Mm.

If Huawei’s theme store still has nothing I like—

I will make it myself.

entry.title: Notes on Carefree Wandering
entry.content:
The first half of Carefree Wandering is mainly concerned with Zhuangzi’s view of the world and of cognition. Human beings always begin from themselves when trying to understand the world. Almost without noticing, they make themselves its measure, using their own experience, situation, and knowledge to confine everything that exists. This is, I think, one of the meanings behind the “distinction between the small and the great.” The enormous Peng, the cicada and the little dove, and many of the figures that follow all reveal the same tendency.

Zhuangzi therefore goes on to say: “The perfected person has no self; the spiritual person has no achievement; the sage has no name.” My present understanding is that we should try to step outside our habitual point of view. We should neither turn that viewpoint into an absolute nor mistake it for the world itself; at the same time, we should not allow external standards to imprison us in return. What Zhuangzi calls “carefree wandering” may be a condition of movement and freedom within the Dao, through which heaven, earth, and the myriad things continuously change. One does not cling to a fixed identity, scale, or judgment, but changes flexibly with the world until no single framework can hold one fast.

The second half first uses Xu You to develop the idea that “the sage has no name.” Xu You does not pursue titles that appear splendid but may have no genuine connection with his own life. Other people chase fame and profit, competing within a particular system of value. From his perspective, there is no compelling reason to enter the game at all; participation may simply bring disturbance, exhaustion, and injury.

“When the tailorbird nests in the deep forest, it occupies no more than one branch; when the mole drinks from the river, it fills no more than its belly.” What I truly require need only be enough to sustain my own life and allow me to remain free. You, Yao, may regard the empire, the throne, and the achievement of governing well as matters of the greatest importance. I have no obligation to enter your coordinate system, nor do I want to confine myself within identities such as “sage king” and “Son of Heaven.” What you value need not be what I value. What I seek is my own path of wandering.

The story of the spiritual person on Mount Gushe, meanwhile, criticizes the habit of standing within the boundaries of one’s own knowledge and experience and casually using them to judge everything in existence. Something should not be declared impossible merely because it exceeds what we have encountered. To put the point in a rather crude and not entirely accurate but intuitive sentence: “How can you prove that a god does not exist?”

This continues the earlier distinction between the small and the great. Human experience is always limited, yet limited experience readily disguises itself as the world in its entirety. It is precisely this intellectual complacency against which Zhuangzi warns us.

At the same time, the spiritual person of Mount Gushe represents an extreme condition of freedom imagined by Zhuangzi. To such a person, even the achievements of Yao and Shun, admired to the highest degree by ordinary society, weigh very little. The point is not necessarily that the spiritual person’s “ability” exceeds theirs. Rather, from the perspective of the freedom they seek, governing the world and accomplishing great deeds have ceased to be the most important standards of judgment.

The achievements of Yao and Shun may of course be pursued. There is simply no need to rely upon them as proof of oneself, or to let them harden into one’s identity. This is roughly what “the spiritual person has no achievement” means: not that such a person lacks ability or refuses to act, but that “what I have accomplished” no longer serves as the fundamental measure defining who I am.

At the end, the discussion returns to Huizi through the stories of the enormous gourd and the useless tree. Put in the bluntest possible way, the gourd story says: Huizi, you idiot, someone gives you this splendid enormous gourd, yet all you can think about is whether it can be used as a ladle. At this point you resemble a ladle yourself. Zhuangzi asks why Huizi did not use it as a vessel and float across the rivers and lakes. The problem was never the gourd. Huizi had already imprisoned it inside a fixed conception of “use.”

That was why the Confucian phrase “the gentleman is not a vessel” first came to mind. The comparison is not completely accurate, but there is some common ground. What Zhuangzi truly opposes is the attempt to use a rigid and predetermined social category to dictate what something “ought to be useful for.” First allow a thing to be what it is. Do not conclude that something is defective merely because it does not fit the purpose you had assigned in advance. Change the scale, the relation, or the mode of use, and what once appeared “useless” may become useful in another way.

If the enormous gourd means, “You think it is useless only because you do not know how to use it,” the enormous tree goes further: even if something truly does not count as useful by ordinary standards, so what? Precisely because the tree cannot be measured by the carpenter’s line, does not conform to his rules, and attracts no interest from him, it will not be cut down. It can grow undisturbed in “the village of nowhere, in the broad and boundless wild.” People may wander beside it or sleep beneath it, while the tree itself remains whole. This is approximately the “usefulness of the useless.”

Something regarded by society as “useless” does not therefore lack value. At times it is precisely because it remains on the edge, outside a utilitarian system, that it gains a space free from interference—a space more favourable to preserving itself and even to pursuing freedom.

Understood in this way, there are indeed parts of Zhuangzi’s thought with which I agree strongly.

The first is his warning about cognition: do not remain confined within your own field of vision and then assume that the world must be identical to what you see. The size, rightness, usefulness, and value of things often depend upon the position of the observer. The greatest danger lies not in possessing a scale, but in making that scale absolute—in mistaking one’s map for the world itself.

I also admire the lightness with which Zhuangzi regards his own existence. He no longer requires life to carry so many burdens of self-justification. A person need not become something, prove something, or leave something behind before earning the right to live freely. This lightness of spirit, this carefree wandering, is indeed an ideal condition that I deeply value.

Still, I probably cannot achieve so complete a freedom in Zhuangzi’s sense. At present I continue to feel that some of his thought contains a slight tendency to withdraw from the world. What I desire may be closer to “the greatest hermit lives in the marketplace,” or “doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone.”

For now, I would summarize what Carefree Wandering has given me in four layers:

In cognition, do not measure other things solely by oneself.
In value, do not define oneself through reputation and achievement.
In action, do not cut everything down to fit a fixed purpose.
In existence, do not assume that because you are “useless” by conventional standards, you must be remade into something else.

These four layers eventually converge into the first, incomplete idea of “carefree wandering” that I can presently understand.

The size, rightness, usefulness, and value of all things depend upon the scale and relation occupied by the observer. What matters, therefore, is not the possession of an absolutely correct scale, but the refusal ever to make one scale absolute.

If, upon reaching such an understanding, one can still enter the world, act, and create without allowing those things to bind one again—then that is probably the form of carefree wandering I myself would rather pursue.

entry.title: The Topology of Thought
entry.content:
The topology of thought (a provisional English rendering of the Chinese term) is a proposed framework for analysing the structure of thought through language and sustained conversation. Through a person’s habitual vocabulary, sentence-forming logic, methods of connecting concepts, and paths of topical development, it attempts to reconstruct a relatively stable shape of thought. It then uses that reconstruction to judge approximately how the other person thinks, align with that mode, and allow the conversation to continue deepening.

The word “topology” borrows topology’s concern with “which relations remain unchanged amid transformation.” The topology of thought describes the connections that repeatedly appear behind the changing words used in conversation.

Its basic claim may be summarised as follows:

Language is the observable trace left by thought. If a sufficiently long trace is observed, one may attempt to infer the space that generated it; after entering that space, one may continue the conversation along the other person’s habitual paths.

I. Name and Definition

“Language is the boundary of thought” forms the initial premise of the topology of thought. A person does not necessarily complete a clear and whole thought in the mind before translating it into sentences. Often, thought begins as a vague feeling or a set of relations not yet separated. Only when the person selects a word, constructs a sentence, and maps the thought onto a particular term does the original idea acquire a recognisable shape for the first time.

Language is therefore not merely the result through which thought is expressed, but also the tool thought employs and the environment it inhabits. A person develops indistinct thought from experience, body, and social circumstances; language then divides, names, and organises it. The resulting linguistic structure participates in the next act of thought in return. When new experience enters, old words and concepts may be revised, and the boundaries of thought move accordingly.

flowchart LR
    A["经验、身体与社会处境"] --> B["模糊思维"]
    B --> C["语言的切分、命名与组织"]
    C --> D["交流与持续对话"]
    D --> E["新的经验与他者反馈"]
    E --> F["被修正的思维"]
    F --> C

In this sense, neither language nor thought determines the other unilaterally. They form together through interaction. A “topology of thought” consists of the relatively stable conceptual relations, levels of abstraction, and path preferences within this process of mutual formation.

II. Basic Theorems

The topology of thought is not currently a rigorously demonstrated formal theory. The expression “basic theorem” refers to several propositions central to the internal framework, rather than claiming that they have become theorems in mathematics or cognitive science.

1. The Linguistic Boundary Theorem

What a person can stably distinguish, name, and organise within his present language forms the boundary of what he can clearly think and communicate at that moment.

This boundary is dynamic. New vocabulary, experience, metaphors, and people may strike the existing language and separate what was previously mixed together. “Shame,” “guilt,” “inferiority,” “embarrassment,” and “humiliation,” for example, may once have formed only one mass of “discomfort.” When these words genuinely become connected with different experiences, the person’s understanding of himself acquires a higher resolution.

Expanding vocabulary and experience can therefore make a conversation more interesting, rich, full, and substantial. Yet possessing more words does not automatically indicate more complicated thought. Vocabulary is closer to the resolution of a space of thought: it determines how finely a person can divide experience, but cannot guarantee that those divisions have been well organised.

2. The Conceptual Compression Theorem

A word that has genuinely been understood can compress a large quantity of concrete information and relations into one conceptual node that can be called repeatedly.

For example, one person may spend a long time describing how, upon entering an environment similar to one from the past, earlier memories, emotions, and bodily responses are activated together, as though what happened before has returned. Another person listens and asks, “Is this a form of scene re-enactment?” If the expression genuinely identifies the common structure within the earlier description, the person has done more than rephrase it; a conceptualisation has occurred:

$$
大量具体信息 \rightarrow 提取共同结构 \rightarrow 形成抽象概念 \rightarrow 用一个词完成调用
$$

When a similar experience occurs later, the person need not run the original long description again. Calling the node “scene re-enactment” can reactivate the complete set of relations behind it. Here, vocabulary is not merely a label attached to a thing, but an instrument of mental compression. In programming language, it resembles the name of a cognitive function: understanding the word means not only remembering the name, but knowing what will unfold when it is called.

What truly matters is therefore not only how many words a person possesses, but how many high-quality “packages of conceptual compression” are available. “Sunk cost,” “path dependence,” “self-fulfilling prophecy,” “discipline,” “alienation,” “projection,” and “metacognition” are useful not because they sound more advanced, but because each compresses a complicated phenomenon, a set of relations, or an extensively discussed theory.

Once the other person learns such a word, it alters observation in return. Events previously treated as unrelated may later reveal a shared structure because they fall under one concept. Experience produces language; language compresses experience; the compressed concept then becomes a tool for observing new experience. The expansion of vocabulary changes not merely how a person speaks, but what he will more readily notice in the future.

Compression, however, always loses information. “This is projection” may accurately identify a common mechanism, but it may also cover a complicated particular situation with an elegant term. Whether a concept has genuinely been mastered cannot be judged only from the ability to name it. One must also determine whether the person can decompress it when necessary: explain the relations it contains, the conditions under which it applies, what it omits, and why the present example genuinely belongs to it.

3. The Linguistic Projection Theorem

Language is an observable projection of thought, but does not equal thought itself.

What a person says is jointly affected by occasion, emotion, education, linguistic ability, conversational partner, and willingness to express. Silence may indicate an absence of thought or an unwillingness to speak. A simple statement may come from a simple judgement, or from complicated thought that has been compressed. One sentence therefore cannot justify announcing that “this person’s thought is exactly like this.”

Yet a projection, although not identical to the original, is not unrelated to it. If the sample is sufficiently long and contains enough contexts, the repeated appearance of one relation is more likely to come from a relatively stable habit of thought. The topology of thought is not mind-reading. It performs structural inference under limited conditions.

4. The Syntactic-Level Theorem

Sentence-forming logic reflects how a person habitually handles objects, relations, and logical levels at the same time.

“I do not like this” and “I am uncertain whether I genuinely dislike this, or whether, after recognising that other people expect me to like it, I have begun resisting the expectation itself” do not necessarily differ in the rarity of their words. The second, however, sustains more levels of relation:

$$
我 \rightarrow 感受 \rightarrow 对感受的怀疑 \rightarrow 他人的期待 \rightarrow 对期待的反应
$$

Structurally complicated sentences generally require more working memory and more readily expose how a person handles cause, condition, transition, recursion, and another person’s perspective. Yet “a long sentence equals depth” does not follow. Some people merely pile many ideas together, while others compress five levels of relation into one short sentence. What should be observed is not length, but whether a person can unfold levels when necessary and compress them without losing the critical relations. Returning to simplicity does not mean the absence of complicated structure, but the ability to expand and contract that structure freely.

5. The Conversational-Path Theorem

Compared with isolated words and sentences, the path of development in sustained conversation more clearly reflects the shape of a person’s internal world.

One sentence is easily imitated, but continuous dialogue repeatedly forces a person to choose where to go next. Some people habitually continue asking for causes; others make horizontal associations. Some divide a problem into two opposed alternatives. Some first recognise that a judgement is valid, then search for its limits and its opposite. Others continually ask why they themselves have judged in that manner.

These choices form relatively stable preferences for paths. For example:

  • Causal path: phenomenon—cause—earlier cause—condition;

  • Associative path: concept A—adjacent concept—long-distance leap—return;

  • Binary path: problem—two alternatives—elimination or selection;

  • Dialectical path: proposition—boundary—counter-proposition—reorganisation;

  • Metacognitive path: object—judgement of object—how the judgement formed—whether the language used also shaped the judgement.

One person may employ several paths. The topology of thought asks which paths are selected more readily before different problems and which almost never appear.

6. The Attractor Theorem

In a sufficiently long conversation, certain concepts repeatedly become the destination or transfer point of different topics. These concepts may be called attractors of thought.

If a person discusses work, love, study, and family, but readily returns in every case to “how other people see me,” then “other people’s evaluation” may be one attractor. If another person always ends by asking “what mechanism lies behind this?”, then “mechanistic explanation” may be an attractor for him.

One point requires attention: an attractor is not necessarily the person’s highest value. It may also be a frequent loop caused by anxiety, inertia, professional training, or present circumstances. It shows only that certain topics exert strong attraction within the existing sample; it cannot directly show that the person “is essentially like this.”

7. The Thought-Alignment Theorem

If one can approximately judge the path along which another person thinks, one can imitate that habit and continue the conversation along edges familiar to him.

With someone who habitually seeks causes, one may ask, “If we trace this result another step backwards, what produced it?” With someone who values experience, one may ask, “What did your body feel at the time?” With structural thought, one may point out that “there may be three levels here.” With dialectical thought, one may discuss “the conditions under which this judgement holds and how it produces its own opposite.”

Alignment first uses a path the other person can enter, giving new content somewhere to attach. Genuine alignment still permits opposition, correction, and the introduction of unfamiliar concepts. If it becomes mere agreement, it will not move thought forwards, but only deepen an existing loop.

8. The Co-evolution Theorem

Conversation is not the passive exchange of two already completed forms of thought. Language expresses thought while also participating in its formation. The other person’s response then becomes new experience, changing the next round of language and thought.

The process may be written as:

$$
T_0 \rightarrow L_0 \rightarrow D \rightarrow E_1 \rightarrow T_1 \rightarrow L_1 \rightarrow \cdots
$$

Here, $T$ represents a state of thought, $L$ linguistic expression, $D$ dialogue, and $E$ new experience formed through another person’s feedback. A conversation deepens not merely because one side “guesses” the other more accurately, but because both sides construct, through continuous response, a shared structure which did not previously exist.

III. Representing a Topology of Thought

To describe a person’s topology of thought, it may provisionally be represented as a directed weighted graph containing information about levels and paths:

$$
\mathcal{T}=(V,E,W,H,C,P,A)
$$

Symbol Meaning Appearance in Conversation
$V$ Conceptual nodes Repeated words, objects, values, and questions
$E$ Relational edges Connections of cause, analogy, opposition, inclusion, condition, explanation, and so forth
$W$ Edge weight Frequency and stability of a particular connection
$H$ Level of abstraction Ability to rise from concrete experience to rules, models, and meta-judgements
$C$ Conceptual clusters Concepts that frequently appear together within a person’s worldview
$P$ Paths of transfer Preferred paths when moving from one topic to another
$A$ Attractors of thought Core questions to which different topics readily return

What genuinely corresponds to “topology” is the question of which connections remain stable after vocabulary has been replaced.

In strict mathematical terms, however, this representation currently lies closer to graph theory and dynamical systems than topology. The name “topology” is retained to preserve its original intuition. If future formalisation is attempted, it must answer which transformations are permitted, which relations count as invariants, and how different graphs of thought should be compared.

IV. Development of the Idea

The topology of thought developed through approximately six stages.

The first was “language is the boundary of thought.” This judgement emphasised that people can stably divide and process experience only through the language available to them. Vocabulary, conceptual distinctions, and expressive ability therefore affect the space of possible thought.

The second stage discovered that vocabulary not only distinguishes experience, but also compresses it. An accurate concept can replace a long description and make structures of the same kind easier to recognise in the future. Vocabulary therefore involves not merely the number of nodes, but the amount of information genuinely contained behind those nodes and whether it can be unfolded again when necessary.

The third stage moved from vocabulary into sentence-forming logic. Vocabulary determines which nodes can be called; syntax determines how those nodes establish relations at the same time. The complexity of thought appears not merely in how many words a person knows, but in how many levels of condition, cause, perspective, and self-correction can be maintained.

The fourth moved from the isolated sentence into sustained conversation. A genuinely stable shape of thought does not remain within one sentence, but appears in the movement of dialogue: what the person asks first, where he goes next, how he treats a counterexample, and which question always returns at the end.

The fifth introduced the metaphor of “topology.” The object of study was no longer particular words, but the connections preserved while language continued to change. Conceptual nodes, relational edges, levels of abstraction, paths of transfer, and attractors together formed an observable graph of thought.

The sixth moved from recognition to alignment and added the effect of language upon thought. Judging the shape of another person’s thought is not the end. Once the other person’s path has been entered, both sides construct new words, connections, and questions together; the original topology may change accordingly. At this point, the topology of thought ceased to be only a static portrait of personality and became a framework for the co-evolution of language, thought, and other people.

V. Method of Analysis

A relatively complete analysis of a topology of thought requires at least the following steps:

  1. Collect continuous conversations across topics and periods of time, rather than extracting the single most representative sentence;

  2. Mark frequently appearing concepts without treating word frequency directly as importance;

  3. Observe which words can replace a complete description, and check whether they can be unfolded again and whether their conditions of application remain consistent;

  4. Identify repeated causal, analogical, oppositional, inclusive, and conditional relations among concepts;

  5. Record where topics begin, which transfer points they cross, and where they eventually return;

  6. Distinguish stable habits from contextual responses, such as examination anxiety, professional terminology, or defensiveness towards a particular person;

  7. Test existing judgements through new questions and observe whether the other person genuinely continues along the predicted path;

  8. Allow the other person to correct the analysis, and treat the correction itself as new information.

VI. Applications

The topology of thought is first applicable to deep conversation. It may help a participant discover that the other person’s difficulty does not necessarily arise from the absence of an answer, but from the failure to connect the question with a familiar path. Asking again through a different relation is sometimes more effective than continuing to add conclusions.

In education, it can distinguish whether a student lacks a concept, lacks levels, cannot transfer knowledge, or has already understood but not found an appropriate means of expression. In writing, it can help an author judge whether an article possesses terms but no connections, or complicated sentences but no genuine movement. In human-machine dialogue, it may distinguish imitation of surface tone from alignment with the structure of thought, allowing the system not merely to repeat the user’s words, but to understand how the user habitually constructs a problem.

It may also be used for self-observation. Looking back through long-term conversations and articles, a person may discover certain attractors: every problem finally becomes self-justification, every relationship becomes control and withdrawal, or every difficulty of action is rewritten as a larger theoretical question. Seeing the path does not automatically make it disappear, but at least allows a person to know where he has arrived once again.

VII. Relationship with Existing Fields

The topology of thought overlaps with several established areas of research, but cannot replace them.

  • Linguistic relativity asks whether and how linguistic structures influence cognition;

  • Cognitive linguistics and psycholinguistics study the relations among language, concepts, attention, memory, and reasoning;

  • Idiolect studies examine an individual’s relatively distinctive and stable habits of vocabulary and expression;

  • Conversation analysis emphasises turns, sequences, and the way a statement acquires meaning through its dependence upon earlier dialogue;

  • Discourse analysis and computational linguistics can extract conceptual relations, dialogue acts, and patterns of information flow from corpora;

  • Graph theory and dynamical systems provide tools for formalising nodes, edges, paths, weights, and attractors.

The topology of thought differs from these fields by concentrating upon the relatively stable “shape of paths” within one person’s sustained conversations, and by asking further how alignment can be achieved along that shape. At present, it resembles an interdisciplinary observational framework rather than a formal discipline with independent methods, experimental standards, and a shared research tradition.

VIII. Limitations and Criticism

The framework first faces a problem of observability. Language presents only one part of thought; unspoken feeling, bodily response, visual thought, and habitual action may all be omitted. Limited expressive ability does not imply equally limited thought. Strong expression does not imply that one’s judgements are closer to reality.

Second, complexity can easily be mistaken for depth. Long sentences, advanced vocabulary, frequent quotation, and multilayered self-reflection can all be trained or imitated, and may simply be circuitous. The depth of thought must still be judged by whether these structures can address real problems, accept counterexamples, expand when necessary, and compress when expansion is unnecessary.

Third, a shape of thought is not a fixed personality. A person may use different paths during an examination, in an intimate relationship, at work, over drinks, and upon an anonymous network. Familiar and unfamiliar fields likewise reveal different powers of abstraction. Every analysis should specify the corpus and context. A permanent essence cannot be inferred from one conversation.

Thought alignment also raises an ethical problem. Understanding another person’s paths can assist communication, but can also be used for persuasion, manipulation, and the creation of dependence. The legitimate boundary of alignment should be to improve the other person’s ability to express and judge, rather than bypassing judgement. The more one understands how another person thinks, the more one must preserve that person’s right to refuse, remain uninterpreted, and change paths.

Finally, a shared structure emerging within dialogue does not belong solely to either side. A new concept produced through sustained exchange may neither have existed originally in person A nor been introduced independently by person B, but have grown within the dialogue itself. Insisting upon returning it to a pre-existing “inner world” would overlook the generative role of conversation.

IX. Conclusion

The topology of thought may be compressed into three levels:

First, vocabulary determines the resolution of a space of thought and compresses complicated experience into concepts that can be called repeatedly; sentence-forming logic reflects how those concepts establish relations. Second, the paths and attractors of sustained dialogue reveal the shape of a person’s internal world more clearly than isolated words and sentences. Third, after these structures have been identified, one may attempt to align with the other person’s thought and allow the conversation to move in a direction where it can continue growing.

Language, however, is not a transparent shell around thought. It is both a product of thought and a participant in its formation. A person’s topology of thought is therefore not a fixed map hidden inside the mind and waiting to be surveyed, but a structure continuously changing among experience, expression, other people, and action.

Whether the name itself is defensible still requires clearer definitions, more conversational samples, and methods genuinely capable of being refuted. At present, it at least offers one way of seeing:

Conversation is not two people taking turns to output sentences, but two shapes of thought testing and connecting with each other, and changing together after the connection is made.

References

  • Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, 5.6: “The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.”
  • The Language of Thought Hypothesis — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
  • Philosophy of Linguistics — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
  • John J. Gumperz, Stephen C. Levinson (eds.), Rethinking Linguistic Relativity, Cambridge University Press, 1996.
  • Harvey Sacks, Emanuel A. Schegloff, Gail Jefferson, A Simplest Systematics for the Organization of Turn-Taking for Conversation, 1974.
  • Andreas Stolcke et al., Dialogue Act Modeling for Automatic Tagging and Recognition of Conversational Speech, 2000.
  • Laurence A. Clarfeld et al., A General Model of Conversational Dynamics and an Example Application in Serious Illness Communication, 2020.

entry.title: Neither Escort nor Welcome; Respond without Storing
entry.content:
Yesterday, I read an article which said that some people enjoy analysing, making deductions, and constructing theories. At first, their object of study is the external world. Gradually, they also place themselves inside it: why do I think this way, why do I need an answer, and who is the person observing me? Whenever an explanation is obtained, the explanation itself becomes a new problem. In the end, the observer continues to observe the observer, and reflection reflects upon reflection reflecting. Reason not only deals with problems; it can also turn its own process of dealing with them into another problem, and this process has no necessary end.

People imagine that they are seeking truth, when what they sometimes seek is only certainty. The answer itself need not be beautiful; it is simply that having no answer causes unease. They do not necessarily have to understand the world, but cannot accept that, for the moment, the world refuses to obey an explanation. Then “why do I need certainty?” also becomes an object of analysis, and even “I should accept uncertainty” can turn into a new demand.

This first made me think of Buddhism. Yet after discussing Laozi and Zhuangzi, the feeling remained somewhat different. They do not seem interested in installing another, more advanced observer above reason. Their questions are these: when is a form of knowledge already sufficient? Why do people always want to treat their own distinctions as the world itself? And after understanding, can they first go and live?

The Laozi begins, “The Dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao; the name that can be named is not the constant name.” Of course, translating this directly into “language determines the boundaries of thought” would move far too quickly. The early Wittgenstein was concerned with how propositions picture facts; the later Wittgenstein with how language is used within life.

Even so, the claim that “names cannot exhaust reality” gives me enough to consider for a long time. Student, engineer, successful person, failure—each name provides information. Without concepts, people could neither communicate nor act. Trouble begins when a name no longer merely describes certain facts, but requires the facts to obey it. Then we have fallen into the trap of language.

“Being and non-being generate each other; difficult and easy complete each other; long and short give form to each other; high and low incline towards each other” adds another layer. Many judgements are not fixed properties carried independently by an object, but arise within relations and comparisons. High requires low. Success requires a scheme for distinguishing failure. Excellence first requires the question: excellent according to which standard? This does not mean that every evaluation is false. Scores genuinely affect admission, and whether a project runs is governed by highly specific standards. But the distance from “this result is poor” to “this entire person is poor” is actually enormous.

When I then read that “reversal is the movement of the Dao,” certain things connect. A person who wants to control everything perfectly is eventually led by the desire for control. A person who wants to remain constantly lucid ends up continually checking whether he is lucid. A person who wants to prove that he is sufficiently excellent must ask before every action whether “this can prove me.” When a force is pushed to an extreme, it may indeed begin producing its opposite.

I naturally understand this through feedback and reaction. The analogy helps me enter the text, and should stop there. Laozi was not writing control theory. He was saying only that excessive effort is not merely exhausting. It can sometimes alter the thing itself, until the action gradually serves what it originally intended to escape.

Hence wuwei, or non-coercive action.

It obviously does not mean doing nothing. Describing it as “less control” is still insufficient, because less control can itself become a more sophisticated technique of control. In the Laozi, wuwei is also connected with spontaneity, desire, cultivation, and politics. It was not written specifically as a commentary upon modern procrastination. What I initially took from it was probably only one sentence: “Do not add anything else.”

Yet stopping here would reduce Laozi to a technique for managing anxiety, as though the entire meaning of wuwei were to make me consume myself less.

Laozi also pursues something positive called ziran. Here, it does not mean forests and rivers, nor doing whatever one pleases. It is closer to “being so of itself”: the countless things are not forcibly prescribed by an external will, but grow and change according to their own conditions. Laozi repeatedly writes of infants, the uncarved block, valleys, and water, probably because all approach a state of life not yet excessively shaped by reputation, desire, and artificial standards. What he seeks to reduce is not action itself, but the human impulse to prescribe a shape for everything.

“Giving birth without possessing, acting without relying upon achievement, helping to grow without ruling” may come closer than “doing nothing.” Something is nurtured without being claimed as property; a task is completed without grasping its credit; growth is assisted without thereby obtaining the right to rule. Human beings still participate in the world, but do not announce that the world belongs to them because they have participated.

Thus, wuwei in the Laozi is not merely individual cultivation. In discussing politics, the text says, “I practise non-action and the people transform themselves; I value stillness and the people correct themselves.” This ancient political vision obviously cannot be transferred to the present without distinction. At the very least, however, it shows that Laozi was not seeking an individual more skilled at self-management, but an order that does not depend upon constantly stimulating desire, manufacturing competition, and imposing intervention. If the ruler undertakes less self-important shaping, people may regain room for “self-transformation.”

Seen in this light, “do not add anything else” is no longer merely negative subtraction. It creates room for something to happen by itself.

“Being provides advantage; non-being provides use” probably describes the same kind of empty space. A wheel turns because the centre of its hub has not been filled; a vessel holds something because its interior is empty. “Non-being” here is neither deficiency nor the destruction of everything already present. It merely reminds me that certain functions occur precisely where a space has not been occupied.

Whenever I discover a problem, I feel that I ought to add something: one more explanation, one more plan, one more review, one more angle from which to inspect myself. Yet some problems do not lack a step; they have already been crowded full of steps. Writing another analysis of “how to stop excessive analysis” does nothing except add another layer to the recursion.

I am therefore now more willing to ask whether this step actually addresses reality, or merely relieves the anxiety created by my inability to control reality.

The two are often entangled. I may not be able to distinguish them.

Still, having spoken of Laozi and Zhuangzi together, I should pause here. Laozi retains a direction of “return”: return to the uncarved block, the infant, and softness, withdrawing from a condition disturbed by desire and artificial standards. Zhuangzi does not necessarily promise one authentic position to which everyone ought to return. He asks not only how to return to nature, but who is standing where when the words nature, correct, and original are spoken.

One speaks of returning; the other of wandering. They are not two successive stations along the same road.

In the “Discussion on Making All Things Equal,” the problem returns to the person who is knowing the world. “There is a ‘this’ and a ‘that’ for every right and wrong.” Each person begins from a “this,” seeing his own “right” and another’s “wrong.” This does not mean that truth and falsehood do not exist, still less that every opinion possesses equal quality. A frog at the bottom of a well does not know the sea. The existence of its own perspective does not suddenly give it as much information as someone who has seen the sea.

The real difficulty of Zhuangzi is that he restores the position of the judge which an analysis had removed. What I see also depends upon where I see it from, what I have experienced, what language I use, and what kind of life I am presently defending. I may still say that something is wrong, and must remain responsible for the statement. I can no longer pretend, however, that I speak from an absolute position which does not exist.

The expression “pivot of the Dao” is especially interesting. A pivot is the axis of a door. It stands upon neither side, but allows the door to turn. It does not demand that a person possess no position forever. I may make a judgement now and act accordingly; when new facts arrive, I may also turn. This does not mean occupying every perspective in advance. It means only admitting that I stand here now, and that here is not the centre of the universe.

Then again, this reminder about perspective cannot be reduced to the sentence “everyone has a point.” I have just written that “everyone possesses the right to experience the world,” but not everyone’s judgement produces equal consequences. The partial view of someone who controls institutions, resources, and the authority to define things is more likely to become the conditions under which other people must live. Particular harm cannot be erased by saying that “each side is limited,” nor can responsibility. Knowing that one occupies a position should restrain absolutism, not provide an excuse.

Zhuangzi’s loosening of the “self” cannot be identified directly with the Buddhist idea of non-self either. “I have lost myself” and “the perfected person has no self,” at least in this reading, are closer to refusing attachment to one particular self. Student, lover, son, a person preparing for an examination—each identity is real and participates in forming me. None has the right to possess me alone, and none may announce that the whole person has failed merely because it temporarily fails.

Connected with “depending upon nothing,” this can easily be presented as “needing nothing.” But how could a concrete person possess no dependencies? People need food and sleep, money, a body, and assistance from others. Their room for choice is also constrained by real conditions. As I wrote in the article on feminism, telling someone to become courageous and true to herself does not create freedom from nothing when she lacks safe housing and the resources for life. Zhuangzi should not be used to cancel those conditions.

I therefore dare to offer only a highly personal translation: “depending upon nothing” does not mean having no conditions, but refusing to mortgage the right to exist completely to any single condition. The postgraduate entrance examination remains important, but passing it does not grant me permission to exist. Relationships remain important, but being chosen by someone does not issue the certificate proving whether I deserve love. Ability must still grow, but its strength does not determine whether I may first experience the world as a human being.

This certainly represents one level of free wandering, yet now it seems insufficient. Behind “do not let conditions define me” there remains a very solid self: external identities may change, but inside them there seems to be one true self that must be protected whole. Zhuangzi may not intend to preserve even that “true self” for me.

The opening of the “Free and Easy Wandering” is strange. The giant Kun and Peng still require sufficiently deep water and powerful wind before taking flight; the cicada and little dove cannot fly high, but have their own suitable elm and sandalwood trees; Liezi can already ride the wind, yet Zhuangzi still says that “he remains dependent.” Thus, the essay does not first imagine someone who needs no conditions and then call him free. On the contrary, it spends a long time describing how all beings depend upon something before asking: “If one rides the proper course of heaven and earth, and commands the changes of the six energies in order to wander through the inexhaustible, upon what would such a person depend?”

I now prefer to place the emphasis upon the word “wander.” Free wandering does not mean finally locating a position that will remain correct and safe forever. It means not being nailed permanently to any position. Heaven, earth, and the six energies continue to change, while people continue to act through them. The difference is that a person no longer requires one condition to support him forever, but retains the capacity to turn, move, and respond again when change arrives.

Seen this way, “the perfected person has no self, the spiritual person has no achievement, and the sage has no name” does not eliminate people, action, and names. Having no self means no longer making one fixed self the centre of everything. Having no achievement means not freezing oneself through achievement after acting. Having no name means using names without allowing them to become the final judgement. This is less a defence of a true self untouched by influence than the preservation of life’s capacity to continue changing.

At its end, “Free and Easy Wandering” deliberately offers two “useless” things. The enormous gourd is too heavy to hold water and, when divided into ladles, fits nothing. The tree-of-heaven grows contrary to every carpenter’s rule and is ignored by the woodcutter. Huizi sees only that they fail to meet existing purposes. Zhuangzi asks why the great gourd cannot float upon rivers and lakes, and why the tree cannot be planted in the land of nothing whatever, so that one may wander freely and sleep beneath it. Not every existence must first prove that it has the same kind of use. Being declared useless by one purpose sometimes means only that it can travel somewhere that purpose has never imagined.

Free wandering is therefore not a flight from reality out of nothing, still less the declaration of spiritual freedom behind a closed door. It must still “ride things” and pass through particular conditions; only the “wandering mind” is no longer detained by them. The external world changes me, relationships change me, and every failure and success leaves something behind. Zhuangzi probably does not guarantee that a complete self will survive the change. His question is closer to this: if I already exist within change, why must the preservation of my present self become the measure of every change?

Of course, everything written so far remains inside my head. Yet Zhuangzi also describes Cook Ding cutting up an ox: “I meet it with the spirit and do not look with the eyes; sensory knowledge stops and the spirit moves as it desires.” This sounds like mystical intuition, but beneath it lie Ding’s many years of experience with the knife. Even reducing it to the bodily intuition produced by expertise would still make the passage too narrow. Ding also says, “There are spaces between the joints, while the knife-edge has no thickness; use what has no thickness to enter where there is space.” His knife remains as new after nineteen years not because he controls the ox more completely, but because he does not strike directly against tendons and bones. He travels through the gaps which already exist within the thing. Action no longer depends upon pressing forward with greater force. It makes itself thin and passes through where the thing allows passage.

Fasting of the mind and sitting in forgetfulness are the same. They are not anti-intellectual slogans; they merely prevent existing judgements from occupying every position the moment reality appears. To act “according to what is already so,” one must still encounter things, be limited by them, and be corrected by them. Without practice, so-called movement with the tendency of things may simply follow one’s own imagination. This joins closely with my existing understanding: reality exists independently; people use body, experience, and language to form limited knowledge, then act to encounter it; reality pushes back, allowing knowledge to be corrected again.

Laozi and Zhuangzi have not proved that models should not be built, nor told me to follow feeling from now on. What they add is an answer to what should happen after a model has completed one task.

My default answer was always further improvement. Discover a deviation and update; discover that the update also contains deviation and reflect upon the update. Openness slowly became a task that was never allowed to end: I must remain open, must constantly revise, must guard against becoming rigid. Eventually, even “continue using it without fully believing it” became a self-image that required continual proof. Laozi and Zhuangzi provide no still higher method of remaining open. They merely say that, sometimes, I can stop inspecting for a while.

I am probably incapable of truly stopping the construction of models. Perhaps even this article is another outbreak of the same symptom. But can I at least stop turning every event immediately into a judgement about “what kind of person I am”?

This also explains why the eight characters I finally remembered came from “Responding to Emperors and Kings”:

Neither escort nor welcome; respond without storing.

The original says that “the perfected person’s mind operates like a mirror”: it does not follow what leaves or anticipate what arrives; when something comes, it reflects it, and when it passes, nothing is retained. In conversation, we interpreted this as follows: do not force the past into the present, and do not cover the present with the future in advance; respond when something comes, and stop grasping it once it has passed. Reading the words through past and future is the modern use I have taken from them, not the only interpretation of the original. More directly, the source says: do not follow, do not anticipate; respond upon arrival and retain nothing after departure.

The word “respond” is also important. A mirror does not avoid contact with external things, nor remain cold towards everything. On the contrary, whatever comes is reflected. It avoids injury not by escaping events, but by refusing to detain them permanently in the mind after they have passed. This clearly does not oppose preparation and review. It says only that preparation need not mean living through failure in advance, and review need not preserve one outcome as a permanent identity.

In the end, many events never occur only once inside my head. Before they happen, I simulate them; while they happen, I interpret them; after they happen, I continue writing them into a self-narrative. Eight characters cannot solve these things. They merely offer an order I did not previously know very well: allow the event to arrive, respond to it genuinely, and finally permit it to pass.

Looking back now, Laozi and Zhuangzi seek more than an “admission that knowledge is limited.” Laozi worries that people use names, desire, and coercion to shape the countless things into what they want before those things can unfold. He therefore returns to ziran, allowing things to arise and transform by themselves, acting without possession. Zhuangzi worries that people become trapped in one position by prejudice, identity, and achievement. He therefore seeks not merely to loosen judgement, but to “wander,” allowing the mind to continue moving with the changes of things.

One says: do not seize the countless things and turn them into mine. The other says: do not seize myself and turn me into a thing. The two finally meet in refusing to let what has already formed block the life still occurring.

Non-action cannot excuse procrastination; the equality of things cannot abolish truth, falsehood, and responsibility; dependence upon nothing cannot erase the real limits imposed by resources, institutions, and other people. If I cannot solve a problem, that means I genuinely cannot solve it now. If I injure someone, I remain responsible for the consequences. Laozi and Zhuangzi remove only the additional layer added too rapidly afterwards: I cannot solve this problem, therefore my complete life is a failure; I did not control this event, therefore something must be wrong with the world.

Knowledge is meant to participate in reality, not replace it. Once used, it can sometimes be placed to one side.

entry.title: Everyone, Feel
entry.content:
I
