b_n=\frac1l\int_{-l}^{l}f(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{l}dx.
$$

For an odd function, only sine terms remain; for an even function, only cosine terms remain. If a function is given only on $[0,l]$, an odd extension produces a sine series, while an even extension produces a cosine series.

Under common assumptions such as the Dirichlet conditions, a Fourier series converges to $f(x)$ at a point of continuity and to the average of the two one-sided limits at a jump:

$$
\frac{f(x^-)+f(x^+)}2.
$$

A Taylor expansion uses local derivatives to encode a function as powers, whereas a Fourier expansion uses inner products over a whole interval to encode it as frequencies. Both choose a set of simple basis functions and use coefficients to record how much of each component a complex object contains. One is more local and suited to analytic structure; the other is more global and suited to periodic structure.

15. Differential Equations: Prescribing How an Object Changes Rather Than Describing It Directly

15.1 From Functional Models to Laws of Evolution

An equation containing an unknown function and its derivatives is called a differential equation. The order of its highest derivative is the order of the equation. A general solution usually contains as many independent arbitrary constants as the order; a solution determined by initial conditions is called a particular solution.

A differential equation performs a more radical compression: we do not know the complete shape of $y(t)$, but we know how its rate of change depends on the current state and input. Solving the equation means reconstructing the whole trajectory from a local rule of evolution.

15.2 First-Order Differential Equations

Separable equation:

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=g(x)h(y)
$$

Rearrange it as

$$
\frac{dy}{h(y)}=g(x)dx
$$

and integrate both sides. Before dividing by $h(y)$, check whether $h(y)=0$ corresponds to a constant solution that would otherwise be lost.

Homogeneous-type equation:

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=F\left(\frac yx\right)
$$

Let $u=y/x$, so $y=ux$ and $y’=u+xu’$, reducing it to a separable equation.

First-order linear equation:

$$
y’+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Its integrating factor is

$$
\mu(x)=e^{\int P(x)dx},
$$

and hence

$$
y=e^{-\int Pdx}
\left(\int Qe^{\int Pdx}dx+C\right).
$$

Bernoulli equation:

$$
y’+P(x)y=Q(x)y^n,
\qquad n\ne0,1,
$$

Let $z=y^{1-n}$ to reduce it to a first-order linear equation. Again, check whether the transformation loses solutions such as $y=0$.

Exact differential equation:

$$
M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0.
$$

If $M_y=N_x$ and the regional conditions are suitable, the left side is the total differential of some potential function $u(x,y)$, and the solution is $u(x,y)=C$.

15.3 Higher-Order Equations That Can Be Reduced in Order

If the equation does not explicitly contain $y$, as in

$$
y’’=f(x,y’),
$$

let $p=y’$ to reduce the second-order equation to a first-order equation for $p(x)$.

If the equation does not explicitly contain $x$, as in

$$
y’’=f(y,y’),
$$

let $p(y)=y’$ and use

$$
y’’=\frac{dp}{dx}=\frac{dp}{dy}\frac{dy}{dx}=p\frac{dp}{dy}
$$

to reduce the order.

Epistemologically, order reduction uses the symmetry represented by a missing variable to remove an unnecessary degree of freedom.

15.4 The Superposition Structure of Linear Differential Equations

An $n$th-order linear equation can be written as

$$
y^{(n)}+a_1(x)y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+a_n(x)y=f(x).
$$

For a homogeneous equation, the right side is zero. Linearity means that homogeneous solutions can be superposed; the general solution of a non-homogeneous equation is

$$
y=y_h+y_p,
$$

namely the general homogeneous solution plus one particular non-homogeneous solution.

For the second-order homogeneous equation with constant coefficients

$$
y’’+py’+qy=0,
$$

setting $y=e^{rx}$ yields the characteristic equation

$$
r^2+pr+q=0.
$$

  • For two distinct real roots $r_1,r_2$: $y=C_1e^{r_1x}+C_2e^{r_2x}$;

  • for a repeated real root $r$: $y=(C_1+C_2x)e^{rx}$;

  • for conjugate complex roots $\alpha\pm i\beta$:

$$
y=e^{\alpha x}(C_1\cos\beta x+C_2\sin\beta x).
$$

Characteristic roots turn a differential operation into an algebraic equation. Since differentiation changes an exponential function only by a multiplicative factor, exponential functions are the natural eigenfunctions of linear constant-coefficient differential operators.

15.5 Non-Homogeneous Particular Solutions, Euler Equations, and Systems of Equations

When the right side is $e^{\lambda x}P_m(x)$ or $e^{\alpha x}[P_l(x)\cos\beta x+Q_n(x)\sin\beta x]$, the method of undetermined coefficients can be used to propose a particular solution. If the proposed form overlaps with a homogeneous solution, it must be multiplied by a sufficiently high power of $x$ to remove the resonance.

For the Euler equation

$$
x^2y’’+pxy’+qy=f(x)
$$

set $x=e^t$ to transform the variable-coefficient structure into a constant-coefficient equation.

A system of linear differential equations with constant coefficients can be eliminated or written in matrix form:

$$
\mathbf x’=A\mathbf x+mathbf f(t).
$$

Eigenvalues control the growth, decay, and oscillation of the modes of the system. Here advanced mathematics begins to connect with linear algebra, signals and systems, and automatic control: the same desire to “diagonalise the differential operator” repeatedly returns under different names in different courses.

15.6 What a Modelling Problem Truly Lacks Is Not a Solution Formula

Models of growth, decay, cooling, and vibration usually follow these steps:

  1. choose the state variables;

  2. identify the conservation or change relation over a small interval of time;

  3. write a differential equation;

  4. add initial or boundary conditions;

  5. solve it and check dimensions, signs, and long-term behaviour.

Obtaining a function does not mean that the model is complete. We must still ask whether the solution lies in the domain, whether it satisfies the initial values, whether its long-term tendency agrees with reality, what happens as parameters change, and when omitted factors begin to push back against the model.

16. Compressing the Entire Subject Again

The generative logic of advanced mathematics can now be compressed into one table.

Module The gap it fills Central object Most important awareness of boundaries
Functions Relations in reality cannot be processed directly Correspondence from input to output Domain and rule jointly determine a function
Sequences Continuous models do not suit discrete states Functions indexed by integers Terms tending to zero do not imply convergence of a series
Limits Unreachable points and infinite processes cannot otherwise be discussed A stable value in a process of approach A limit concerns a neighbourhood, not the point value
Continuity Tendency and actual value may be disconnected Local stability Continuity does not imply differentiability
Derivatives Static correspondences lack speed of change Local rate of change Differentiability implies continuity, not conversely
Differentials A local curve remains complicated Best linear principal part Existence of multivariable partial derivatives does not imply differentiability
Mean-value theorems Local derivatives cannot directly describe the whole interval A bridge between local and global Check continuity, differentiability, and endpoint conditions one by one
Indefinite integrals The rate of change is known, but the original object is not A family of antiderivatives Do not omit arbitrary constants or special solutions
Definite integrals Countless local contributions must be combined Limit of Riemann sums Area requires sign handling; improper integrals require convergence first
Analytic geometry in space Multivariable objects lack a descriptive language Vectors, planes, and surfaces The equation form must serve the geometric object
Multivariable differentiation One output is influenced by several inputs Partial derivatives, gradients, and total differentials All local directions must be controlled uniformly
Multiple integrals The domain of accumulation extends from lines to surfaces and volumes Area and volume elements A substitution requires a Jacobian and a rewritten region
Line/surface integrals The domain of accumulation is itself curved Circulation and flux First-kind integrals have no orientation; second-kind integrals do
Series Infinite addition need not become stable Partial sums and function expansions Test endpoints separately; absolute and conditional convergence differ
Differential equations The object is unknown, but its law of change is known Unknown functions and their derivatives A solution is only a model output and must still be checked against conditions

Compressed once more, it becomes:

$$
\boxed{
\text{关系}
\to\text{趋近}
\to\text{局部变化}
\to\text{整体累积}
\to\text{多维推广}
\to\text{无限叠加与演化规律}
}
$$

Another hidden line runs through the subject from beginning to end:

$$
\boxed{
\text{选取变量}
\to\text{建立模型}
\to\text{在条件内运算}
\to\text{让现实或题目检验}
\to\text{修正模型}
}
$$

I once understood advanced mathematics as “building a functional model and then adding derivatives and integrals.” That view now seems too narrow. What the subject repeatedly trains are two inverse movements: dividing a whole into infinitesimal local parts and accumulating those parts back into a whole; projecting a complex object onto coordinates or a basis in which it is easier to handle, and then calculating within that representation.

This is why limits are not a tool to be discarded after the first chapter. A derivative is the limit of a difference quotient, a definite integral is the limit of a sum, a series is the limit of partial sums, and multivariable continuity and improper integrals are still asking about limits. The rooms keep changing throughout the building, but the load-bearing structure remains the same.

Still, let me turn the argument back. Being able to draw this map only shows that I can compress the subject at present. Whether I can unfold it depends on whether I can state the conditions of each theorem one by one, derive the formulas myself, and recognise a problem after its surface has changed. Whether the whole system can run in the examination room is yet another question concerning “action.”

I can even feel a slight impression that “this part is not so formidable after all.” Usually, when that feeling appears, it is not because I have mastered the material, but because I have not yet encountered a problem capable of pushing the model back at me.

So the map ends here. I had better return to solving problems.

entry.title: Islands and the Continent
entry.content:
No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main.

—John Donne, Meditation XVII

0. Two People Apparently Saying the Same Thing

Feynman once conducted a rather interesting little experiment.

He practised counting at a steady pace in his head and used the number he reached to estimate one minute. Once he became skilled at it, he could read while silently counting and still remember roughly what he had read. Yet the moment he spoke aloud, the counting broke off.

John Tukey, a mathematician he knew at Princeton, was precisely the opposite. Tukey could count and speak at the same time, but could not read simultaneously.

After investigating for a while, they discovered that when Feynman counted, a voice in his mind recited one, two, three; Tukey, by contrast, seemed to watch a ribbon printed with numbers pass before his eyes. Speech collided with the voice in Feynman’s head, while reading blocked Tukey’s visible numbers.

If you are interested, open any Zhihu answer and try it: count inwardly while reading, then keep counting and attempt to read the words aloud. Feynman later tried to find a way to count while reading aloud, but failed; Tukey could not do it either. Apparently, providing voice-overs for Zhihu answers was slightly beyond the syllabus for both gentlemen.

Both said, “I am counting,” yet what they actually experienced was not the same thing.

Human communication is probably always like this. We use the same set of words: happy, sad, lonely, caring, fine. Yet in different people, those words connect to entirely different memories, feelings, and lives. One person has said everything he can say, while the other still receives only a part.

And friendship somehow arises within precisely this part.

We cannot enter another person’s consciousness in full, yet we gradually learn when he really is fine and when we had better ask once more. We remember details meaningless to everyone else, and after misunderstanding him once, we may still be willing to listen again.

Limited understanding has not prevented people from knowing one another.

I find that romantic in itself.

1. How Friendship Begins

Two People Must First Look at Something Together

Friendship seldom begins with, “I want to establish a friendship with you.”

It usually begins with a third thing: a course, a dormitory, a job, a ball game, a video game, a book, or perhaps some person whom both find equally absurd.

Two people first look at something together, and only then notice each other beside it.

This may be one important difference between friendship and love. Love often begins with “I noticed you,” whereas friendship frequently begins with “So you noticed this too.” If two people sit solemnly opposite each other at their first meeting and demand that each present reasons for being suitable as a friend, the scene rather resembles a job interview without a job description.

Shared activity makes closeness natural and gradually reveals a person. Does he take defeat in a game out on others? Can he keep a promise? Does he constantly interrupt? When trouble comes, does he first shift blame or first handle the problem? Much of personality does not live in self-introductions; it lies scattered among small events.

Friends, therefore, are often not selected. They are gradually recognised while doing things together.

Friendship Also Contains Need

Aristotle divided friendship into friendship for utility, for pleasure, and for admiration of the other person’s character.

This classification is easily read as a hierarchy of contempt: people who work on a project together are merely connected by interest, gaming companions are fair-weather friends, and only those who admire each other’s virtue possess true friendship. By that standard, friends should begin dinner by discussing the Idea of the Good—or, failing that, at least exchange their ideals of life instead of merely eating.

Real relationships are not so clean.

Inviting a friend to dinner requires his time; confiding in him requires his attention; working together requires his ability; staying with an interesting person is pleasant to me. From the beginning, friendship includes need, convenience, pleasure, and accident.

The issue is not whether I receive anything from a friend.

The issue is whether, when he temporarily cannot provide those things, a person still remains before my eyes.

A friend who always comforts me is exhausted today: can I allow him not to catch me? The project is over: do I still want to eat with my collaborator? A formerly entertaining friend has little to say lately: do I immediately decide that he has lost his value?

If the person disappears together with his usefulness, perhaps I never knew more than a function.

But if friendship cannot rest on utility alone, when does it begin to care about this particular person?

That is no longer a question of why people meet, but of how a relationship changes.

2. How Friendship Changes

“Being with You Is Quite Nice”

At first, friendship depends on a shared setting.

The same class, dormitory, or organisation repeatedly places people together. They eat, slack off, rush to meet deadlines, and incidentally complain about several mutual acquaintances. The environment arranges the meetings, concrete events supply the topics, and the two people need only avoid disliking each other too much.

The relationship may perfectly well stop here.

“There Is Something I Want to Tell You”

After repeated contact, the other person begins to step out of the setting.

I see something and want to send it to him; when arranging dinner, I naturally leave him a place; when something happens, I imagine beforehand what he might say. At first we merely happened to meet; later I began to expect the meeting. At first we discussed only what was before us; later, lives unrelated to the shared activity gradually entered the relationship.

It looks like only a few more messages, yet an important change has occurred within them: a friend begins to participate in how I understand my own life.

Trust Is Not the Number of Secrets Exchanged

Later still, people hand over parts unsuitable for public display: failure, jealousy, fear, ambition, childish wishes, and certain deeds that remain rather difficult to evaluate even now.

Secrets alone, however, do not prove intimacy. Two people may exchange childhood traumas at three in the morning and still not become close friends the next day. They may finish reporting their entire family histories before the waiter even serves the first dish. Secrets prove only that the other person knows more. Trust comes from what happens after a secret is given: whether it becomes gossip, whether it is turned into a weapon during an argument, and whether a friend who has seen one terrible version of me uses that version to pass a life sentence.

What truly deepens a relationship is not how much was said once, but the many later occasions on which what was known was not abused.

A Shared History Makes Someone Particular

A friend’s particularity does not arise entirely from his virtues.

There are, of course, people in the world who are cleverer, funnier, or better at comforting others. Yet nobody can participate again in a past that has already happened. Who was there during the hardest period? Why did some apparently trivial event matter so much at the time? Through how many transformations did an old joke pass before becoming what it is today? None of this can be regained simply by meeting someone with better qualifications.

A shared history does not make a friend eternally right, but it does make him impossible to replace casually.

From here, friendship acquires a little responsibility. I know that my silence may worry him, that a certain remark may hurt him, and what he has recently been enduring. My choices are therefore no longer wholly unrelated to him.

But trouble arrives as well.

If shared history, trust, and daily participation all make someone particular, does a friendship necessarily become superior when people have known each other longer, know more, and communicate more often? Is a playmate merely an ordinary friend awaiting an upgrade, and an ordinary friend a best friend still loading?

Obviously not.

3. Friends Are Not Ranks but Different Shapes

“Playmate—ordinary friend—growth companion—best friend” may roughly describe relationships, but it cannot be treated as a single route of promotion. A playmate need not eventually become a best friend, and a best friend may not suit every activity in my life.

Some people are good travel companions but poor colleagues. Some can discuss my most private troubles, yet seldom contact me in ordinary times. Others are bad at comforting words but arrive fastest when something really happens.

Instead of asking what rank a friendship occupies, we might ask what shape it has. That shape contains at least three elements.

Where the Relationship Grew From

It may arise from a shared interest, class, dormitory, or organisation; from working on a project, enduring difficulty together, mutual admiration, mutual understanding, or simply the comfort of being with this person.

Its origin influences the relationship’s most natural form. Friends who met through an interest may always depend upon a fixed activity. Those who endured hardship together may have little to say in ordinary times, yet retain a deep confirmation through shared experience. Still others did nothing remarkable together; they merely happened to share many ordinary days.

What the Relationship Can Carry

It may carry play, cooperation, and everyday company, or intellectual exchange, exposed vulnerability, mutual criticism, practical help, and responsibility in emergencies. Plainly, these capacities do not appear automatically as one package.

Being able to confide does not mean being suited to cooperation. Knowing someone for years does not make every subject discussable. Meeting every day does not guarantee reliability in a crisis. The person who listens to my trauma may not be good at helping me move house, while the person who helps me move may have no idea how to comfort me.

We easily demand every other capacity once one is present. If you can listen to my heart, you should understand me at all times; if you are an old friend, you should support every choice; if you are called a best friend, you should preferably provide companionship, advice, entertainment, emergency assistance, and lifelong witness all at once. This is no longer a friend but a full-stack position. The job description is excessively long, and the salary is paid mainly in reaction memes. One can hardly blame the applicant.

What Keeps the Relationship Alive

Some friendships rely on frequent meetings, others on a regular activity or shared project. Some require both sides to volunteer news of their lives; others rest mainly upon shared history and long-standing trust. Some relationships pause for years, yet grow new content when both people remain willing to approach each other again.

Frequency of contact alone therefore proves neither closeness nor distance. Friends who talk every day may chiefly share the present; people who meet once in several years may preserve profound historical trust. The former is not shallow, nor is the latter necessarily truer. They exist through different things.

The same friend may be “low-frequency contact, high historical trust, highly reliable in emergencies,” or “high-frequency contact, high entertainment value, low capacity for vulnerability.” Neither stands above the other; their shapes differ.

“Best friend” still has meaning, of course. It usually means that a relationship is deep in several respects and has endured time and reality. But it is not every friendship’s graduation certificate. A relationship that honestly carries what it is suited to carry, without being forced to take charge of an entire life, is already very good.

These three dimensions explain how friendship operates, but not why, if a friend is merely a collection of functions, someone with similar functions cannot replace him when the relationship fades.

The reason is that a friend eventually enters more than my schedule.

4. Friends Enter “Who I Am”

Nobody grows in a sealed room.

How I see myself, remember my past, decide what is funny, and speak to comfort myself when things happen—all bear, to some degree, the traces of other people’s participation. Friends especially do so.

Some friends remember versions of me that I have forgotten. They know what I once sincerely believed before doing what I do today; they know that a decision now fit for a joke tormented me badly at the time; and they know how a part of my character that now seems natural first developed within a shared life.

This is why meeting an old friend can feel strange. Although neither has participated in the other’s daily life for years, after several sentences I suddenly remember a manner of speaking long unused. The relationship has not automatically returned to the past. Rather, the other person preserves a road towards my former self.

Friends also become reference points.

When something happens, I imagine how he would judge it. When choosing, I remember what we once argued about. When a friend follows another road, his life reveals a possibility I did not choose. This includes not only support, but comparison, jealousy, and defiance. In My Brilliant Friend, Lenù and Lila admire one another while continually treating the other as a coordinate for measuring their own lives. A friend’s light does not always merely illuminate; sometimes it is rather dazzling.

This explains why drifting apart hurts.

What is lost may be more than someone to chat, dine, or ask for help. Sometimes it is a shared language, a witness to an earlier self, and a part of life to which I could once return through that person. Another equally interesting and reliable individual cannot reproduce this history.

Yet someone’s entry into “who I am” does not mean that he belongs to me.

Precisely because a friend has acquired weight in my life, I can easily replace “you matter to me” with “I am entitled to demand things from you.” Here begins friendship’s real difficulty.

5. Closeness Does Not Create Ownership

A friend is not another version of me. Even after the relationship deepens, he will still refuse and change, and live in ways unfamiliar to me.

Knowing Someone Does Not Mean Explaining Him Completely

The more familiar we become with a person, the more readily we skip the question.

He has not replied, so he must be withdrawing. She says “whatever,” so she must be unhappy. A friend did not follow my advice, so he must reject my judgement. After guessing correctly several times, we easily promote guesses into facts, then complete our understanding, disappointment, and downgrading of the relationship alone, before the other person even knows what has happened.

The most valuable part of “I know you” is not that I never need to ask again, but that I know where guessing is insufficient.

A friend is not somebody who never misunderstands me. Such a person probably lives only in my imagination, rent-free at that.

A friend is closer to someone who lets me explain myself, and who updates his judgement after discovering a misunderstanding. I must also allow him to overturn the version I wrote for him.

Help Must Not Secretly Become Control

When I advise a friend, I may sincerely wish him well.

Yet advice also contains other things: a wish that my ability be recognised, that the time I spent produce a result, and that he act according to my method, thereby proving that I understood the problem.

So when he listens but does nothing, I feel my time has been wasted and do not want to interfere again.

But rejecting my advice does not necessarily mean rejecting me. The method may be unsuitable; he may be unprepared; or he may merely have wanted to speak, rather than open a public tender for a complete solution to his life.

I may offer a view and decide how far I am willing to help. Yet if so-called help does not permit refusal, it has already begun to resemble control.

A Friend May Say I Was Wrong

True friendship neither rationalises everything I do nor takes my side unconditionally within a shared social circle.

A friend may believe both that “you handled this terribly” and that “you are not reducible to this one act.” Understanding someone does not cancel consequences; criticising one act need not burn his entire history with it.

Of course, a friend has the right to be disappointed and to change the distance of the relationship. Friendship is not a card of absolution with a clause saying, “Since you understand me, you must forgive me.”

My wish that a friend not summarise me by one mistake may be real; his unwillingness to continue the former relationship may also be real. Holding both together is painful, but pain does not make only one of them true.

Being Particular Does Not Mean Being Owned

Friends enter new circles, devote more time to work, partners, and new lives, decline invitations, cease sharing everything first, and become somewhat different from who they were.

The deeper a relationship is, the easier it becomes to interpret these changes as betrayal: we have known each other for so long—why did you not put me first?

Shared history makes someone particular; it does not make him mine. Closeness gives me reasons to care and requires me to bear some consequences of my actions. It does not qualify me to manage his life.

If friendship contains freedom without responsibility, it becomes two people always prepared to retreat. If it contains responsibility without the freedom to refuse or leave, it becomes a contract nobody signed and nobody may resign from.

A real relationship can only remain between the two.

This sounds quite complete in principle, but friends do not live inside principles.

They face unanswered messages, promised dinners, contact after graduation, and the question of whether one person will actually be present when the other truly needs him.

6. Reality

Friendship has real costs; nobody simply sends the bill most of the time.

Some Time May Be Entirely Useless

Two people may discuss literature, philosophy, trauma, and the future until they feel they have reached each other’s souls. Yet profound conversation creates a sense of closeness, not necessarily a reliable relationship.

Real friends also eat, play games, do separate things in the same room, and say nonsense forgotten the next day. Nobody solves the other’s life, and no minutes are produced.

If a friend must provide insight, mutual growth, or crisis rescue, usefulness has merely taken over friendship under a more progressive name.

Relationships Require Maintenance

In the same class, dormitory, or organisation, the environment delivers people to each other every day. After graduation, relocation, or the end of a project, automatic meetings stop, and only then must both sides walk towards each other themselves.

Nobody needs to report daily. An occasional “still alive?”, a ridiculous image only the other person understands, or a meal without a theme adds a little present to a shared history. The past matters, but it does not send messages to today by itself.

Reciprocity Is Not Settled Transaction by Transaction

Friendship certainly requires reciprocity. If one person alone keeps initiating, listening, and helping while the other appears only in need, even a tolerant person grows tired. Yet reciprocity does not require every matter to be repaid immediately, nor reply times, gift prices, and minutes of confiding to be equal. People possess different energy at different stages and care in different ways.

Mutuality means something closer to this: over enough time, both people are sometimes willing to walk towards the other, and neither treats the other’s presence as natural entitlement. If every meal, confidence, and favour is recorded exactly, friendship may achieve quantitative management, but the people will probably be dismissed by the accounting system.

Drifting Apart

Love at least has the word “break-up.” Friendship usually ends without notice: messages become fewer, and “let’s meet next time” never reaches a next time. One day, two people discover that they still call each other friends, yet no longer know what life the other is living.

The later ending of a relationship does not rewrite the fact that it once happened. Someone may no longer participate in my life today, yet already have participated in the process by which I became who I am today. The past can have been real, and departure can also be real.

At this point, friendship need no longer be arranged into a checklist of qualifications. Everything above grew from the initial facts. Because nobody can directly enter another consciousness, understanding depends upon repeated questions and revisions. Because a friend has no duty to bind himself to me, remaining is a choice. Because that choice forms a shared history over time, a particular person becomes impossible to replace casually. And because he remains independent, this particularity brings only limited responsibility, never ownership.

So for now, I would probably understand friendship like this:

Friendship is the approach of two independent people who can never understand each other completely, brought close by sharing a part of life; through repeated contact, they gradually care about this particular person and form trust and a shared history; without compulsory obligation, they nevertheless remain willing to give one another limited but genuine care, freedom, and responsibility.

It does not demand that two people become each other’s only answer, nor promise that they will never drift apart. It asks only that while the relationship exists, I treat the person before me seriously and take seriously what my actions may leave in him.

7. Reflection

All the preceding principles are convenient when used to analyse other people. Turning them back upon myself is less dignified.

Maintenance and Accounting

I desire a free and mutual friendship, yet often interpret “freedom” as freedom from maintenance, and “mutuality” as the other person’s duty to know when to find me. I hope friends understand what I leave unsaid, then quickly doubt the entire relationship when they occasionally fail to catch it.

To put it unpleasantly, I sometimes treat friends as old archive files that never expire: I do no maintenance in ordinary times, yet when needed, expect to read them from the old location—with version compatibility, complete data, and preferably no rubbish explanation after opening. This is plainly unreasonable. A person is not a cloud-storage subscription; besides, even that subscription renews only when the other side acts.

I once judged best friends by several things: whether we knew each other’s secrets, had seen each other at our worst, told each other important news first, maintained contact over time, and kept the relationship sufficiently equal. These standards are not wholly wrong, but I readily turned them into rankings. Who hears first may indicate closeness, but also become an examination. Knowing many secrets may indicate trust, but cannot ensure mutual understanding. Equality, if it means receiving the same response for every effort, ends only in a meticulously kept account book.

I also valued whether someone could “understand me.” When a friend failed to catch my meaning or adopt my advice, I sometimes instinctively wondered whether the relationship was less deep than I thought, or whether my ability had gone unrecognised.

Yet this still turns a friend’s response into confirmation of me.

He may be willing to listen but not know what to say; he may understand and still choose another method; or he may genuinely lack energy today. A friend who does not care for me in the manner familiar to me is not necessarily uncaring. Rejecting my answer does not mean rejecting me.

Keep in Touch, Even When Nothing Is Wrong

Another obvious problem is that most of my friends came from shared settings.

Classmates, organisations, people with whom I did things. While the setting remained, I could be devoted because the environment handled meetings and topics for me. Once it disappeared, I scarcely knew how to contact people for no particular reason. I seemed to require a sufficiently proper excuse before daring to appear.

Consequently, I do not share ordinary life in ordinary times, yet suddenly remember somebody when disaster comes and hope the relationship can immediately recover its former depth. Afterwards I fear having disturbed him and become even less willing to make contact. The cycle can hardly be called ingenious. I mainly manage to claim the benefits on both sides: solitude in ordinary times and a relationship waiting at attention during emergencies.

More contradictorily, I want friendship to be mutual while often waiting for the other person to come first. When he does not appear, I suspect the relationship is fading; from his perspective, however, the person who seldom initiates may be me.

Understanding and Criticism

The shared social circle left by my previous intimate relationship also made me reconsider what “understanding” and “criticism” mean.

I did make mistakes and hurt someone. Naturally, I hope friends can believe I acted wrongly without sentencing my whole person to death for a single mistake. Yet when somebody really remains willing to associate with me, I feel indebted to his tolerance and become constrained. The ideal scene appears to be one in which he simply curses me for a while. On reflection, this also hides an account: as if, once I accept a scolding, the punishment is complete and the relationship should automatically return to normal.

But criticism is not a fine, and friendship is not automatically unfrozen after payment. Friends may be disappointed and choose their distance anew. What I can do is admit what happened and change how I treat people afterwards, rather than demand that somebody stay to prove I have improved.

What to Do

So perhaps I need to do several things that are not particularly grand.

  • I may contact people even when nothing important has happened—friends need communication. Before confiding, ask whether the other person has energy. Before advising, ask whether he wants me merely to listen or to think of a solution together. When a friend does not follow my advice, resist imagining myself as an unappreciated strategist.

  • I must also accept that different relationships have different shapes. A playmate need not understand my whole self, and somebody who listens to my heart need not remain on call. If another person stays, I may be grateful without immediately recording a debt of tolerance.

  • Finally, allow friends to know me again, and allow myself to know them again.

People truly are islands. We can speak only across our separate experiences, and some part will never cross. A friend cannot live for me and has no duty to remain docked here forever. Yet people truly are also pieces of a continent. Not because boundaries finally disappear, but because limited understanding, time spent together, and the influence we leave upon one another genuinely change a person.

A friend does not make the island disappear. But the island’s shape is no longer quite what it would have been had they never met.

entry.title: An Unauthorized Structure in the Mind
entry.content:
Love is probably when one person gradually enters the consciousness of another person, and finally a “we” grows between the two people. But when did this “we” become love, and when did it become nothing more than habit, debt, or unwillingness? Only time can give the result, but time is never responsible for writing the standard answer.

〇. Why does a third thing grow between two people?

I finished writing Gears, Industry and Civilization a few days ago, and now I want to write about love again.

It’s not that love and gears have anything in common. To put it bluntly, it probably sounds when both of them are inappropriate. However, if the gear sounds, you can stop it for inspection. If the gear sounds, people usually say “It’s okay” and then go back to sleep.

After falling in love once, I began to doubt many novels.

Of course, the novel is not really a lie. It’s just that stories always like to write about encounters and heartbeats for a long time: looking at each other in the rain, recognizing each other in the crowd, and saying words that only two people can understand one night. As for how two people arrange time, deal with suspicion, how to talk when they are tired, how to face money, distance, body and each other’s bad temper, they are often compressed into the ending sentence “live happily ever after”.

But it’s only after you actually enter a relationship that you realize that “from now on” may be the main text.

Love certainly has romance, attachment, and sexual attraction, but it also has values, desires, power, boundaries, responsibilities, misunderstandings, projections, and reality conditions. It’s not a pure occurrence like a miracle, or just two people sitting down and calculating what each other has to offer.

So I want to ask again from the beginning: Why does one person fall in love with another person? How does love go from a flutter of heart to a shared history between two people?

1. The birth of love

It is impossible for a person to be loved apart from his own attributes

People cannot be loved apart from their own attributes, Kafka said.

The reason why a person is seen by another person always depends on something specific: appearance, voice, body, personality, ability, experience, expression, or a small action. Maybe she looked at you seriously when she spoke, maybe she stopped to wait for someone when everyone was moving forward, or maybe she was sitting there when the sun was shining brightly one day, and you happened to see her.

The so-called “I love your soul” cannot really separate the soul from the body and experience. At the same time, a person completely devoid of appearance, voice, character, history, and social relationships does not exist. The soul must have something concrete to show its face, otherwise it will be a problem for two people to meet anywhere.

But on the other hand, people are not simply the sum of these attributes.

Family, class, education, gender roles, past relationships and hurts all shape a person. But what truly makes up a person is not just what she goes through, but how she responds to those experiences. People who have also been hurt can choose to retaliate, avoid, remain silent, or they can learn to trust again after a long time.

So I would rather say:

Man is not only the result of the shaping of social relations, but also a subject who can respond to these relations and form his own history.

What love loves is exactly this kind of thing: she carries the traces left by the world, but is not completely determined by these traces. She is already someone and continues to be someone at the same time.

There is always “use” in love

This may not sound very romantic, but it probably can’t be avoided.

If you want the other person to eat with you, you are using her time; if you talk to her, you need her attention; if you want her to be loyal, you want to gain stability from the relationship; hugging, sex, care, recognition, belonging, and living together, all of them satisfy certain human needs.

Even “I just wish her the best” may not be entirely selfless. Seeing that she is doing well makes me feel at ease; helping her confirms that I am a person capable of loving others. If the ledger is burned, the ledger does not necessarily cease to exist. It just changed to a more noble cover.

But discovering this does not mean that love is therefore a scam.

The question is never whether I get something from you, but: Do I see you as a person who can satisfy my needs, or do I just see you as a tool to satisfy my needs?

The former recognizes that intimacy necessarily involves mutual need. The latter will immediately degrade the other person from a person to a failed function when she is temporarily unable to provide value.

Mature love is not about declaring “I don’t need you at all.” If it’s really not needed at all, it’s hard to say how intimate it is. It’s closer to:

I do need you and will get a lot from you; but when you can’t satisfy me, you are still you, not something that suddenly breaks.

Desire and love are not the same thing

Desire says: I want to be close to you, to have you, to touch you, to have you stay with me.

Love gradually takes on another layer: I want you to live better for who you are, even if your “better” sometimes doesn’t fully serve me.

But the two cannot be cut cleanly. Without desire, love can easily become a kind of moral appreciation through glass; with only desire, the other person can easily be compressed into an object that satisfies me.

The real difficulty is not to eliminate desire, but to admit that:

My urge to have you is true, and it is also true that you do not belong to me.

Love starts to get troublesome from here. Sigh, it would be great if I were only responsible for my heartbeat.

2. How Love Changes

A relationship does not rise uniformly from ten per cent affection to one hundred per cent, before a prompt suddenly appears: “Congratulations, you have obtained mature love.” Please do not live real life as though it were a galgame!

It is more like passing through several transformations. Both before and after, we call it love, yet what it contains is no longer quite the same.

“I want to be close to you”

There is attraction, curiosity, and a lot of projection at this time.

Part of the person we fall in love with is a real person, and part of the person we fall in love with is an image we make up based on limited information. She understands me, she is different from others, she can heal me, and she may accompany me for a long time - these judgments sometimes come from her, sometimes from the fact that I needed such a person too much at the time.

Attraction is real and so is imagination. It’s just her in my imagination, not necessarily her.

The two people in “Romeo and Juliet” met, fell in love, got married, went into exile, and both died in a very short period of time. The feelings are certainly strong, but they have little chance of experiencing disenchantment over a long relationship. This story proves that love can burn to a high level at once, but it does not prove that high temperature itself is maturity.

Those two in Verona rushed the schedule rather fiercely. Married life had not even entered the calendar before both of them were gone—a little like Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai. Then again, had they actually survived long enough to live as a married couple, perhaps this love story would not exist at all.

“I’m starting to look forward to you”

After repeated contact, the other person begins to enter everyday life.

When something happens, I want to tell her. I pick up my phone and wait for her message. When I reach a place, I wonder whether she would like it. When planning the future, I begin to leave a place for her. Love is no longer merely a momentary feeling; it has become a stable expectation.

Later, shared memories, habits, commitments and future plans gradually accumulated, and the relationship underwent its first real qualitative change.

Originally there was only “I” and “you”, but then “we” appeared.

A decision is no longer just about “do I want to do it?” but also about: Will this damage our trust? Did it violate our agreement? Where will it lead our common future?

This “we” is not really a third person, but it has its own history and weight, and begins to affect the two people in turn.

However, here, some people don’t like the existence of the concept of “we” and feel that this will restrict their freedom. This is a matter of opinion. Just like a popular saying on the Internet, marriage is to use trouble to resist loneliness.

After the charm is gone, love begins for the second time

Real dealings will expose differences sooner or later.

It is impossible for your partner to understand you forever. Your partner is also a human being. He or she will also be tired, selfish, silent, bored, have a life that you cannot participate in, and will disappoint you at some point. In fact, no one is different. If people live a little longer, it will be difficult to always maintain the refined version when they first met.

Disenchantment does not necessarily mean that you no longer love. It may also be the first time love truly escapes projection:

From loving someone who meets my expectations to loving someone who continues to exceed my expectations.

I saw her limitations and allowed her to overturn my judgment of her. Not because she had proven herself perfect, but because I finally got to face a concrete person.

Mechanism, Calling, and Endurance Are Three Different Questions

Many explanations for why love occurs can be found in physical attraction, attachment needs, upbringing and social conditioning. These are mechanisms.

But the mechanism cannot explain another problem: so many people have similar attributes, why is it this person who made me feel bright at a specific moment?

This is closer to a calling. It’s not that I listed the conditions first and then judged her worthy of liking; it was that she first appeared there as a specific person, my heart moved first, and the reasons came to the scene later.

But calling is only responsible for letting people walk over. It is not responsible for teaching people how to get along, let alone how to continue after many years.

When the initial intensity wears off, what really sustains the relationship becomes something less dazzling: reliability, habits, candor, order in living together, and a willingness to respond to the other person on ordinary days.

Put plainly, mechanism explains why ignition is possible; calling makes the fire actually burn; endurance must answer where the next bundle of firewood will come from. Two people cannot embrace the matchbox of their first heartbeat and expect it to keep them warm for a lifetime.

Time will change love, but it will not testify for love

In “Love in the Time of Cholera”, Ariza waited for fifty years, nine months and four days, but experienced more than 600 relationships during the long wait. It doesn’t seem right to say that he doesn’t love Fermina; to say that he has been pure and loyal for more than fifty years, it’s hard not to think it’s a bit abstract.

Time did not write the answer on his face. It just marinates love, desire, obsession and stories about oneself in the same jar, and then opens them together fifty years later.

So what time tests is not only whether love is still there, but also what this love has become over the long years.

Sometimes it’s trust, sometimes it’s responsibility, sometimes it’s habit, and sometimes it’s just unwillingness to admit that I’ve waited for so long. More often than not, several things are mixed together and no one wants to go out first.

Of course, we still see a tendency to only regard the love in literature as love, and to deconstruct real love into symbols such as desire and obsession in reality. Wittgenstein criticized these things, so I won’t go into detail here.

3. The Unauthorized Structure in the Mind

After the relationship deepens, the other person is no longer just a person in the outside world.

She taps into my emotions, identity, daily habits, memories, and future plans. The original “what do I do on the weekend” gradually becomes “what do we do on the weekend”, and the original “where do I go in the future” becomes “where do we go in the future”. When I encounter something, I will even automatically imagine how she will evaluate it before it is my turn to speak. These are also supported from a neuroscience perspective.

In this sense, love does make another person a part of yourself.

But a patch must be made immediately: she is part of my consciousness, which does not mean that she is my possession. She entered my life without losing her independent life.

The pain of breakup

If the other person has participated in my self-structure, breaking up is not just about losing an external object, it is more like a part of the consciousness that was originally maintained by two people and suddenly lost the support of reality.

People will subconsciously want to tell her things, will automatically think of shared experiences when passing a certain place, will continue to imagine how she will respond, and even the grammar of “we” will remain when planning the future.

That person is no longer there, but the position formed for her is still there. This is very much like a phantom limb: it’s not that the body is really missing another piece, but that the consciousness still interprets the world according to the original layout.

Therefore, the recovery of broken love is not to prove that she was never important, nor is it to judge all memories as errors. What really needs to be done is to re-answer: Who am I without this relationship? What life belongs to me? How should the original future be rewritten? Where should she be placed in my life history? In other words, falling out of love is a self-destruction.

Maturity does not mean completely devaluing your ex. It seems that as long as you prove that she is not worth it, you have not lost anything. I personally feel that this approach is quite tasteless. A more honest statement might be:

That relationship was once real, she was once in my life and shaped a part of me, but she is no longer a part of my current life.

Love Brain

There may be a lot of things mixed in the “love brain”: the high level of attention during the love period, the fear of being abandoned, the lack of self-worth, too few fulcrums in life, the hope that the partner will compensate for past deficiencies, and the addiction caused by the other person’s hot and cold mood.

If a person lacks stable friends, study, work, interests and his own order in his life, his partner can easily become the only emotional outlet, source of recognition, future meaning and focus of life at the same time.

If the other party moves slightly, the whole world will sway.

This does not necessarily mean that love is too big, it may just be that it is too empty elsewhere. How can I put it, when there is only one pillar in the house, that pillar does seem to be very important. Mainly because it’s also scared.

There are also some relationships that people cannot let go of, not because they are happy, but because they are extremely unstable. Sometimes intimate, sometimes cold; sometimes committed, sometimes withdrawn. People keep waiting for the next time intimacy will reappear, and then mistake this anxiety for affection.

Therefore, the intensity of pain cannot directly prove the depth of love. There may be love in it, but there may also be lack, unwillingness, competition and the desire to be chosen again.

Allow to be loved

Some people are good at taking care of others, but not very good at taking care of others.

When someone treats you well, your first reaction is not to feel reassured, but to doubt what the other person is up to; when you accept a little help, you immediately think about how to return it in equal value; when your needs are exposed, you feel that you have lost your dignity, as if you are worthy of being loved only if you are complete, strong, and not troublesome to anyone.

But true intimacy requires one to allow oneself a certain degree of dependence, acceptance, and vulnerability. Accepting being loved does not mean handing over life, it just admits: I will be tired, and there are things I can’t do, and I can also let another person help me at certain times.

Of course, being helped does not mean taking off the leg and giving it to the other person on the spot. There is still some scale in between.

4. Distance creates beauty

The most difficult part of love is probably not how to get infinitely close, but that after getting close, you still admit that the other person is not you.

Power in love

Who is more dependent on whom, who is more afraid of losing, who has more money and life resources, who is better at expressing, who determines the rhythm of the relationship, and who has the power to interpret “normal” - these all create asymmetries.

A mature relationship is not about pretending that power does not exist, but about realizing how you can influence the other person and refraining from abusing it. You cannot repeatedly leave the other person to force her to give in because you are more afraid of losing. You cannot declare her feelings as irrational because you are more reasonable. You cannot turn caring into control because the other person relies on you. What is this? This is a fucking scumbag.

In “Othello”, a handkerchief bears the burden of evidence that it should not bear. Suspicion gradually replaces inquiry, and deep love quickly turns into surveillance, judgment and destruction. Othello finally describes himself as a person who does not love wisely but loves too deeply. But it is also obvious that this sentence is beautiful as an epitaph, but not as a defense statement.

Deep love cannot automatically excuse harm. In fact, the more you can influence a person, the more you should know how much weight your actions will leave on her.

Summoning does not confer qualifications

I am moved by a person and want to be close to her, take care of her, and protect her. This feeling can be completely true, but it can only prove that she has special meaning to me. It cannot just say that I have special meaning to her, nor can it prove that I have gained a ticket to her life.

She doesn’t have to accept my love and doesn’t owe me a response. Nor can I claim to know what is good for her better than she does just because I am sincere. Let’s not turn “I’m good for you” into a master key, trying to open all the doors she doesn’t want to open.

In other words:

Love gives me a reason to care about her, but it doesn’t give me the qualification to own her.

She can refuse, she can change, she can leave. The calling was real, it could be real that she no longer needed me. If two things are true at the same time, they will not erase each other.

“We” cannot destroy “me” and “you”

If a relationship only has integration but no independence, it can easily lead to possession, control, symbiosis and emotional kidnapping. If there is only independence and no integration, they may become two people who are ready to retreat at any time. They have a clear calculation and can move smoothly when difficulties arise. “Husband and wife are originally birds in the same forest, and they fly separately when disaster strikes.”

Mature love does not draw a perfect line from the middle, but continues to bear this tension:

You are an important part of me, but not my possession.

Your destiny is related to me, but your life is not determined by me.

I am willing to adjust myself for you, but I will not destroy myself in exchange for you staying.

We form a community, but the community cannot cancel “I” and “you”.

This is not a problem that can be solved once and for all. I thought clearly today, but tomorrow the other party doesn’t reply for two hours, and my mind starts to build scaffolding downstairs again. Theory is one thing, but actually standing in the relationship is another. Of course, this has to do with the unity of knowledge and action.

5. How does love survive reality?

Love cannot only happen in the spiritual world.

Of course two people can talk about philosophy, literature, trauma and the future until three in the morning, feeling that each other has reached the depths of their souls. But in-depth chat creates a sense of intimacy, not necessarily a reliable relationship.

One person understands me very well, but may not be suitable to live with me; another person is not good at talking about grand issues, but may bring me water when I am sick, and stay to finish my words after a conflict.

Self-disclosure makes people feel close, and shared responsibility gradually creates trust.

Love has a material foundation and a body

Real love also has to face money, city, distance, work, school, family, living space, housework and caring responsibilities.

Where two people live, who adjusts careers for whom, how much time and travel expenses it takes to meet each other, who does more housework, how both parties use their joint money - these questions are not suitable for writing love poems, but they will determine the shape of the relationship day by day.

Love happens physically, too. Sexual attraction, touch, fatigue, illness, aging, differences in desire, all enter into relationships. The body is not a express box containing the soul, which can be thrown away after using the packaging. People really become impatient when they are sleepy, they really need care when they are sick, and they may feel alienated if they are not touched for a long time.

Calling all of this “not spiritual enough” will only result in a love that is beautiful but no one can live in.

Of course, admitting that material conditions are important does not mean that if your income falls below a certain level, you are not worthy of love. It just reminds me that feelings cannot pay all the real costs for two people. Roses are very beautiful, but landlords usually don’t collect roses when the rent is due.

Responsibility is usually not very romantic

Responsibility is not “I am willing to sacrifice everything for you” which is suitable for shouting in the rain. This is very idol drama, but not very realistic. It more often manifests itself as something without background music: try to do what you promised and explain in advance when you can’t do it; don’t punish the other party with silence; be willing to come back and communicate after a conflict; admit that your behavior has indeed caused harm; don’t escalate every quarrel into a relationship life or death.

Romance often happens at night. Responsibilities usually come the next morning, in the form of remembering to buy medicine, take out the trash, buy breakfast, and finish what you left off last night. This doesn’t sound earth-shattering enough, but most things that can live for a long time are not earth-shattering every day. It was shaking every day, and the neighbors couldn’t stand it.

Responsibility does not equal redemption of relationship

After a person hurts the other person, he can apologize, change, and bear the consequences, but these cannot exchange for the other person’s forgiveness, nor can he ask her to come back, nor can he ask her to be responsible for witnessing “I have finally changed for the better now.” If my growth still requires her to come back for approval, then there may still be an old account hidden in this growth: I have changed, so you should choose me again.

But the relationship is not about make-up exams. You don’t have to retake the wrong question and ask the same person to reissue it.

A more radical responsibility may be: I change the way I treat people in the future, but I don’t require the people I have hurt to prove that I have changed. Some repairs can only happen within myself, and the relationship itself will not be restored; nor is she a teaching aid specially sent to teach me how to grow. She is a person who has been truly affected, hurt, and has the right to close the book.

6. The minimal structure of mature love

Writing here, it seems that I can try to summarize it.

Of course, the discussion here is not about whether unrequited love counts as love, nor is it about giving a certificate to everyone’s relationship. All I want to ask is: What are the minimum requirements for a mature, two-way love relationship?

The first is speciality.

Indeed, love begins with mutual attraction and requires this motivation; love also supports both parties to gain something from the relationship and be willing to give. But as to why I only fall in love with him and why he is special, it is because I care about this specific person, not any substitute for the function she provides. Shared history makes her irreplaceable.

Second, it is two-way subjectivity.

Both people have the right to express, refuse, change and leave. Love cannot exist only in one person’s grand narrative and then require another person to co-star.

Third, it is trust that has been tested by reality.

Not only were we able to talk about souls, but we also faced time, fatigue, conflicts and interests together. Whether words and deeds are consistent, whether promises can be fulfilled, and whether injuries can be repaired are slower and heavier than a night of deep chatting.

Fourth, is responsibility for each other’s consequences.

Her happiness, pain, and dignity would truly influence my choices. I knew I had the power to hurt her, and I restrained myself from using it. We may have conflicts, but we must also have the ability to re-understand, apologize, adjust and restore links.

Fifth, there is interdependence within boundaries.

We allow ourselves to need each other, but we do not require one person to take on the other person’s entire life; we allow “us” to form, but do not eat “me” and “you” together.

So now I probably understand love like this:

Love is two limited people with desires, needs and realistic conditions who get close to each other because of each other’s specialness; trust, attachment and a common history are formed in repeated interactions, and in intimacy they recognize that the other person is still a subject that cannot be swallowed up by oneself; ultimately, through responsibilities, boundaries and continuous choices, a “we” is formed that does not eliminate “I” and “you”, but truly exists.

There is no “always understanding” or “never wavering” in this definition. These words are too big and difficult to place in reality.

All it requires is that while the relationship is still there, I treat you as a concrete person and take seriously what my actions will do to you.

7. In the end, the words fall back on yourself.

At first, I imagined love as meeting someone special enough, and then naturally gaining stability, understanding, and mutual salvation.

After I actually entered into a relationship, I was a very difficult person to judge. Rather than finding a partner, it would be better to say that I found a mother, or a super wishing machine.

Now I am more willing to admit that love has mechanisms, exchanges, bodies, and realistic conditions. But these explanations cannot erase the meaning that a specific person once gave me.

Explainable does not mean digestible. She was once real, and her departure is also real.

As for the future, I probably need to do a few less ambitious things.

First, establish more fulcrums for your life. Study, work, friends, interests, body and one’s own order should all continue to exist. Not to act independent, but to not let your partner bear the weight of the world.

Secondly, increase real contact. You can’t keep waiting for yourself to become good enough and then expect love to knock on your door automatically. If a person doesn’t go out, it’s probably difficult for him to master the art of walking through walls.

Then, slowly form the “we”. Get along first to see if each other is comfortable; then experience together to see if trust grows; and finally talk about long-term integration. Don’t just meet someone and then secretly arrange for her to play roles in the next few decades before they even receive the script.

You also need to learn to express yourself directly. Instead of rehearsing an entire tragedy in your head based on the speed of responses, ask, “I’ve been a little uneasy with the lack of contact lately. I wonder where we are now.”

When a conflict occurs, first distinguish whether the other party needs companionship and solutions at the moment, or whether there is indeed a long-term conflict that cannot be avoided. Don’t hold a seminar when someone is crying, and don’t judge every mood swing as a sign that the relationship is about to die.

No more pain to prove affection. Insomnia, rumination, and loss of order in life may mean that love is very important, or it may mean that other fulcrums are falling. Pain deserves to be seen, but the sound of pain does not mean the love is right.

Finally, learn to accept being loved. Allow others to take care of me and not be in a hurry to pay off the debt; allow myself to have needs, and allow others to say they can’t do it.

These words are quite clear now. I don’t know how much I can really do in the next relationship. Theorists usually sit on the shore and talk about swimming in a clear and logical manner.

But probably still have to go into the water.

Love is probably when one person gradually enters the consciousness of another person, and finally a “we” grows between the two people. It’s just that this “we” cannot obtain the freehold property rights, nor can we in turn evict the two people.

I don’t know when it is love and when it becomes habit, debt or unwillingness.

Time may tell.

But time is never responsible for writing standard answers.

entry.title: After a Thousand Sails
entry.content:
Something rather irritating keeps happening when I work through exercises. My mind remains quiet while I eat, sleep, or scroll through videos. The moment I begin serious mathematics—especially when I cannot solve a question—my former partner, the stupid things I once did, and the possibility of failing the postgraduate entrance examination all arrive together. It begins with an unsolved limit and soon accelerates into the question of whether my entire life is finished. Not one additional symbol appears on the page.

Today I came across an explanation. The human brain, it seems, is not nearly as modern as we imagine. A tiger attempting to eat you is obviously a danger. To the brain, however, an action that may fail, cause humiliation, or prove one’s inadequacy is dangerous too. This is especially true of the postgraduate entrance examination, into which I have placed far too many other things. It is no longer a collection of mathematics problems; it is connected to education, the future, and the question of whether I am an idiot.

When I cannot solve something, uncertainty and the fear of being classified as a failure rise together. The sympathetic nervous system starts first. Adrenaline and noradrenaline prepare the body for conflict; the slower HPA axis and cortisol response follow. The heart accelerates, attention narrows, and the body assumes that I am about to fight or flee. In reality, I am calculating a limit.

To be precise, cortisol does not carry a loudspeaker through the brain ordering it to “begin searching the archive of shame.” The process is closer to this: once stress rises, working memory and quiet reasoning are impaired, while attention tilts toward danger. The feeling that “I may fail again” becomes a retrieval cue in its own right. Memory is recovered through association, so earlier failures, embarrassments, and moments of shame become easier to call up, as though old surveillance footage had suddenly begun playing on a loop.

But the system is probably not attacking me.

It has merely detected a scent resembling an earlier danger and is trying to prevent me from falling into the same trap. The program was written a long time ago, when rejection by the group or a mistake during a hunt might genuinely have been fatal. In the twenty-first century, it still cannot reliably distinguish “I cannot solve this question” from “the tribe is about to cast me out.”

Damn it. The firmware needs an update.

Once I understood this, the experience became slightly easier to interpret. The reason old memories return whenever a question defeats me may not be that those events urgently need to be discussed. The present state of “perhaps I am incapable” simply points toward earlier moments in which “I genuinely failed to do well.” The memories are not appearing without cause. The mind is searching for like terms.

Love is among them. I think I understand a little better why she may once have liked me, although this is only a model I have fitted to the past from one side; I do not know what she actually thought. Perhaps the person I was then genuinely did think about many things and, after all that thought, remained willing to love something. Later, as the models multiplied and I learned more unpleasant facts, I grew colder. Love was a transaction, friendship an exchange of needs, dreams a release of dopamine, and research an evaluation system. Everything could be explained. Nothing remained interesting.

Love, however, is only one example. What truly concerns me is the person I want eventually to become.

I do not think I want to return to the self who knew nothing. Innocence untouched by experience is beautiful, but part of its beauty comes merely from not having seen. Once it encounters interest, failure, departure, and helplessness, it can break at once. Then a person begins to call himself mature: everyone is selfish; love is false; ideals cannot purchase food; look after yourself first.

None of these statements is entirely wrong. Yet if maturity ends by seeing an interest behind every person and a fraud behind every object, has one not merely travelled from one kind of childishness to another?

What I want may be one step farther on. I want to see something of the world: to know how society operates, how to speak, how to handle affairs, how to keep accounts, and how to make something real. I want to have been rejected and defeated, to have watched relationships dissolve, and to understand that effort does not always produce a result. After passing through all of that, I do not want to pickle myself into a smooth old cynic. I want to remain capable of believing in something again.

To believe that love can exist; that a formula can truly be beautiful; that a problem may deserve investigation for reasons beyond papers and employment; that one person sometimes reaches out simply because another person is in pain. Not because I remain ignorant of the mechanisms, interests, and hormones beneath these events, but because knowledge of a mechanism does not make the event false.

This is probably what I meant by those earlier sentences: idealism at its furthest point becomes inseparable from realism; complete maturity from complete innocence; a genuine dream from the power to act. If an ideal is real, it must understand how reality operates. If maturity is real, it cannot stop at “I have seen through everything and therefore believe in nothing.” If a dream is real, it must eventually become the number of exercises completed today.

The innocence that remains after a thousand sails is not the innocence present at the beginning. The first believes because it does not yet know. The second knows and remains willing. It is not a return to the point of origin. It is arriving there after a long circle, carrying both the wounds and the abilities acquired along the way.

As Romain Rolland is so often quoted that the sentence has nearly worn smooth: true heroism consists in loving life after recognising its truth. I used to regard that as another correctly phrased piece of nonsense. Now I can feel a little of its weight.

What I should do next, then, has two sides. I must learn the operations of reality, become shrewder, acquire the ability to act, earn money, and assume responsibility. At the same time, I must avoid pickling myself entirely into an old cynic. I would like to become someone who can still be delighted by a flower, a formula, or a particular person.

An innocent person who has passed a thousand sails.

Or, to put it differently, a father who has retained the spirit of a boy.

That phrase is rather good.

Of course, this entire essay emerged while I was supposed to be solving problems. Once again, I have successfully explained why I was not working and substituted the explanation for the work itself. How the hell is it still the same recursion?

At least this version can be shorter.

Let the alarm sound. Its sounding does not mean that a tiger is present, nor that the old events must be resolved now. If I cannot solve the question, then I cannot. Read the solution, cover it, and write the answer again. If the brain insists on playing old footage, it may do so in the background. I will finish the next line first.

entry.title: The Beast's Method of Studying
entry.content:
Original version:

Recently I have been thinking about a kind of beast’s method of studying. The idea is to treat myself as a beast: stop thinking about everything, stop applying a whole moral code in order to condemn myself, and regard myself as an idiot. I am simply too stupid for this question, so I have to study it more. I am a beast that must pile up enough hours before these things can be learned properly. If I think of myself as a work animal and get on with the labour, there seems to be much less internal friction. Different parts of the brain also need to take turns; I cannot study the same subject without interruption. I have done mathematics for two days in a row and now feel close to vomiting. I need some English, politics, or a major course in the middle to slow down and recover. Sometimes philosophy should remain philosophy. Too much thought, philosophising, and summarising of methods delays actual study, just as listening to lesson after lesson without producing any output interferes with progress.

GPT-organised version:

I have recently been considering a beast’s method of studying. That means, first of all, ceasing to treat myself as a defendant before a moral court and treating myself as a beast instead.

If I cannot solve the question, it is not because my life has failed, my soul is inferior, I lack the mentality of the strong, or I have not discovered some ultimate method of learning.

I am simply bad at it.

If you are bad, practise. If you are slow, look again. If you do not know, put in the hours.

I am an idiot. I cannot solve this question, and this concept has not yet grown inside my brain. What can be done? Nothing particularly clever. Read it again. Write it again. Get it wrong tomorrow, then crawl back the day after that.

It sounds unpleasant, but the statement has a peculiar advantage: it produces much less internal friction.

Once I admit that “I am simply slow,” a great deal of additional judgment disappears. Previously, the process after a wrong answer looked something like this: get the question wrong; ask why I got it wrong again; wonder whether I am unsuited to mathematics; wonder whether I will fail the postgraduate entrance examination; and eventually arrive at existentialism, family structure, the education system, and the limitations of human civilisation.

The question remains uncorrected.

Good grief. Why am I writing a sociological elegy for another wrong answer?

Here is a rougher model:

flowchart TD
    A[做错题] --> B[我不会]
    B --> C[看答案]
    C --> D[遮住重做]
    D --> E[明天再做]

The process is not elegant. It contains no epistemological beauty and no philosophical depth. It is effective. Or perhaps it is effective precisely because it is not elegant. It leaves the brain too little room for performance and prevents my overdeveloped analytical mind from calling another meeting.

The second thing I have felt very clearly is that different parts of the brain really do need to take turns.

After two consecutive days of mathematics, I feel close to vomiting. This is not the ordinary “oh, I do not feel like working hard” kind of nausea. A particular region of the brain genuinely feels as though it has been rubbed with sandpaper. Show me another limit, derivative, or integral and I want to throw both the book and myself out of the room.

The book cannot be thrown away, of course. It was rather expensive.

So the same task cannot remain at full load indefinitely. When mathematics makes me sick, I switch to English. When English vocabulary turns numb, I switch to politics. When politics makes me feel that I am memorising a pile of correctly phrased nonsense, I switch to a major course. When that material begins to scatter, I return to basic mathematics problems.

This is not avoidance.

Avoidance means opening Bilibili and announcing, “I am taking a short break.”

Switching mental gears is still study. It simply stops one part of the brain from being squeezed to death. Even a work animal cannot pull the same cart without pause; a beast occasionally needs a different trough. The language is crude, but the fact is real.

The third rule is that philosophy should shut up for a while.

The sentence makes even me laugh. One of my strongest abilities is turning a specific problem into an abstract one.
