If I merely failed to review vocabulary today, I can transform the matter into the question of “whether language acquisition is essentially the subject’s domestication of a symbolic system.” It sounds cultured.

The vocabulary remains unlearned.

If I merely failed to produce solutions in mathematics, I can diagnose a “knowledge–action gap between input and output.”

The questions remain unwritten.

That is idiotic.

I am not saying that the analyses are wrong. On the contrary, most of them may be correct. That is precisely the problem. A correct idea can still delay the work, and its correctness may make the delay even easier to defend.

The same applies to lessons. The teacher explains everything smoothly; you follow without difficulty; the notes fill page after page in several carefully distinguished colours. The brain develops the illusion that the knowledge has already been mastered.

Then the video ends and the exercise sheet comes out.

Oh dear.

Who was the person who had mastered the subject a minute ago? Has he logged off?

I may therefore need a brutal rule: input that is not received by output counts only as passing traffic.

A lesson without exercises is passing traffic. A book that cannot be restated is passing traffic. Vocabulary that cannot be recalled is passing traffic. Understanding a worked solution without covering it and solving the question again is also passing traffic.

Knowledge entered through the eyes and ears, took a tourist photograph at the gate of the brain, and left. You cannot claim that it moved in merely because it once visited.

In plain language:

I am a beast.

I am a work animal.

I am a slow creature that can be built only through time and repetition.

The sentence sounds insulting, yet it contains a certain kindness. A beast does not question the meaning of life because it cannot differentiate today. A work animal does not write an existentialist essay because it pulled the mill poorly.

It continues pulling.

I do not literally want to become a beast. A human being must still think; without thought, one merely reaches a different form of numbness. At this stage, however, excessive thought is not the ability in short supply.

For me, what is scarce is the ability not to think.

At least during these hours at the desk, think a little less.

Write a little more.

If you do not know, admit that you do not know.

If one subject makes you sick, change subjects.

After input, produce output.

When you want to summarise another methodology, ask one question first: have today’s exercises been completed?

If not, this essay should not become too long either.

It is already long.

Damn it.

Sleep.

entry.title: Chapter One: Functions, Limits, and Continuity—The First Foundation of Calculus Viewed Through Epistemology
entry.content:
This is the single-chapter version of Chapter One. The same epistemological thread was later expanded into Advanced Mathematics: An Epistemological Map from Functions to Fields.

Wang Yangming said that before you looked at a flower, it and your mind both returned to silence; when you came to look at it, its colours became clear at once. The rough meaning is that the world does not enter the mind in a completely naked form. When you find a flower beautiful, the beauty does not arise merely because the flower is “objectively beautiful.” Its colour, form, light, and shadow produce an image in your mind, and your mind brightens with it.

Epistemologically speaking, human beings are continually compressing, abstracting, and modeling the objective world. We do not know the world itself directly. Instead, we compress its enormous, confused, and complicated information into models that can be understood, used, and transmitted. This is particularly evident in natural science: physics compresses motion and force into formulas; chemistry compresses changes in matter into structures; mathematics uses still more abstract symbols to compress relations themselves.

A good model cannot be excessively bulky. Ideally, it consumes little energy, remains concise and elegant, and is nevertheless useful. As for beauty, I currently suspect that it may be whatever reduces information entropy. Symmetry, unity, and the sudden appearance of a simple structure beneath a complicated phenomenon all have this quality. Upon seeing such a structure, one thinks, “So that is how it works.” This is a kind of cognitive pleasure. At a more fundamental level, perhaps the pleasure arose from the pressure for survival written into human genes?

Consider the first chapter of advanced mathematics. Calculus studies change, but before studying change we must identify the object that changes. We therefore begin with functions.

A function is a model of material, quantitative, and changing relations, represented through algebra and graphs. Reality contains many complicated relations: time and position, temperature and time, voltage and current, cost and profit. Mathematics abstracts them into a correspondence between an independent and a dependent variable: y=f(x). A complicated relation in reality is thereby compressed into a model that algebra and a graph can describe together.

We consequently study a function’s domain and range; inverse, implicit, and composite functions; and such properties as monotonicity, parity, periodicity, and boundedness. These topics are all asking what the model looks like. Over what range does it hold? Can it be understood in reverse? Can several simpler relations be composed to produce it? Does it contain symmetry, repetition, boundaries, or order?

At this point, the model called a function has been provisionally established.

A function alone, however, is insufficient. It describes a correspondence but does not adequately answer questions about approach. Often, what concerns us is not an isolated point, but the tendency shown by f(x) as (x) gradually approaches a value or travels towards infinity.

We therefore introduce the limit.

A limit enables us to study stability within a process. It is concerned not with the static result at one point, but with the destination approached by one variable while another continually draws nearer. Infinitesimals and infinities enter mathematical language in the same way. An infinitesimal is not simply a very small ordinary number; it is a quantity tending towards zero within a process. Infinity is not a number that can literally be held in one’s hand, but a tendency for function values to increase without bound.

Within the rigorous system used for postgraduate mathematics, limits are normally defined over the real numbers through the language of $\varepsilon-\delta$. For purposes of understanding, however, I find it illuminating to imagine extending the reals into the hyperreals. Hyperreal numbers offer a more intuitive picture: beyond ordinary real numbers, there seem actually to exist infinitesimal quantities “infinitely close to zero without being zero,” as well as infinite quantities greater than every ordinary real number.

As a proof, 1=3/3=3*1/3=0.33333333*3=0.99999999 is of course valid. The real-number system is continuous and complete and contains no infinitesimal gaps; infinitesimals belong to the hyperreal system. In other words, there is no gap between 0.999999999 and 1 among the reals.

This does not mean that a postgraduate examination will test hyperreal numbers. Rather, they provide a cognitive model for understanding limits. “Approach” ceases to be merely a formal definition and becomes something that can almost be handled in imagination. Standard analysis constrains approach rigorously with $\varepsilon-\delta$, whereas non-standard analysis seems to place infinitesimals directly inside the number system. The former is more rigorous and the latter more intuitive. At different levels, both help us understand the same thing.

The limit thus adds a sense of process to the model of a function. A function states what a relation is; a limit states what happens to it at a boundary, during an approach, or at infinity.

We then study the definition and properties of limits and the methods by which they are calculated. Arithmetic operations on limits, the squeeze theorem, the two important limits, and equivalent infinitesimals are all devices for treating relations of approach more effectively.

L’Hôpital’s rule and the Taylor formula can be regarded as more advanced instruments for calculating limits.

L’Hôpital’s rule is particularly interesting. Many limits are difficult because they appear in an indeterminate form such as $\frac{0}{0}$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$. Looking directly at the function values tells us little. L’Hôpital’s rule says that we may instead examine the rates of change of numerator and denominator. When both quantities tend towards zero or both towards infinity, we compare not the quantities themselves but the speeds at which they change.

This, too, is a form of modeling. When the original model is difficult to interpret or calculate, we change perspective from the “size of a quantity” to its “rate of change.” If two runners are both standing at the starting line at one instant, their positions do not reveal who is faster. Their velocities do.

The Taylor formula is an extreme form of model compression. A complicated function may be difficult to understand near a point, but Taylor tells us that a polynomial can approximate it:

$$f(x)\approx f(a)+f’(a)(x-a)+\frac{f’’(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2+\cdots $$

This is remarkably beautiful. Polynomials are among the most familiar and easily calculated objects in mathematics, yet near a point a complicated function can be decomposed into a constant term, a linear term, a quadratic term, a cubic term, and so on. It is as though an intricate curve were opened near one point and revealed as an ordered sequence. Adding more terms makes the model more precise; retaining only the first few makes it simpler. The aesthetic force is strong: complexity is compressed into simplicity, a curve into a polynomial, and local variation into information carried by derivatives.

L’Hôpital and Taylor are therefore more than techniques for solving examination questions. Both have an epistemological meaning. When a model is difficult to handle in its original form, we replace it with a more workable model that approaches the same object. L’Hôpital compares change through rates of change; Taylor approximates a complicated function locally through a polynomial.

Continuity and discontinuity then appear as natural applications.

If a limit studies the tendency of a function near a point, continuity asks whether that tendency meets the function’s actual value at the point. If, as $x$ approaches $x_0$, the limit of $f(x)$ equals $f(x_0)$, the function is continuous there.

Continuity means that the model does not break locally. Its tendency and value connect. A discontinuity means that the connection has failed: perhaps a removable point has not been filled; perhaps the left and right sides move towards different values; perhaps the function rushes towards infinity; or perhaps it oscillates without settling.

Seen in this way, the first chapter of advanced mathematics does not merely pile functions, limits, and continuity together. It establishes the most basic cognitive model of calculus. First, functions compress relations found in reality. Limits then describe the tendencies of those relations during a process of approach. Infinitesimals, infinities, and the intuitive picture of hyperreal numbers help us imagine such tendencies. Methods of calculation allow us to handle them, and continuity finally judges whether the local model remains stable and joined together.

This is my present understanding: mathematics does not move away from the world. It recompresses the world in a form that consumes less energy and is more concise and beautiful. A function models a relation; a limit models a tendency; L’Hôpital models comparison through rates of change; Taylor models local approximation; and continuity models stability. The whole structure of calculus begins here.

entry.title: Fitness Research Report
entry.content:
This is a comprehensive research report on natural fitness, ranging from exercise physiology and standards of lean-muscular aesthetics to physical assessment, training systems, and nutritional strategies. The main text remains available as a Markdown version for online reading, while a compiled PDF can be downloaded below and at the end of the article.

Source note: The material comes from a personal fitness research project, and the PDF is a compiled product.

PDF Download

  • Click to Download the PDF

Reading Guide

This report consists of eleven chapters and an appendix, covering the complete chain from basic physiology to practical training. Chapters One to Three establish the theoretical and conceptual foundations; Chapters Four and Five define aesthetic standards and methods of assessment; Chapters Six to Eight move into practical training; Chapters Nine to Eleven discuss nutrition, integration with daily life, and advanced development.

Fitness Research Report

Fitness Research Report

From Physiology to Aesthetics · From Assessment to Training · From Nutrition to Life

July 2026

Chapter One: Exercise Physiology and Medical Foundations

Before formally beginning a fitness journey, understanding how the body’s precise machinery operates is far more important than lifting weights blindly.

1.1 Anatomy of the Musculoskeletal System

The seven major muscle groups are the chest (pectoralis major), back (latissimus dorsi and trapezius), shoulders (the anterior, lateral, and posterior heads of the deltoid), arms (biceps and triceps), legs (quadriceps, hamstrings, and gluteus maximus), core (rectus abdominis and external obliques), and forearms.

Types of Muscle Fibre

Type Contraction Speed Resistance to Fatigue Suitable Training
Type I (slow-twitch) Slow High Endurance training
Type IIa (intermediate) Fast Medium Combined strength and endurance
Type IIx (explosive) Extremely fast Low Heavy strength work and explosive power

1.2 Molecular Mechanisms of Muscle Growth

The Three Principal Drivers of Hypertrophy

  1. Mechanical tension—the strongest signal: heavy compound movements directly activate mechanoreceptors
  2. Metabolic stress—the science behind the pump: high-repetition training accumulates metabolic waste and triggers a cellular-swelling response
  3. Muscle damage—reconstruction produces growth: training creates microscopic tears; after supercompensation, the muscle fibres become thicker and stronger

1.3 Energy Metabolism Systems

Energy System Duration Typical Application
ATP-CP system 6-10 seconds Maximum loads and sprinting
Glycolytic system 30-90 seconds Strength training at 8-15RM
Aerobic oxidative system Several minutes to several hours Low-intensity aerobic exercise

1.4 The Endocrine System

  • Testosterone: the king of anabolic hormones. It rises briefly after heavy compound movements
  • Growth hormone and IGF-1: promote fat breakdown and tissue repair
  • Cortisol: a double-edged sword. A persistently high level → muscle breakdown and fat accumulation
  • Insulin: the manager of nutrient distribution. Greater sensitivity means a lower tendency to store fat

1.5 Adaptation of the Nervous System

During the first month of strength gains, the muscles have not yet grown larger, but have already become stronger—this is neural adaptation.

The mind-muscle connection has a scientific basis—when attention is concentrated upon the target muscle, activation measured by EMG may rise by 10-20%.

Chapter Two: The Underlying Logic of the Lean-Muscular Male Physique

2.1 Definition and Measurement

Body-Fat Range: 10-14%

Body-Fat Range Visual Appearance
10-12% Abdominal definition is visible; facial contours are clear
12-14% Abdominal muscles are faintly visible; clothes produce the best appearance
15-18% Abdominal definition is unclear, but the body looks generally solid

A body-fat percentage below 10% carries costs including reduced testosterone and weaker immunity.

Reference Muscle Mass for a 175 cm Man

A fat-free mass index, or FFMI, of approximately 19-20; upper-arm circumference of 35-38 cm; chest circumference of 95-100 cm.

2.2 Aesthetics of Key Proportions

The V-shaped physique and shoulder-to-waist ratio: a ratio above 1.6 produces an obvious inverted triangle. Increasing shoulder width by 4-5 cm while keeping the waist between 72 and 76 cm is sufficient to reach this standard.

The ideal head-to-shoulder ratio is 2.5-3.0:1. East Asian men commonly measure 2.1-2.4, so shoulder training offers an exceptionally high return.

2.3 Nature versus Training

The skeleton and the shape of muscle bellies are genetically determined, but most people remain far below their limits.

Body-fat percentage, muscular circumference, posture, flexibility, and neuromuscular efficiency can all be changed.

2.4 Metabolic Advantages

A lean-muscular physique possesses greater insulin sensitivity, so carbohydrates enter muscle glycogen stores in preference to fat storage.

Chapter Three: Self-Assessment of Constitution, Body Type, and Posture

3.1 Classification of Body Types

Body Type Characteristics Difficulty of Gaining Muscle
Ectomorph (long and lean) Narrow shoulders and rapid metabolism Difficult
Mesomorph (well proportioned) Broad shoulders and narrow waist Easy
Endomorph (rounded) Broad hips and a tendency to store fat Easy to gain muscle but difficult to lose fat

3.2 Estimating Body-Fat Percentage

Visual comparison + skinfold callipers + bioelectrical impedance—cross-check the result through several methods.

3.3 Postural Assessment

Upper crossed syndrome (rounded shoulders, forward head, and hunched back): stretch the chest and strengthen the upper back.

Lower crossed syndrome (anterior/posterior pelvic tilt): for anterior tilt, stretch the iliopsoas and strengthen the glutes and abdominal muscles; for posterior tilt, stretch the hamstrings and strengthen the iliopsoas.

Order of priority in postural correction: breathing pattern → pelvic position → thoracic mobility → scapular stability.

Chapter Four: Aesthetic Standards for a Lean-Muscular Male Physique—A Detailed Guide by Body Part

4.1 Shoulders—Three-Dimensional Capped Deltoids

The ideal ratio among the anterior, lateral, and posterior heads of the deltoid is 1:1.5:1. The lateral head determines shoulder width, while the posterior head must not be neglected.

4.2 Chest—Square Rather than Rounded

The upper chest is the first priority: it determines the visual effect around the collar of a T-shirt. Avoid excessive development of the lower chest.

4.3 Back—The V-Shaped Inverted Triangle

The latissimus dorsi determines the V-shaped outline, while the middle and lower trapezius and the rhomboids determine thickness. Width first > thickness > detail.

4.4 Arms—Filling the Sleeves

The target upper-arm circumference for a lean-muscular physique is 37-40 cm. The triceps account for two-thirds of upper-arm size and contribute more to “large arms” than the biceps.

4.5 Core—Definition First

Whether the abdominal muscles appear depends upon body-fat percentage; 10-12% is sufficient. The external obliques are easy to “overtrain”—excessive development damages the V-shaped outline.

4.6 Overall Bearing

Muscle alone does not equal attractiveness. An upright and confident person looks far better than a heavily muscled person with rounded shoulders and a hunched back.

Chapter Five: Aesthetic Methods—Scientific Observation and Judgement

Standardised circumference measurements (once per week): shoulders, chest, waist, upper arms, and thighs. Focus particularly upon the shoulder-to-waist ratio.

Standardised photographic protocol (every 2-4 weeks): use the same lighting and pose, taking front, side, and rear photographs.

Trust trends rather than individual points; trust data rather than emotion; trust time rather than shortcuts.

Chapter Six: Preparing for Fitness—From Zero to One

6.1 Health Screening

Complete a routine physical examination before training. Anyone with an old injury should adjust the choice of movements accordingly.

6.2 Setting SMART Goals

Short-term goals should be completely controllable—for example, “complete four training sessions every week without absence.” Accumulate confidence through victories over small goals.

6.3 Choice of Venue

Type Advantages
Commercial gym Wide range of equipment; convenient progressive overload
Dumbbells and barbells at home No commute; one-off investment of 2,000-8,000 yuan
Bodyweight training No cost, but limited opportunities for overload

Chapter Seven: The Training System—Daily Process and Detailed Movements

7.1 Training Splits

Model Frequency Suitable Stage
Full-body training Three times per week Beginner
Upper/lower split Four times per week Novice
Push/pull/legs split Four to six times per week Advanced

7.2 Progressive Overload

This is the principal driver of muscle growth. Increase the training demand each week through weight, repetitions, number of sets, or shorter rest periods.

7.3 The Five Golden Compound Movements

Squat, deadlift, bench press, overhead press, and pull-up—place them near the beginning of each session.

7.4 Training Intensity

For a lean-muscular route: compound movements at 8-12RM × 3-4 sets, and isolation movements at 12-15RM × 2-3 sets. Rest for 90-180 seconds between compound sets and 60-90 seconds between isolation sets.

Chapter Eight: Customising the Training Programme

8.1 Choosing a Split

Three sessions per week → full-body training; four sessions → upper/lower split; five to six sessions → push/pull/legs split.

8.2 Sample Programme: Four Sessions per Week

Day Content
Monday Upper-body push (bench press, overhead press, lateral raise, triceps)
Tuesday Lower body (squat, Romanian deadlift, leg curl)
Thursday Upper-body pull (pull-up, row, biceps, face pull)
Friday Lower body + assistance (deadlift, split squat, hip thrust, abdominals)

Chapter Nine: Nutrition—the Materials from Which the Body Is Rebuilt

Muscle gain: a caloric surplus of 200 to 300 kcal per day. Fat loss: a caloric deficit of 300 to 500 kcal per day.

Protein: 1.6-2.2 g per kilogram of body weight per day, divided among 3-5 meals.

Recommended supplements: protein powder (★★★★★), creatine (★★★★★, the strongest evidence base), caffeine (★★★★), and vitamin D (★★★★).

Chapter Ten: Integration with Daily Life—Muscle Growth beyond the Gym

Sleep: 7-9 hours; secretion of growth hormone reaches its peak during deep sleep.

Stress management: prolonged high stress → persistently elevated cortisol → muscle breakdown.

Daily posture: check your seated posture every hour—draw the shoulder blades back and tuck the chin slightly. All-day posture matters more than one hour of training.

Chapter Eleven: Advanced Development and Additional Notes

Breaking through a Plateau

Increase volume (total weekly sets +10-20%), change movement variations, schedule a deload week, and optimise nutrition.

Common Misconceptions

❌ “The more I train, the faster I grow”—recovery matters more than training
❌ “Every set must reach failure”—failure increases fatigue and is unnecessary for every set
❌ “Fat can be reduced locally”—it cannot; fat loss occurs throughout the body

A Sustainable Attitude towards Fitness

Fitness is a lifelong practice, not a sprint lasting several months. What matters is long-term average quality, rather than perfection in a single session.

Appendix

A. Standard Circumference Record

Measurement Initial Month 1 Month 2 Month 3 Month 6
Shoulder circumference — — — — —
Waist circumference — — — — —
Upper arm (flexed) — — — — —
Thigh — — — — —

B. Body-Fat Reference

Body-Fat Percentage Appearance
10-12% Clearly visible abdominal muscles and definition
12-14% Faintly visible abdominal muscles and clear contours
14-16% Flat abdomen and softer muscular definition

entry.title: A Crash Course in Facial Aesthetics
entry.content:
This is a scientific guide extending from aesthetic principles to changes that can be made after birth. The first part asks “why,” examining the four underlying channels through which the brain evaluates a face. The second asks “how,” playing every available card, from body-fat percentage to hairstyle, clothing, and social presence. The main text remains available as a Markdown version for online reading, while a compiled PDF can be downloaded below and at the end of the article.

Source note: The material comes from a personal research project on facial aesthetics, and the PDF is a compiled product.

PDF Download

  • Click to Download the PDF

Reading Guide

This book is divided into Part One, which discusses principles, and Part Two, which focuses upon practice. The first explains how the brain evaluates a face, while the second provides practical methods of improvement. Readers interested only in “what to do” may proceed directly to Chapter Six. Yet if they understand the principles in the first part, they will also understand the reasons behind those actions.

A Crash Course in Facial Aesthetics

A Scientific Guide from Aesthetic Principles to Acquired Improvement

Symmetry · Proportion · Sexual Dimorphism · Attention Allocation · Dynamic Beauty · Practical Improvement

July 2026

Prologue: Aesthetic Judgement Is a Skill That Can Be Learned

“Beauty is difficult.” — Plato, Hippias Major

“Aesthetic judgement is subjective; different people prefer different things.”

This is probably the most frequently repeated claim in discussions of appearance. It sounds fair, inclusive, and unlikely to cause offence. Yet it is wrong—or, at least, only half right.

Personal preferences certainly differ, just as some people prefer coffee and others tea. When we discuss “handsomeness” and “beauty,” however, studies across cultures and historical periods repeatedly reveal one fact: human judgements of faces follow highly consistent underlying rules.

When a member of a Nigerian tribe, an office worker in Tokyo, and a university student in Stockholm evaluate photographs of faces belonging to different ethnic groups, the correlations among their ratings of “attractiveness” reach 0.7-0.9 (Langlois et al., 2000). This agreement crosses race, culture, sex, and even age. Infants only three months old look for longer at the faces which adults have rated more highly (Slater et al., 1998).

Three popular myths require correction:

Myth One: “Aesthetic judgement is subjective and cannot be explained.” In reality, while subjective elements exist, the underlying mechanisms—detection of symmetry, calculation of proportion, and assessment of sexual dimorphism—are hard-wired cognitive modules whose operation is highly consistent.

Myth Two: “A handsome face is inherited and cannot be changed.” Genetics certainly establishes a broad range, but within that range, body-fat percentage, muscular definition, the condition of the skin, hairstyle, habitual expressions, and posture each exert an influence no weaker than that of the skeleton itself.

Myth Three: “Money is all that matters; whether someone is handsome is irrelevant.” This is less an aesthetic judgement than a cynical simplification of social rules.

The position of this book is perfectly clear:

Aesthetic judgement follows rules, and most aspects of appearance can be improved after birth.

We shall answer two central questions:

  1. What exactly is “handsomeness”?—what does the brain actually assess when it evaluates a face?
  2. What can I do?—once the rules are understood, which particular and practical directions are available?

Chapter 1: Symmetry and Averageness—the Brain Sweeps for Mines

“Symmetry is the receipt for health.” — Evolutionary psychologist Randy Thornhill

1.1 Symmetry

The Developmental Stability Hypothesis

The Developmental Stability Hypothesis tells us that the degree of symmetry between the two sides of the body provides an external measure of whether development proceeded smoothly.

Development encounters various forms of “noise”: parasitic infection, malnutrition, inbreeding, genetic mutation, and maternal stress or illness during pregnancy. Every disturbance leaves a minute trace upon the face.

Research finding: a cross-cultural study discovered a highly consistent preference for “symmetrical faces” among participants in Britain, Japan, China, India, and South Africa (Perrett et al., 1999).

A Common Misunderstanding about “Perfect Symmetry”

No perfectly symmetrical human face exists in nature. Every face is slightly asymmetrical, and research employs the concept of a degree of symmetry. Interestingly, a perfectly symmetrical face is instead regarded as unnatural, because it lies beyond the biological range of variation in human faces.

1.2 The Averaging Effect

During the nineteenth century, the researcher Francis Galton conducted an experiment in which he superimposed photographs of several criminals. He discovered that the resulting average face appeared more regular than any of the originals. An average face is a face “without an obvious problem”: its nose is neither too large nor too small, and its chin neither excessively receding nor excessively projecting.

Limitation: The Problem of Distinctiveness

An average face has one fatal weakness: it lacks distinctiveness. A face that truly reaches the highest level must build upon the foundation of “averageness” while making a controlled departure in certain directions. That is precisely the subject addressed by sexually dimorphic characteristics.

1.3 Their Essential Meaning

This judgement requires only approximately 13 milliseconds (Olson & Marshuetz, 2005).

Chapter 2: Sexual Dimorphism—the Theory of Honest Signals

“A peacock’s tail is not used for flight, but for display. Its display is credible because it is costly.” — Amotz Zahavi

2.1 What Are Sexually Dimorphic Characteristics?

A List of Masculine Characteristics

During puberty, rising testosterone promotes the growth of male facial bones in particular directions: stronger brow ridges, a squarer and broader chin, higher and wider cheekbones, a larger nose, more obvious mandibular angles, and deeper eye sockets.

A List of Feminine Characteristics

Oestrogen acts in a different direction: a rounder facial outline, a thinner and narrower chin, fuller lips, larger eyes, a smoother region around the brow ridge, and a more delicate skin texture.

How Testosterone Shapes the Skeleton

Testosterone does not simply “make you more manly.” During puberty, it acts directly upon the growth plates of the facial skeleton. Facial bones differ among individuals in their degree of response, which explains why some people possess high testosterone without displaying especially prominent masculine facial characteristics.

2.2 The Theory of Honest Signals

If masculine features are so “attractive,” why have all men not evolved the most exaggerated square chins and heavy brow ridges? The answer is that the cost is too high.

Testosterone is an immunosuppressive hormone: high levels suppress the operation of the immune system. This means that if a male with high testosterone during puberty lacks a sufficiently strong immune system, he will fall ill repeatedly during development.

In the language of game theory, this is an “honest signal.” Only an individual of sufficiently high genetic quality can bear the immune cost imposed by high testosterone.

The Handicap Principle, proposed by the Israeli biologist Amotz Zahavi, provides the best framework for understanding this phenomenon. Masculine facial characteristics are, in essence, the human version of the peacock’s tail.

2.3 Dependence upon Context

Women do not possess one fixed “aesthetic preference,” but adjust their strategy flexibly according to their physiological condition:

Stage Preference Underlying Strategy
Ovulation, with high probability of conception A more masculine face Short-term mating strategy—obtain high-quality genes
Luteal/non-ovulatory phase A softer, more feminine face Long-term mating strategy—find a partner willing to invest resources

2.4 Cross-Cultural Observations

One notable characteristic of East Asian cultures is that they accept soft male faces to a far greater degree than Europe and North America do. Possible reasons include the stronger emphasis agricultural civilisation places upon communal cooperation, the magnified risks of high aggression in densely populated societies, and traditional admiration for “cultivated elegance” and “delicate good looks.”

Every culture is sensitive to sexually dimorphic characteristics, but each culture calibrates a different optimal degree.

Chapter 3: Proportion and Line—the Brain Conserves Energy

“The brain is a lazy organ: its highest principle is not the pursuit of beauty, but the reduction of processing cost.”

3.1 Three Sections and Five Eye-Widths

Three Sections

The three-section principle divides the frontal face vertically into equal thirds: the upper section, from the hairline to the glabella; the middle section, from the glabella to the base of the nose; and the lower section, from the base of the nose to the tip of the chin. Ideally, the three areas are roughly equal in height.

Five Eye-Widths

The five-eye principle divides the frontal face horizontally into five equal parts: facial width is approximately equal to the width of five eyes.

The brain requires no ruler to calculate proportion. Facial recognition involves the fusiform face area, or FFA, which automatically extracts the relative positions and sizes of different parts while processing a face. This process occurs before attention.

3.2 The Truth about the Golden Ratio

The real status of 1:1.618 in facial aesthetics is as follows:

  • It genuinely exists—the proportions of some faces widely regarded as beautiful approach the golden ratio
  • It is not a “formula for beauty”—many highly attractive faces do not conform to the golden ratio

The prominent position of the golden ratio in aesthetic literature is to a considerable extent the result of publication bias.

Processing Fluency Theory

When the brain processes a stimulus, a smooth and effortless process produces a positive aesthetic experience. The advantage of the golden ratio is that 1:1.618 is a simple numerical relation: simple relation = easy for the brain to process = low processing cost = a feeling of “comfort.”

3.3 Smoothness of Line

Three principal forms of smoothness are critical: the outer contour (the complete outline from hairline to chin), the profile line (the S-shaped curve from forehead to chin), and internal transition lines (the transitions among different regions).

As a person ages, full contours are replaced by hollows and angles. The brain may have learned to use “smooth lines” as a proxy for “this person is not old.”

East Asian aesthetics places far greater weight upon smooth lines than European and North American aesthetics do. The preference for a V-shaped face, inward movement of the cheekbones, and filling of the temples all express this tendency.

3.4 Evenness of Skin Tone

If any aesthetic indicator is genuinely universal across cultures, it is that “an even skin tone” is more fundamental than “light skin.”

Preference Cross-Cultural Consistency Evolutionary Logic
Even skin tone Extremely high Even skin tone = no infection = health
Light skin Medium, limited to East Asia Lightness may be associated with signals of social class

The Brain’s Algorithm for Evaluating Facial Attractiveness

Chapter 4: Attention Allocation and Peak Shift—the Contest between Distinctiveness and Risk

4.1 The Effect of Visual Focus, or the Attention-Seeker Principle

The visual system automatically assigns its budget of attention to the most striking characteristic. The greater the difference, the greater the weight.

Positive version: an excellent feature becomes the anchor of the complete face. Negative version: one obvious small defect can similarly absorb all attention.

Facial aesthetics is not a scoring system, but a system of attention allocation.

4.2 The Peak Shift Effect

During development, the brain constructs a statistical template of a “normal human face.” When it calculates the distance between a particular face and the average template, if the departure occurs in a pleasing direction, the departure itself becomes a source of attractiveness.

This produces an inverted U-shaped curve: insufficient departure = too close to average; appropriate departure = peak attractiveness; excessive departure = disgust is triggered.

4.3 The Contrast Effect

A face permits only one feature to stand out—that is distinctiveness. If two or more features stand out together, the face slips from “distinctive” towards “genuinely ugly.”

Distinctiveness = peak shift in one direction, with all other aspects remaining average or better.
Ugliness = simultaneous departure in two or more directions, each competing for attention.

4.4 Baby Schema

Large eyes, a small nose, a round face, and a high forehead—across species, these characteristics trigger an adult desire to protect.

Baby schema + sexually dimorphic characteristics form the strongest combination in aesthetics. This is why the “beautiful youth” type of face appeals to every age group.

4.5 Facial Width-to-Height Ratio and Edge Contrast

A high fWHR, or broad face, is perceived as more dominant; a low fWHR, or narrow face, is perceived as gentler.

Edge contrast refers to the transitional region between hard and soft tissue. Edge contrast suits men, producing strength; a smooth transition suits women, producing softness.

Chapter 5: A First-Principles Question—Where Does Aesthetic Judgement Begin?

5.1 Tracing Upwards

Every aesthetic preference is, in essence, the brain performing an ancient task of detection: assessing genetic quality and the expected return from a potential mate.

The underlying derivation of every aesthetic principle ultimately points towards two drivers: sexual selection, or reproductive value, and survival selection, or survival value.

5.3 Cognitive Spillover

If sexual and survival selection are the final sources of aesthetic judgement, why are people moved by non-living things? What do sunsets, mountains, and symphonies have to do with genetic quality?

This article supports the idea of Cognitive Spillover: the brain’s aesthetic system is a detector that remains continuously online. When it receives no input related to sexual selection, it does not shut down. Instead, it projects its remaining processing capacity upon every object available to perception.

5.4 The Core Framework of the Book

Chapter 6: Foundational Improvement—Complete the Free Steps First

Before spending ten thousand yuan upon your face, reduce your weight to a standard body-fat percentage. This has greater leverage than any medical-aesthetic procedure.

6.1 Body-Fat Percentage—the Greatest Lever

Body-Fat Range Condition of Jawline Overall Facial Appearance
Below 12% Sharp jawline Clearly defined, approaching a model’s appearance
Around 15% Visible jawline Clean and sharp; the best range for most people
18%-20% Unclear jawline Insufficient three-dimensional definition
Above 20% Jawline disappears Puffy appearance

For most Asian men, reducing body fat from 20% to 15% improves facial attractiveness more than any skincare product, hairstyle, or adjustment of clothing.

6.2 Skin Management

Order of priority: sun protection > moisturising > cleansing > acne control > everything else.

The three skincare essentials for men: facial cleanser, specifically an amino-acid cleanser + moisturising lotion/cream + sunscreen, SPF30+.

6.3 Sleep, Stress, and Swelling

Long-term sleep deprivation → increased cortisol → redistribution of facial fat, increased sebum, and reduced collagen synthesis.

6.4 Minimum Standards of Cleanliness

Item Standard
Bathing At least once per day
Oral hygiene Brush for two minutes + floss + clean the tongue
Fingernails Trim short, leaving no more than 1 mm
Nasal hair Not visible outside the nostrils
Lips Neither dry nor peeling

A sense of neatness = the absence of obvious negative details that attract attention.

Chapter 7: Refining the Head—Your Face Can Be Adjusted

The correct combination of hairstyle, eyebrow shape, facial hair, and glasses can approach the effect of surgery upon the soft tissues of the face, at less than one-tenth of the cost.

7.1 Hairstyle

Facial Characteristic Hairstyle Strategy
High forehead/receding hairline Use a fringe or side part for coverage
Long face Retain volume on both sides
Broad/round face Add height on top and tighten the sides
Broad jaw/square face Add volume on top to balance the lower facial section

7.2 Eyebrow Shape

For men: remove stray hairs and give the eyebrows a clear shape. Have them shaped once, then maintain them yourself every week.

7.3 Facial Hair

First principle: if there is insufficient density, do not grow it. A clean shave is ten thousand times better than a sparse beard.

Facial Defect Facial-Hair Strategy
Receding chin Grow a goatee or retain greater length at the chin
Unclear jawline Keep a line of short hair along the edge of the jaw

7.4 Masseter Muscles and Expression

Chewing on only one side over a long period causes facial asymmetry. Record a video upon your phone while behaving naturally: most people will be shocked by their default expression, which looks as though they are angry.

7.5 Glasses

Align the upper edge of the frame with the eyebrows. Above the eyebrows → a strange expression; below them → a tired appearance.

Chapter 8: The Body—the Frame around the Face

Training the lateral deltoid through lateral raises is the single most efficient movement for changing bodily proportions.

Do not overtrain the trapezius—a highly developed upper trapezius shortens the visual length of the neck.

With the head carried 5 cm forward, your face appears 5%-10% heavier than it really is. The simplest correction is to stand against a wall for five minutes every day.

The language of the hands: clean and neatly trimmed nails = “I take care of my own life.”

Chapter 9: Clothing and Environmental Signals

Fit matters more than brand. Spend 500 yuan upon an ill-fitting garment → passers-by will assume it was borrowed.

The three-colour principle: main colour 60% + secondary colour 30% + accent colour 10%. Wear no more than three colours across the complete outfit.

Layering: three layers > two layers > one layer. Every additional layer suggests that you have given the outfit more thought.

Small details: fingernails, nasal hair, shoes, collars, and smell. Each seems unimportant in isolation, but together they form the boundary between a polished and a careless appearance.

Chapter 10: Invisible Weapons

Three levels of scent: cleanliness, the foundation → the smell of laundry detergent, a social signal → perfume, the background music.

Voice: speed, 120-160 Chinese characters per minute; pitch, no rise at the end of a sentence; resonance, chest resonance.

The golden ratio of eye contact: look into the other person’s eyes for 60%-70% of the time while speaking.

The key to a smile is not duration, but timing. Smile when meeting, when hearing something interesting, and when saying goodbye.

Chapter 11: Overall Order of Priority

Complete the free steps first. Before spending any money, finish everything that costs nothing.

Most people skip the first step and rush directly into a medical-aesthetics clinic. They spend the money, but the effect is completely cancelled by a high body-fat percentage and unhealthy habits.

Final Chapter: The Ultimate Answer to Every Principle of Aesthetics

First, aesthetic judgement follows rules. It is not mysticism, but the result of sexual selection, survival selection, cognitive processing, and cultural learning operating together.

Second, rules are meant to produce understanding, not anxiety.

Appendix

A. Twenty-Item Rapid Self-Assessment Checklist

# Item Standard
1 Body-fat percentage below 15% Abdominal definition is visible
2 Skincare every morning and evening Cleanser + moisturiser + sunscreen
3 At least seven hours of sleep each day Seven to eight continuous hours
4 No obvious body odour or bad breath No unpleasant smell detectable from half an arm’s length
5 Fingernails cleanly trimmed White edge no longer than 1 mm
6 Nasal hair not exposed Invisible from every angle
7 Lips not dry or cracked No peeling or fissures
8 Hairstyle matches facial shape Deliberate adjustment for facial shape
9 Stray eyebrow hairs trimmed Eyebrow shape clearly visible
10 Facial hair shaved cleanly or deliberately shaped No awkward transitional period
11 Forward head posture under correction Stand against a wall every day
12 At least three well-fitting sets of basic clothing Shoulder seams, sleeve length, and garment length all checked
13 Know the best photographic angle Completed the “choose three from fifty” test
14 Possess a suitable perfume Selected after testing the fragrance
15 Have listened to and adjusted a recording of your voice Adjusted speed and pitch
16 Deliberately practise eye contact Apply the golden ratio of 60%-70%
17 No more than three colours across the complete outfit Follows the 60-30-10 colour principle
18 Glasses match facial shape Upper edge of frame aligned with eyebrows
19 Loose hair at the back of the head and behind the ears is neat Confirmed as neatly treated during the haircut
20 Know your facial shape Can accurately identify round/square/long/heart-shaped/diamond/oval

entry.title: Men's Skincare Research Report
entry.content:
This is a comprehensive research report on men’s skincare, extending from physiological differences and the identification of skin types to daily routines, product selection, lifestyle, and the management of problems. The main text remains available as a Markdown version for online reading, while a compiled PDF can be downloaded below and at the end of the article.

Source note: The material comes from a personal skincare research project, and the PDF is a compiled product.

PDF Download

  • Click to Download the PDF

Reading Guide

This report contains thirteen chapters and follows the logical chain of “building understanding → theoretical foundations → practical system → responses to problems → advanced extension.” The first four chapters establish the conceptual foundation; Chapters Five to Eight construct the practical system; Chapters Nine to Eleven address particular situations; and Chapters Twelve and Thirteen provide extensions and a conclusion.

Men’s Skincare Research Report

Men’s Skincare Research Report

From Science to Aesthetics · From Skin Type to Routine · From Selection to Persistence

July 2026

Chapter 1: Introduction—Why Men Need Skincare

1.1 An Overlooked Basic Need

For a long time, Chinese society has treated skincare as the exclusive territory of women. An invisible wall stands between men and skincare, built jointly from the stereotype that “roughness is masculine” and a lack of knowledge about skincare products.

Yet the global market for men’s skincare is undergoing unprecedented growth. In 2023, the global market for men’s facial skincare exceeded 18 billion US dollars, while the Chinese market reached approximately 18 billion yuan.

The principal drivers of this growth are the visual turn of social media, the rise of the “male economy,” and pressure arising from professional and social situations.

1.2 Core Position

This report adopts three principles: scientific, systematic, and sustainable. All claims of effectiveness should be supported first by evidence-based medicine, while every stage should ask one question: “What do the distinctive properties of men’s skin mean here?”

Chapter 2: The Development of Skincare

Ancient Egypt: men and women used almost identical skincare products—castor and olive oils for moisture, and Kohl eyeliner for protection against ultraviolet radiation.

Ancient Greece and Rome: the public bathhouse sequence of “cold water → warm water → hot water → steam” formed a prototype for the modern skincare routine.

Ancient China: literati during the Tang and Song dynasties used facial preparations containing traditional ingredients such as Angelica dahurica and Sichuan lovage; Su Shi and others discussed formulas for such preparations. Bathing beans and various scented ornaments were popular among Song scholar-officials.

The twentieth-century “silent period”: the two World Wars reinforced the model of “men = roughness,” and skincare products came to be regarded as a sign of effeminacy.

The Japanese and Korean wave: Shiseido took the lead in launching a men’s skincare line during the 1990s. K-Beauty then carried men’s skincare to a new level.

The Chinese market: emergence in the 2000s → growth in the 2010s → rapid expansion in the 2020s.

Chapter 3: Skin Physiology and Medical Foundations—the Male Version

3.1 Structural Differences in the Skin

Indicator Men Women
Thickness of the dermis Approximately 20-25% thicker Thinner
Quantity of sebum 1.5-2 times greater Lower
Subcutaneous fat Lower Higher

Wrinkles appear later in men but are deeper, while collagen is lost at a steady rate. The sebaceous glands are stimulated by DHT and produce 1.5-2 times as much sebum as those of women. Daily shaving increases transepidermal water loss by 20-50%.

3.2 Skin Ageing—the Male Version

Extrinsic ageing is men’s weak point: they participate in more outdoor activity but use sunscreen at a far lower rate than women. Glycation causes the skin to become yellow and dull.

Typical signs include enlarged pores, a dull and yellow complexion, hollow eye sockets, and deep, coarse wrinkles.

3.3 A Care Path Designed for Men

Dimension Key Action
Correct shaving Warm towel → lubrication → shave with the grain → after-shave care
Moderate cleansing Avoid alkaline soap bases
Moisturising Choose lightweight moisturisers such as gels or lotions
Sun protection SPF30+ for daily life and SPF50+ outdoors
Regulation of metabolism Niacinamide to control oil; retinol against ageing

Chapter 4: Identifying Skin Type

4.1 The Four Everyday Categories

Oily (oil across the complete face) → dry (tightness and flaking) → combination (oily T-zone and dry cheeks) → normal (extremely rare)

Cleansing test, at no cost: wash the face with warm water and observe—oil after 30 minutes = oily; tightness after one hour = dry.

4.2 Distinctive Features of Acne in Men

Men produce 1.5-2 times as much sebum as women, and acne appears more often in the beard region. The vicious cycle between shaving and acne is a management problem specific to men.

Common triggers of adult acne include whey-protein supplements, stress, a high-GI diet, and masks.

Skin type should be reassessed every quarter.

Chapter 5: Aesthetics, Bearing, and Skincare Strategies

Type of Bearing Skincare Priority
Fresh and clean Oil control + moderate cleansing + basic moisturising
Rugged Moderate oil control + contour care + after-shave repair
Mature and steady Anti-ageing + sun protection + deep moisturising
Cheerful and athletic Antioxidants + sun protection + lightweight moisturising
Cool and refined Detailed care + pore management + brightening

Men’s central requirements when choosing products: Fast + Invisible + Effective.
Preferred texture: light and non-sticky > rapidly absorbed > no film-like feeling.
Preferred fragrance: fragrance-free > woody > citrus.

Chapter 6: Facial Preparation and Preconditions

The Correct Shaving Process

  1. Apply a warm towel to the face for 1-2 minutes to soften the hair
  2. Apply shaving cream for lubrication
  3. Shave with the grain to minimise irritation
  4. Shave against the grain only where necessary
  5. Rinse with cold water + apply an after-shave product

Facial Cleansing

The feeling of “scrubbing a plate” does not mean that the face is clean—tightness indicates that excessive cleansing has damaged the skin barrier.

Choose an amino-acid cleanser for everyday use and occasionally use a combined cleanser for deeper cleaning. Say goodbye to soap-based cleansers completely.

Chapter 7: A System for the Daily Skincare Routine

Core Principle

A routine that can be maintained is far better than one that is optimal only in theory.

The Basic Three-Layer Framework

Cleanse → Moisturise → Protect/SPF

Morning Routine

Water or a gentle cleanser → after-shave care if shaving → vitamin C serum, optional → moisturiser → sunscreen, the most important step

Evening Routine

Cleanse → after-shave care if shaving → active serum → moisturiser

Retinol is the first-choice anti-ageing ingredient for men. Begin at a concentration of 0.25%-0.3%, use it twice per week, and gradually build tolerance.

Advanced Active Ingredients

Goal Ingredient Starting Concentration
Oil control Niacinamide 2%-5%
Blackhead removal Salicylic acid (BHA) 0.5%-2%
Anti-ageing Retinol 0.25%-0.3%
Brightening Vitamin C 10%-15%
Repair Ceramide/B5 —

Chapter 8: Lifestyle—the Invisible Half of Skincare

Diet: high-GI foods are positively associated with acne. Whey protein increases acne in some users.

Fitness: the first fifteen minutes after exercise are the golden window for facial care.

Sleep: insufficient sleep → increased cortisol → overactive sebaceous glands + greater inflammation.

Smoking: produces a “smoker’s face,” with a dull, grey-yellow complexion. Within one week of stopping smoking, the complexion brightens; within three months, wrinkles decrease.

Chapter 9: A Practical Guide to Product Selection

The Core Logic of Selection

Ingredients > brand > packaging. Before every purchase, ask yourself: What does my skin need? What is the core ingredient? Can I continue using it?

Understanding the Ingredient List

Rule of decreasing quantity: ingredients are listed from highest to lowest content. The 1% threshold: preservatives are generally added at below 1%, so ingredients appearing before them have a concentration above 1%.

Brand Selection

Type Recommended Brands Suitable Users
Dermocosmetics CeraVe, La Roche-Posay, and Paula’s Choice Those focused upon ingredients
Men’s lines Lab Series and Biotherm Homme Those seeking convenience
Japanese Shiseido Men Those prioritising the experience upon the skin
Chinese brands Simpcare and Proya Those seeking value for money

Budget Distribution

Sunscreen (¥100-300/month) + serum (¥150-500/month) + savings on cleanser (¥50-150/month). The average daily cost is approximately ¥10-15.

Chapter 10: Decision Trees and Typical Cases

A 25-Year-Old Programmer with Oily Skin (¥143/month)

Morning: amino-acid cleanser → niacinamide → lightweight lotion → sunscreen
Evening: amino-acid cleanser → salicylic acid every other day → lightweight lotion
Weekly: clay mask upon the T-zone 1-2 times

A 32-Year-Old Office Worker with Combination Skin (¥280/month)

Morning: water → vitamin C 10% → light moisturising lotion → sunscreen
Evening: amino-acid cleanser → retinol 0.1-0.3% every other day → repairing cream

A Mature 40-Year-Old (¥480/month)

Morning: gentle cleanser → vitamin C → peptide eye cream → rich face cream → high-SPF sunscreen
Evening: cleanser → retinol 0.3-0.5% → peptide eye cream → repairing night cream

A 22-Year-Old University Beginner (¥80/month)

Buy only three products: amino-acid cleanser + moisturising lotion + sunscreen. The goal is to establish a habit, not to obtain the most extreme result.

Chapter 11: Standard Procedures for Handling Problems

Level Symptoms Response
L1 mild Slight stinging or redness Reduce frequency and strengthen moisturising
L2 moderate Widespread redness and stinging Stop active ingredients and use repair products only
L3 severe Swelling or blisters Seek medical care immediately

Situations in which a doctor must be consulted: severe nodular or cystic acne, a rash lasting more than two weeks, widespread urticaria, or changes in a mole according to the ABCDE rule.

Chapter 12: Supplementary Topics

Routes for Different Age Groups

Age Core Goal
20-25 Control oil, maintain stability, and use sunscreen
25-30 Introduce vitamin C and retinol
30-40 Upgrade retinol and moisturising
40-50 Comprehensive anti-ageing and consideration of medical aesthetics
50+ Strengthen moisturising and place gentleness first

Economic Observations

Between the factory and the shop, the price of a pair of glasses increases five to ten times. A reasonable transaction price for Zeiss or Essilor is 25%-30% of the advertised market price. Do not buy a package offering “free frames with the lenses”—the frames supplied cost less than 20 yuan.

Sustainability

Bio-based acetate, recycled titanium, and replaceable modular designs are emerging environmental trends. Old glasses can be donated through Lions Clubs International, retained as a spare pair, or resold.

Chapter 13: Conclusion and Programme of Action

Three Core Principles

  1. Sun protection is the only skincare behaviour supported by overwhelming evidence
  2. Consistent performance of three basic steps > an occasional ten-step routine
  3. Understand ingredients > worship brands > follow trends blindly

A 90-Day Beginner Programme

Stage Goal
Month 1 Establish the habit—complete the three basic steps every day without interruption
Month 2 Introduce vitamin C in the morning and retinol at night, beginning twice per week
Month 3 Observe and adjust—assess the effects and optimise the plan

Guide to the First Action

Decide today to “buy three products first”:

  1. Amino-acid cleanser (≤¥80)
  2. Lightweight moisturiser (≤¥100)
  3. Daily sunscreen SPF30+ (≤¥100)

Keep the total budget below ¥300—less than the cost of a dinner with friends.

Men’s skincare is not intended to turn you into somebody else, but to make you the best version of yourself. Skincare is a healthy habit, like brushing your teeth or taking a shower: it is basic maintenance of your body.

Beginning matters more than perfection, and persistence matters more than intensity.

entry.title: Hairstyle Research Report
entry.content:
Extending from historical origins to scientific foundations, and from aesthetic principles to practical operation, this report covers almost every aspect of hairstyles. The main text remains available as a Markdown version for online reading, while a compiled PDF can be downloaded below and at the end of the article.

Source note: The material comes from a personal hairstyle research project, and the PDF is a compiled product.

PDF Download

  • Click to Download the PDF

Reading Guide

This report consists of twelve chapters and systematically reviews every dimension of hairstyles: from history to physiology, from aesthetics to practice, and from ideas to tools. It may be read from beginning to end or selectively according to the reader’s interests. The first five chapters focus upon fundamental theory, while the remaining seven place greater emphasis upon practical operation.

Hairstyle Research Report

Chapter One: A Brief History of Hairstyle Development

As an important part of human society and culture, hairstyles reflect not only changes in aesthetic ideas, but also historical information drawn from several dimensions, including politics, economics, religion, and technological development.

1.1 The Evolution of Hairstyles in the Ancient World

Changes in Chinese Hairstyles across the Dynasties

During the Shang and Zhou dynasties, the belief that “the body, hair, and skin are received from one’s parents and must not be damaged” was deeply rooted. Both men and women grew their hair long, arranged it in a bun, and fixed it with a hairpin. During the Qin and Han dynasties, men generally wore a bun beneath a crown, and crowns and headcloths became central marks of social identity and position. The Tang dynasty represented the high point of Chinese hairstyling. Women’s styles flourished in extraordinary variety: towering buns rose like clouds and were combined with magnificent gold and silver ornaments and decorative forehead flowers, expressing the graceful splendour of the Tang empire. The Song dynasty turned towards restraint and inward elegance. Cloth caps and the Dongpo hat became popular among men, while women’s styles placed greater emphasis upon flowing lines and overall harmony.

During the Ming and Qing dynasties, the Qing government imposed the “queue order,” compelling men to shave the front of the head and retain a braid. From the Republican period onwards, the movement to cut off queues after the 1911 Revolution marked the end of the feudal age, while new short styles such as the Zhongshan cut and the 70/30 side part quickly spread.

The Evolution of Western Hairstyles

The ancient Egyptians developed the culture of wigs to its furthest extent. In ancient Greece and Rome, hairstyles became closely connected with aesthetic ideals. During the Renaissance, golden curls were regarded as the standard of ideal beauty. The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries marked the peak of Western wig culture, when enormous, full wigs worn by men became the ultimate symbol of power and position. After the nineteenth century, the modern system of short hairstyles for men gradually took shape.

1.2 The Modern Hairstyle Revolution

1920s: slicked-back hair and side-parted pompadours became standard equipment for a gentleman.
1950s: the Pompadour became popular throughout the world under the influence of Elvis Presley.
1960s: the Beatles’ mop-top hairstyle broke the fixed assumption that “men must wear short hair.”
1970s-80s: the punk movement introduced the Mohawk, while disco promoted curls and high-volume styling.
1990s-2000s: simple styles such as spiky cuts and crew cuts returned, while fade techniques matured.
2010s to the present: the Undercut spread across the world, and men’s hairstyling entered an “age of precision.”

1.3 Contemporary Hairstyle Trends

Popular trends for men: the fade remains the technical core; the Textured Crop is widely popular; curled fringes break the stereotype that Asian men must have straight hair; and the wolf cut is rapidly gaining popularity among younger people.

Popular trends for women: the wolf cut, butterfly cut, and Korean perming techniques such as the air-cushion perm, C-curl perm, and cloud perm remain highly fashionable.

1.4 Comparison between Eastern and Western Hairstyle Cultures

Eastern hairstyle culture pursues refinement and order, placing emphasis upon the texture and shine of the hair. Western hairstyle culture places greater weight upon volume and visible texture. Under globalisation, Eastern and Western hairstyle cultures are blending at an accelerating pace.

Chapter Two: Hair Physiology and Medical Foundations

2.1 The Anatomical Structure of Hair

A complete strand of hair contains three layers from the outside in: the cuticle (the outermost layer, consisting of 5-12 layers of scale-like keratinised cells), the cortex (more than 90% of the strand, determining mechanical strength and colour), and the medulla (the central layer).

2.2 The Hair-Growth Cycle

Stage Duration Proportion
Anagen 2-7 years 85%-90%
Catagen Approximately 2-3 weeks Approximately 1%
Telogen Approximately 3-4 months 10%-15%

2.3 Principal Factors Affecting Hair Quality

Factor Specific Effects
Genetics Colour, thickness, degree of curl, follicle density, and tendency towards hair loss
Nutrition Protein, iron, zinc, biotin, vitamin D, and Omega-3
Hormones DHT attacks hair follicles, mainly in men; thyroid hormone; cortisol
Environment and lifestyle Ultraviolet radiation, heated tools, chemical perming and colouring, sleep, and smoking

2.4 Androgenetic Alopecia

Androgenetic alopecia, or AGA, is the most common form of hair loss among men—affecting approximately 30% by the age of thirty, 50% by fifty, and as many as 80% by seventy. In essence, it is a process in which DHT causes the hair follicles to become progressively smaller.

The Norwood-Hamilton scale extends from Stage I, involving slight recession of the hairline, to Stage VII, in which only a horseshoe-shaped region of hair remains. Early intervention is critical. Drugs approved by the FDA include oral finasteride and topical minoxidil.

2.5 Common Problems of the Scalp and Hair

Problem Response Strategy
Androgenetic alopecia Finasteride for men, minoxidil, and hair transplantation
Seborrhoeic dermatitis Shampoo containing ketoconazole or selenium sulphide
Premature greying Primarily genetic; cover with hair dye

Chapter Three: Identifying and Classifying Hair Type

3.1 Four Basic Hair Types

Hair Type Typical Characteristics
Oily hair The scalp appears oily within half a day to one day after washing
Dry hair No oily feeling for 2-3 days after washing; prone to split ends
Normal hair A moderate amount of oil 2-3 days after washing
Combination hair Oily scalp but dry ends

3.2 Methods of Self-Testing at Home

  1. Blotting-paper test—measures the quantity of oil secreted
  2. Elasticity test—measures the elasticity of the hair shaft
  3. Float test—measures porosity
  4. Stretching test—measures breaking strength
  5. Comb test—measures the smoothness of the cuticle

3.3 Suitable Hairstyles for Different Hair Types

Hair Type Recommendations for Men
Oily hair Short textured cut, graduated short cut, or Undercut
Dry hair Short side part or classic pompadour
Fine, soft hair Keep the length below 5 cm and use volumising powder
Thick, coarse hair Heavily textured short cut or thinning to reduce weight

Chapter Four: Aesthetics and Bearing

4.1 Analysis of Seven Facial Shapes

Facial Shape Recommendations for Men Avoid
Oval Almost every hairstyle Very few restrictions
Round High-top Fade, side part, or voluminous Top Rounded bowl cut
Square Side part, long texture, or voluminous Top Buzz Cut and level lines
Long Heavy fringe or short Fade High-top quiff
Heart-shaped Short hair, texture, or side-swept style Styles that expose the forehead
Diamond-shaped Graduated Fade or voluminous Top Slicked-back hair close to the scalp

4.2 Matching Hairstyle with Bearing

Masculine Bearing Recommended Hairstyle
Business professional Side Part, pompadour, or Undercut
Athletic and cheerful Crew cut, short textured cut, or Crop Top
Artistic and refined Slight Japanese-style curls, lightly parted textured fringe, or centre-parted texture
Street fashion Fade + textured perm, dreadlocks, or wet slicked-back style
Mature and steady Crew Cut, classic side part, or short slicked-back style

4.3 Hair Quantity and Choice of Style

Limited hair/receding hairline: a short Fade transfers visual attention towards the clean temples rather than the thinning top.

Thick hair: thinning or a textured perm reduces visual volume while increasing control.

Chapter Five: An In-Depth Analysis of Aesthetic Principles

5.1 Proportion and Mathematical Aesthetics

Three sections and five eye-widths: a hairstyle visually “redistributes” the proportions of the three regions of the face. A long upper section → fringe; a long middle section → broaden the sides horizontally; a long lower section → let the ends fall at the jawline or collarbone.

The golden ratio of 1:1.618: in hairstyle design, this appears across three principal dimensions—facial proportions, the relationship between hairstyle height and facial width, and the ratio of a side part.

Crown ratio and the effect of “the head enclosing the face”: when the crown ratio is at least 1/3, the face is visually “contained” within the frame of the skull and therefore appears smaller. East Asian skulls tend to have flatter crowns; principal corrective methods include root perms and blow-drying techniques that create a higher crown.

5.2 Principles of Visual Design

The language of lines: horizontal lines convey stability, vertical lines confidence, diagonal lines movement, and curves softness.

Contrast in texture: high shine (oil-based pomade/vintage), natural finish (water-based pomade/everyday), and matte finish (hair clay/street fashion).

The law of volume: the essence of a Fade is the creation of an extreme contrast in volume. Low, Mid, High, and Skin Fades each produce a different degree of visual impact.

5.3 Gestalt Principles

Figure-ground relationship: the hairstyle is the “ground,” while the face is the “figure.” The hairstyle must not steal the scene.

Law of closure: the proportion of the outline is a hundred times more important than perfection in the details.

5.4 Colour Aesthetics

Guide to choosing hair colour:

  • Cool skin tone: cool brown, ash brown, or grey-purple shades
  • Warm skin tone: caramel brown, chestnut, or reddish brown
  • Neutral skin tone: almost every colour can be attempted

A special note for men: “cooling” the hair colour is the key to making Asian men’s skin appear lighter—the blue tones in natural black hair complement yellow skin.

5.8 Differences between Eastern and Western Aesthetics

Eastern aesthetics: an aesthetics of concealment, including fringe culture, thick hair, and a full outline. The preference for a high crown in East Asia has roots in physiognomy—the “full heavenly court,” or upper forehead, is regarded as a sign of great fortune.

Western aesthetics: an aesthetics of exposure, displaying the complete hairline and the bone structure of the face.

5.10 Core Aesthetic Decision Tree

Begin with the question, “What do you want people to notice?” Eyes → open the face; facial outline → expose the forehead + jawline; overall bearing → unify the style; something you do not want noticed → conceal it selectively.

Chapter Six: Aesthetic Methods Related to Hairstyles

6.1 The Art of Coordinating Hairstyles and Glasses

Frame Type Core Strategy Recommendations for Men
Square/rectangular frames Soften with curves Textured curls or lightly parted curls
Round/oval frames Break the roundness with clean lines Textured fringe or Buzz Cut
Cat-eye/upswept frames Echo the structure Side-parted pompadour
Large/Oversize frames Principle of subtraction Crop Cut or short textured cut
Wellington/browline frames Classic gentleman Side-parted pompadour or Pompadour

6.2 Hairstyles and Accessories

Hats, earrings, and beards—the relationship between each accessory and the hairstyle determines the overall impression. Coordination between beard and hairstyle is an exceptionally important part of male aesthetics.

6.3 Choosing Hair Colour

Hair colour is the most rapidly changing and immediately influential dimension of hairstyle aesthetics. The central principle is compatibility with skin tone: keep the hair colour and skin tone within the same colour-temperature system.

Chapter Seven: How Hairstyles Modify Head Shape and Attractiveness

The central function of a hairstyle is to optimise facial proportions by reshaping the outline. A good hairstyle can make the face look “one size smaller and one degree more three-dimensional.”

High forehead/receding hairline → use a fringe or side part for coverage. Flat head shape/low crown → use a root perm, or pull the roots in the opposite direction while blow-drying. Wide cheekbones → grow the sides below the cheekbones to soften their appearance.

Modification of the jawline: in men, the jawline is the part of the face with the strongest sexual characteristics. By treating the sides and adjusting volume on top, a hairstyle can make the jawline visible to exactly the right degree.

Chapter Eight: Preparation before Changing Your Hairstyle

Before entering a salon, complete the following tasks. Take five photographs in advance: front, left and right at 45 degrees, and left and right at 90 degrees. Collect 3-5 reference images, taking care to find models whose hair type and facial shape resemble your own.

When communicating with the stylist, do not merely say “cut it a little shorter.” State the desired length, fade height, whether thinning is required, and the position and length of the fringe.

Chapter Nine: How to Choose a Barbershop or Salon

Type Suitable Customers
Chain express-cut shop Extremely short or simple hairstyles
Traditional long-established shop Conventional styles and those who trust a long-term barber
Barbershop Men seeking a refined hairstyle
Japanese/Korean salon Fashionable styles and perming or colouring needs
Independent stylist’s studio Those who need one regular stylist over the long term

Chapter Ten: The Process of Cutting and Styling Hair

Complete Process of a Men’s Haircut

  1. Discuss requirements → 2. wash hair → 3. cut hair (establish the outline before treating the details) → 4. shave the face/shape the eyebrows → 5. style

An Explanation of Men’s Perms

Type of Perm Effect Duration
Textured perm Natural slight curl 2-4 months
Root perm Increased volume 1-2 months
Directional perm Shapes the hair in a specified direction 2-3 months

Daily Styling at Home

Choosing Styling Products for Men

Pomade: oil-based products hold firmly but are difficult to wash out; water-based products are easy to clean. Suitable for pompadours and side parts.
Wax: provides a matte finish and is suitable for natural texture. It is used most frequently in Japanese and Korean styles.
Clay: the most popular product in recent years. Strong hold + matte finish, suitable for short to medium-length hair.
Hair Spray: provides the strongest final hold.

Steps for Styling Men’s Hair at Home

Wash → press with a towel to absorb water → blow-dry to 80% while shaping → apply styling product in several small quantities → make precise adjustments → set with hair spray

The most common mistake is using too much product. Use an amount the size of 1-2 soybeans for short hair and 2-3 soybeans for medium-length hair.

Chapter Eleven: Supplementary and Extended Topics

11.1 Seasonal Hairstyle Strategies

Season Recommendations for Men
Spring Short side part or Crop Cut
Summer High Fade, Skin Fade, or Buzz Cut
Autumn Textured Crop or side-swept texture
Winter Medium-length hair or full texture

11.3 The Psychology of Hairstyles

“Hairstyle anxiety”: men experiencing hair loss score significantly lower in self-esteem than men of the same age without hair loss. “The confidence of a shaved head”: actively choosing to shave the head can increase feelings of confidence and control.

The “haircut effect”: changing one’s hairstyle after a breakup, change of job, or move is a ritual form of “self-reconstruction.”

11.4 The Scientific Selection of Hair-Care Products

Surfactants: sulphates clean strongly but easily remove too much oil; amino-acid surfactants are gentler.

Ingredients that genuinely prevent hair loss must be delivered through leave-on products—minoxidil and finasteride. Anti-hair-loss shampoos remain upon the scalp for only 1-3 minutes and therefore have limited effects.

11.5 Special Hairstyles and Services

Hair transplantation: FUE, which leaves no linear scar and costs 10-30 yuan per follicular unit, is the mainstream approach in the Asian market. SMP scalp micropigmentation: a non-surgical option that imitates the “dark stubble” left by a shaved head.

11.6 Future Hairstyle Trends

Short Korean textured styles will continue to lead Asian fashion. A wave of curled hairstyles for men is approaching. Gender-neutral hairstyles are rapidly emerging among Generation Z. AI-assisted hairstyle design is moving from concept towards reality.

Conclusion

The best hairstyle is neither the most popular nor the most expensive, but the one most suitable for you. It should fit the condition of your hair, match your facial and head shapes, and become part of your way of life.

Hairstyles can be changed, aesthetic judgement can be cultivated, and one’s image can be improved. Every occasion on which you sit in a barber’s chair is an opportunity to understand yourself again.

July 2026

entry.title: Eyewear Research Report
entry.content:
This is a comprehensive research report on eyewear, extending from the refractive index and Abbe number of lenses to frame materials and their coordination with facial shapes; from the underlying logic of aesthetics to effects in social psychology; and from the process of in-person selection to correct methods of maintenance. The main text remains available as a Markdown version for online reading, while a compiled PDF can be downloaded below and at the end of the article.

Source note: The material comes from a personal eyewear research project, and the PDF is a compiled product.

PDF Download

  • Click to Download the PDF

Reading Guide

This report is not a “guide to buying glasses.” It is closer to an in-depth examination of eyewear from several perspectives, including technology, aesthetics, psychology, and economics. The report contains eight chapters and may be read in full or selectively according to the reader’s interests. The first four chapters focus more heavily upon technology and aesthetics, while the final four are oriented towards practice and culture.

Eyewear Research Report

Eyewear Research Report

From History to Aesthetics · From Lenses to Frames · From Eye Examinations to Maintenance

July 2026

Chapter 1: The Past and Present of Eyewear

Have you ever considered that the small object resting upon your nose every day carries more than two thousand years of civilisation? From the first convex crystal lens polished by a craftsman of the Eastern Han dynasty to today’s smart glasses, which can be customised, used to control myopia, and even connected to a network, every stage in the evolution of eyewear reflects humanity’s persistence in pursuing the simple desire to “see more clearly.” Understanding this history not only gives you greater confidence when making a purchase, but also reveals that glasses have never been an ordinary commodity.

1.1 Timeline: From Crystal Lenses to Smart Glasses

Eastern Han—the Earliest Known Prototype of Eyewear

In 1980, a gold ring containing a convex crystal lens was excavated from the Eastern Han tomb of Liu Jing, Prince of Guangling, in Hanjiang County, Jiangsu Province. Approximately 2 cm in diameter and 0.5 cm thick, it could magnify an object four to five times. Archaeology currently recognises it as the earliest prototype of a human “magnifying glass,” dating from almost two thousand years ago. Although it was probably a royal object for amusement rather than daily wear, it demonstrates that Chinese craftspeople had mastered the polishing of crystal lenses as early as the first or second century AD. [Source: archaeological report of the Nanjing Museum]

Eleventh Century—Europe’s “Reading Stone”

In medieval European monasteries, monks used a translucent quartz sphere known as a Reading Stone. They placed it upon a manuscript to magnify the text. This was the earliest European prototype of spectacles.

Southern Song—“Aidai”

The word “aidai” appears in documents of the Song dynasty: “When an old person cannot distinguish fine writing, covering the eyes with this makes it clear.” Lenses were polished by hand from crystal or agate, while frames were made from tortoiseshell, copper, or ivory. This was not simply a magnifying glass, but a genuine visual aid held before the eyes. Zhao Xigu, a scholar of the Southern Song, wrote in Dongtian Qinglu: “Aidai: when an old person cannot distinguish fine writing, covering the eyes with this makes it clear.” This is one of the world’s earliest unambiguous written records of reading glasses.

1268-1289—Modern Spectacles Are Born in Italy

Italian craftspeople—sometimes said to include Salvino D’Armate—joined two convex lenses with a hinge so that they could rest upon the bridge of the nose. The design is regarded as the formal birth of “modern spectacles.” Venice and Florence became early centres of spectacle production.

Late Ming and Early Qing—Sun Yunqiu and History of Mirrors
