A systematic philosophy cannot pretend to be complete. The following subjects have been identified as lying explicitly outside the framework. Listing them is not an apology but a marking of unexplored territory. The act of marking is itself part of the unity of knowledge and action.

Missing Field In One Sentence Severity
Axiology/ethics I know how to travel but not where to go. The framework does not directly answer “what is worth doing?” “Eating fried chicken and drinking IPA” is a signal to pause, not a direction. 🔴
Ethics of the Other I know how relationships operate but not what I owe other people. “I will owe her for the rest of my life”—this sentence contains an ethical judgment for which the framework supplies no theoretical foundation. 🔴
Time and growth There is structure but no process. How did Alpha become v1.0? Not by thinking it through, but by running into a wall. “Collision” has not been theorized as a mechanism of change. 🟡
Philosophy of the body The unity of knowledge and action remains extremely brain-centered; the body is treated as an external device that must be driven. Yet the body at two in the morning, the body that nearly drowned in Qingdao, and the body in the wind on the rooftop are not the same body. 🟡
Philosophy of language I write every day but do not reflect upon writing. “The most important things cannot be said but only shown” has not been pursued: what can language capture, and what is distorted as soon as it is written? 🟢
Philosophy of death Ten Years weighed it; Briefly weighed it; Qingdao nearly drowned. The experiences are scattered and have never been assembled into a position. 🟢
Free will People can be modeled and driven by positive-feedback loops, yet they can also count 5-4-3-2-1 and move. No bridge connects the mechanical description with autonomy in action. 🟢

VIII. Overview

Axis Central Proposition Key Ideas Source Articles
Epistemology Human beings understand the world through compression and unfolding; models are tools rather than truth Compression/unfolding, fractals, survivorship bias, unity of knowledge and action as the dynamic version The Radar Equation, The SOP Article
Ontology The observer is never present in his own equation; this is not a bug but an architectural property Blind spot, logical impossibility, Wang Yangming Audit Report, The Radar Equation
Theory of relationships Alpha parasitism → v1.0 transaction → what cannot be modeled; also applicable to self-relations Three stages, listening-to-needs and provision, quantum computer Audit Report, Half a Year, Briefly, The SOP Article
Theory of practice Write, act, shut down + five practical mechanisms; action produces motivation Coordinate system, five-second countdown, pre-decision, do it three times before writing an SOP Ten Years, Audit Report, Meow, The SOP Article
Aesthetics Dry humor is a brake and the only way to avoid stack overflow during infinite recursion Self-mockery, what cannot be modeled, recursive-function pseudocode Meow, Audit Report, Ten Years, The SOP Article
Theory of action Unity of knowledge and action: do not let “thought” intercept “action” Wang Yangming, Step Zero, debug toolkit The SOP Article, Pavlov’s Dog, Briefly, Half a Year
Recursive self-reference Any self-analysis can be exposed by a higher-level analysis—a safety limiter Gödel’s incompleteness, metacognition, sweet self-deception Briefly, Audit Report, The SOP Article

Conclusion

One year ago, Pavlov’s Twenty-Eight Dog complained about having no energy to work. The Unknown asked why one should live. Briefly lay motionless in a dormitory and wrote that self-reflection was a sweet form of self-deception.

One year later, on the same person’s same computer, there appeared CVE vulnerability numbers, pseudocode for a recursive function, seven axes, and a table marking known gaps.

This is not progress. Progress implies that the old is bad and the new is good. Yet the first epistemological principle I wrote states that a model has no final version, only a version sufficient at the present level of precision.

This is unfolding. It begins with a vague confusion, compresses it layer by layer, unfolds it again layer by layer, and makes the coordinate system increasingly dense. Nothing more.

To quote the sentence from The Unknown, written last autumn and still valid today:

“I write these words not to seek an answer, but merely to confirm that I have passed through this life truthfully, contradictorily, and passionately.”

The gaps remain in Section Seven. Whether the next article will fill the gap in axiology or simply involve eating barbecue, I do not know. Either would be fine.

That is probably all.

entry.title: The Final Three Kilometres from Knowledge to Action
entry.content:
0. A Piece of Dark Humour

Last night, I spent half an hour discussing with DeepSeek why I never execute an SOP after writing it. When the conversation ended, I did something perfectly consistent with my character: I organized the chat into a new SOP.

If you find that funny, congratulations. You have located one of the central loops in my mental life with remarkable precision.

Still, it is not entirely a joke. I have spent a long time colliding with the problem of execution, and recently, after all those collisions, something has finally loosened a little. At two in the morning, I therefore decided to record the process by which it loosened—even though I know perfectly well that the act of recording it is itself an ideal example of the problem I am describing.

Look. I have begun again. This is exactly how it works.

I. The Gap Between Knowledge and Action

The problem is hardly new. Wang Yangming said several centuries ago:

“To know and not to act is not yet to know.”

In modern language: if you think you understand something but do not act upon it, you never truly understood it.

The first time I read the sentence, I felt that he was scolding me. Later I discovered that he really was scolding me, and that the scolding was thoroughly deserved. Of course, saying that does not prove I am McDonald’s.

I had been making a subtle substitution, passing off the ability to summarize as knowledge. After completing something, I would review it and write an elegant SOP. At that instant the brain released a strong sense of completion and decided that the matter had been settled. But the satisfaction corresponded not to “the task is complete,” but to “the summary is complete.” These are separate accounts; the brain quietly settled them together.

To put it plainly, I did not write an SOP to guide my next action. I wrote it to give the previous action a respectable conclusion. Here the SOP was not an operating manual, but a congratulatory address—or an elegy.

The better the address or elegy was written, the less necessary genuine change became next time. The brain had already received the reward it wanted.

Oh, Wang Yangming said something else:

“Knowledge is the beginning of action; action is the completion of knowledge.”

Knowledge begins in action, and action completes knowledge. Notice the wording. He does not say, “First finish knowing, and then go and act.” He says that action is the final form of knowledge. In his system, knowledge that has not passed through action does not count as knowledge. It is a hallucination.

This has exactly the same structure as the “compression and expansion” discussed in my essay on the radar equation. An SOP is compression; execution is expansion. You performed the compression and never expanded it. A zip archive that is never extracted is about as useful as—well, never mind. It is useless.

Another layer is added by CVE-0003 from the audit report: the observer is absent. The self who writes the SOP and the self expected to execute it are not the same. The former is calm, rational, and looking down upon the whole system; the latter is sleepy, irritated, and wants to scroll through a phone. When the first writes the plan, he repeatedly forgets that the second does not want to move.

Wang Yangming called this “the separation of knowledge and action.” People treat knowing and acting as two things, he argued, even though “the moment a thought is aroused, it is already action.” The thought “I do not want to do this,” arising in your mind, is itself a kind of action. Knowledge and action were never separate; they have always been feeding one another. You imagine the problem as “I know what to do but cannot do it.” In reality, every action—including lying there and doing nothing—acts in return upon what you “know.”

Suppose you know that waking early is beneficial, and then turn off the alarm. The act of turning it off is itself knowledge: it teaches you more deeply that “getting up early is optional.” Every failure to act patches the cognitive system, except that the patch says, “This item may be skipped.”

The gap between knowledge and action is therefore not an obstacle to be crossed. It is a false problem. There is no gap. Everything you do corresponds precisely to what you truly “know” at that moment. Your résumé is judged not by the SOPs you wrote, but by what you actually did.

II. The Six Steps from Ten Years

In Ten Years, written a few days ago, I answered a question: when confronted with an entirely unfamiliar problem, how does one move from knowing nothing to proposing the first workable solution? I gave six steps:

  1. Define the problem.
  2. Break it down.
  3. Transfer a model by analogy.
  4. Clarify the central solution.
  5. Design an executable scheme.
  6. Verify and iterate rapidly.

There is nothing fundamentally wrong with the framework. When I read it again, it does describe how I think upon entering an unfamiliar field.

But it contains a fatal defect. It never answers one question: what makes me actually begin the first step?

The six steps describe the operation of a system that has already started. The real difficulty is getting the damned and beautiful machine to turn.

The central sentence of Ten Years was, “You cannot solve, merely by thinking, the problems that thinking has produced.” What is missing, then, is not a seventh step. It is a “Step Zero.”

III. Step Zero

Wang Yangming’s answer is radical. Knowledge and action were always one thing; if they appear separate, private desire has cut them apart. Remove that desire, and their unity returns naturally.

The claim may be philosophically sound. In practice, however, I need something more concrete—methods that bypass the analytical brain and make the hand begin to move.

Here are several small pieces of material I have collected.

1. Count Down from Five

When the thought “I should do X” appears, you have a window of about five seconds. After those seconds, the brain—an organ shaped by millions of years of evolution and primarily committed to conserving the two thousand calories it consumes each day—constructs a complete argument proving that now is not the ideal time and another five minutes of preparation would be wiser.

The countdown works very simply. By occupying working memory, it prevents the system of rationalization from starting in time. Count from five to one. At one, the body must move. Before a choice can be made, you have already boarded the vehicle.

2. Reduce the Friction of Beginning to an Absurd Degree

The greatest enemy is not “I cannot finish,” but “I do not want to begin.” The latter arises because “beginning” has been defined as something too heavy.

Not “write the paper,” but “open Word, type the title, and close it if you want.”
Not “review Principles of Communication,” but “open the book, read one line of a formula, and close it if you want.”
Not “organize the SOP,” but “create a Markdown file, type a title, save it, and declare today’s task complete.”

When action is reduced to something absurdly small, the brain decides that launching the procrastination system would cost more than the task itself.

This is more effective than one might expect. Once Word is open and the title has been typed, the system has warmed up; continuing is far more probable than beginning from a cold stop. Did not our great Sir Isaac tell us that a body at rest tends to remain at rest, while one in uniform motion tends to remain in uniform motion?

3. Decide in Advance

If most internal conflict occurs at the moment of asking whether to do something, eliminate that moment.

The night before, write down three things to be done the following morning. Specify when, where, what, and for how long. When the appointed time arrives, you are not “making a decision.” You are “executing a decision already made.”

The brain resembles any embedded processor: the fewer interruptions it receives, the fewer resources it spends handling them and the more steadily the main loop runs. “Should I do this?” is the most expensive interrupt in the system. Pre-decision moves that interrupt outside the main loop.

4. Let Action Precede Motivation

This is the most important of the five and the one I took longest to accept.

I used to believe that motivation must precede action: a feeling arrives → work begins → work is completed. The model appears perfectly natural, but reverses cause and effect.

When you type the final word of a blog post at two in the morning, did motivation exist before you began? No. It grew by itself somewhere in the middle.

Motivation does not produce action. Action produces motivation.

The proper sequence is therefore: begin → acquire the feeling while working → continue → finish. Do not become stuck upon “wanting to do it” as a prerequisite. It is not a prerequisite. It is an intermediate product.

5. Do It Three Times Before Writing the SOP

Of the five methods, this one is most directly prescribed for my condition.

I am too skilful at building a model before doing anything. Once the model is complete, the brain releases its satisfaction and the motivation leaks away. Anything completed once in imagination suffers a dramatic decline in marginal attraction when it must be done in reality.

So I impose a rule: before writing an SOP for anything, do it three times. The results may be terrible. Summarize them only after the third attempt.

Wang Yangming stated the philosophical foundation long ago: train through concrete affairs. Grind against the actual thing, not against an image inside the head. The usefulness of an SOP depends on the time spent “doing,” not the time spent “thinking.”

Good. Step Zero is complete.

Except that I have suddenly noticed what happened: I built another SOP about how to execute SOPs. There is a certain dark humour in this. Heh.

If it were a recursive function:

I do not know its termination condition. Perhaps none exists. I can only hope that the value returned by each iteration comes slightly closer than the last to the thing called “having done it.”

If Wang Yangming can see this from heaven, he is probably shaking his head. “I spent five hundred years saying that knowledge and action are one, and this boy translated it into five little tricks. Fine. At least it is better than doing nothing.”

IV. The Six Steps, Plus a Patch

Since I have already come this far, I may as well add one:

Stage The difficulty you imagine The actual difficulty Patch
① Define the problem Not knowing what to ask “I have not thought it through” becomes infinite delay Method 2: write one line; Method 1: count down from five
② Break it down Not knowing where to divide it Each subproblem becomes a black hole of internal conflict Method 3: decide in advance where the decomposition will stop
③ Transfer by analogy Finding no model to borrow “I do not know enough” turns research into another name for inaction Method 5: act three times before summarizing; Method 4: action produces motivation
④ Clarify the central solution The formula is not elegant enough Perfectionism repeatedly demolishes and rebuilds the scheme in the mind Method 3: decide beforehand what counts as “good enough”
⑤ Design an executable scheme Not knowing the order of the steps Treating “designing the scheme” as though it were execution Method 5: do it three times before writing the SOP; Method 1: begin in five seconds
⑥ Verify and iterate Not knowing how to obtain feedback Fear that verification will prove you wrong Method 4: action precedes motivation; only after acting have you earned the right to judge

The six-step method is sound. It merely assumes, without saying so, that whenever a step begins, you possess the ability to begin with it. For someone accustomed to substituting analysis for action, that assumption is precisely the problem requiring a solution.

V. Epilogue

After finishing, I read the piece again. To be honest, I will probably forget it immediately.

Not because it is badly written. On the contrary, because it is rather good, it may activate the brain’s standard procedure: “A good article! Completed! Release the reward!” The article itself may become the perfect excuse for failing to execute it.

That is what dealing with one’s analytical brain feels like. Every act of “self-examination” can become a new round of escape. There is no end, only deeper recursion. Recursion upon recursion—how abundant recursion is!

Still, I have to write.

Not because writing will solve the problem, but because “every word you type at the keyboard helps me maintain a traceable coordinate system.”

Today I wrote, “I may not execute anything in this article.” If the person I am three days from now really fails to execute it, at least the evidence is available: look, you predicted this three days ago. Perhaps the next encounter with the sentence will be slightly different.

If the person I am ten years from now sees it, he may laugh—

and then continue writing his own Final Three Kilometres Between Knowledge and Action.

That is about it, I suppose.

entry.title: 2026-06-27 Interpersonal System Audit Report
entry.content:
0. Version Overview

Version Period Core Characteristics
Alpha My previous relationship and the period before it No operating system; driven by raw anxiety; emotional parasitism
v1.0 From the breakup to the present Transaction system online; needs-diagnosis and supply model
Audit Now A line-by-line inspection of the two versions above, with self-criticism included

There is no vulnerability report for the Alpha period. It did not even qualify as a system; it was a simple programme running on bare metal. The analysis of Alpha will therefore take the form of a memoir.

I. Alpha Version: The Bare-Metal Era

1.1 Input Layer: I Could Not Hear What You Were Saying

When my ex-girlfriend spoke to me, my ears—the receiver—were certainly working. Yet during the later stage of our relationship, what the receiver was waiting for had nothing to do with her sentences. It was waiting for “me.” Every word she said would automatically be translated into a signal: Does this sentence prove that she cares about me? Does it mean that she is going to leave? Where am I located within it?

From this perspective, I never actually knew what she was saying. Unfortunately, love has to be built upon two people seeing each other.

She might tell me that she felt more relaxed when she went out on her own, but I did not really hear it. My first reaction was not to ask what problem between us might lie behind her statement. I heard only that “her tone was not enthusiastic enough when she told me this.” Then my receiver began to overheat. I would consume myself with questions: Does she no longer care about me? She did not speak to me like this before.

She merely wanted to be seen. Unfortunately, what she encountered was a genuine bare-metal system, with a receiver best described as a pile of shit.

In this version, input was never extracted; it was merely detected. Once a negative signal was detected, the whole system began to overheat abnormally. Once a positive signal was detected, the system simply continued operating in power-saving mode.

1.2 Output Layer: Dumping Is Not Sharing

Throughout the relationship, I constantly poured a great many things out to her, believing that I was sharing myself. I told her about the day’s uneasiness, my anxiety about the future, my doubts about myself, and my desire to control everything.

Look, I am willing to tell you all this. See how much I trust you. Hehe.

Yet a well-hidden displacement was taking place. What I told her was not “who I am,” nor did it meet any need of hers. What I was really saying was “how badly I need you right now.” Every sentence was sincere, but beneath every sentence lay the same invoice: now that I have told you these things, should you not respond and comfort me?

She had no choice in the relationship. She was not a willing listener; she was a supplier of security who had been dragged into the role. Or, to borrow the fashionable language of the Internet, she had the misfortune to encounter an NPD.

This was the Alpha version’s output pattern: not communication, but emotional dumping and the transfer of anxiety. I believed that holding nothing back was love. I had it backwards. What I held nothing back from expressing was not love, but need. Love means caring about the other person’s present condition. Need means demanding that the other person respond to mine.

1.3 Testing Loop

Once anxiety reaches a certain level, a rather strange behavioural pattern appears: one deliberately causes harm and then observes the other person’s response.

I would become cold on purpose, deliberately say ambiguous things, push the other person away, and then watch to see whether she returned, using the result to obtain a sense of security.

The unconscious script ran as follows: I have made myself unlovable, even hurtful. Are you still willing to stay? If you are, that proves you truly love me. This seems more reliable than “you like me because I treat you well”—in the latter case, she may merely have been attracted by my kindness; in the former, she chooses to remain even when she has no reason to do so.

Unfortunately, no one can pass this kind of test in the long run.

A person will not love you more because she has received an unlimited stream of emotional blackmail. She will only be drained and then leave. Leaving is the greatest responsibility the test subject can show towards herself.

1.4 Boundaries: A Module That Was Never Installed

I may have heard the word “boundaries” at the time. I did not know what boundaries looked like in real life.

I could not distinguish between “my pain” and “her responsibility.” I turned my own anxiety into her problem. If she became distant for a while, I turned it into a crisis of my existence.

Nor did I understand that “a person needs time alone.” When she wanted some quiet, I interpreted silence as rejection and sent more messages in an attempt to break it. This produced a deeper silence, which made me still more frantic. In systems theory, this is a positive-feedback loop, and the result of positive feedback is the collapse of the system.

In a blog post written half a year later, I said that I had “no ability to maintain an intimate relationship… From childhood onward, I had turned myself into a tool.” Looking back, that sentence was not wrong, but it was far too gentle. What it failed to state clearly was this: the Alpha version of me did not even know that there was a difference between a relationship and parasitism.

1.5 An Inevitable Collapse

She fell in love with me. We passed through a very sweet period. Then I treated her as an emotional stabiliser; she lost hope; she left. Every step in the process was reasonable, and the entire process possessed a certain historical inevitability. Perfectly normal, my friend.

For a long time after the breakup, I hated myself intensely. How had I become this person? Later, that self-hatred slowly developed into something calmer: no matter how far I had advanced before then, during those months I really was exactly like that.

It was time for the Alpha version to leave the stage.

II. The v1.0 Transaction System

After the breakup, I read many books related to psychology and philosophy, began writing the blog again, and started to handle interpersonal relationships in a way completely opposed to my earlier approach.

The Alpha era was bare metal, driven entirely by instinct, burning both other people and myself. Apart from instinct, however, what am I best at? Abstracting all sorts of things into models. Thus v1.0 was born.

On closer examination, however, it is as extreme as Alpha, only at the opposite end. Alpha had no model; v1.0 does not know how to speak to people without one. It therefore still requires improvement. Let me first set out the basic framework of v1.0.

Core Framework of v1.0

I. The essence of interpersonal interaction is exchange.

When someone comes to talk to you, that person either needs emotional value—empathy, recognition, the experience of being seen—or practical help: a plan, resources, or information.

II. Listening is a form of diagnosis.

Within the first few sentences spoken by the other person, the system should have completed its classification of the need. Does the person want a certain amount of emotional value, or advice? Once this has been determined, call the corresponding output template: emotional request → mirroring + extension; practical request → analysis + advice.

III. Cut your losses promptly in an unequal transaction.

You offered mirroring and extension, but received no response. You provided analysis, but the person kept charging down the same dead end. After this happens several times, there is no need to continue.

IV. Self-disclosure is acceptable, but its dosage must be calculated.

Sincerity is a limited resource. Give too much and the other person cannot digest it; give too little and trust cannot be established. The amount should be precise enough for the other person to receive it.

V. Be a creditor in relationships; do not owe debts of favour.

I can diagnose a friend’s problem accurately and give him what he needs. This means that I will no longer live as a parasite upon other people, as I did during the Alpha period.

At the same time, I should not owe favours to others. Such debts can never be settled clearly.

All right. That is v1.0’s understanding of itself.

When I first constructed this logic, I was fairly satisfied with it. It counted as a calculable model, perhaps? It gave me enough security to know what I should do. Yet it is now obvious that the model contains problems, and that the entire idea of building one model and depending upon it for the rest of my life is itself mistaken. What follows is a list of the model’s vulnerabilities, together with possible directions for advancement.

CVE-2026-0001 — Misclassification by the Needs Classifier

Severity: Medium

Affected module: listening.zhw

Relationship with Alpha: The Alpha version could not understand what the other person was saying at all. Before incoming sound and light waves reached the layer of understanding, they were completely drowned by the noise of my own anxiety. The classifier was designed specifically to oppose this noise: it tried to begin from the other person’s position and determine what that person needed. The problem is that it compressed an entire human being into two labels. This is an advanced form of deafness. It is slightly better than Alpha’s total deafness, but it still counts as a disability.

Observed behaviour:

Whenever I speak with someone, the system automatically runs a needs-classification programme in the background. It takes a sentence as input and produces one label: a need for emotional value, or a need for a solution. Once the label is fixed, the corresponding template is retrieved—the first category triggers mirroring + extension, while the second triggers analysis + advice.

It sounds like a decent customer-service system. Yet the purpose of customer service has never been to understand people; it is to make them feel understood. Replacing a genuine attempt to understand someone with an approximate algorithm that approaches the same goal is a problem.

Vulnerability mechanism:

All the classifier’s training data came from the psychology I had read. Like the rest of Western philosophy, it naturally tends to cut living things apart with a cold surgical knife and to treat the person opposite as a deterministic signal. But a person is not a signal. People do not necessarily know what they want. Someone who says, “Could you help me think of a solution?” may only be trying to say, “I have done my best, but you need to see how hard this has been for me.” Someone who says, “I feel terrible” may really be saying, “Tell me I am strong.” Going further, how can you be sure of the classifier’s robustness? How can you prove that it is correct in most cases?

Many needs lie buried in noise, beyond the reach of such a simple classifier.

Conditions for reproduction: Any conversation in which the thought “I have solved this kind of problem before” arises in your mind.

Recommended fix: No standardised patch is available. From time to time, deliberately produce less output and allow more silence in a conversation, giving both the other person and yourself room to say things outside the classification system. This recommendation cannot be carried out through deliberate practice, because deliberate practice itself belongs to the territory seized by the classifier.

Note: This vulnerability is fatal only in close relationships. In the workplace, with strangers, and in ordinary social interaction, the classifier is instead a best practice.

CVE-2026-0002 — Withdrawal upon Inequality

Severity: High

Affected module: investment_tracker.zhw

Relationship with Alpha: The Alpha version gave endlessly and invested without considering cost—with the result that all the money was spent and the person was somehow left owing even more. This vulnerability is essentially an excessive correction after trauma: the system jumped straight from “unconditional dumping” to “settlement by the second,” while the module for flexible giving was never implemented.

Observed behaviour:

You offer someone a passage of mirroring, an insight, or an analysis. Three days later, there has been no response. In your mind, you quietly mark the investment as a bad debt. The next time the person sends a message, your reply naturally becomes shorter. You do not think he is a bad person. You simply do not want to conduct this transaction again.

Vulnerability mechanism:

The system treats a single interaction as one settlement period by default. Yet the settlement period of a human relationship is much longer than a single conversation. The other person may have failed to reply not because he feels no gratitude, but because his own ability to function has temporarily gone offline. Your tracker does not care about the cause. It sees only the short-term account.

There is also a more concealed variation. After doing many things “without seeking anything in return,” your mind secretly opens a new account: “I have done so much for other people; I am a good person now.” When the other person fails to meet your moral expectation, you feel more wronged than you would have under an openly stated price. Previously, you kept accounts of emotional value; now, you keep accounts of moral nobility. The latter is harder to notice because it wears the clothing of “selflessness.”

This may be the most sinister bug in the entire system. It keeps moral accounts on your behalf, while leaving you convinced that you are performing good deeds.

Conditions for reproduction:

  • Any moment when you begin counting the time until the other person replies after sending a message.
  • Any moment when the thought “I have done so much for this person” enters your mind.
  • Any moment when “I really am a good person” flashes through your head.

Recommended fix: With people you like and those close to you, stop calculating gains and losses so carefully; it is enough that you are happy to do the thing. In addition, the moment you notice yourself striking the pose of “doing good,” stop. Good deeds performed with an account book are more likely to produce resentment than conduct with a clearly stated price.

CVE-2026-0003 — The Observer Is Missing from the System Equation

Severity: Critical

Affected module: The entire v1.0 runtime environment

Relationship with Alpha: In the Alpha version, the observer was completely immersed in the system and could not separate himself from his emotions. v1.0 corrected that problem, but placed the observer outside the system altogether.

Observed behaviour:

You can analyse a friend’s condition precisely. You may understand, for instance, that a friend’s first stirrings of romance are not love, but a desire to find a clean vessel for emotion. You can infer your ex-girlfriend’s situation accurately and understand why she left. You can write an entire audit report on your own transaction model—including the paragraph you are reading now.

Yet the living you is absent from your equation and cannot be quantified and inserted into it.

Vulnerability mechanism:

The self who builds models of other people is itself the most unstable disturbance variable in those models. A person cannot remain rational at all times.

When you are talking to a friend, your output is not merely a solution produced after diagnosis. It is also disrupted by your emotional state, your degree of fatigue, and your real-time monitoring of the question, “Did I respond well this time?”

This is not the absence of some equation or module. It is a structural problem: once you place yourself in the position of observer, you cannot simultaneously observe yourself in full. Any analysis of “what kind of person I am” must leave out the person currently conducting the analysis. Meanwhile, that unobservable part exerts enormous influence upon your judgement and decisions.

Conditions for reproduction: None at present

Recommended fix: None at present

CVE-2026-0004 — The Strategic Use of Vulnerability

Severity: Medium

Affected module: self_disclosure.zhw

Relationship with Alpha: Alpha’s vulnerability was genuine and exposed without reservation, but it injured both other people and myself. v1.0 learned to control the amount disclosed, and that was not a mistake. The problem is that, as control became increasingly precise, “disclosure” itself turned into a carefully calculated asset.

Observed behaviour:

You deliberately reveal to someone a genuine flaw, a shameful piece of your past, or a present weakness.

The second you finish speaking, an expectation automatically launches in the background: the other person should now trust you more because of this disclosure. Or, at the very least, should offer a response that can be interpreted as “you understand me.”

Then the person responds. But not in the way you wanted.

Then something feels wrong.

It is like giving someone a present: before the moment when you say “there is no need to thank me,” you have already begun waiting for the person to say thank you.

Vulnerability mechanism:

The system cannot distinguish between two statements: “I let you see what is rotten in me because I want to be seen by you,” and “I let you see what is rotten in me because I want to obtain your trust in exchange.” Deliberate awkwardness is an exceptionally difficult signal to process, because it is perfectly isomorphic with genuine awkwardness and honesty. Their observable behaviour is identical; the only difference lies in the expectation running in the background.

Conditions for reproduction: Any moment when you reveal a weakness while secretly expecting a particular response from the other person. This includes the present moment, in which I am writing this report and discussing the fact that “I have already recognised the strategic use of vulnerability.”

Recommended fix: Remove honesty from the transaction completely, but do not attempt to do so by command. It can arise naturally only when you happen to forget to calculate something.

CVE-2026-0005 — The Saviour Verification Loop

Severity: Medium

Affected module: friend_rescue_handler.zhw

Relationship with Alpha: The Alpha version had no saviour complex; it could not even save itself. The saviour is a privilege unique to v1.0. At last, you possess the ability to help others. When you help them, therefore, your mind performs two tasks: helping the person + testing how well you are helping. Yet in many situations, the second task should not exist at all.

Observed behaviour:

A friend falls into difficulty. You decide to help him. At the exact moment the thought of helping appears, another process quietly launches in the background: “If I manage to help him, it will prove that I have truly left the Alpha era behind.” He is testing his own incompetence; you are testing your own growth. He has become your laboratory mouse, though you would never admit it aloud.

Vulnerability mechanism:

The act of helping is bound to a hidden condition: the loop is considered complete only if the other person improves by following your solution. This is a polite form of narcissism. You think you are looking at him, but in fact you are checking whether he reflects enough light for you to see what you now look like.

Conditions for reproduction: Before you are about to say, “Stop thinking about it; let me buy you some barbecue,” you discover that you have already begun calculating in your mind how he ought to respond after the meal.

Recommended fix: Accept one premise: after listening to everything you say, he remains free to continue going round in circles. That is his freedom. It is also your release. If one day he truly runs into the wall, feels the pain, and comes back to find you, only then will the glass in your hand cease to be a mirror.

III. Audit Conclusion

This audit report is itself a paradox. It uses the language of systems to audit a system and the method of modelling to dismantle a model. Writing a vulnerability report, giving it CVE numbers, and then calling the result “self-knowledge” is itself an extremely v1.0 thing to do.

To put it bluntly, I have merely built a higher floor for myself inside the model. I stand on that floor and look down, saying, “The version of me below is rather stupid.” Then, after finishing the article, I feel that I have somehow become an even stupider idiot than he was.

But I do not intend to delete it.

The Alpha version of me possessed the heat of instinct, but could only burn everyone who came near. The v1.0 version possesses structural elegance, but is sealed within a resin shell of its own construction; other people can touch only the casing. Alpha was unquestionably bad for everyone. v1.0 has unquestionably turned me into a machine that does nothing but calculate. Neither version is good enough. Yet I probably cannot depend upon reason alone to construct a perfect version either. Perfection now seems more like a concept that exists only because too much information has been omitted; it cannot run within a genuinely complex system.

Human beings always attempt to describe everything with equations. Nature, however, is complex, and so are people. An equation may be concise and beautiful—for details, see the blog post on radar equations and love—but no set of equations can contain everything.

So where should I go from here? Leading physicists and engineers have recognised the limits of today’s large computers and have therefore attempted to use quantum computers, employing quantum phenomena to simulate the countless things of the world. Perhaps I, too, can learn something from their approach.

The ideal condition may therefore be to use a little of each version without allowing either one to take complete control. From time to time, let v1.0 handle professional and ordinary social interaction. At other times, release a little of Alpha’s recklessness and do something impulsive or awkward.

DS told me that a genuine connection requires “a little awkwardness and irrationality.” I think the sentence is right, but the sentence itself can also be modelled. See? I have started again. That is how it is.

That will do. Today, I would like some fried chicken and a glass of IPA—after I finish the final Introduction to Artificial Intelligence assignment, of course.

entry.title: Ten Years
entry.content:
It is an afternoon in 2036. You, who are also me ten years from now, are sitting before a computer and typing this letter.

I thought for a long time before deciding to write it, because the act itself is rather strange. You want to say something to the person you were ten years ago, while knowing perfectly well that he will not listen. He cannot even manage what is immediately before him and is still talking about whether life is worth living. Why would he have the patience to hear the voice of some old fellow a decade away?

Still, I want to write. Some things are not said because anyone is expected to listen.

Let me begin with the warnings.

First, almost everything that now seems impossible to survive will pass. Notice that I said almost, not everything. Some things pass and are truly over, but the marks they leave do not disappear. You continue to live with them and gradually become accustomed to carrying the weight. This is not an attractive lesson, but it is true: people do not really forget pain; they merely learn to live beside it.

Second, most of your self-analysis is, frankly, a matter of walking in circles. You think you are deconstructing yourself, when in fact you are using thought to escape action. Put less politely, you are a daydreamer. You spend a great deal of time asking, “Why am I like this?” and “What should I do?” Yet some answers cannot be reached by thought alone. Even if you complete the reasoning in your head, it is useless unless you act. Only when you do something, strike the world, and feel it push back can you discover your own shape.

The most important thing I have learned in these ten years is this: you cannot solve, merely by thinking, the problems that thinking has produced.

Third, about her.

You are probably still immersed in the feeling that you will owe her for the rest of your life, convinced that you ruined everything. Ten years later, I can tell you that you did not ruin everything. You ruined that particular relationship. It is certainly nothing to celebrate, but you did not commit some unforgivable wrong. At the time, you simply did not yet possess the ability to maintain an intimate relationship. That is hardly surprising; no one had taught you.

What I want to say, however, is something else. You later meet some people and miss some others. Yet the feeling of “I miss her so much” returns on an ordinary afternoon without explanation, like a needle that has somehow entered your finger unnoticed. You cannot deal with it, and it does not disappear. All you can do is grow used to its presence.

To put it plainly, regret is not a problem to be solved. It is something one carries. Nevertheless, one must move forward—keep moving forward and do not turn back.

Then come the thanks.

The first thing I must thank you for is beginning to write all this. At the time, you wrote a blog for no grand reason. Certain words hurt when held inside, and there was nowhere to put them. You kept the habit for so long that writing became one of your principal ways of dealing with the world. Every word you now type helps me preserve a traceable coordinate system. Without those words, I could never recall what I was like at twenty. The sleepless nights, the inexplicable moments of obsession, and every “I don’t know” written at half past two in the morning—all of them have acquired meaning when viewed ten years later.

The second thing I must thank you for is not actually killing yourself.

I know that you considered it seriously. It was not the joking kind of thought; you weighed it in earnest. Thank you for not taking the final step. This is not because life ten years later becomes wonderfully good—it does not. The Earth still turns, and time continues to pass. But if you had ceased to exist, many things would genuinely have become impossible for both of us.

There is, for example, a summer evening when you sit with friends on a rooftop as the wind blows past. Perhaps you have brought two bags of craft beer, or perhaps just Corona. You sit there drinking without saying anything, and for a moment you think it is good to be alive. Had you not been there, that moment would not have existed. There are many such moments. None appears important, yet not one can be spared.

The third thing I must thank you for is recording honestly how bad your life was.

You did not pretend on the blog that everything was fine. You wrote about lying in a dormitory bed and scrolling through your phone until four in the morning; about ruining a relationship; about making a complete mess of your studies; about not knowing why you should remain alive—and then about continuing forward. These articles are embarrassing to read now. Yet precisely because they are sufficiently truthful, they are reliable. When you look back many years later, you are surprised to discover that the things you once found most shameful are exactly the things in you most worth preserving.

Honesty is the hardest quality to sustain, but you began practising it at twenty.

At this point the whole thing suddenly feels rather funny.

Here I am, a man ten years in the future, telling twenty-year-old you this and that as though I could provide an answer. In truth, I am like you: there are still many answers I do not know.

The only difference is that I can now accept the condition of “not knowing” more readily, move forward anyway, and make the ideas in my head take material form.

You now demand an answer to every question because an answer offers security. You depend heavily upon that security, much as you depended throughout the first eighteen years of life on the existence of a correct answer. It feels reassuring. Thus you pursue a general solution and place your faith in certainty. Unfortunately, the world is not like that. It is an AWGN channel in continual change. You will never understand it completely; you can only learn to coexist with it.

There is, however, one thing of which I am certain: ten years from now, you will not regret the time spent writing these pieces. Compared with the things done to satisfy other people’s expectations, and the energy spent feeding what you called the ego, this writing without any utilitarian purpose becomes the only real evidence that you once lived.

That is about it, I suppose.

The next time you cannot sleep, remember to pour yourself a glass of water.

One more thing: two questions are attached below.

Faced with a problem in a wholly unfamiliar field—for example, “How can the pollination routes of urban bee colonies be optimized?”—describe the steps by which you move from complete ignorance to the first workable hypothesis. Be as specific as possible.

Step 1: Define the problem

Do not rush to search for solutions. First determine what is actually to be done. What is the objective, and how can it be expressed more precisely in natural or mathematical language? How far must the solution go, and where are its boundaries?

Step 2: Break the problem down

Divide the large problem into smaller ones: data acquisition, mathematical modeling, algorithm selection, dynamic adjustment, and practical deployment. Deal with them one by one. In a team, the division also makes work easier to assign.

Step 3: Transfer by analogy

Actively search other fields for mature solutions. A “bee-colony route,” for example, may be compared with the traveling salesman problem in logistics. The key is to identify structural similarities beneath surface differences—route planning and resource allocation, in this case—so that an existing algorithmic framework or method of reasoning can be borrowed.

Step 4: Clarify the central solution further

Express the central method first in the simplest possible formula. This makes it clearer what we are doing and exposes both the principal variables and the real constraints: missing data, a bottleneck in computational complexity, or something else. Hidden difficulties are thus brought into view.

Step 5: Design an executable scheme

Use the simplest logic currently available to assemble the smallest process that can actually run. Then patch its largest defect. Continue iterating, layer by layer, until a better version emerges.

Step 6: Verify and iterate rapidly

Test the main hypothesis with a small experiment or simulated data, while actively seeking criticism from domain experts or opponents. Verification has two sides: it asks whether the scheme can run, and it introduces an opposing perspective to expose defects and omissions. Each round of feedback can act upon the product and improve the next iteration.

Suppose you discover that your entire life is a simulation and that you have just found a vulnerability in its console. Would you exploit it to become the “god” of this world, or use it to send the system a command saying, “I want to exit”? Why?

I would exit.

Once I knew about the vulnerability, I could no longer experience the world as I had before. The option of “pretending not to know” would have been destroyed at the instant of discovery.

There is a further problem. If this whole life were a simulation, our universe could be summarized by a theory. Everything would have an answer, but, being inside the system, I could never reach it. There is a vast sadness in that thought. Everything you investigate each day may have been calculated and prescribed by the system in advance.

Under that condition, what use would any of my abilities be? If the entire stage were false, every skill I had developed upon it would also fail to be fully real. Its meaning would be enclosed by the boundary of the system. I do not want merely to play a character in a game.

I am reminded of the people watching firelight in Plato’s cave; the resemblance to this question is close. The person who left the cave must have spent a long time doubting, confused, and unable to endure the light, yet he did not walk back inside. I hope to be such a person. I want to move forward and face reality. Whatever lies outside, I want to see it for myself. I refuse to sink into a falsehood once I know it to be false.

entry.title: 2026-06-25 Have You Gone to Work Today, Meow?
entry.content:
I have recently noticed something rather strange: human beings seem exceptionally fond of finding themselves a boss. If no boss is readily available, they insist on manufacturing one.

At first, people manufactured gods. Later, deciding that the gods took payment every day while doing no actual work, they manufactured all manner of institutions instead: I become the Brahmin while you become the Dalit; I become the emperor while you become the eunuch. A magnificent collection of peculiar arrangements.

After these institutions had run for a while, people found them insufficiently flexible and invented capital.

Then they discovered that, while drowning, one probably ought not place too much faith in Hayek’s invisible hand. So they began to trust algorithms. An algorithm may not be able to fish you out of the water either, but it can certainly persuade people to work for it.

I suspect that, several decades from now, humanity’s greatest technological breakthrough will be the invention of a supervisor capable of monitoring us twenty-four hours a day—and everyone will voluntarily renew the subscription.

At this point, it occurred to me that the human species possesses a rather distinctive sense of humour. Perhaps the essence of humanity is McDonald’s after all.

Later, however, an old man informed me that the proper word for all this was alienation.

To be honest, I do not particularly like the term. That is not because the old man failed to pay me an advertising fee for this essay, nor because he was wrong. The word simply resembles a standard answer, a piece of flatbread somebody else has already chewed. I have never cared for indirectly kissing old men.

I would rather understand the matter in another way: human beings are remarkably good at raising tools until they become masters.

At the beginning, a tool exists merely for convenience. Later, it begins to dictate what convenience means. Money, for example, arose to make exchange easier, yet gradually became the centre around which life was organised. An academic qualification was once no more than evidence that someone had studied certain things; later, it became a label declaring how much that person was worth.

These objects were created to satisfy certain needs. The charming part is that, in the end, they themselves became the needs.

Well, well. The dragon slayer becomes the dragon.

Think about it again, though, and perhaps this is not entirely bad. Slaves no longer have to cultivate a master’s land, and serfs are no longer bound to the soil for life. Today’s workers can resign; programmers can change employers. Human beings do seem to have become progressively freer. They also seem to have been progressively restrained all over again.

Sometimes I suspect that human history is not a history of pursuing freedom so much as a history of repeatedly fitting ourselves with new chains.

Yet even as I write this, a few exceptions come to mind. When I am writing a blog post, or sometimes when I used to write code, I occasionally enter a state in which time suddenly disappears. Nobody is urging me on; there is no target to meet; no voice in my head asks what bloody purpose the thing is supposed to serve. I do not even think about what I am doing. The thing simply grows forward, little by little, on its own.

By the time I become aware of myself again, it is already two in the morning. The file has been saved, the sky has darkened a little further, and my roommate’s snoring sounds beautiful and sexy. For those few minutes, I seem genuinely free. Probably free, anyway.

Some people call this state flow. Game developers are forever trying to pull you into it, while online success gurus are forever teaching you how to reach it. Its sexiness is undeniable. Still, I do not think it means that one has acquired something. Perhaps, for a moment, one has merely ceased to lose something.

Then another, more interesting problem occurred to me. These disordered thoughts were not produced entirely by me. Some of them grew out of conversations with Instructor D, who offered several of the ideas that led me here. There is a certain black humour in that.

At this point I can no longer tell who is using the tool, who invented whom, or who has remade whom.

It probably does not matter. We have always behaved this way: first invent a thing, then gradually learn to obey it, until we have taken its shape.

The only difference is that kneeling before an idol used to look rather undignified. Sitting in front of a computer is at least a more civilised posture.

entry.title: 2026-06-24: The Radar Equation and Love
entry.content:
When you have not seen this flower, it and your mind are together in stillness. When you come to see it, its color becomes clear for a moment. From this you know that the flower is not outside your mind.

— Wang Yangming, Instructions for Practical Living

0. The Starting Point

While studying the radar equation, I noticed a problem.

The formulas of high school physics are generally clean: F=ma, three characters; U=IR, three characters; the law of universal gravitation, a bit longer, but still no more than one line. At that stage, solving problems did not require understanding many premises. You just took a few tidy equalities and plugged numbers in, and the world felt like exactly that.

The radar equation is, of course, not like that. It looks like this:

$$
P_r = \frac{P_t G_t G_r \lambda^2 \sigma}{(4\pi)^3 R^4 L}
$$

And even at this level of detail, each symbol — G, σ, L — separately expands into an entire course. How antenna gain is computed, what the radar cross-section specifically depends on, how many kinds of losses exist. Behind each term lies another book, and behind each book, yet another.

This reminded me of a similar experience in mathematical modeling. Using mathematical models to simulate the real world is essentially the same operation: take a real problem, strip away countless influencing factors, keep only a few variables you can actually write down, and then build a relationship. You know that the model differs from reality by a factor of a million, but as long as it is useful at that level of precision, it suffices.

Why is it that the closer you get to the real world, the more complex the formulas become?

The answer is: the elegance of classical mechanics is not a property of nature; it is the result of deliberate omission. F=ma does not care about relativistic corrections, quantum effects, or the microscopic mechanisms of friction. It hides all of them. And the more it hides, the prettier the formula becomes.

The ugliness of the radar equation does not mean it is imprecise — quite the opposite. Engineering demands higher precision, so it can afford to omit less. Yet both share the same underlying operation: from an infinitely complex reality, select a few key variables, and establish an equality among them.

In other words, a formula is not truth; it is a compressed expression of reality.

This idea later became a thread that strung together several seemingly unrelated domains.

1. Core Concept: Compression and Expansion

If we break down what it means “to understand a system,” it contains two dual abilities.

Compression: folding a large amount of information into a small number of elements. A book compresses into a page, a page into a sentence, a sentence into a formula. Information decreases; structure increases.

Expansion: reconstructing the full derivation in reverse from a compressed form. Given a formula, one should be able to answer: what are the assumptions? What is the physical origin of each term? What happens when the boundary conditions break down? What is the chain of reasoning for each conclusion?

These two abilities are often split apart in students. Those with only compression can state conclusions but cannot withstand probing — ask one question, get an answer; ask “why,” and they freeze. Those with only expansion can talk for three hours without stopping, but ask “so what is this course really about,” and they cannot summarize. The former has only the trunk; the latter, only the leaves.

Only when one possesses both abilities — and can switch freely between different levels of granularity — can knowledge be truly internalized.

This framework itself is not complicated. But as a general-purpose cognitive tool, it can be transplanted into entirely different domains.

2. The Structure of Knowledge: Fractals and Multiple Scales

The framework above leads to a corollary: knowledge is organized neither as a flat list nor as a simple tree hierarchy.

Take the radar equation. If you stare at the RCS symbol and keep asking “where does it come from,” the path is: radar cross-section → scattering center theory → edge diffraction → Maxwell’s equations → electromagnetic boundary conditions → deeper physics. Each layer down, the interior contains a complete, self-consistent structure. The tree model is not enough — a tree has a definite root and leaves, but knowledge unfolds without a clear endpoint. It is closer to a fractal: pick any local region, zoom in, and there is a whole new world inside.

Another discovery came from cross-disciplinary comparison. The same physical object — an airplane — is modeled as completely different things in different disciplines. Radar engineering describes it as an RCS value; materials science, as a distribution of dielectric constants; aerodynamics, as lift and drag; the pilot sees attitude, heading, and altitude.

Which description is “correct”?

All of them are. But their ranges of correctness differ; they serve different observational goals and precision requirements. The radar engineer does not need the aerodynamic properties of the aircraft, and the pilot does not care about its scattering cross-section.

A more general judgment follows: there is no uniquely correct model; there are only models that hold at a specific scale and remain valid at a specific precision. Science does not provide ultimate truth; it provides an ever-iterating set of compression schemes. A model is accepted not because it is “fully real,” but because it works well enough at the current precision demanded.

Or perhaps one could say that truth valid under all conditions is, itself, impossible.

3. Interpersonal Cognition

If we transplant the modeling framework of physical systems onto the cognition of people, the structure is perfectly isomorphic.

A person cannot directly perceive the “totality” of another. The brain automatically compresses the other’s behavior into a limited set of observable variables: reaction speed, emotional stability, reliability, interests. It then performs an implicit weighting on these variables and outputs a prediction — whether this person is worth cooperating with, worth trusting, or worth keeping at a distance. The formal logic of the whole process is no different from an engineering formula: input limited variables, output a predicted value.

This framework explains a deep source of interpersonal conflict: many arguments are not disagreements about facts, but two parties using different compression models. One side explains the other’s silence with the model “no response = no concern”; the other side natively runs on “not expressing ≠ not caring.” The same behavioral input produces opposite predictions in the two models. The conflict at the output layer looks like an attitude problem, but the root lies in model specifications that were never aligned from the start.

Yet this analogy has one crucial break. Physical systems do not explain themselves. A stone will not become less friendly because you think it is unfriendly.

People can.

You say something; the other interprets it as cold; their mood worsens; their behavior cools; you detect the cold behavior and further confirm that “he really doesn’t want to talk to me,” so you also withdraw. A loop closes. Interpretation itself becomes part of the dynamical system. This recursive structure has no counterpart in physical systems; it keeps interpersonal models perpetually in a state of “being used while being modified.”

This leads to a distinction between two levels of understanding a person:

  • Shallow understanding: judging the current values of that person’s state variables — what are their abilities, motivations, and emotions.
  • Deep understanding: tracing how these state variables were generated step by step over time — what the family system input, what constraints the work system imposed, what feedback the social network provided, and how the person themselves interpreted and digested these inputs.

The latter does not ask “what kind of person is he,” but “how did he come to be where he is today.”

4. Learning Methods

If the preceding discussion holds — that knowledge is a hierarchical compressible structure; that mastering knowledge means switching freely between compression and expansion; that cognition is essentially modeling the world — then improvements to learning methods should also be derived from this framework.

Learning a subject efficiently is not about storing more knowledge items in the head, but about rebuilding, in the mind, a runnable system capable of generating that subject’s core conclusions. Concretely, it can be broken into four stages.

Stage One: Build the skeleton. Do not start from details. Use the table of contents as a guide and clarify three questions: what does this subject study? What are the core variables? What are the inputs and outputs? This round does not seek to understand details, only to form a global contour in the mind — knowing “what this course looks like,” not “what each cell looks like.”

Stage Two: Fill in the derivation chains. For every core formula or theorem encountered, do not settle for memorizing the final form. Ask three things: from which more basic assumption was it derived? What are the boundary conditions under which it holds? What happens when they break down? This step transforms each knowledge point from “an item to memorize” into “a reasoning path that can be reconstructed.”

Stage Three: Reverse compression. After finishing each chapter, force yourself to summarize the chapter’s core generative rule in one sentence — not writing an abstract, but writing “what mechanism this chapter uses to produce output from input.” Without this step, the fruits of the first two stages remain scattered and, over time, unrecoverable.

Stage Four: Reconstruction from zero materials. Close all reference materials and independently complete the full derivation from basic assumptions to core conclusions. If you can do it, knowledge has transformed from external information into an internally runnable cognitive model. If you cannot, some link in the previous three stages has not closed — most likely Stage Three was skipped.

Most complaints about “inefficient learning” do not have slow learning as their root cause, but rather that the learning path stops after Stage Two, always lacking the closed loop of compression and reconstruction.

5. Underlying Logic: Abstraction and Switching

Let us take an overview of the previous layers:

Level Core Question Key Concept
Trigger Why do formulas become more complex? Compression, omission, precision hierarchy
Epistemology What does it mean to truly understand a system? The dual ability of compression and expansion
Theory of knowledge How is knowledge organized in the mind? Fractal structure, multi-scale models
Interpersonal What do understanding a person and understanding a formula have in common? Implicit modeling, recursive loops, generative paths
Methodology How to learn efficiently? Skeleton → derivation → compression → reconstruction from zero

What runs through all levels is not any single concrete conclusion, but one repeatedly appearing pattern:

Faced with an infinitely complex input — whether the physical world, a disciplinary system, or another person — extract a limited set of key variables, establish the relational structure among them, and then move freely between different levels of abstraction.

6. Extension: Why Can Mathematics Describe the World?

All of the above, in turn, makes me think of another question: why can mathematics be used to describe the world at all?

Mathematics is not a product of nature. It is a symbolic system invented by humans. Natural numbers come from counting; the equals sign comes from the concept of conservation; calculus comes from an abstraction of motion and change — every branch can be traced back to some primal human impulse to understand and predict the environment. But the question is: why would an artificial language be so particularly good at describing nature?

This is not a question that modeling experience alone can answer. Historically, several major explanations have been offered. Let me examine each, and compare it with the foregoing reflections.

1. Platonism: Mathematics Was Always There

This position holds that circles, pi, and exponential functions “existed” before humans — not as physical entities, but as abstract forms independent of matter. The physical world merely happens to instantiate these mathematical structures. Planetary orbits are elliptical not because you invented the ellipse equation, but because the ellipse already existed in a Platonic world, and nature chose to use it.

The appeal of this view lies in its directness; it requires no further explanation. But its weakness is equally obvious: why would nature choose these structures rather than others? And further, branches of mathematics developed purely out of human interest (group theory, number theory) later found uses in physics — if they exist independently, is this “pre-installation” too coincidental?

Relation to the preceding reflections: The farthest. Everything previously argued rests on “formulas are compressions, models are man-made,” and Platonism stands exactly opposite — it holds that mathematical forms exist independently of humans, who merely discover them. If formulas were “original truth,” there would be no issue of compression ratios, nor any discussion of the boundaries of model validity.

2. The Evolutionary Explanation: The Human Brain Is Itself a Modeling Machine Trained by Nature

This account starts from the other end. When your ancestors were fleeing on the savanna, if they could not subconsciously estimate the distance, speed, and number of prey or predators — that is, if they could not perform a kind of “quasi-mathematical” computation — their genes would not have been passed down. Hundreds of thousands of years of natural selection have hardwired “performing approximate mathematical calculations of the physical world” into the circuits of the human brain.

People find F=ma intuitive not because it is truth, but because the perceptual system of the species to which you belong understands motion through approximations consistent with F=ma.

Relation to the preceding reflections: Partial overlap. The preceding reflections mentioned “the concept of conservation → the equals sign, the concept of counting → natural numbers,” which aligns with the direction of the evolutionary explanation — the origin of mathematics is indeed instrumental, grown out of experience. But evolution can only explain “why humans can learn mathematics,” not “why humans later developed group theory and topology, abstract systems entirely detached from everyday experience.” It explains the hardware, not the software.

3. Instrumentalism: Mathematics Does Not Describe the World; It Compresses It

This is the position used throughout the preceding sections.

Instrumentalism holds that mathematics is not at all a set of statements about the essence of the universe. It is just a symbolic system plus rules of operation. The usage is as follows: first, through observation, determine a few variables of interest; then experiment with different mathematical expressions until the computed results align with observations to an acceptable precision. If it matches, the formula enters the textbook; if not, discard it and try another.

In other words, behind “mathematics can describe nature” lies a severe survivorship bias: what you see is only the formulas that passed the test; behind every successful formula are hundreds of derivations that were overturned, written nowhere.

Relation to the preceding reflections: This is the core operational framework of the preceding sections. The radar equation and F=ma are essentially the same kind of act — select variables, ignore details, establish relationships. Their difference is only in compression ratio. This position is highly consistent with everything argued above and requires no correction.

4. Structural Realism: The World Does Have Objective Structure, and Mathematics Happens to Describe It

This position holds that reality can be decomposed into two levels: substance and structure. Substance — what “material” electrons are made of, how consciousness actually arises — may never be directly accessible. But structure — the decay law between electric force and distance, the quantitative proportions of energy transfer — is stable, repeatably measurable, and independent of the observer.

Mathematics happens to be a language that cares only about “structure” and never asks about “substance.” It does not care what a thing “is”; it only cares what relation the thing has to other things. F=ma does not tell you the ontological definition of force and mass; it only tells you that a linear relationship exists between two quantities. Because this orientation perfectly matches the pattern of external relations among objects, mathematics is particularly useful.

Relation to the preceding reflections: Ambivalent. When arguing that “the same airplane is modeled as different objects in different disciplines, yet all models are valid,” a premise was already implied: there is a sufficiently stable airplane there, allowing different models to converge around it. This premise itself is a mild form of structural realism. But the preceding reflections fundamentally do not want to go as far as “structure is a property of the world itself” — preferring to say “we do not know whether structure belongs to the world or is imposed by humans.” This ambiguity is real; preserving it is more honest than forcibly resolving it.

5. The Kantian View: It Is Not That Mathematics Describes the World, but That Humans Can Only See the World Through the Lens of Mathematics

The subversiveness of this position lies in its direct reversal of the question.

You think you are using mathematics to “see” the world. But by Kant’s reasoning, time, space, quantity, and causality — these categories are themselves the a priori structures of your cognition, not things you learned from the external world. You did not learn to see the world with mathematics; your brain is simply innately capable of organizing sensory data only in quantified, structured ways.

A tree — you think you “see” a tree; in fact, the actual process is: photons strike the retina, convert to neural signals, pass through multiple layers of cortical processing, and are finally constructed by your brain into a perceptual model called “tree.” You are never directly in contact with the world; you are only in contact with the output of your own perceptual processing. Mathematics appears omnipresent because, from the very first instant you touch the world, it has already been “mathematicized” by your cognitive structure.

Wang Yangming, in an entirely different discourse system, said something similar: when the flower is not seen, it and the mind are together in stillness — not that the flower does not exist, but that its color, shape, and kind have not yet been illuminated by the light of the “mind,” not yet co-generated. Kant and Wang Yangming, though separated by three centuries and two civilizations, almost converge on this point.

Relation to the preceding reflections: This layer is neither a supplement to nor a replacement for the preceding arguments; it is their bedrock foundation. Everything said above — “models are man-made, compression involves trade-offs, cognition has boundaries” — if pursued to the end, all stops at this place: everything “objective” that humans can speak of cannot escape the fact that “subjective cognitive structure participated in its construction.” This does not lead one into nihilism; it leads one into a sober self-awareness: knowing that one is not directly watching the world, but participating in its constitution.

Overview of the Six Positions and Their Relation to This Essay

Position Relation to the Core Framework Verdict
Platonism Formulas as original truth, directly opposed to “compression” Farthest; incompatible
Evolution Explains “why humans can” model, does not touch “the boundaries of modeling” Partially useful but not central
Instrumentalism Formulas as disposable compression tools — consistent with the operational logic throughout Core at the methodological layer
Structural realism Suggests objective constraints that make models converge; this essay remains open to it Held in suspension
Kant/Wang Yangming The observer participates in the construction of the observed — provides the underlying conviction Foundational layer

My Position

Comparing each one, my own position can, in fact, be described fairly clearly.

First, mathematics is a tool invented by humans, not truth fallen from the sky. The concept of conservation was abstracted, and so the equals sign appeared; the impulse to count was formalized, and so natural numbers appeared. Humans first invent these symbols and rules, then turn around and use them to frame nature — what frames successfully is kept; what fails is discarded or iterated. The Platonic idea that “mathematics has been waiting in the sky to be discovered” — I do not accept it. If formulas were innate truth, then what would overturned formulas be? Truth evolving?

Second, at the operational level, I basically stand with instrumentalism. The radar equation, F=ma, and the various fittings in mathematical modeling are all essentially the same operation — select variables, cut details, build equalities. Whether a formula is good does not depend on how “true” it is, but on whether it works at the current precision required. Compression ratios may differ, but the underlying logic is invariant. This position dovetails seamlessly with the analytical framework of this essay; no separate patching is needed.

But instrumentalism pushed to its extreme gives a sense that “everything is fictional; just whatever works,” which does not quite match my actual experience. When the same airplane can be effectively described by models from different disciplines, these models are all pointing to the same “constrained direction” — there is something objectively there, restricting the space in which all models can operate, forcing them to converge in a certain direction. So I retain a certain tolerance for structural realism — not elevating it to truth, but admitting that models are not entirely free; something underneath is pressing down. What that “something” is, I cannot yet say.

Finally, and most importantly, at the more foundational level of belief, I incline toward Kant and Wang Yangming. Whatever nature humans see — however rational, however objective — is ultimately seen through one’s own cognitive structure. Space, time, causality, quantity — these are human frames, not nature’s own. Mathematics appears so useful not because it happens to match the essence of nature, but because humans can only see the “mathematized face” of nature. As Yangming said, the flower does not not exist; its color only becomes clear when illuminated by the mind. This does not mean the world is an illusion; it means that everything “objective” humans discuss cannot possibly excise the observer from the equation.

So, all together, my position is roughly: with the cognitive stance of Kant and Yangming as the foundational floor, practicing instrumentalism at the methodological level, and maintaining a degree of openness, without forcing the issue, toward structural realism. Platonism is clearly rejected. Evolution explains some hardware-level matters, but does not reach the core of the question.

Afterword

This bout of thinking was considerably heavier than my usual blog writing. Starting from a single formula, it ran through the construction of an analytical framework, the discussion of knowledge structure, the transfer of an interpersonal model, the derivation of learning methods, and finally collided with a fundamental question about “why mathematics can describe the world.”

This piece is different from my usual casual essays. It is more systematic — because what it faces is itself systematic. Writing it in fragments would only have made it scattered.

The final landing point is not a single concrete conclusion, but a question that can be used repeatedly:

When faced with any complex system — a formula, a course, a person, a decision — which model am I using right now? What variables does this model select, and which does it omit? Is there another model that holds equally well at another scale?

Internalizing this habit is, I suppose, indeed more useful than memorizing the radar equation itself!

entry.title: A Guide for Station Assistants
entry.content:
