The state space—the range of states, or the probabilities of the possible results—is $E={E_1,E_2,…,E_J}$, while the symbol alphabet, which is effectively its set of subscripts, is $X={a_1,a_2,…,a_q}$.

Definitions:

  • Emission probability: $p(a_k|E_i)$

  • State-transition probability: $p(E_j|E_i)$

If these probabilities are independent of time, the process is called a homogeneous Markov chain.

In the state-transition diagram of a Markov chain, every circle represents a state and a directed line between two states represents a transition from one to the other. The symbol and number beside a directed line represent, respectively, the emitted symbol and conditional probability.

For an mth-order source:

$$H_{m+1} = -\sum_{x_{1}^{m+1}} P(x_{1}^{m+1}) \log P(x_{m+1}|x_1…x_m)$$

Moreover, $H_0 \ge H_1 \ge H_2 \ge … \ge H_\infty$.

Ergodicity and limiting entropy:

If the Markov chain is ergodic, a unique stationary distribution exists:

$$Q(E_i) = \sum_j Q(E_j)p(E_i|E_j)$$

The limiting entropy is:

$$H_\infty = -\sum_{i,j} Q(E_i)p(a_j|E_i)\log p(a_j|E_i)$$

It should also be noted that the limiting entropy of an mth-order Markov source equals its mth-order conditional entropy; that is, $H_m = H_{无穷}$.

Source Redundancy and the Entropy of Natural Language

Approximating a Real Source

Real sources are often non-stationary, and the limiting entropy $H_\infty$ does not necessarily exist.

By measuring the conditional probability $P(X_N|X_1X_2…X_{N-1})$ of a sufficiently long sequence, we may approximate:

$$H_N(X) \approx H_\infty$$

(2) Approximation with a Markov Source

The entropy of a stationary source is difficult to calculate, so it may be approximated by the entropy $H_{m+1}$ of an mth-order Markov source:

$$H_{m+1} \approx H_\infty$$

The accuracy of the approximation depends on the memory length $m$.

(3) Correlation Among Source Symbols and Average Information

$$\log_2 q = H_0 \ge H_1 \ge H_2 \ge … \ge H_m \ge H_\infty$$

The stronger the dependence, the lower the entropy; the more independent the symbols, the higher the entropy.

IX. Source Redundancy and Communication Efficiency

(1) Definitions

  • Relative entropy rate:

$$ \eta = \frac{H_\infty}{H_0}$$

  • Source redundancy:

$$ \gamma = 1 - \eta = 1 - \frac{H_\infty}{H_0}$$

(2) Meaning

  • ( \gamma ) reflects the dependence among symbols.
  • The greater ( \gamma ) is, the more compressible the source becomes.

For example, the redundancy of English is:
[
\gamma = 1 - \frac{1.41}{\log_2 27} \approx 0.71
]
→ Seventy-one per cent of the information in English is predictable, leaving only 29 per cent as free variation.

(3) Conclusions

  • High redundancy → easy compression and strong resistance to noise.
  • Low redundancy → high efficiency but greater vulnerability to interference.
  • Coding must balance efficiency against reliability.

X. Communication Efficiency and Reliability

  • Source coding reduces redundancy and improves efficiency.
  • Channel coding adds redundancy and improves reliability.

Together they form the fundamental tension and point of balance in an information-transmission system.

📘 Summary

The essence of this chapter is to understand entropy as a measure of information.
Markov sources describe the finite memory of real sources,
while redundancy and limiting entropy reveal both the compressibility of linguistic information and its resistance to interference.

entry.title: Chapter 3 — Random Processes: Spectral Analysis
entry.content:
So tired, meow QAQ. I really do not want to write any more, meow QAQ.

1 Spectral Analysis of Random Processes

As usual, before analysing random signals, let us begin with deterministic signals and establish an initial intuition.

1.1 Review of the Spectrum of Deterministic Signals

(1) Energy Signal

This is a relatively simple idea. Consider, for example, a sudden “duang” sound: once it has been played, it is over, and its finite energy can be calculated directly.

A signal may be highly irregular in time, yet what often matters is the frequencies at which its energy is concentrated.
Thus, in moving from the time domain to the frequency domain, the first step is to define energy:

$$
E = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} |x(t)|^2 , dt
$$

If $E<\infty$, the signal is called an energy signal, as in the case of a finite-duration, non-periodic signal.

Its Fourier transform is:
$$
X(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x(t)e^{-j\omega t} dt
$$

The squared magnitude gives the distribution of energy over frequency and is called the energy spectral density:

$$
|X(\omega)|^2
$$

Parseval’s theorem:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} |x(t)|^2 dt = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} |X(\omega)|^2 d\omega
$$

The energy spectral density reveals how a signal’s energy is distributed in the frequency domain.

Intuitively, the theorem converts the integral of a squared signal in the time domain into a corresponding integral in the frequency domain. Energy can therefore be calculated from two different perspectives.

(2) Power Signal

$X(t)$ generally does not come to an end, so its energy is infinite.

We therefore adopt a different perspective and examine only the average energy per unit time—that is, power:

$$
P = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{2T} \int_{-T}^{T} |x(t)|^2 dt
$$

A periodic signal with finite power is called a power signal. Our concern then shifts to the distribution of power over frequency, namely, power spectral density (PSD).

Power spectral density is defined as:

$$
S_x(\omega) = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{E[|X_T(\omega)|^2]}{2T}
$$

Here, $X_T(\omega)$ is the Fourier transform within the time window $[-T, T]$.

PSD is therefore the distribution of average power along the frequency dimension.

1.2 Average Power Spectral Density of a Random Signal

The power spectral density of a random signal $X(t)$ is defined below.

It represents the average power of the signal in the neighbourhood of a particular frequency.

$$
S_X(\omega) = \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{E[|X_T(\omega)|^2]}{2T}
$$

Its supposed characteristics include the following:

[!WARNING]
These characteristics have not yet been verified and need to be checked in the next revision.

  1. A sample signal is generally a power signal;

  2. Different sample signals possess different spectral densities;

  3. $S_X(\omega)$ is a random function, and its mathematical expectation is generally taken;

  4. The random-signal power $P_X = E[|X(t)|^2]$ is a random variable, and usually only its mean is of interest.

1.3 Power Spectral Density and the Complex-Frequency Plane

The power spectral density $S_X(\omega)$ is defined on the complex-frequency plane $s=j\omega$:
$$
S_X(s) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} R_X(\tau)e^{-s\tau} d\tau
$$
If $S_X(\omega)$ is a rational spectrum, it can be expressed as:
$$
S_X(s) = K \frac{\prod (s - \alpha_i)(s + \alpha_i)}{\prod (s - \beta_i)(s + \beta_i)}
$$
A real signal satisfies:
$$
S_X(s) = S_X^*(-s)
$$

For the detailed method of solution, I need to return to signals and systems and review the Laplace transform.

2 Properties of the Power Spectral Density of a Random Process

  1. Real-valued evenness:
    $$
    S_X(-\omega) = S_X(\omega)
    $$

  2. Non-negativity:
    $$
    S_X(\omega) \ge 0
    $$

  3. Parseval relation:
    $$
    R_X(0) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} S_X(\omega)d\omega
    $$

  4. Finiteness of the integral:
    For a stationary process, $\int S_X(\omega)d\omega$ converges.

  5. Rational spectral factorisation:
    If the spectrum is a rational function, its poles lie in the left half-plane, while its zeros lie on the imaginary axis or in the left half-plane.

3 Relationship between Power Spectral Density and the Autocorrelation Function

Wiener–Khinchin Theorem

If the random process $X(t)$ is wide-sense stationary (WSS), then:
$$
S_X(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} R_X(\tau)e^{-j\omega\tau} d\tau
$$
$$
R_X(\tau) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} S_X(\omega)e^{j\omega\tau} d\omega
$$

The average power is:
$$
E[X^2(t)] = R_X(0) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} S_X(\omega)d\omega
$$

The smoother a signal is, the more slowly $R_X(\tau)$ decays, and the more its spectrum is dominated by low-frequency components.
The faster a signal changes, the more rapidly $R_X(\tau)$ decays, indicating stronger high-frequency components.

4 Power Spectral Density of a Discrete-Time Random Process

Suppose that $X(n)$ is a wide-sense stationary random sequence obtained by uniformly sampling $X(t)$ at a sampling interval $T$.

If $X(n)$ is a stationary discrete random sequence:

$$
R_X(m) = E[X(n)X(n+m)] = R_X(mT)
$$

Its power spectral density is:

$$
S_X(\Omega) = \sum_{m=-\infty}^{+\infty} R_X(m)e^{-j\Omega m}
$$

Its inverse transform is:

$$
R_X(m) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} S_X(\Omega)e^{j\Omega m} d\Omega
$$

The average power is:

$$
E[|X(n)|^2] = R_X(0) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} S_X(\Omega)d\Omega
$$

When the sampling interval is $T$:

$$
S_X(\omega) =\frac{1}{T} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} S_c(\omega - k\omega_s)
$$

This is the sampling theorem for power spectral density.

Here, $\omega_s = \frac{2\pi}{T}$.

[!NOTE]
The sampling theorem was not explained in much detail, and I still do not understand it very well. Since I did not learn this part of signals and systems properly, I barely listened to it—including the spectral factorisation theorem, which I understand even less.

5 Cross-Spectral Density of Jointly Stationary Random Processes

To be honest, I can no longer follow what she is deriving on the slides. All the notes below were therefore completed by AI.

If $X(t)$ and $Y(t)$ are jointly stationary processes, their cross-power spectral density is defined as:
$$
S_{XY}(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} R_{XY}(\tau)e^{-j\omega\tau} d\tau
$$

It has the following properties:

  1. $S_{XY}^*(\omega) = S_{YX}(\omega)$;
  2. For real processes, $S_{XY}(-\omega) = S_{YX}^*(\omega)$;
  3. If $X,Y$ are uncorrelated, then $S_{XY}(\omega)=0$.

6 White Noise

(1) Definition

  • If the power spectral density is constant:
    $$
    S_N(\omega) = \frac{N_0}{2}
    $$
    the noise is called white noise.

  • Its autocorrelation function is:
    $$
    R_N(\tau) = \frac{N_0}{2}\delta(\tau)
    $$

(2) Ideal White Noise

Its characteristics include:

  • A mean of zero;
  • A constant $S_N(\omega)$;
  • Infinite average power;
  • Non-existence in practice, meaning that it can only be approximated.

(3) Band-Limited White Noise and Coloured Noise

  • If $S_N(\omega)$ is constant within the finite bandwidth $[-W, W]$:
    $$
    S_N(\omega) = N_0/2, \quad |\omega| \le W
    $$
    it is called band-limited white noise;

  • If the spectral density varies with frequency, the noise is called coloured noise.

(4) Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)

It is defined as:
$$
\mathrm{SNR} = \frac{P_s}{P_n}, \quad \text{(dB)} = 10\log_{10}\frac{P_s}{P_n}
$$

Example:
Suppose $s(t)=4\cos(\omega_0 t)$, while $n(t)$ is low-pass white noise with a bandwidth of $2$ kHz and a power spectral density of $S_N(\omega)=2$:

$$
P_s = \frac{A^2}{2} = 8, \quad P_n = 2W/\pi = 8000
$$
$$
\mathrm{SNR} = 10\log_{10}\frac{8}{8000} \approx -30 \text{ dB}
$$

entry.title: Chapter 2 — Random Processes: Time-Domain Analysis
entry.content:
1 Basic Concepts and Statistical Characteristics of Random Processes

1.1 Basic Concepts of a Random Process

A random process $X(t,s)$ can be understood from both macroscopic and microscopic perspectives:

Perspective Description Fixed quantity Variable quantity Result
Macroscopic view (a family of time functions) A mapping from the sample space to a function space None Both $t$ and $s$ vary Random process
Sample function One realisation of a random process $s$ is fixed $t$ varies Known time function
Microscopic view (a time-varying random variable) At every specified time $t_i$, it is a random variable $t$ is fixed $s$ varies Random variable
Deterministic value Both the sample point and time are fixed Both $t$ and $s$ are fixed None Deterministic value

Definition 1 (family of time functions/macroscopic view):

Let the sample space of a random experiment be $S={s_i}$. For every sample $s_i \in S$, there is a corresponding time function $X(t,s_i)$, where $t \in T$. All samples in $S={s_i}$ therefore correspond to a family of time functions ${X(t,s_i), s_i \in S}$. The mapping from the sample space to this function space is called a random process.

Definition 2 (time-varying random variable/microscopic view):

For every specified time $t_i$, if $X(t_i,s)$ is a random variable, then $X(t,s)$ is called a random process.

This idea has already become fairly clear in the course on communication principles, so I will not go into it again.

1.2 Classification of Random Processes

I. Classification by whether time and amplitude (state) are continuous or discrete

  • Continuous random process: continuous in time and continuous in state.
  • Discrete random process: continuous in time and discrete in state.
  • Continuous random sequence: discrete in time and continuous in state.
  • Discrete random sequence: discrete in both time and state.

A pile of empty distinctions. No need to spend much time on them.

II. Classification by the properties of sample functions

  • Uncertain (unpredictable) random process

  • Deterministic (predictable) random process: for example, the random-phase signal $A\sin(\omega t+\Phi), \Phi \sim U(0,2\pi)$.

III. Classification by the characteristics of probability distributions

  • Stationary random process: a process whose statistical characteristics do not vary with time, such as thermal noise.
  • Normal random process
  • Markov random process
  • Independent-increment process
  • Independent random process

There is no need to inspect every category in detail. It is enough to know that these classifications exist; for now, they are not particularly useful.

1.3 Probability Distributions of Random Processes

The “certainty” contained in randomness means that the overall properties of a random process can be described by statistical averages, including moments, characteristic functions, and probability distribution or density functions.

I. One-Dimensional Probability Distribution

  • One-dimensional distribution function: $F_X(x;t) = P{X(t) \le x}$, which is a deterministic function.

  • One-dimensional probability density: $f_X(x;t) = \frac{\partial F_X(x;t)}{\partial x}$, which may be a time-varying probability density.

II. Two-Dimensional Probability Distribution

  • Two-dimensional distribution function: $F_{X_1X_2}(x_1,x_2;t_1,t_2) = P{X(t_1) \le x_1, X(t_2) \le x_2}$.

  • Two-dimensional probability density: $f_{X_1X_2}(x_1,x_2;t_1,t_2) = \frac{\partial^2 F_{X_1X_2}(x_1,x_2;t_1,t_2)}{\partial x_1 \partial x_2}$.

III. Obtaining a Probability Density through a Transformation of Random Variables

  • Monotonic invertible transformation: $Y = g(X), X = h(Y)$

    $$f_Y(y) = f_X[x=h(y)] \left| \frac{dh(y)}{dy} \right| = f_X(x) \left| \frac{dg(x)}{dx} \right|^{-1} \Big|_{x=h(y)}$$

  • Non-monotonic invertible transformation: $Y = g(X)$, with multiple roots $X_k = h_k(Y)$

    $$f_Y(y) = \sum_{k} f_X[x=h_k(y)] \left| \frac{dh_k(y)}{dy} \right|$$

  • Two-dimensional transformation (Jacobian determinant): $Y_1=g_1(X_1,X_2), Y_2=g_2(X_1,X_2)$

    $$f_{Y_1Y_2}(y_1,y_2) = \left| J_h(y_1,y_2) \right| f_{X_1X_2}[x_1=h_1(y_1,y_2), x_2=h_2(y_1,y_2)]$$

    Here, $|J_h|$ is the absolute value of the determinant formed by the partial derivatives of $X_1, X_2$ with respect to $Y_1, Y_2$.

Chapter 1 already covered most of this material, so there is no reason to repeat it in detail.

1.4 Numerical Characteristics of Random Processes

  • Mean function $m_X(t) = E[X(t)]$

Note: this is also called the second-order raw moment.

  • Variance function $D_X(t) = E{[X(t)-m_X(t)]^2}$

Note: this is also called the second-order central moment.

  • Autocorrelation function $R_X(t_1, t_2) = E[X(t_1)X(t_2)]$

  • Covariance function $K_X(t_1, t_2) = R_X(t_1, t_2) - m_X(t_1)m_X(t_2)$

2 Differentiation and Integration of Random Processes

2.0 Preliminary Concept: Mean-Square Limit

  • Second-order process: a random process satisfying $\forall t \in T, E[X^2(t)] < \infty$.

  • Mean-square limit (l.i.m.): A sequence of random variables ${X_n}$ is said to converge to $X$ in the mean-square sense, written as $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\mathrm{l.i.m.}} X_n = X$, if:

    $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} E|X_n - X|^2 = 0$$

Here, l.i.m. is short for “limit in mean square”.

Mean-square convergence is defined because it differs from ordinary convergence: what must converge is the mean square, not every individual sample point.

Of course, when it comes to solving exercises, we still end up using much the same machinery as in ordinary calculus.

Properties of the Mean-Square Limit

$$\underset{n \to \infty}{\text{l.i.m}} c_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} c_n = c$$

$$\underset{n \to \infty}{\text{l.i.m}} Z = Z $$

$$\underset{n \to \infty}{\text{l.i.m}} c_n Z = cZ$$

  • Algebraic properties: The order of a mean-square limit may be exchanged with addition, multiplication by a constant, and expectation ($E$).

    $$\underset{n \to \infty}{\text{l.i.m}} (aX_n + bY_n) = aX + bY$$

    $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} E X_n = E X = E \left[ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} X_n \right]$$

  • Criterion for mean-square convergence (Cauchy criterion): A necessary and sufficient condition for ${X_n}$ to converge in the mean-square sense is:

    $$\lim_{n,m\rightarrow\infty} E|X_m - X_n|^2 = 0$$

2.1 Stochastic Continuity: Mean-Square Continuity

  • Definition: $X(t)$ is said to be mean-square continuous at time $t_0$ if:

    $$\lim_{\Delta t\rightarrow0} E{[X(t_0+\Delta t)-X(t_0)]^2} = 0$$

  • Criterion for mean-square continuity (necessary and sufficient condition):

    A second-order process $X(t)$ is mean-square continuous at $t_0$ if and only if its correlation function $R(s,t)$ is continuous at $(t_0, t_0)$.

    In other words, the mean-square continuity of a second-order process can be determined through the ordinary continuity of its correlation function.

  • Properties:

    • If $X(t)$ is mean-square continuous at $t_0$, its mean function $m_X(t)$ and variance function $D_X(t)$ are also continuous at $t_0$.

    • The order of “E” and “l.i.m.” may be exchanged.

2.2 Differentiation of a Random Process (Mean-Square Differentiability)

  • Criterion for mean-square differentiability (necessary and sufficient condition):

    A second-order process $X(t)$ is mean-square differentiable at $t_0$ if and only if its correlation function $R(s,t)$ possesses a generalised second derivative at $(t_0, t_0)$. In plain terms, when the two independent variables of the correlation function are equal, a continuous second-order mixed partial derivative must exist.

  • Properties of the mean-square derivative:

    • If $X(t)$ is mean-square differentiable at $t$, then $X(t)$ is mean-square continuous at $t$.

    • The order of “E” and “$\frac{d(\cdot)}{dt}$” may be exchanged. That is, $E[\frac{d}{dt}X(t)] = \frac{d}{dt}E[X(t)]$.

2.3 Integration of a Random Process (Mean-Square Integrability)

  • Sufficient conditions for mean-square integrability:

    • For a second-order process $X(t)$, if the double integral of its correlation function $R(s,t)$ exists and is finite, then $X(t)$ is mean-square integrable on $[a,b]$.

    • If $X(t)$ is mean-square continuous on $[a,b]$, then $X(t)$ is mean-square integrable on $[a,b]$.

  • Property of the mean-square integral:

    • The order of “E” and mean-square integration may be exchanged. That is, $E[\int_a^b X(t)dt] = \int_a^b E[X(t)]dt$.

3 Stationary and Ergodic Random Processes

3.1 Stationary Random Processes

  • Stationary random process: a random process whose statistical characteristics do not change as time passes.

  • Such processes are divided into strict-sense stationary (SSS) and wide-sense stationary (WSS) processes.

I. Strict-Sense Stationary Random Process (SSS)

  • Definition: For a random process $X(t)$, every $n$-dimensional probability distribution function $F_X(x_1,\dots,x_n; t_1,\dots,t_n)$ remains unchanged under a translation in time. It is therefore independent of the starting point in time and depends only on the time differences $\tau_k=t_k-t_1$.

    $$F_X(x_1,\dots,x_n; t_1,\dots,t_n) = F_X(x_1,\dots,x_n; t_1+\tau,\dots,t_n+\tau)$$

  • Properties of lower-order moments:

    • The mean function $m_X(t)$ is independent of time $t$ and is therefore a constant.

    • The autocorrelation function $R_X(t_1, t_2)$ depends only on the time difference $\tau=t_2-t_1$, and can thus be written as $R_X(\tau)$.

This condition is plainly too demanding to be satisfied in most cases, and its range of application is therefore rather narrow. We consequently need wide-sense stationarity to do the practical work.

II. Wide-Sense Stationary Random Process (WSS)

  • Definition (Khinchin): A random process $X(t)$ must satisfy the following conditions:

    1. Its mean function $m_X(t)$ is independent of time $t$ and is therefore a constant $m_X$.

    2. Its autocorrelation function $R_X(t_1, t_2)$ depends only on the time difference $\tau=t_2-t_1$, and may therefore be written as $R_X(\tau)$.

  • Relationship:

    • Strict-sense stationarity $\implies$ wide-sense stationarity, but the reverse does not hold, except for a normal process.
  • Properties:

To be honest, I did not read this part carefully enough to understand it.

Next, the correlation time is introduced:

A smaller $\tau_0$ means that the correlation coefficient decays more rapidly as $\tau$ increases, indicating that the random process changes more sharply over time.

3.2 Cyclostationary Random Processes

3.3 Ergodic Processes (Ergodicity)

The point is to replace a statistical average with a time average.

  • Basic idea: The statistical average, taken over a family of samples, is equal to the time average taken over a single sample function.

    • Time averages: the time mean $\overline{X}$ and the time correlation function $\mathfrak{R}_X(\tau)$.

  • Definition of a wide-sense ergodic process: Suppose the random process $X(t)$ is wide-sense stationary and is ergodic in both its mean and autocorrelation function. It is then defined as a wide-sense ergodic process.

    1. Mean ergodicity: The time mean converges in the mean-square sense to the statistical mean.

      $$\overline{X} = \lim_{T\rightarrow\infty} \frac{1}{2T} \int_{-T}^{T} X(t)dt \xrightarrow{\mathrm{m.s.}} E[X(t)]$$

    2. Autocorrelation ergodicity: The time autocorrelation function converges in the mean-square sense to the statistical autocorrelation function.

      $$\mathfrak{R}X(\tau) = \lim{T\rightarrow\infty} \frac{1}{2T} \int_{-T}^{T} X(t)X(t+\tau)dt \xrightarrow{\mathrm{m.s.}} R_X(\tau)$$

In practice, as soon as a stationary signal turns up, we simply use these averages without worrying too much about the fine print. Reckless, perhaps, but that is how the exercises tend to go.

4 Joint Probability Distributions and Cross-Correlation Functions of Random Processes

4.1 Joint Probability Distribution of Two Random Processes

Consider two random processes $X(t)$ and $Y(t)$.

  • $(n+m)$-dimensional joint distribution function:

    $$F_{XY}(x_1,\dots,x_n;y_1,\dots,y_m;t_1,\dots,t_n;t_1’,\dots,t_m’) = P{X(t_1) \le x_1,\dots, X(t_n) \le x_n; Y(t_1’) \le y_1,\dots, Y(t_m’) \le y_m}$$

  • $(n+m)$-dimensional joint probability density:

    $$f_{XY}(\dots) = \frac{\partial^{n+m}F_{XY}(\dots)}{\partial x_1 \dots \partial x_n \partial y_1 \dots \partial y_m}$$

  • Points to note:

    1. If the $n+m$-dimensional joint probability distribution of the two processes is given, all their statistical characteristics are determined.

    2. Their lower-dimensional joint probability distributions can be derived from the higher-dimensional distribution.

There is not much else to say. This is simply a generalisation of what was already established above.

4.2 Cross-Correlation Function

  • Definition of the cross-correlation function: It describes the statistical association between the states of two random processes at different times.

    $$R_{XY}(t_1, t_2) = E[X(t_1)Y(t_2)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}xyf_{XY}(x,y;t_1,t_2)dxdy$$

  • Cross-covariance function (centred cross-correlation function):
    $$K_{XY}(t_1, t_2) = E{[X(t_1)-m_X(t_1)][Y(t_2)-m_Y(t_2)]}$$
    $$K_{XY}(t_1, t_2) = R_{XY}(t_1, t_2) - m_X(t_1)m_Y(t_2)$$

Relationships

Relationship Definition Cross-correlation function $R_{XY}(t_1, t_2)$ Cross-covariance function $K_{XY}(t_1, t_2)$
Statistical independence $f_{XY} = f_X f_Y$ $m_X(t_1)m_Y(t_2)$ $0$
Uncorrelated $K_{XY}(t_1, t_2)=0$ $m_X(t_1)m_Y(t_2)$ $0$
Orthogonal $R_{XY}(t_1, t_2)=0$ $0$ $-m_X(t_1)m_Y(t_2)$

[!WARNING]
Something here is not quite right;
also, CXZ is my son.

  • Points to note:

    1. If two random processes are independent of each other and both possess second-order moments, they must be uncorrelated.

    2. For normal random processes, being uncorrelated is equivalent to being independent.

I do not want to study any more. Time for some music QAQ.

Joint Stationarity

  • Joint strict-sense stationarity: The joint probability distribution of $X(t)$ and $Y(t)$ remains unchanged under a translation in time.

  • Joint wide-sense stationarity (wide-sense stationary dependence):

    1. Both $X(t)$ and $Y(t)$ are wide-sense stationary.

    2. The cross-correlation function $R_{XY}(t, t+\tau)=R_{XY}(\tau)$ depends only on the time difference $\tau$.

  • Joint wide-sense ergodicity:

    1. $X(t)$ and $Y(t)$ are jointly wide-sense stationary.

    2. The time cross-correlation function converges in the mean-square sense to the statistical cross-correlation function.

      $$\mathfrak{R}{XY}(\tau) = \underset{T\rightarrow\infty}{\mathrm{l.i.m.}} \frac{1}{2T}\int{-T}^{T}X(t)Y(t+\tau)dt = R_{XY}(\tau)$$

5 Complex Random Processes

  • Complex random signal: $Z(t) = X_c(t) + jX_s(t)$.

The difference between its calculation and that for a real random process is much the same as the difference between complex and real numbers, so there is no need to elaborate here.

  • Wide-sense stationary complex random process:

    1. The mean function $m_Z(t) = E[Z(t)]$ is a constant.

    2. The autocorrelation function $R_Z(t_1, t_2) = E[Z(t_1)Z^*(t_2)]$ depends only on the time difference $\tau=t_2-t_1$, and can therefore be written as $R_Z(\tau)$.

  • Jointly wide-sense stationary complex random processes:

    1. $Z_1(t)$ and $Z_2(t)$ are each wide-sense stationary.

    2. The cross-correlation function $R_{Z_1Z_2}(t, t+\tau) = E[Z_1(t)Z_2^*(t+\tau)]$ depends only on $\tau$.

[!NOTE]
As can be seen, the distinction is much the same as that between real and complex numbers. There is no need to inspect it too closely.

6 Discrete-Time Random Processes

  • Representation: $X(nT)$ or $X(n)$.

  • Method of analysis: In essence, it is the same as the analysis of a continuous-time random signal.

  • Correspondence: the time variable $t \rightarrow n$.

[!NOTE]
As can be seen, there is almost no essential difference from the continuous-time case, so there is no need to inspect it too closely.

7 Normal Random Processes

  • Principal properties:

    1. The $n$-dimensional probability density of a normal random process is completely determined by the collection of its means and the collection of its covariance functions.

    2. For a normal process, strict-sense stationarity and wide-sense stationarity are equivalent.

    3. For a normal process, being uncorrelated is equivalent to being independent.

    4. The output produced when a normal random process passes through a linear system remains a normal process.

[!ERROR]
The stationary normal random process is omitted here, meow.

entry.title: Chapter 1 — Foundations of Probability Theory
entry.content:
Here begins the main text.

1.1 Basic Concepts

  • Random Experiment: an experiment whose outcome cannot be predicted in advance, but which can be repeated.

  • Sample Space $\Omega$: the set of all possible outcomes.

  • Random Event $A \subseteq \Omega$:

    • An elementary event contains only one outcome;

    • A compound event contains several outcomes;

    • $\Omega$ is the certain event, whereas $\varnothing$ is the impossible event.

  • Probability (axiomatic definition)

    1. $0 \le P(A) \le 1$

    2. $P(\Omega) = 1$

    3. If $A \cap B = \varnothing$, then $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$

Note: classical probability, geometric probability, frequentist probability, and axiomatic probability merely offer different ways of understanding the same subject. This course adopts the axiomatic definition together with a formal treatment based on density functions.

1.2 One-Dimensional Random Variables

Definition

A random variable $X(\omega)$ is a function that maps the sample space to the real-number domain.

Distribution Function

$$F_X(x) = P{X \le x}$$

It has the following properties:

  1. It is monotonically non-decreasing;
  2. It is right-continuous;
  3. $\lim_{x\to -\infty}F=0$, and $\lim_{x\to +\infty}F=1$.

Discrete and Continuous Types

Type Description Representation
Discrete $P{X=x_k}=p_k$ Probability mass function (PMF)
Continuous $P{x<X<x+dx}=f(x)dx$ Probability density function (PDF)

The PDF of a discrete random variable can also be expressed in a unified form through the Dirac delta function:

$$f(x) = \sum_k p_k \delta(x - x_k)$$

Transformations of Random Variables

Suppose $Y = g(X)$.

  • If the transformation is monotonic and invertible:

$$f_Y(y) = f_X(x) \left| \frac{dx}{dy} \right|$$

The concrete derivation can be understood as follows:

Look at the diagram. If the distribution of (y) is required, the ratio between $\Delta y$ and $\Delta x$ can be used directly; it gives the corresponding ratio between (y) and (x) in the calculation.

  • If the transformation is invertible but non-monotonic, sum the contributions from its multiple solutions.

Common examples include $Y = \sin X$ and $Y = X^2$.

I will check later whether an exercise of this kind appears in the homework; the example on the slides is not particularly clear.

1.3 Multidimensional Random Variables

Joint Distribution Function

$$F_{XY}(x,y) = P{X \le x, Y \le y}$$

Joint Density Function

$$f_{XY}(x,y) = \frac{\partial^2 F_{XY}}{\partial x \partial y}$$

Marginal Distribution

A marginal distribution is obtained by setting aside one factor and considering only the other.

$$f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_{XY}(x,y) , dy$$

Conditional Density

$$f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \frac{f_{XY}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}$$

If $f_{XY}(x,y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$, the variables are said to be independent.

Transformation of Two-Dimensional Random Variables (Jacobian)

Suppose

$$
Y_1 = g_1(X_1,X_2), \quad Y_2 = g_2(X_1,X_2)
$$

Then

$$
f_{Y_1Y_2}(y_1,y_2) = f_{X_1X_2}(x_1,x_2) \cdot \left| J_g^{-1} \right|
$$

1.4 Numerical Characteristics

One-Dimensional Case

Quantity Discrete Continuous
Expectation $E[X]=\sum x_k p_k$ $E[X]=\int xf(x)dx$
Variance $D[X]=E[X^2]-E[X]^2$ Same as on the left

Two-Dimensional Case

  • Covariance

$$\mathrm{cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]$$

  • Correlation Coefficient

$$\rho_{XY} = \frac{\mathrm{cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{D[X]D[Y]}}$$

  • Property: $\rho \in [-1,1]$. The greater $|\rho|$ is, the stronger the linear correlation becomes.

1.5 Characteristic Function

$$\phi_X(u) = E[e^{juX}]$$

  • It is equivalent to the Fourier transform of $f_X(x)$;
  • It can be used to derive convolution results and prove limit theorems;
  • The characteristic function of a Gaussian distribution remains Gaussian in form.

1.4 Numerical Characteristics of Random Variables

One-Dimensional Random Variables

Quantity Discrete Continuous
Expectation $E[X]=\sum x_k p_k$ $E[X]=\int xf(x)dx$
Variance $D[X]=E[X^2]-E[X]^2$ Same as on the left
Raw moment $\mu_k=E[X^k]$ Same as on the left
Absolute moment $\lambda_k=E[|X|^k]$ Same as on the left
Central moment $v_k=E[(X-E[X])^k]$ Same as on the left
Standardised moment $\tilde{v}_k=E\left[\left(\frac{X-\mu_X}{\sigma_X}\right)^k\right]=\frac{v_k}{\sigma_X^k}$ Same as on the left

Properties of Numerical Characteristics

  1. Expectation of a function: $E[g(\xi)]=\int g(x)f(x)dx$

    • Linearity: $E[a\xi+b]=aE[\xi]+b$

    • Variance: $D[a\xi+b]=a^2D[\xi]$

  2. Relationship between central and raw moments:

$$v_n=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^{n-k}C_n^k\mu_1^{n-k}\mu_k$$

  1. Minimum-variance property: $E[(\xi-E[\xi])^2]\leq E[(\xi-x)^2]$

Two-Dimensional Random Variables

Quantity Discrete Continuous
Joint raw moment $E[X^jY^k]=\sum\sum x_m^j y_n^k p_{m,n}$ $E[X^jY^k]=\iint x^j y^k f(x,y)dxdy$
Joint central moment $E[(X-E[X])^j(Y-E[Y])^k]$ Same as on the left
Correlation $R_{XY}=E[XY]$ Same as on the left
Covariance $K_{XY}=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]$ Same as on the left
Correlation coefficient $r_{XY}=\frac{K_{XY}}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}$ Same as on the left

Important Concepts

  • Covariance matrix:

$$\Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}K_{XX} & K_{XY}\ K_{YX} & K_{YY}\end{bmatrix}$$

  • Uncorrelated variables: $r_{XY}=0 \Leftrightarrow K_{XY}=0 \Leftrightarrow E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]$

Independence implies an absence of correlation, but the reverse is not necessarily true. Correlation describes only the degree of linear association between two random variables, whereas independence is a stronger condition. For a joint normal distribution, however, being uncorrelated is equivalent to being statistically independent.

  • Orthogonality: $E[XY]=0$. If either (X) or (Y) has a mean of zero, the absence of correlation is equivalent to orthogonality.

Linear Minimum Mean-Square Estimation

  • Optimal linear estimate: $\hat{Y}=E[Y]+\frac{K(X,Y)}{D(X)}(X-E[X])$

  • Minimum mean-square error: $\min e=(1-r_{XY}^2)D(Y)$

1.5 Characteristic Functions of Random Variables

Definition

In effect, this is simply a Fourier transform.

$$C(u)=E[e^{juX}]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{jux}f(x)dx$$

Properties

  1. Boundedness: $|C(u)|\leq C(0)=1$

  2. Conjugate symmetry: $C(-u)=\overline{C(u)}$

  3. Linear transformation: if $Y=aX+b$, then $C_Y(u)=e^{jub}C_X(au)$

  4. Moment generation: $E[X^k]=j^{-k}C^{(k)}(0)$

  5. Independence: if $X,Y$ are independent, then $C_{X+Y}(u)=C_X(u)C_Y(u)$

Characteristic Function of a Gaussian Distribution

  • The characteristic function of $X\sim N(a,\sigma^2)$ is:

$$C_X(u)=\exp\left(jau-\frac{\sigma^2 u^2}{2}\right)$$

  • A linear transformation of a Gaussian random variable remains Gaussian.

  • In the multidimensional case, if $X\sim N(m_X,K_X)$, then $Y=AX+b\sim N(Am_X+b,AK_XA^T)$.

entry.title: Chapter 5 — Analogue Modulation Systems
entry.content:
Definition and Purposes of Modulation

Modulation places the message signal $m(t)$ upon a certain parameter of the carrier, such as $\cos(\omega_c t)$, thereby producing a modulated signal.

Purposes

  1. To improve antenna radiation efficiency, which is achieved by shifting the spectrum. A low-frequency signal has a long wavelength and therefore requires an enormous antenna, whereas a high-frequency signal has a shorter wavelength and permits an antenna of reasonable size.

  2. To share spectrum resources. Different signals occupy different frequency bands through frequency-division multiplexing (FDM), making multichannel communication possible.

  3. To improve resistance to interference. Nonlinear modulation, such as FM, can improve the signal-to-noise ratio.

Carrier Signal

The textbook mainly discusses sinusoidal-wave modulation. Pulse modulation is set aside for the moment and may appear later.

A carrier signal is usually written as:

$$
c(t) = A_c \cos(\omega_c t + \phi_c)
$$

Here, $A_c$ is the carrier amplitude, $\omega_c$ is the carrier angular frequency, and $\phi_c$ is its initial phase. Modulation makes $A_c$, $\omega_c$, or $\phi_c$ vary with the baseband signal $m(t)$.

Classification of Analogue Modulation

  1. Amplitude Modulation (AM): the carrier amplitude varies with the signal. This is linear modulation.

    • DSB (double sideband)
    • AM (conventional amplitude modulation)
    • SSB (single sideband)
    • VSB (vestigial sideband)

  2. Angle Modulation (PM/FM): the carrier phase or frequency varies with $m(t)$.

    • FM (frequency modulation)
    • PM (phase modulation)

Linear Modulation Systems (Amplitude Modulation)

In linear modulation, the baseband signal $m(t)$ acts linearly upon the carrier amplitude. The modulated signal can be represented in the time domain as:

$$
s_{AM}(t) = A(t) \cos(\omega_c t)
$$

The general model of an amplitude modulator is:

Its particular type is determined by the different choices of $m(t)$ and $h(t)$.

Conventional Amplitude Modulation (AM)

Time-Domain Expression

An AM signal adds a carrier component to DSB:

$$
s_{AM}(t) = [A_0 + m(t)] \cos(\omega_c t)
$$

Here, $A_0$ is a DC offset and must satisfy $A_0 > |m(t)|_{max}$ so that $[A_0 + m(t)] > 0$ and overmodulation does not occur.

Modulation Index ($\mu$)

$$
\mu = \frac{|m(t)|_{max}}{A_0} \le 1
$$

A value greater than one indicates overmodulation, which causes distortion and a loss of information.

Power and Efficiency

The total power of an AM signal is $P_{AM} = P_c + P_{SB}$. The sideband power $P_{SB}$ carries information, whereas the carrier power $P_c$ carries none.

  • Efficiency: $\eta = \frac{P_{SB}}{P_c + P_{SB}}$. AM efficiency is generally low because the modulation index cannot exceed 1, and the carrier power must consequently be greater than the sideband power.

Demodulation Methods

Direct non-coherent demodulation can be performed with an envelope detector. It amounts to little more than a diode and a capacitor: the circuit is simple and requires no synchronised carrier.

Coherent demodulation is also possible and is relatively more complicated. Since the carrier component is available, however, synchronisation remains fairly easy. Remember that the DC component must be removed after demodulation.

Double-Sideband Suppressed-Carrier Modulation (DSB-SC)

Time-Domain Expression

There is no carrier component.

$$
s_{DSB}(t) = m(t) \cos(\omega_c t)
$$

Note that a reversal point appears when the carrier and input signal change polarity at the same time.

Frequency-Domain Characteristics

The spectrum of a DSB signal is obtained by shifting the baseband spectrum $M(\omega)$ to the left and right:

$$
S_{DSB}(\omega) = \frac{1}{2} [M(\omega - \omega_c) + M(\omega + \omega_c)]
$$

  • Bandwidth: $B_{DSB} = 2f_H$, where $f_H$ is the highest frequency of the baseband signal.
  • There is no carrier component.
  • The amplitude is reduced by half.

Demodulation Methods

The distinction between coherent and non-coherent demodulation can be summarised as follows:

(1) Coherent demodulation can operate with a signal-to-noise ratio below 0 dB;

(2) Non-coherent demodulation requires a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10 dB;

(3) Coherent demodulation offers better signal-to-noise performance, whereas non-coherent demodulation adapts more effectively to mobile conditions and environments with a wide dynamic range of signal-to-noise ratios.

Coherent demodulation is introduced first.

The receiver requires a local carrier $\cos(\omega_c t)$ with the same frequency and phase as the transmitted carrier.

The received signal contains no carrier component, so one must somehow be extracted. When can a frequency-domain component be generated? Through a nonlinear operation. Multiplication is therefore introduced:

  1. Multiplication:

$$r(t) = s_{DSB}(t) \cdot 2\cos(\omega_c t) = m(t) \cos^2(\omega_c t) = m(t) [1 + \cos(2\omega_c t)]$$

$$
r(t) = m(t) + m(t) \cos(2\omega_c t)
$$

  1. Low-pass filtering (LPF): Filter out the high-frequency term $m(t) \cos(2\omega_c t)$ to obtain $m(t)$. In effect, the coherent component is multiplied into the signal, after which the high-frequency part is removed.

Non-coherent demodulation was discussed above and will not be repeated.

Single-Sideband Modulation (SSB)

Spectral Characteristics

SSB retains only one of the upper sideband (USB) and lower sideband (LSB), thereby saving a substantial amount of bandwidth and improving power efficiency.

Because an ideal filter does not exist, however, producing SSB in the frequency domain with an LPF is complicated and only moderately effective. Phase cancellation can also be used, but it is complicated as well.

A conventional AM receiver cannot receive an SSB signal because it can perform only envelope detection, not coherent demodulation.

  • Bandwidth: $B_{SSB} = f_H$.

Time-Domain Expression

$$
s_{SSB}(t) = m(t) \cos(\omega_c t) \mp \hat{m}(t) \sin(\omega_c t)
$$

Here, $\hat{m}(t)$ is the Hilbert transform of $m(t)$. A Hilbert transform shifts a sine or cosine by half of pi. The minus sign may be regarded as producing the upper sideband, whereas the plus sign produces the lower sideband.

Demodulation Method: Coherent Demodulation

SSB can be demodulated only coherently. Why exactly is that?

Vestigial-Sideband Modulation (VSB)

Spectral Characteristics

It is sufficient for the cut-off characteristic of the filter to satisfy the condition of complementary symmetry at the carrier frequency.

VSB retains one complete sideband and part of the other sideband—the vestigial sideband. It is therefore a compromise between DSB and SSB.

  • Bandwidth: $f_H < B_{VSB} < 2f_H$.

Advantage

VSB avoids the filter-realisation difficulty of SSB while retaining low-frequency components. It is consequently suitable for signals rich in low-frequency content, including a DC component, as in television transmission.

Demodulation Method: Coherent Demodulation

Angle-Modulation Systems (Nonlinear Modulation)

This material is not included in our examination, so the course discusses only a little of it. We basically need to know what FM and PM are, that they are nonlinear forms of modulation, that they generate many frequency-domain components and occupy a wider bandwidth, and that the resulting signal quality is better.

Angle modulation is nonlinear: either the carrier’s instantaneous phase or its instantaneous frequency varies with the baseband signal $m(t)$.

Frequency Modulation (FM)

Instantaneous Frequency

The instantaneous carrier frequency $\omega_i(t)$ varies linearly with $m(t)$:
$$
\omega_i(t) = \omega_c + k_f m(t)
$$
Here, $k_f$ is the frequency-modulation coefficient, measured in $\text{rad/s/V}$.

Time-Domain Expression

$$
s_{FM}(t) = A_c \cos[\omega_c t + \phi(t)]
$$
The instantaneous phase $\phi(t)$ is the integral of instantaneous frequency over time:
$$
\phi(t) = \int^t \omega_i(\tau) d\tau = \omega_c t + k_f \int^t m(\tau) d\tau
$$
The FM signal is:
$$
s_{FM}(t) = A_c \cos[\omega_c t + k_f \int^t m(\tau) d\tau]
$$

Modulation Index ($\beta$)

For single-tone modulation $m(t) = A_m \cos(\omega_m t)$, the modulation index of the FM signal is:
$$
\beta = \frac{\Delta \omega}{\omega_m} = \frac{k_f A_m}{\omega_m}
$$
Here, $\Delta \omega = k_f A_m$ is the maximum angular-frequency deviation.

Bandwidth (Carson’s Rule)

The spectrum of an FM signal is infinitely wide, but most of its energy is concentrated within a finite bandwidth. Carson’s rule estimates its effective bandwidth:
$$
B_{FM} \approx 2(\Delta f + f_m) = 2(\beta + 1) f_m
$$
Here, $\Delta f$ is the maximum frequency deviation in hertz.

Demodulation Method

An FM signal is generally demodulated with a frequency discriminator, which converts changes in frequency into changes in amplitude before envelope detection or low-pass filtering is performed.

Phase Modulation (PM)

Instantaneous Phase

The instantaneous carrier phase $\theta_i(t)$ varies linearly with $m(t)$:
$$
\theta_i(t) = \omega_c t + k_p m(t)
$$
Here, $k_p$ is the phase-modulation coefficient.

Time-Domain Expression

$$
s_{PM}(t) = A_c \cos[\omega_c t + k_p m(t)]
$$

Relationship between FM and PM

  • Integrate $m(t)$ and then perform FM modulation on the carrier to obtain a PM signal.
  • Differentiate $m(t)$ and then perform PM modulation on the carrier to obtain an FM signal.

Resistance of Analogue Modulation Systems to Noise

The noise resistance of a communication system is generally measured through that of its demodulator. The performance of different modulation systems is studied in the presence of additive Gaussian white noise in the channel.

Performance-Analysis Model and Measures

Receiver Model

After the modulated signal $s_m(t)$ is mixed with the additive Gaussian white noise $n(t)$ of the channel, it first passes through a band-pass filter (BPF), which removes noise outside the signal band. The signal entering the demodulator is $s_m(t)$ and its noise is $n_i(t)$. The useful output of the demodulator is $m_o(t)$, while the output noise is $n_o(t)$.

Characteristics of Input Noise

The noise $n_i(t)$ entering the demodulator is obtained when stationary Gaussian white noise $n(t)$ passes through a band-pass filter, and can be regarded as stationary narrowband Gaussian noise.

Narrowband Gaussian noise can be represented as:

$$
n_{i}(t)=n_{c}(t)\cos\omega_{c}t-n_{s}(t)\sin\omega_{c}t
$$

Here, $n_c(t)$ and $n_s(t)$ are respectively the in-phase and quadrature components. Both have a mean of $0$ and the same variance.

  • Input noise power: If the one-sided power spectral density of the white noise is $N_0$, and the BPF bandwidth is $B$, equal to the modulated-signal bandwidth $W$:

    $$
    N_{i}=\overline{n_{i}^{2}(t)}=N_{0}B
    $$

Quality Measures

  1. Output signal-to-noise ratio (Output SNR): This measures the quality of the demodulator output.

    $$
    \frac{S_{o}}{N_{o}}=\frac{\overline{m_{o}^{2}(t)}}{\overline{n_{o}^{2}(t)}}
    $$

  2. Input signal-to-noise ratio (Input SNR):

    $$
    \frac{S_{i}}{N_{i}}=\frac{\overline{s_{m}^{2}(t)}}{\overline{n_{i}^{2}(t)}}
    $$

  3. Modulation-system gain: This is used to compare the performance of modulation systems of the same type.

    $$
    G=\frac{S_{o}/N_{o}}{S_{i}/N_{i}}
    $$

Performance Derivation for Linear Modulation Systems

1. DSB-SC Modulation System (Coherent Demodulation)

  • Input signal power: $S_{i} = \overline{s_{DSB}^{2}(t)} = \frac{1}{2}\overline{m^{2}(t)}$.

  • Output signal: $m_{o}(t)=\frac{1}{2}m(t)$.

  • Output signal power: $S_{o} = \overline{m_{o}^{2}(t)} = \frac{1}{4}\overline{m^{2}(t)}$.

  • Output noise power: $N_{o} = \frac{1}{4}\overline{n_{i}^{2}(t)} = \frac{1}{4}N_{0}B$.

  • Modulation-system gain: $G_{DSB} = 2$.

2. SSB-SC Modulation System (Coherent Demodulation)

  • Bandwidth: $B=W$, the baseband-signal bandwidth.

  • Output signal power: $S_{o}=\overline{m_{o}^{2}(t)}=\frac{1}{16}\overline{m^{2}(t)}$.

  • Output noise power: $N_{o} = \frac{1}{4}N_{0}W$.

  • Modulation-system gain: $G_{SSB} = 1$.

3. Performance Comparison between DSB and SSB

Although $G_{DSB}=2$ and $G_{SSB}=1$, these values do not directly prove that DSB performs better, because the input signal powers and bandwidths of the two systems differ.

Conclusion: Under the same input signal power $S_i$, the same noise power spectral density $N_0$, and the same baseband-signal bandwidth $W$, DSB and SSB have an equal output signal-to-noise ratio, indicating that their resistance to noise is the same.

4. Performance of AM Envelope Detection

  • High signal-to-noise ratio: Envelope detection performs as well as coherent demodulation.

  • Low signal-to-noise ratio: A threshold effect occurs. At a low signal-to-noise ratio, the envelope detector confuses the useful signal with noise, and the output signal-to-noise ratio deteriorates sharply.

Performance Comparison of Analogue Modulation Systems

Modulation Transmission bandwidth DC response Equipment complexity Main applications
DSB $2f_H$ (none) None Moderate: coherent demodulation required Analogue data transmission
AM $2f_H$ (present) Present Low: simple modulation and demodulation Radio broadcasting
SSB $f_H$ (none) None High: coherent demodulation required; modulator also relatively complicated Speech communication and frequency-division multiplexing of speech channels
VSB $f_H < B < 2f_H$ (present) Present High: coherent demodulation required; modulator needs a symmetric filter Data transmission and broadband television systems
FM $2(\Delta f + f_m)$ (present) Present Moderate: somewhat complicated modulator and relatively simple demodulator Data transmission, radio broadcasting, and microwave relay

Main Conclusions

  1. Resistance to noise: WBFM, or wideband frequency modulation, performs best; DSB, SSB, and VSB come next, while AM performs worst. When the input signal-to-noise ratio is high, a larger FM modulation index $\beta$ produces stronger resistance to noise.

  2. Spectral efficiency: SSB has the narrowest bandwidth, $B_{SSB}=f_H$, and therefore the highest spectral efficiency. FM occupies the greatest bandwidth, which increases with the modulation index $\beta$, and consequently has the lowest spectral efficiency.

  3. Trade-off: FM is a typical example of sacrificing effectiveness, in the form of bandwidth, in exchange for reliability, in the form of resistance to noise.

Frequency-Division Multiplexing (FDM)

Concept and Purpose

Multiplexing: a technology that addresses how several signals can be transmitted simultaneously through a single physical channel. Its purpose is to make full use of the frequency, time, and spatial resources of a channel, thereby improving channel utilisation.

Frequency-division multiplexing (FDM): a form of multiplexing that divides a channel by frequency.

Principle and Implementation of FDM

  1. Division into frequency bands: Divide the total channel bandwidth into several non-overlapping bands, or subchannels, each occupied by one signal.

  2. Guard bands: Leave an unused guard band between adjacent signals so as to prevent spectral overlap and interchannel interference.

  3. Transmitter: Each baseband signal $m_i(t)$ first passes through a low-pass filter (LPF) and is then multiplied by a different carrier $\omega_{c_i}$ for modulation. A sideband filter ($\text{SBF}_i$) selects the required sideband, after which an adder combines the modulated signals and sends them into the channel.

  4. Receiver: The received composite signal passes through a band-pass filter ($\text{BPF}i$), which separates the corresponding subchannel. It is then multiplied by a carrier $\omega{c_i}$ of the same frequency for demodulation, and finally passes through an LPF to recover the original baseband signal $m_i(t)$.

Advantages and Disadvantages of FDM

Advantages:

  1. High channel utilisation.

  2. A large number of channels can be multiplexed.

  3. Individual channels can be separated conveniently by frequency.

Disadvantages:

  1. The equipment is relatively complicated to manufacture.

  2. Imperfect filter characteristics and nonlinearities within the channel can produce interchannel interference.

entry.title: Chapter 4 — Communication Channels
entry.content:
Definition of a Channel

A channel is a path through which a signal travels, and it is indispensable in a communication system.

Channel in the Narrow Sense

In the narrow sense, a channel refers to the transmission medium—the physical path between the transmitter and receiver.

  • Guided media: optical fibre, twisted-pair cable, and coaxial cable
  • Unguided media: radio and infrared waves

Channel in the Broad Sense

In the broad sense, a channel is an equivalent model that incorporates some of the other equipment in a communication system:

  • A modulation channel extends from the output of the modulator to the input of the demodulator, and concerns modulated signals.
  • A coding channel extends from the output of the encoder to the input of the decoder, and concerns digital sequences.

Modulation-Channel Model

A modulation channel transmits modulated signals, so the main concerns are signal distortion and the influence of noise. Because the instantaneous value of a modulated signal varies continuously, it is also called a continuous channel—or, in some contexts, simply a channel.

Its detailed characteristics do not seem especially important here. They probably belong to general background knowledge, so I will not describe them further.

The textbook states that the great majority of modulation channels are linear. It should be noted, however, that this is merely an approximation adopted at the present stage because our analytical ability is still limited.

Its mathematical model is shown below:

Coding-Channel Model

A coding channel, also called a digital channel, contains and depends on a modulation channel. Its interference is reflected in bit errors, and its principal performance measure is therefore the bit error rate.

Depending on whether the transition probability between successive symbols is dependent on earlier symbols, coding channels may be further divided into channels with memory and channels without memory.

Performance Parameters

The reliability of a communication system is mainly affected by two factors: noise and imperfections in the transmission characteristics of the channel.

Characteristics of Constant-Parameter Channels

Examples

Twisted-Pair Cable

Twisted-pair cable can be used for both analogue and data transmission. Its bandwidth depends on the thickness of the cable and the transmission distance.

It is divided into unshielded twisted pair (UTP) and shielded twisted pair (STP); the latter uses foil shielding to reduce interference.

Coaxial Cable

Baseband coaxial cable: 50 $\Omega$. It transmits baseband digital signals for data communication and is widely used in local area networks.
10 Mb/s, 1 km

Broadband coaxial cable: 75 $\Omega$. It is mainly used in CATV systems to carry frequency-division-multiplexed analogue signals.
6 MHz/300–400 MHz, 100 km

Optical Fibre

An optical fibre is a double-layer cylindrical communication medium that carries information through light waves. It offers high transmission rates, a broad bandwidth, low loss, strong resistance to interference, good confidentiality, and low weight. Yet optical modulators and photodetectors are required at the two ends, making the system relatively complicated. Connections can also be troublesome, and the fibre itself is fragile—step on it once and it is gone.

Three wavelength windows are commonly used:

0.85 um: attenuation is high, so the transmission rate and distance are limited, but the equipment is inexpensive;

1.30 um: attenuation is low; without dispersion compensation or power amplification, the maximum range is 40 km in the worst case;

1.55 um: attenuation is low; without dispersion compensation or power amplification, the maximum range is 80 km in the worst case.

Terrestrial Line-of-Sight Radio Relay

Transmission between two ground stations, point to point.

Distance: 50–100 km; frequency: 2G–40 GHz

Its performance depends on the weather and operating frequency.

Applications include long-distance transmission of speech and television signals, as well as LAN interconnection between buildings.

Communication-Satellite Relay Channel

This classification is becoming absurd. You are seriously telling me that this thing has constant parameters? Who exactly is supposed to believe that?

It uses microwaves.

A transponder receives and retransmits signals.

Advantages include a long transmission distance, broad geographical coverage, stable and reliable transmission, and high capacity.

Applications include television-signal transmission, long-distance speech transmission, and the construction of private networks.

Point-to-multipoint transmission is supported.

C band: 4/6 GHz

Uplink: 5.925–6.425 GHz
Downlink: 3.7–4.2 GHz

Ku band: 12/14 GHz

Uplink: 14–14.5 GHz
Downlink: 11.7–12.2 GHz

Characteristics

In a constant-parameter channel, the channel characteristics do not change with time. More specifically:

$$ h(t) \Leftrightarrow H(\omega) = |H(\omega)| e^{j\varphi(\omega)} $$

Amplitude-frequency characteristic: $|H(\omega)|$

Phase-frequency characteristic: $\varphi(\omega)$

Group-delay characteristic: $\tau(\omega) = -\frac{d\varphi(\omega)}{d\omega}$

Characteristics of Time-Varying Channels

Examples

Short-Wave Ionospheric-Reflection Channel

All right, this one certainly varies more than the previous examples.

The ionosphere is an atmospheric layer 60–600 km above the ground. Counting upward from the surface, the atmosphere can be divided into the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, ionosphere, and exosphere. The refractive index of the medium decreases with altitude, so the path of a radio wave gradually bends until total reflection occurs at a certain height.

Short wave: 3–30 MHz (100–10 m)

This mode of transmission has no blind zone and requires only simple, flexible equipment. Antarctic scientific expeditions, for example, use it as a means of communication. The ionosphere reflects the frequency bands used by ordinary radio broadcasting, but it cannot reflect radio waves with shorter wavelengths. Television happens to use shorter radio waves, which is why a television set cannot receive programmes from a distant station by this mechanism.

Transmission reliability is poor, and the operating frequency must be changed frequently.

Applications include short-wave broadcasting, emergency communication, disaster-response communication, and military communication.

The most basic reason short-wave communication attracts users is that long-distance communication requires only modest transmission power and moderately priced equipment. It also possesses a relay system—the ionosphere—that is not easily “destroyed”. Practice has shown that short-wave communication modernised with contemporary technology can provide high-quality, reasonably priced links with high availability. It nevertheless has several shortcomings, mainly in the following two respects:

  1. It cannot overcome the weaknesses inherent in the high-frequency medium itself;

  2. It cannot resist interception or various forms of deliberate interference.

It can also produce multipath propagation:

Tropospheric-Scatter Channel

The troposphere is the part of the atmosphere below an altitude of roughly 10–12 km.

It is used with very-high-frequency and microwave bands.

Its advantages include strong survivability, good confidentiality, high mobility, and an ability to adapt to complex terrain.

It supports point-to-point communication in military applications, between islands and the mainland, and in emergency or disaster-relief communication.

Other Examples

Other examples include short-wave ionospheric reflection, VHF meteor-trail scattering, VHF and microwave tropospheric scattering, short-wave ionospheric scattering, and beyond-line-of-sight VHF diffraction.

Characteristics

With respect to signal transmission, the transmission medium has the dominant influence, whereas the influence of converters is secondary and may even be neglected. The main task is therefore to study the common characteristics of transmission media and their effects on signals.

Characteristics of Time-Varying Channels

In multipath transmission, the attenuation and delay of every path vary randomly. Both the attenuation imposed on the signal and the transmission delay consequently change over time.

In mathematical language:

We can see that R(X) may be regarded as a narrowband random process: multipath propagation turns a deterministic single-frequency carrier into a narrowband signal whose envelope and phase are both modulated—that is, a fading signal.

From the time-domain perspective, the result is multipath delay spread; from the frequency-domain perspective, it is frequency dispersion or broadening.

Statistical Characteristics

When $n$ is sufficiently large, $X_c(t)$ and $X_s(t)$ are stationary Gaussian processes, so $R(t)$ is a narrowband Gaussian process.

The one-dimensional distribution of $V(t)$ is a Rayleigh distribution, corresponding to Rayleigh fading:

$$f(V) = \frac{V}{\sigma^2}\exp\left(-\frac{V^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \quad V \geq 0, \sigma > 0$$

The one-dimensional distribution of $\varphi(t)$ is a uniform distribution:

$$f(\varphi) = \frac{1}{2\pi}, \quad -\pi \leq \varphi \leq \pi $$

Frequency-Selective Fading

This is the fading of certain components in a signal spectrum. After the frequency components of a signal arrive over multiple paths, their phases differ. Components with the same phase reinforce one another when their vectors are added, whereas components with opposite phases cancel. The amplitudes of different frequency components in the received signal therefore change, much as if the signal had passed through a selectively attenuating network; hence the term frequency-selective fading.

Coherence Bandwidth and Types of Fading

Frequency-selective fading in multipath propagation depends on the relative delay difference, represented by the maximum multipath delay difference $\tau_m$.

The coherence bandwidth is defined as:

$$\Delta f = \frac{1}{\tau_m} $$

When the signal bandwidth satisfies $B > \Delta f$, the waveform $R(t)$ is distorted, producing frequency-selective fading;

When the signal bandwidth satisfies $B << \Delta f$, the strength of $R(t)$ varies over time and depends on $\tau$, producing flat fading, or general fading;

To avoid obvious frequency-selective fading, $B$ should be smaller than $\Delta f$. Techniques such as diversity reception may also be adopted to stabilise the signal.

To be honest, I still do not quite understand this part.

Improvement

Diversity

Concept

Diversity reception is an important technique developed in mobile communication to overcome various forms of fading and improve system performance.

Its basic principle is to separate the received multipath signal into several uncorrelated, or independent, signals, and then combine their energy according to a particular rule so as to maximise the useful signal energy at the receiver.

For a digital system, the objective is to minimise the bit error rate at the receiver.
For an analogue system, the objective is to improve the signal-to-noise ratio at the receiver.

Forms of Diversity

Time diversity uses time interleaving and channel coding to provide replicas of a signal in the time domain.

Frequency diversity transmits symbols on different carrier frequencies, thereby providing replicas in the frequency domain.

Space diversity is realised through multiple antennas.

Combining

Selection combining chooses the branch with the highest signal-to-noise ratio; naturally, the result will tend towards a limiting value at a later stage.

Equal-gain combining adds the signals from all branches directly with the same gain.

Maximum-ratio combining sets the gain of each branch in proportion to the signal-to-noise ratio of that branch.

entry.title: Chapter 3 — Random Signal Analysis
entry.content:
Random signal analysis is actually the subject of another course. Here it is treated only briefly, almost as an outline; the teacher did not expect us to understand all of it at this stage either.

The Concept of a Random Process

What Is a Random Process?

A random signal in communication is unpredictable and therefore random, yet it still follows statistical regularities. We consequently need the mathematical concept of a random process to describe it. It is not deterministic.

A random process is the collection of the time evolutions produced by different outcomes of a random experiment. Put differently, it is a time function whose value at each moment remains uncertain and is therefore a random variable.

A sample function is a concrete realisation of a random process, whereas the sample space consists of all such realisations. Taken together, all the sample functions and their statistical characteristics constitute the random process.

A random process is essentially an extension of the concept of a random variable, with a time variable added.

General Representation of a Random Process

Like many other methods of analysis, this one moves from a single fragment to several fragments, and from the characteristics at one point to the relationships among multiple points.

Distribution Functions and Probability Densities

One-Dimensional Case

A random process can be characterised by a distribution function and a probability density. The underlying idea is as follows.

At any given moment, a random process is a random variable. If we take a slice at that moment and regard the various probabilities within the slice as an independent distribution, we can obtain the one-dimensional distribution function and probability density at that time.

The formulas are:

$$F_1(x_1, t_1) = P\left{ \xi(t_1) \leq x_1 \right}$$

$$f_1(x_1, t_1) = \frac{\partial F_1(x_1, t_1)}{\partial x_1}$$

Note that $t_1$ is treated as a fixed value in both the one-dimensional distribution function and the probability density.

n-Dimensional Case

A one-dimensional distribution or density function describes only the statistical characteristics of a random process at a single instant. This idea can then be extended to the probability distribution and density at any fixed set of n moments. The larger n becomes, the fuller—and more complicated—the description of the statistical characteristics will be.

$$F_1(x_1, x_2; t_1,t_2) = P\left{ \xi(t_1) \leq x_1,\xi(t_2) \leq x_2 \right}$$

I seem to remember that second-order quantities were usually enough in the random signal analysis course. For those of us working on communication, such precision is generally unnecessary; the numerical characteristics of a random process are sufficient.

Numerical Characteristics of a Random Process

Mean or Mathematical Expectation

For a random process, the mean is calculated at each time slice. It is a function of time, but it should be noted that this function is deterministic. I will omit the detailed calculation.

Variance

Omitted.

Both the mean and variance depend only on the one-dimensional probability density function, and they reflect the characteristics of the random process at each moment.

Correlation Function

The correlation function describes an internal relationship within a random process—namely, the relationship between two random variables belonging to the process at any two moments.

Autocorrelation Function

$$R(t_1, t_2) = E\left[ \xi(t_1)\xi(t_2) \right] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x_1 x_2 f_2(x_1, x_2; t_1, t_2) dx_1 dx_2$$

It reflects the correlation between the values of a random process at different times—admittedly a rather vague sentence—and is often used to analyse periodicity or stationarity in time-series signals. The following offers one way to understand where the formula comes from.

Consider what may happen when two sets of data are multiplied element by element and the products are then added.

If the signs in both sets are random, will the average product not approach zero? Once some relationship exists between their signs, however, the result of multiplying and adding will deviate to one side or the other of zero.

We can therefore match this multiply-and-add operation to the analysis of a random process. Is it not, in effect, an average of products? In this way, it can reveal the correlation between the values of the process at different moments.

Autocovariance Function

$$B(t_1, t_2) = E\left{ \left[ \xi(t_1) - a(t_1) \right] \left[ \xi(t_2) - a(t_2) \right] \right} = R(t_1, t_2) - a(t_1)a(t_2)$$

By the same reasoning, the autocovariance function improves upon the autocorrelation function by adopting a centred form, thereby preventing an offset from distorting the result.

Correlation Coefficient

$$
\rho(t_1, t_2) = \frac{B(t_1, t_2)}{\sigma(t_1)\sigma(t_2)}$$

If $\rho(t_1, t_2) = 0$, then $\xi(t_1)$ and $\xi(t_2)$ are said to be uncorrelated.

Joint Distribution Function and Probability Density

I did not quite understand this part. I will leave it for the random signal analysis course; it is not central here, and the textbook does not even include it.

Examples of Random Processes

Stationary Random Processes

Definition

If the statistical characteristics of a random process are independent of the starting point in time and always obey the same statistical pattern, the process is strictly stationary.

Equivalently, every finite-dimensional probability density must be independent of the starting time. The one-dimensional probability density is independent of time t, while the two-dimensional distribution depends only on the time interval $\tau$. The criterion is shown below:

The mean of a strictly stationary process is constant, and its autocorrelation function depends only on the time interval.

This condition is, of course, relatively strict and rarely needed in ordinary work. We generally use wide-sense stationarity instead.

A wide-sense stationary process need only satisfy two requirements: its mean is constant, and its autocorrelation function depends solely on the time interval.

Property

Ergodicity

Take any one realisation of a random process, and over time it will pass through all the possibilities contained in that process.

To put it more vividly, imagine turning on a switch in an unchanging environment and never turning it off. The random signal it produces over time contains all the information.

This is convenient because temporal characteristics can replace statistical ones. We no longer need to know the distribution function of the random process: whenever an average is required, a time average may replace a statistical average.

Note that an ergodic process must be stationary, but a stationary process is not necessarily ergodic. The two conditions are not mutually necessary and sufficient.

Postscript

The autocorrelation function of a real stationary random process has several further properties. I will not discuss them here; they can wait until the exercises require them.

There are also several calculations involving its power spectral density:

Gaussian Random Processes

Definition

If every n-dimensional distribution of a random process is normal, the process is called a Gaussian random process, or a normal process.

Important Properties

  • The n-dimensional distribution of a Gaussian process is completely determined by the mathematical expectations and variances of the n random variables $x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n$, together with the normalised covariance function between every pair of variables;

  • A wide-sense stationary Gaussian process is also strict-sense stationary;

  • If the values of a Gaussian process at different moments are uncorrelated, they are also statistically independent:

$$f_n(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n; t_1, t_2, \cdots, t_n) = f(x_1, t_1) f(x_2, t_2) \cdots f(x_n, t_n) $$

  • For Gaussian variables, being uncorrelated is equivalent to being independent;

  • A Gaussian process remains Gaussian after a linear transformation, or after passing through a linear system, although its numerical characteristics change;

  • The algebraic sum of several Gaussian processes remains Gaussian, although its numerical characteristics change:

Suppose

$$X_1 \sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2) ， X_2 \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2) $$

Then

$$aX_1 + bX_2 \sim N(a\mu_1 + b\mu_2, a^2\sigma_1^2 + b^2\sigma_2^2) $$

Two more slides of material are omitted here.

Narrowband Random Processes

The output produced when a random process passes through a narrowband system centred at the frequency $f_c$ is a narrowband process.

A narrowband system is one whose passband width satisfies $\Delta f<<f_c$, where $f_c$ is far from zero frequency.

In practice, most communication systems are narrowband. Any signal or noise that passes through a narrowband system must itself be narrowband; if the signal or noise is also random, it is called a narrowband random process.

If the waveform of one realisation is observed on an oscilloscope, it appears as shown in Figure 2-4: a sinusoid whose frequency is approximately $f_c$ and whose envelope and phase vary slowly and randomly. The slow variation matters; otherwise, the bandwidth of the baseband signal would not remain narrow.

A Sinusoid Plus a Narrowband Gaussian Process

This is an application of the preceding sections.

One common method of modulation uses a sinusoid—the simplest waveform—as the carrier. The receiver then accepts a composite waveform containing the modulated sinusoidal signal and narrowband Gaussian noise.

Gaussian White Noise and Band-Limited White Noise

Definition

White noise is noise whose power spectral density is constant at every frequency. Thus:

Two-sided power spectral density: $P_n(f) = \frac{n_0}{2} (-\infty < f < +\infty )$

One-sided power spectral density: $P_n(f) = n_0 (0 < f < +\infty)$

Here, $n_0$ is a positive constant.

Autocorrelation function of white noise: Taking the inverse Fourier transform of the two-sided power spectral density gives the correlation function:

$$ R(\tau) = \frac{n_0}{2} \delta(\tau)$$

entry.title: 2025-10-12 One Plus One
entry.content:
One

It seems that, in the course of a life, one must leave the place where one stands before the existence of distance can be understood. And so, at a midnight already touched by cold, I arrived at the airport. Familiar classmates travelled beside me; what truly kept me company was a question that appeared quietly at the beginning of the journey: why was I setting out?

Under the lights of the departure hall, I watched aircraft rise and land beyond the glass and thought about my own familiar cycle of sleeping and waking. The immense terminal appeared empty and indifferent. Someone stood by the railing with a book, taking shelter from one part of reality after another; someone else folded loneliness into a quiet posture across several seats. Leaning against an automatic massage chair while a meaningless mechanism pushed at my rigid back, I suddenly realised that what prevents sleep is never the hardness of a chair. It is the drifting sensation of belonging nowhere at that moment—no longer at the point of departure, not yet at the destination, suspended like a pendulum in mid-air and uncertain toward which end it should fall.

—Why was I setting out?

Guangzhou possesses a kind of low-voiced prosperity. Walking through the city, I passed the carved beams and painted rafters of the Chen Clan Ancestral Hall, where fine patterns of light turned across the walls like cloth wrinkled by time. Red flags lined the roads of Shamian Island, as if retelling the fierce years of past uprisings. I walked through damp old lanes, ate fragrant beef, drank a bowl of cool sweet soup, watched moss spread across mottled stone, and climbed Canton Tower to look down upon the lights of countless homes unfolding like a river of stars.

At that moment, however, I felt a desolate truth with unusual clarity. No matter how far one looks upward, how high one climbs, or how persistently one searches, a human being remains no more than a grain in the sea. Perhaps an entire life is enough only to light one’s own small candle.

The last time I looked upon a scene like this, I was travelling south from Beijing and sitting beside the aircraft window. The ground seemed to lie beneath my feet; the whole city could be taken in at a glance. I had the pride of youth, flowers and a spirited horse. Why, then, did the same view produce such a different state of mind now?

Perhaps it is time to seek the spirit of those honoured people of the past: neither delighted by external things nor saddened by personal fortune. Even if a lifetime purchases only one candle and one inch of light—unable to measure boundless space or disperse a night black as lacquer—that may be enough. That inch of light is sufficient to prove that we once stood and once breathed.

Sunset followed sunrise. At the old site of the Whampoa Military Academy, time acquired a solemn voice. The wind in the corners resembled an echo of the past; it raised no great wave and merely sighed beside the ear. Had I come several years earlier, I would probably have been full of confidence, discussing the fate of nations and writing with extravagant force. Now I lowered my head and walked in silence. I listened instead: to history turning itself into story within silence, and to the self distinguishing sincerity from performance within the returning echo. Memory and reality crossed beneath my feet. Many expectations and desires that had been enlarged and trusted proved to be little more than long acts of self-deception. What mattered was often only a small action in the present, a rational thought, or a quiet answer.

—Why was I setting out?

I reached Shenzhen at night. The city surged in the darkness like a tide. Skyscrapers stood without speaking, silent giants above the streets, while a helicopter cut a cold path overhead and crowds gathered only to disperse again. Beside the lake in Talent Park, I received news from home. The vibration of the phone felt unusually abrupt in my palm.

At that moment, a strange estrangement appeared. I was a grain of dark sand in an ocean of light, unable to enter the world’s current no matter how violently it moved. The louder the surroundings became, the more clearly one heard the echo inside oneself.

—For what did the person I was three years ago set out?

I entered Hong Kong through Lo Wu. Hong Kong seemed an absurd city, where prosperity existed beside decay and inclusion beside discrimination. Kowloon Walled City had become history, yet something of it still hid beneath the street’s neon lights, in the narrow lanes and in the rough, cold sound of Cantonese.

Inside an art exhibition, dismantled and reconstructed installations stood beside declarations against tradition. Under the neon lights, several questions flashed repeatedly: “What do you believe?” “Where do you stand?” I had no answer. I had imagined that travel meant looking at scenery; instead, the scenery had turned around to examine me.

I climbed the mountain road toward Victoria Peak. Every step pressed the questions again:

—What am I seeking? Why do I continue walking?

I remained silent. I did not know.

That night I watched the fireworks. Wind from Victoria Harbour moved across my face, while the city’s outline was softened by the water into a blurred line of verse. The fireworks and the light offered more than a moment’s splendour. Somewhere between immensity and smallness, they restored a sense of balance: the world remained vast, yet I could still breathe within it.

I still did not know why I had set out.

Beyond the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macao Bridge, the cities changed rapidly. Macao resembled a hollow city concealed beneath a fading shell of gold. The casinos remained brilliantly lit. People revolved through them, placed bets, shouted in triumph, then lost and left. Magnificence had hardened into an almost absurd stillness: the more splendid the surroundings, the smaller the people appeared. We held up our chips believing ourselves to be gambling with fate, without recognising that what we were spending was our own capacity for hope.

I suddenly understood that this journey had not been a search for answers. It had been an opportunity to observe the many forms of the world, to use other lives as mirrors, and to strip away one false and immature self after another until only a candle willing to burn remained.

I was setting out toward the beginning.

The return journey unfolded at the airport. The aircraft crossed the clouds and left behind the sea and lights of Lingnan. Beyond the window lay plains and mountains without apparent end, and a peculiar calm arrived. I had found no answer on the journey. Yet through repeated questions and fatigue, I had confirmed that I was still searching.

Perhaps that was already enough.
