We do not enter the world in order to win a particular ending. We enter it so that, in the limitless dark, we may remain willing to raise a small candle of our own. It may be weak and the wind may extinguish it at any moment. Yet as long as I choose to shelter it, it continues to burn.

I paused among the lights of the south. Now I carry one of them back within me. It does not illuminate the distance, but it illuminates the person I am at this moment.

—I am still on the road. I still have to set out.

Two

Before acting, one should certainly weigh advantages and harms. More important, however, is the recognition that every action moves some interest from one place to another. Whether the movement appears lighter than a feather or heavier than a mountain, it will touch another person’s boundary and disturb some invisible string.

There is therefore no need to be terrified of offending people. As long as the world continues to operate and people remain in contact, even a silent glance or an apparently casual answer contains movement—of resources, emotion, or position. Wherever something moves, friction follows. The promise that one can avoid offending everyone is little more than self-deception.

There are only three circumstances in which nobody is offended:

First, the other person voluntarily cuts away part of themselves and remains grateful for the opportunity.

Second, the sacrifice ends with you, while everyone else only receives.

Third, you are so insignificant that nobody cares even when you shout.

If that is so, one need ask only three questions: is my action logically consistent? Can I answer for it to my own conscience? Does it meet the standards by which I have chosen to conduct myself? If the left side of the brain has no reason to attack the right and one’s values do not begin fighting inside the chest, there is no need to tremble. A clear position should be followed by a steady step.

By contrast, if one hesitates over everything, retreats before everyone, and refuses to state a position, what others eventually see is not gentleness but transparency. To be understood is fortunate. To be ignored is a slow and silent disappearance.

entry.title: Principles of Communication, Chapter 1: Introduction
entry.content:
This textbook is, in fact, an introduction to an introduction. It provides the background of communication: what communication is, how its quality may be judged, and how information can be transmitted both efficiently and reliably.

This chapter supplies that initial background.

1. Basic Concepts of Communication

Objects of study: signals, messages, and information. Their distinctions can be left aside for the moment.

The basic system model is shown below:

An analog communication system uses a modulator and a demodulator. The frequency of an electrical signal suitable for transmission through free space is generally different from that of the source signal, so modulation is needed to transform it. The resulting signal is called a modulated signal, or a bandpass signal, because its spectrum is usually bandpass in character.

A digital communication system uses source coding, channel coding, and the corresponding demodulation and decoding procedures. It does not modulate information in quite the same way as an analog system. What it requires is digital modulation and demodulation, which amounts to shifting the spectrum, together with efficient AD conversion and interference suppression.

PS:

One disadvantage of digital communication is its relatively large demand for bandwidth. Its time-domain waveform is rather square and therefore contains high-frequency components. Even an approximation in the frequency domain cannot be too narrow without causing serious distortion.

Moreover, common digital modulation schemes, including ASK, PSK, and QAM, also carry digital information within a frequency band.

The higher the modulation order—for example, 16QAM or 64QAM—the more bits can be transmitted within the same bandwidth. This is what is commonly meant by an improvement in spectral efficiency.

Other classifications, such as half-duplex and full-duplex, need not be memorized at this stage. For now, it is enough to know what the field studies: the units of its objects and the model formed from those units.

2. Measuring Information

Information theory has already covered this part once. What operation did it use? Take the reciprocal and then the logarithm, and one obtains the self-information:

$$
I=-log_aP(x)
$$

This definition neatly satisfies two requirements:

  • The less probable an event is, the more information it carries.

  • The information carried by a message composed of several independent events equals the sum of the information carried by those individual events.

The information entropy $H$ of a discrete source is then defined as:

$$
H(x) = \sum P(x_i)I(x_i)
$$

It is simply a weighted sum describing the average amount of information.

One point deserves attention: the weights are determined by the probability distribution as a whole rather than by the observed sample. The following exercise illustrates the distinction:

3. Principal Performance Measures of a Communication System

The first measure is effectiveness, which describes whether a system can transmit signals efficiently. More specifically, it is judged through transmission rate.

In a digital communication system, bandwidth efficiency is defined as the transmission rate per unit bandwidth:

$$
\eta = \frac{R_B}{B}(Baud/Hz)
$$

or

$$
\eta_t = \frac{R_b}{B} \quad (\text{b/(s·Hz)})
$$

$R_B$ is the symbol transmission rate, or simply the symbol rate. It is the number of symbols transmitted per unit time, normally per second. Its unit is the baud (Baud), which is why it is also called the baud rate.

If the duration of each symbol is $T_B(s)$, then:

$$R_B = \frac{1}{T_B} \quad (\text{Baud}) $$

$R_b$ is the information transmission rate, also known as the bit rate. It is the average amount of information transmitted per unit time and is measured in bits per second (b/s).

Since each symbol in an $M$-ary system carries $\log_2 M$ bits of information, the symbol rate and information rate have the following definite relationship:

$$R_b = R_B \log_2 M \quad (\text{b/s})$$

or

$$R_B = \frac{R_b}{\log_2 M} \quad (\text{Baud})$$

For example, if the symbol rate is 1200 Baud and an octal system is used, the information rate is 3600 b/s.
If the duration of each binary symbol is T_b, then T_B and T_b are related as follows:

$$T_B = T_b \log_2 M$$

A good communication system must not merely transmit information; it must also ensure that the transmission is correct and reliable.

In an analog communication system, reliability is normally measured by the ratio of output signal power to noise power at the receiver, namely the signal-to-noise ratio (S/N). The value of S/N is related to the modulation scheme, a subject to be discussed later.

In a digital communication system, reliability can be represented by the error rate. It reflects the probability of an error during transmission and is often defined as the proportion of incorrectly transmitted symbols among all transmitted symbols. More precisely, the symbol error rate is the probability that a symbol is received incorrectly:

$$P_e = \frac{\text{错误码元数}}{\text{传输总码元数}}$$

or

$$P_b = \frac{\text{错误比特数}}{\text{传输总比特数}}$$

entry.title: Unknown
entry.content:
The brush suddenly descends. Its point barely touches the paper, yet, not knowing where the stroke should go, it can only spread into an enormous stain of ink, like a question waiting for someone to answer.

Why have I taken up the brush again to write sentences like these?

Perhaps this apparently useless act of writing, this murmur witnessed by nobody, comes closer to genuine usefulness than anything else.

Philosophers often say that meaning can be assigned to everything: birdsong becomes a courtship song, and the opening flower a promise of pollination. Yet ask one further question—what is the meaning of reproduction? Every species will eventually become extinct, and the universe will ultimately fall silent. Before that vast and intricate emptiness, “meaning” begins to look painfully thin. Reproduction ends in extinction; accumulation ends in dispersal. What difference is there between measuring the universe’s boundless void with a system of meaning constructed by the brief human mind and illuminating an eternal night with the light of a firefly? Every solid interpretation is a castle made of sand before everlasting silence. The tide arrives, and no trace remains.

To grieve over boundless space and the passage of time, however, is not necessarily to lead oneself toward the abyss of nihilism. On the contrary, once the emptiness of life has been admitted, those moments formerly dismissed as “wasted time” acquire a peculiar radiance. Like the stain spreading across the paper, the useless branches of ink extending freely in every direction are precisely what give it a form that cannot be repeated.

If the tower of meaning is ultimately a castle in the air, might the experience of complete absorption and the warmth of a genuine connection with another person constitute a form of existence that is both more real and more durable?

Perhaps I took up the brush only to write a sentence like that.

Have not the past two months at the radio station been just such a real existence? In Room 407, meaning no longer requires a grand defence. Planning, publicity, and organisation become pure because these trivial tasks possess no larger purpose. I am not trying to erect an eternal monument in the hope that someone at the station will remember me many years from now. I am simply greedy for the warmth of existence at that moment—for proof that, here and now, I am standing in Room 407, still breathing, my heart still beating.

We usually decide whether something should be done by calculating advantage and disadvantage. Yet some actions need not be justified by utility, just as some relationships need not be weighed for profit and loss. At this moment, you are looking at my words and I am imagining your existence. Though we have never met, in some sense we are already keeping one another company. That warmth need not be converted into money. It is, in itself, the purest consolation.

This hunger for existence may also explain why, even when I no longer need extra points for postgraduate recommendation, I remain willing to spend additional effort. Once stripped of their utilitarian clothing, the days and nights spent conducting experiments and writing documents become small acts of resistance against emptiness. I still remember the evening when the patent draft was finally complete. After dinner with my teacher, I rode back from Paradise Walk. Night had deepened; the wind was strong; shadows of roadside trees moved against the ground. It felt as though a tiny candle had at last been lit on an endless wasteland. I knew the wind might extinguish it at any moment, but for that instant its light revealed my own hand and barely illuminated an inch of the road ahead. It proved that I was still alive in the pitch-black night.

Or perhaps I wrote these sentences merely so that I could take up the brush.

As a wild goose leaves a trace in passing, I too would like to leave a small claw mark in the increasingly crowded field of object detection—perhaps a line bearing my name in some obscure journal. Yet research into fine-grained detection resembles a forest drowned in fog. Every hypothesis opens another fork in the path; the farther one travels, the more lost one becomes. Every paper warns of the effort demanded by datasets, computing power, model design, and repeated experiment.

I ask and ask. The empty valley returns only an echo, and even that eventually fades.

More troubling still are the delay and estrangement within me. Ambition wants to build a city, while action collapses like running sand. I long for an imagined self who advances without pause, yet move steadily in the opposite direction.

Even in hardship, remain resolute; never let the ambition of the clouds fall.

Seen differently, is this anxiety not itself evidence of existence? It arises from a desire not yet extinguished, rather than from the stillness of surrender. It resembles a trapped animal struggling, not dead water reflecting the sky. The circling and collision may not be futile; perhaps they are the necessary hesitation and gathering of strength through which life searches for its actual form. What matters is not whether I reach some shore selected in advance, but whether, during this hesitation, I can still feel the candle within. It flickers, but it has not gone out.

Heaven and earth are the inn of all things; time is the traveller of a hundred generations. If all of us are passing through, then every step—fast or slow, singing or weeping—is already a response to nothingness. Perhaps true victory lies not in achievement, but in knowing that life is like a dream and nevertheless cherishing this good night enough to carry a candle through it.

Once, I too was the naive person holding the rough ruler called “meaning” and attempting to measure the limitless sky. Now I would rather be an ordinary traveller who settles, for a while, within time that can actually be touched. Whether before a microphone at the radio station, beside an instrument in the laboratory, or at a desk buried under books, the important thing is no longer the result of the measurement. It is the walking itself.

Along a long journey, one occasionally encounters an unexpected view. Beside the road, for example, a graceful reed may stand in silence, its mere existence making the surrounding wasteland feel less absolute. Like the distant beloved in an ancient poem, it remains on the opposite bank. I neither need nor wish to struggle upstream and approach it, thereby destroying the perfection of the distance. The act of looking is already a gift. Like a breath of clean wind crossing the wasteland, it does not disperse the long night, but gives the candle’s movement an accompaniment. That wordless brightness, that distant reflection, reminds me that the world still contains beauty worth contemplating in silence. This alone is the gentlest confirmation of existence.

There is no preventing flowers from falling; the returning swallows seem familiar. Every frustration, heaviness, and unattainable thing resembles a season of blossom already gone. The marks of ink, the laughter carried by radio waves, the solitary lamp burning late in the laboratory, and even a distant blessing offered to that reed are the swallows returning with undiminished warmth.

Perhaps I have written these words not to obtain an answer, but simply to confirm that I am passing through—truly, contradictorily, and passionately. I am still alive.

Do not go gentle into that good night. Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

I took up the brush for no other reason. I merely wrote these sentences.

entry.title: A Review of Mathematical Modelling
entry.content:
The entire body of mathematical modelling can be organized into a framework consisting of three major pillars and a solid foundation. The framework classifies methods according to the central aim of the problem.

  • The first pillar is mechanism-driven modelling, or the white-box approach, whose central question is why. It builds differential or difference equations from known scientific principles, such as physical and biological laws, in order to explain and predict the dynamic behaviour of a system from first principles. It is particularly suitable when data are sparse or even absent but the governing mechanism is clear. It captures the essential laws of development rather than superficial patterns in the data. The process is: identify variables -> analyse the governing rules -> construct equations.

  • The second pillar is data-driven modelling, or the black-box approach, whose central question is what. When the internal mechanism of a system is too complicated to understand but abundant data are available, statistical and machine-learning techniques can learn the mapping from inputs to outputs directly from the data, allowing precise prediction, classification, and pattern recognition. The process is: collect and prepare data -> select a modelling paradigm -> train and validate the model.

  • The third pillar is decision-driven modelling, or optimization, whose central question is what should be done. It seeks the best solution to real-world problems such as resource allocation and route planning by optimizing an objective, such as profit or efficiency, under various constraints. Its main tools are mathematical programming and optimization algorithms. The process is: determine the decision variables -> construct the objective function -> specify the constraints.

  • The solid foundation consists of general tools and ways of thinking that support every modelling activity. These mainly include data interpolation and fitting, which bridge data and models, and a model-evaluation system, which safeguards model quality.

In practice, the three pillars are not independent and are often combined. An epidemic model, for example, may use mechanism-based modelling together with data fitting to estimate its parameters, while many sales problems join prediction to decision-making. Combining the strengths of different methods makes it possible to solve more complex real-world problems. Understanding this framework helps us recognize the essence of a new problem quickly and select the most appropriate modelling path.

Preface

As the opening article in this series on mathematical modelling, this review surveys the central ideas, methodology, and common technical branches of the subject. The material studied and organized here covers the following topics. The aim is to make the core idea of each method clear and provide a basis for later discussions of its implementation.

  • Methodology of mathematical modelling

  • Optimization modelling

  • Statistics and data mining

  • Data fitting and interpolation

  • Differential- and difference-equation modelling, or dynamic-process modelling

  • Machine learning and ensemble methods

  • Model evaluation

I. The Methodology of Mathematical Modelling

Mathematical modelling is the process of translating a real-world problem into mathematical language. However much the setting may change, the core process follows a scientific and systematic set of principles, which can be summarized in six steps.

  1. Problem understanding, or business understanding: first clarify the requirements and ultimate purpose of the problem. In a mathematical competition, this means analysing the question carefully, examining relevant literature and the current state of research, and rapidly identifying the available methods, their technical feasibility, expected performance, strengths, and weaknesses.

  2. Data understanding: examine the quantity and quality of the available data and assess their completeness and correctness. Calculate descriptive statistics and conduct exploratory data analysis, or EDA, to discover the inherent characteristics and patterns of the records and variables. Together with the literature, this allows us to judge which variables may be relevant to the target, whether the data need balancing, and which modelling method appears suitable at first sight.

  3. Data preparation: clean, transform, and reconstruct the raw data. This includes imputing missing values, handling outliers, and selecting variables relevant to the analytical objective. In regression analysis, for example, nominal variables such as sex and region must be converted into dummy variables. At times, derived variables constructed from expert knowledge—BMI calculated from height and weight, for instance—are more useful for modelling.

  4. Model selection and construction: select an appropriate modelling method according to the nature of the problem and the characteristics of the data. Parameters may be adjusted manually or determined through automated methods such as grid search and random search. If a single model performs poorly, or it is unclear which model is best, several can be trained and combined through ensemble learning to produce a model with better performance and stronger robustness.

  5. Model evaluation: assess the performance and effectiveness of the model objectively. Cross-validation and similar methods are commonly used to avoid fluctuations in measured accuracy caused by different divisions of the training and test sets. The central task is to determine whether the model underfits or overfits.

  6. Deployment and reporting: summarize and present the modelling results clearly and scientifically. The structure and logic of a scientific journal article can guide the organization of the result, helping ensure that the model is scientifically sound and innovative and that its conclusions are reliable.

II. Core Modelling Methods

2.1 Optimization, or Mathematical Programming

An optimization problem seeks the best values of its decision variables under a set of constraints, so that its objective function reaches a maximum or minimum.

  • Linear programming, LP: both the objective and every constraint are linear functions. This is the most fundamental optimization model, and an optimal solution must occur at a vertex of the feasible region. Its principal solution algorithms are the simplex method and interior-point methods.

  • Integer programming, IP: one or more decision variables in a linear program are required to take integer values. 0-1 integer programming, in which variables can equal only 0 or 1, is often used for yes-or-no decisions. It is much harder to solve than linear programming, and common algorithms include branch and bound and cutting planes.

  • Nonlinear programming, NLP: at least one objective or constraint function is nonlinear. This is the broadest and most complicated class of problems. Solutions usually depend on gradient descent, Newton’s method, or, for constrained problems, the method of Lagrange multipliers and the KKT conditions.

  • Combinatorial optimization: the decision variables are discrete, and the purpose is to “combine” a large number of possibilities into the best plan, as in the traveling salesperson problem, or TSP, and facility-location problems. Most such problems are NP-hard. Large instances are commonly approached with heuristics such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, and ant-colony optimization.

2.2 Data Interpolation and Fitting

When we face a series of discrete data points, interpolation and fitting provide two ways to turn them into a continuous function, but their underlying assumptions are entirely different.

  • Interpolation:

    • Central idea: assume that every data point is perfectly accurate and require the constructed curve to pass strictly through each one.

    • Methods: classical polynomial interpolation, including the Lagrange and Newton methods, encounters Runge’s phenomenon, or violent oscillations near the boundary, in high-degree problems. Spline interpolation, especially cubic splines, was developed to overcome this difficulty. By joining low-degree polynomial pieces smoothly, it balances precision and smoothness exceptionally well and is now the most robust interpolation method.

  • Data fitting:

    • Central idea: assume that data contain random error or noise. Instead of forcing the curve through any point, find the curve that best represents the overall trend.

    • Methods: the foundation is least squares, which seeks a curve that minimizes the sum of the squared differences, or residuals, between observed values and function predictions. According to the form of the function, fitting may be linear, polynomial, or nonlinear. A nonlinear relationship is often linearized through a change of variables before it is solved.

2.3 Statistics and Data Mining

When the internal mechanism of a problem is unclear but sufficient data are available, statistical and data-mining methods—the black-box approach—can discover regularities and patterns in the data.

  • Exploratory data analysis, EDA: before modelling, calculate descriptive statistics such as the mean and variance and produce visualizations such as histograms, box plots, and scatter plots. These reveal internal structures, patterns, outliers, and relationships among variables.

  • Hypothesis testing: determine whether the situation reflected by a sample differs significantly from a proposed null hypothesis. Assuming that the null is true, calculate the probability—the p-value—of observing the current sample result. If that value is sufficiently small, below 0.05 for example, reject the null. Common methods include the t-test for means, the F-test for variances and analysis of variance or ANOVA, and the chi-squared test for associations among categorical variables.

  • Correlation and regression analysis:

    • Correlation analysis measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two continuous variables, using Pearson’s coefficient, or of an ordinal relationship, using Spearman’s coefficient.

    • Regression analysis builds a quantitative model of the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables for prediction and explanation. Linear regression is fundamental and assumes linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, and normality. Regularized methods such as ridge regression and Lasso regression were developed to address multicollinearity.

  • Classification modelling is used when the dependent variable is categorical. Despite its name, logistic regression is a binary classification model. Other common models include decision trees, support vector classification or SVC, and random forests.

  • Cluster analysis is an unsupervised-learning method. With no predefined classes, it automatically groups samples according to their similarity—birds of a feather, so to speak. The best-known method is K-Means.

2.4 Differential and Difference Equations: Dynamic-Process Modelling

When a process evolves through time or space and its internal mechanism is clear, differential and difference equations are the preferred white-box tools.

  • Difference equations describe discrete, stepwise change, such as a population updated once a year. The central task is to establish the relationship between the present state $x_{n+1}$ and one or more earlier states $x_n, x_{n-1},…$. The classic Logistic model describes discrete population change under resource constraints and can even display chaotic behaviour.

  • Differential equations describe smooth, continuous dynamic development. The central task is to identify the relationship between the rate of change and the current state. For example, $\frac{dx}{dt} = kx$ describes unrestricted exponential growth or decay.

  • Qualitative analysis: analytical solutions to either difference or differential equations are often difficult to obtain. It is therefore essential to study the long-term behaviour of a model, chiefly by finding its equilibrium points and judging their stability. Stability analysis tells us whether a system will return to equilibrium or collapse after a small disturbance.

  • Partial differential equations, PDEs: if the object under study changes not only over time but also with spatial position, partial differential equations are needed. One example is the diffusion of a pollutant through lake water.

2.5 Machine Learning and Ensemble Methods

  • Machine learning, at the intersection of statistics and computer science, offers a large collection of powerful modelling tools and is particularly effective for high-dimensional and complicated nonlinear problems. Decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks, all mentioned above, belong to this field.

  • Ensemble learning is an advanced modelling strategy. Instead of relying on one model, it combines several “weak” learners into a more capable “committee of experts,” improving overall accuracy and robustness.

    • Bagging trains several models in parallel, as random forests train decision trees, and improves performance by voting or averaging their outputs.

    • Boosting trains models in sequence. Each new model concentrates on the samples predicted incorrectly by the preceding one and thereby “corrects” its errors. Representative algorithms include AdaBoost and XGBoost.

    • Stacking uses the outputs of several first-layer models as features for training a second-layer meta-model. It is a more complex form of ensemble learning.

III. Model Evaluation

Once a model has been built, objective standards are required to measure its performance. Evaluation metrics differ according to the type of model, particularly classification or prediction.

  • Metrics for classification models, calculated from the confusion matrix:

    • Accuracy: the proportion of all samples that are classified correctly. It can be misleading when the sample is imbalanced.

    • Precision: the proportion of samples predicted as positive that are genuinely positive. It matters when the cost of a false positive is high.

    • Recall: the proportion of all genuine positive samples that are successfully identified. It matters when the cost of a false negative is high.

    • F1-score: the harmonic mean of precision and recall and thus a combined measure.

  • Metrics for regression models:

    • Root mean squared error, RMSE: the square root of the mean of the squared differences between predicted and observed values. It has the same unit as the original data and is easy to interpret.

    • Mean absolute error, MAE: the mean of the absolute differences between predicted and observed values. It is less sensitive to outliers.

    • Coefficient of determination, $R^2$: the percentage of variation in the dependent variable that the model can explain. A value closer to 1 is better.

    • Adjusted coefficient of determination, or adjusted $R^2$: it accounts for the number of independent variables in addition to $R^2$, making it fairer when models of different complexity are compared.

IV. Summary of Applications and Tools

  • Problems governed by physical laws: if precise physical or natural laws underlie the problem, white-box models such as differential equations are preferred because they describe the system through its mechanism.

  • Statistical and financial problems: if the mechanism is unclear but data are abundant, black-box methods such as statistical models, data mining, and machine learning are generally used to discover data-driven patterns. Derivative pricing in financial mathematics, such as the BSM partial differential equation, is an exception.

  • Decision and planning problems: resource allocation, route selection, strategy design, and similar tasks centre on optimization and require an objective function and constraints.

Whatever the problem, a powerful mathematical-modelling toolbox should include at least:

  • data fitting and interpolation for preprocessing data and turning observations into functions;

  • optimization for solving decision problems;

  • machine-learning and statistical models for learning and prediction from data;

  • approximation methods for solving differential and difference equations;

  • linear programming.

entry.title: A Review of Data Fitting and Interpolation
entry.content:
Abstract

This article presents two fundamental approaches to transforming discrete observations into continuous functional models: data interpolation and data fitting. Interpolation requires the resulting curve to pass strictly through every data point. It is therefore suited to local estimation and exact reconstruction when the available data are highly accurate. The discussion begins with classical Lagrange and Newton polynomial interpolation, examines the Runge oscillations that arise when high-degree polynomials are used, and then turns to spline interpolation, which evolved from piecewise strategies. Cubic splines in particular have become the standard means of balancing global smoothness with local fidelity.

Data fitting, by contrast, seeks to remove the influence of random errors and reveal the broad patterns within the data. Taking least squares as its theoretical foundation, this article explains the optimization principle of finding the best trend function by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. It covers linear models, polynomial models, and nonlinear models that can be linearized, while stressing the importance of objectively evaluating goodness of fit through such measures as R² and adjusted R².

Through comparison, the review clarifies the essential differences between interpolation and fitting in their underlying assumptions, appropriate applications, and technical implementation. Its purpose is to help researchers make a sound methodological choice in response to different levels of data quality and different analytical aims, thereby supporting quantitative analysis that is both more precise and more revealing.

1. Overview

In scientific research and engineering practice, raw data usually take the form of a series of discrete observations, (x_i, y_i). To conduct deeper analysis, predict unknown values, or uncover an underlying pattern, however, we must construct a continuous function f(x) that represents those data. Data fitting and interpolation are the two principal ways of doing so. They rest on different assumptions and serve different analytical purposes.

  • Interpolation: its central assumption is that the data are perfectly accurate. The constructed curve must pass strictly through every given data point; in other words, f(x_i) = y_i must hold for every i. Interpolation is primarily used to make precise, local numerical estimates between known observations. In essence, it “fills in the gaps.”

  • Fitting or approximation: its central assumption is that the data contain noise. The curve need not pass through any particular observation. Instead, it should be smooth and reflect the overall trend of the data as closely as possible. Fitting seeks to separate random errors from the data and capture the fundamental relationship between variables. In essence, it “looks for the rule.”

2. Interpolation: Constructing an Exact Path

2.1 Polynomial Interpolation

An n-1 degree polynomial is used to pass exactly through n data points.

  • Lagrange interpolation:

    • Idea: this is a constructive method. For each data point (x_i, y_i), it carefully designs a basis function L_i(x). That function equals 1 at x_i and 0 at every other x_j (j ≠ i). The final interpolation polynomial is the weighted sum of these basis functions, with the corresponding values y_i serving as weights.

      $$ P(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} y_i L_i(x) \quad , \quad L_i(x) = \prod_{j=0, j \neq i}^{n-1} \frac{x - x_j}{x_i - x_j} $$

    • Comment: the method is theoretically elegant but computationally limited. Whenever a data point is added, all basis functions must be recalculated, so previous calculations cannot readily be reused. More seriously, it cannot avoid the inherent risk of high-degree polynomial interpolation.

  • Newton interpolation:

Idea: the polynomial is constructed iteratively. By introducing divided differences, the method allows each new data point to be accommodated by appending only one additional term. It therefore offers good inheritance and computational efficiency.

$$ P(x) = f(x_0) + fx_0, x_1 + \dots + f[x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}]\prod_{i=0}^{n-2}(x-x_i) $$

Comment: it is computationally superior to the Lagrange method, but it still faces the following problem.

  • Runge’s phenomenon:

This is a danger that must be taken seriously in high-degree polynomial interpolation. When a high-degree polynomial is fitted to equally spaced nodes, violent oscillations may appear near the boundaries of the interval even if the original function is smooth, producing substantial prediction errors. The lesson is clear: blindly forcing a single high-degree polynomial through every point is a hazardous approach.

2.2 Piecewise and Spline Interpolation

A more robust way to avoid Runge’s phenomenon is to abandon a single global polynomial and adopt a piecewise, divide-and-conquer strategy.

  • Piecewise linear interpolation:

Idea: this is the simplest piecewise method; adjacent data points are connected successively by straight lines.

Comment: it is simple and fast, and it never produces oscillations. The cost, however, is the presence of sharp corners at the data points. The first derivative is discontinuous, and the curve as a whole lacks the smoothness required by most physical laws.

  • Spline interpolation:

Idea: spline interpolation is a major improvement on elementary piecewise methods and is designed to ensure global smoothness. It connects low-degree polynomial pieces, usually cubic ones, and imposes continuity conditions on their derivatives at the junctions, which are called knots.

Cubic splines are the most widely used. They ensure not only that the function itself is continuous, but also that its first and second derivatives remain continuous at every knot. Consequently, the curve has no sharp corners, while its curvature also changes continuously; it is highly smooth both visually and mathematically.

Comment: spline interpolation is now the most extensively used and consistently reliable interpolation method in scientific computing. It balances exactness and smoothness remarkably well, avoids Runge’s phenomenon, and has become the standard choice for interpolation tasks.

3. Fitting: Capturing the Underlying Pattern of Data

3.1 The Method of Least Squares

Least squares is the foundational method of fitting. It turns the idea of a “best fit” into a measurable criterion.

Central idea: define the residual between a data point (x_i, y_i) and the fitted function f(x) as e_i = y_i - f(x_i). The best fitted function is the one that minimizes the sum of squared residuals, or SSR.

$$ SSR = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - f(x_i))^2 \rightarrow \min $$

Squaring is chosen not only because it has convenient mathematical properties, including differentiability and convexity, but also because it assigns a greater “penalty weight” to large errors, or outliers.

3.2 Selecting and Implementing a Fitted Model

  • Linear fitting:

    • Model: the functional relationship is assumed to be linear.

    • Solution: take partial derivatives of SSR with respect to all unknown parameters, such as a, b, and so forth, and set them to zero. This produces a system of linear equations known as the normal equations. Solving that system yields the best parameter estimates.

  • Polynomial fitting:

    • Model: the function is assumed to be a polynomial, such as f(x) = a_nx^n + \dots + a_1x + a_0.

    • Solution: its least-squares solution can likewise be reduced to a system of normal equations.

  • Nonlinear fitting:

    • Model: when theory indicates that variables have a nonlinear relationship, such as an exponential, logarithmic, or power relation, nonlinear fitting is required.

    • Strategies:

      1. Linearization: a suitable change of variables can transform a nonlinear relationship into a linear one. For example, taking logarithms on both sides of y = ae^{bx} gives ln(y) = ln(a) + bx, after which linear fitting can be applied to (x, ln(y)). This is a common and efficient technique.

      2. Iterative optimization: when a complex model cannot be linearized, numerical optimization algorithms, such as gradient descent or the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm, must search iteratively and gradually approach the parameter combination that minimizes SSR.

3.3 Evaluating Goodness of Fit

Once a model has been fitted, its quality must be evaluated quantitatively.

  • Coefficient of determination, R-squared or R²:

    • Definition: it measures the percentage of the total variation in the dependent variable that the model can explain. Its value lies between 0 and 1; the closer it is to 1, the stronger the explanatory power of the model.

      $$ R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - f(x_i))^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2} = 1 - \frac{SSR}{SST} $$

  • Adjusted R²:

    • Purpose: R² has a weakness: increasing model complexity, for example by raising the degree of a polynomial, can only increase its value. Adjusted R² therefore introduces a penalty for the number of model parameters. When models of different complexity are compared, it provides a fairer measure.

4. Conclusion

Interpolation and fitting are both foundations of data analysis. Interpolation follows a philosophy of “trusting the data” and constructs exact bridges between one point and the next. Fitting follows a philosophy of “questioning the data” and searches for an underlying rule amid noisy observations. In practice, if the data source is reliable, the error is very small, and the aim is local estimation, interpolation—especially spline interpolation—is the better choice. Conversely, if measurements contain error and the aim is to explore a global pattern or make predictions, fitting, with least squares at its core, is necessary. A clear understanding of their differences and appropriate applications is a prerequisite for effective quantitative analysis.

entry.title: A Review of Differential- and Difference-Equation Methods
entry.content:
Abstract

This article reviews two important methods for modelling dynamic processes: differential equations and difference equations. It first introduces the background of dynamic-process modelling and the choice of methods from a broad perspective, before examining the fundamental ideas and modelling grounds of each kind of equation. Applications include changes in populations, the diffusion of pollutants, and the sales of new products. Difference equations are suited to processes that change in distinct stages over discrete time, whereas differential equations describe continuous and smooth development. Particular attention is given to analytical solutions, numerical solutions, and qualitative analysis, especially the identification of equilibrium points and the judgement of stability. Their practical value for prediction and intervention is also emphasized. Finally, examples such as epidemic models show how increasingly complex models can incorporate impulses, time delays, and different dimensions, including both time and space, and how such models may be improved through repeated revision.

1. Overview of Dynamic-Process Modelling

1.1 The Concept

Many models discussed earlier, such as linear regression, analyse the internal composition of an object statically. They can clearly display its internal structure and relationships at a particular moment. The world, however, is in motion. What matters more often is how an object evolves through time or space. When the characteristics of the object under study are continually changing, dynamic-process modelling has its part to play.

1.2 Choosing a Modelling Method

Route One: Abundant Data but an Unclear Mechanism—the “Black-Box” Approach

Methods: data fitting and statistical regression.

We may not know how a machine works internally, yet possess many sets of input-output data. Our task is then to find a mathematical function that imitates the machine’s behaviour as closely as possible. Whether the function itself has a physical meaning is not our chief concern; it is enough if the imitation is convincing.

Common methods:

Polynomial fitting is the simplest and most direct tool, though pursuing apparent goodness of fit may lead to overfitting.

Other forms of fitting should be selected according to the “shape” of the data:

  • If the growth rate becomes progressively slower, like someone who is nearly full, try logarithmic fitting.

  • If the data grow ever faster, like a snowball rolling downhill, try exponential fitting.

  • If the data form a bell shape, high in the centre and low on both sides, try Gaussian fitting.

  • If the data fluctuate periodically, Fourier-series fitting is the natural choice.

Time-series analysis is needed when the data appear disordered but seem to possess a kind of inertia—today’s observation is related to yesterday’s. More advanced time-series models, such as ARIMA, can then be employed.

Statistical regression is also a form of fitting, but it more “honestly” acknowledges the presence of an error term e and provides a complete theoretical framework for testing the significance of both the model and its coefficients.

Route Two: A Well-Understood Mechanism but Insufficient Data—the “White-Box” Approach

Methods: differential or difference equations and random processes.

Although we may lack abundant data, we understand the rules governing the internal operation of the system. The task is to express its dynamic behaviour in equations derived from physical, chemical, or biological laws.

Models constructed in this way are generally more robust and are particularly suitable for long-term prediction, since they capture the essential laws of development rather than merely reproducing superficial patterns in the data.

2. Modelling with Difference Equations

2.1 Basic Concepts

Appropriate situation: use difference equations when change occurs step by step, in jumps, and is divided into distinct stages.

We do not care about what happens between individual frames. We care about the relationship between frame n and frame n+1, or perhaps several previous frames. For example, population may be counted by year, stock closing prices updated by day, and population size calculated by reproductive cycle.

2.2 Basis of a Difference-Equation Model

The central principle is to link what came before with what comes next: describe the present state by means of past states.

  • xn+1​=f(xn​): the simplest model, in which “tomorrow” depends only on “today.”

  • xn+2​=f(xn​,xn+1​): a slightly more complicated model, in which “the day after tomorrow” depends not only on “tomorrow” but also on “today,” thus allowing for “inertia.”

2.3 Applications of Difference Equations

2.3.1 A Population Model: A Gradually Refined Line of Thought

  1. Model V1.0: The Utopian Model, or the Malthus Model

    • Idea: assume a “utopia” with unlimited resources, where population growth depends only on fixed birth and death rates.

    • Problem: this model is too naive. It predicts either exponential explosion or exponential extinction, neither of which can continue for long in reality.

  2. Model V2.0: The Real-World Model, or the Logistic Model

    • Idea: introduce resource constraints and competition. When the population becomes too large, food grows scarce and living space contracts, causing the birth rate to fall and the death rate to rise.

    • Conclusion: this is a much more advanced model. It predicts that the population will approach a stable upper limit imposed by the carrying capacity of the environment, which agrees closely with natural processes. Yet it also reveals more complicated behaviour: depending on the parameters, a population may settle at the limit, fluctuate periodically around it, or even enter an unpredictable state of chaos.

  3. Model V3.0: Allowing for Generational Differences

    • Idea: introduce a time lag. Many organisms cannot reproduce immediately after birth and require a period of growth. Today’s birth rate may therefore be determined by the number of adults k cycles earlier.

  4. Models V4.0 and V5.0: Incorporating More Realistic Factors

    • Sex: only females can give birth, so introducing the female proportion s makes the model more precise.

    • Age structure, or the Leslie model: this is a major advance. The population is no longer treated as a single number but as a vector, each element of which represents the population in one age group. A state-transition matrix M can then describe precisely how the age structure of the entire population changes from one generation to the next.

  5. Model V6.0: Allowing for Sudden Shocks, or Impulse Effects

    • Idea: the real world is full of unexpected events. Some occur regularly, such as fishing during a fixed season each year, while others are triggered by the state of the system, such as large-scale pesticide spraying once the locust population exceeds a threshold.

    • Modelling: by introducing a switching function, T(n) or S(x), we can simulate such “impulsive” interventions in the equation. This is essential when modelling matters such as epidemic control and economic regulation.

2.4 Stability of Difference Equations

  • Central question: as time approaches infinity, where will the system eventually go? Will it settle at one point, grow without limit, or oscillate back and forth?

  • Equilibrium point: the state at which the system remains motionless, namely x* = f(x*). It is a possible “destination” of the system.

  • Judging stability:

    • In plain language: if we give the system a gentle push near its equilibrium, will it roll back by itself, which means it is stable, or move ever farther away, which means it is unstable?

    • Mathematical tool: the effect of this “push” is described by the derivative |f'(x*)|.

      • |f'(x*)| < 1: the disturbance is gradually “absorbed,” and the system converges back to the equilibrium, so it is stable.

      • |f'(x*)| > 1: the disturbance is “amplified,” and the system moves away from the equilibrium, so it is unstable.

3. Modelling with Differential Equations

3.1 Overview

Appropriate situation: use differential equations when change is smooth and continuous.

3.2 Principal Tasks

  1. Finding an analytical solution: this resembles obtaining a universal formula from which the state at any time can be calculated. Such solutions are rare, however, and are available only for a small number of simple equations.

  2. Qualitative analysis: this is the next-best alternative. Although we have no universal formula, we can analyse the equation itself, draw a “sketch” of its solutions—a phase portrait—and understand the system’s long-term behaviour, equilibrium points, possible periodicity, and so forth. This can offer more insight than a particular numerical solution.

  3. Finding a numerical solution: this is the most practical and powerful method. Given initial conditions and parameters, a computer “iterates” step by step to obtain an approximate solution at any time. We may not know the exact equation of a rocket’s trajectory, for example, but we can calculate its positions at 1 second, 1.01 seconds, 1.02 seconds, and so on. Joining these points gives the trajectory.

3.4 Basis of a Differential-Equation Model

  • The central task is to identify the relationship between the rate of change and the state.

  • Classic example: dx/dt = kx. In ordinary words, “the speed at which something x changes is proportional to its own size.” This relationship can describe unrestricted population growth, radioactive decay, compound interest, and many other phenomena.

3.5 Applications of Differential Equations

  1. A Model of New-Product Sales, or the Logistic Model:

    • Mechanism: sales growth is driven by two factors. The first is word-of-mouth promotion by existing buyers, which is proportional to the quantity already sold, x. The second is market demand among potential buyers, which is proportional to the unsold quantity, K-x. Multiplying them gives the classic Logistic model.

  2. An Age-Structured Population Model:

    • This is the continuous counterpart of the Leslie model. Instead of updating once a year, we examine at every moment how many people move from “youth” to “middle age” and from “middle age” to “old age.”

  3. The Influence of Exceptional Factors: like difference equations, differential equations can incorporate impulses, delays, and other complex factors to bring the model closer to reality.

  4. Mathematical-Physics Equations, or Partial Differential Equations, PDEs:

    • When the object under study varies not only with time but also with spatial position, partial differential equations are required.

    • In plain language: we care not only about how the total amount of a pollutant in a pond changes over time, but also about how its concentration changes over time at different positions, (x, y, z), in that pond. This requires partial derivatives.

3.6 Qualitative Analysis of Differential Equations

  • Central idea: as with difference equations, we find equilibrium points and judge their stability.

  • Method: for a two-dimensional system, stability is judged by analysing the eigenvalues of the linear approximation’s Jacobian matrix at an equilibrium point. The real part of an eigenvalue determines whether the system converges or diverges in the corresponding direction. The equilibrium is stable when the real parts of all eigenvalues are negative.

3.7 Continuing Improvement and Deeper Discussion: An Epidemic Model

This is an excellent example of modelling as a process of repeated iteration towards reality.

  1. Begin with the classic SIR model: it provides the simplest “skeleton.”

  2. Add population movement: turn it into SIRS by allowing recovered individuals to lose immunity again.

  3. Add real-world constraints: incorporate births and deaths so that the total population is no longer fixed.

  4. Add temporal features: include an incubation period, as in the SEIR model, and impulse effects during holidays.

  5. Add social interventions: include vaccination and quarantine.

  6. Add biological characteristics: include viral mutation and vertical transmission.

  7. Add randomness: use stochastic differential equations to describe random disturbances in such parameters as the infection rate due to environmental noise.

By applying one “patch” after another, we can turn a rough toy model into a powerful tool capable of informing public-health decisions.

entry.title: A Review of Statistics and Data Mining
entry.content:
Abstract

This article reviews the basic concepts and methodology of statistics and data mining, together with their applications in data analysis. It begins with the processes of data understanding, preparation, and modelling and introduces the principal evaluation metrics for classification and regression. It then compares ensemble-learning methods—Bagging, Boosting, Stacking, and Blending—and explains how they improve model performance and robustness. The statistical section covers hypothesis testing, contingency analysis, correlation, regression, and analysis of variance, emphasizing their value in exploring relationships and verifying significance. The discussion then turns to predictive modelling, classification, clustering, association and sequential-pattern mining, and typical techniques in Web data mining. By combining the rigorous methodology of statistics with the practical algorithmic framework of data mining, the review offers a systematic way to understand and solve real problems and provides useful background for mathematical modelling and interdisciplinary data analysis.

1. Introduction

1.1 Concepts

Data mining discovers characteristics expressed in large databases and generalizes them into new knowledge and methods.

Statistics is a methodological science concerned with measuring, collecting, organizing, and analysing data that reflect objective phenomena, thereby helping people understand the quantitative laws of the objective world. It includes statistical methods for data acquisition, processing, and analysis.

1.2 Methodology

A cross-industry standard process for data mining consists of the following steps.

  1. Business understanding means examining the state of research at home and abroad. In other words, clarify the requirements and ultimate purpose of the analysis and determine what data mining can contribute. In a mathematical competition, the objective is usually explicit. The task is to consult relevant literature, identify appropriate methods, and assess the difficulty of reproducing them and the room for improvement.

  2. Data understanding means determining what preprocessing the data require, examining their completeness and correctness, forming a preliminary view of their possible characteristics, and deciding which modelling methods may be suitable.

  3. Data preparation means preprocessing the data.

  4. Select an appropriate modelling method. Parameters may be adjusted manually, or grid search can traverse specified combinations of hyperparameters before fitting the model. Random search and Bayesian search are other possibilities. The relevant material and code should be prepared in advance. If it is unclear which model is better, several can be trained and combined through a suitable strategy into a stronger ensemble.

  5. Evaluate model performance.

  6. Present the modelling results.

1.3 Model-Evaluation Metrics

After building a model for classification or prediction, we need objective standards by which to measure its performance.

Metrics for Classification Models

These models predict categories, such as yes or no, classes A/B/C, or diseased and healthy. Their evaluation usually begins with a confusion matrix, a table summarizing the different ways in which the model is right or wrong.

Predicted positive Predicted negative
Actually positive True positive (TP) False negative (FN)
Actually negative False positive (FP) True negative (TN)
  • Positive is usually the class of greater interest, such as “diseased” or “spam.”
  • TP, true positive: the model is correct; the sample is positive and is predicted as positive.
  • FN, false negative: the model is wrong; the sample is positive but is predicted as negative. This is a missed detection.
  • FP, false positive: the model is wrong; the sample is negative but is predicted as positive. This is a false alarm.
  • TN, true negative: the model is correct; the sample is negative and is predicted as negative.

The matrix gives rise to the following metrics.

  • Accuracy

    • Definition: the proportion of all samples that the model classifies correctly.

    • Formula: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)

    • Limitation: with an imbalanced sample, accuracy can be deceptive. Suppose a cancer-detection dataset contains only one patient among 1,000 people. A lazy model that labels everyone healthy achieves an accuracy of 99.9 per cent. It looks excellent but fails to find even the single patient and is therefore useless.

  • Precision

    • Definition: among the samples predicted as positive, the proportion that really are positive.

    • Formula: TP / (TP + FP)

    • Application: high precision is desirable when a false positive is costly. In spam detection, for example, an important work email should not be classified as spam, even if that means letting some spam through.

  • Recall

    • Definition: among all genuinely positive samples, the proportion successfully found by the model.

    • Formula: TP / (TP + FN)

    • Application: high recall is desirable when a false negative is costly. In screening for an infectious disease or cancer, missing a real patient can have grave consequences, so it is better to ask some healthy people to undergo further examination.

  • F1-score

    • Definition: the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

    • Formula: 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

    • Precision and recall often conflict: raising one may lower the other. The F1-score seeks a balance and becomes high only when both are high, making it a more comprehensive and robust measure.

Metrics for Continuous-Variable Prediction, or Regression

Such models predict numerical values, including house prices, temperature, and stock prices.

  • Mean squared error, MSE

    • Definition: the mean of the squared differences between predicted and actual values.

    • Formula: (1/n) * Σ(y_true - y_pred)²

    • Limitation: it is sensitive to very large deviations.

  • Root mean squared error, RMSE

    • Definition: the square root of MSE.

    • Formula: sqrt(MSE)

    • Its advantage is that it has the same unit as the original data. If the model predicts house prices in units of ten thousand yuan, RMSE is expressed in the same unit. We can then understand directly the scale of the average prediction error, making RMSE easier to interpret than MSE.

  • Mean absolute error, MAE

    • Definition: the mean of the absolute differences between predicted and actual values.

    • Formula: (1/n) * Σ|y_true - y_pred|

    • In plain language: it also measures how far predictions miss the target. Because it uses absolute values rather than squares, it is less sensitive to extraordinary outliers, behaves more gently, and better reflects ordinary prediction error.

  • Coefficient of determination, R-squared or R²

    • Definition: a goodness-of-fit measure representing the percentage of variation in the dependent variable explained by the model’s predictions.

    • Formula: 1 - (Σ(y_true - y_pred)² / Σ(y_true - y_mean)²)

    • In plain language: its value is commonly interpreted between 0 and 1. If we use no model and simply guess that every sample equals the mean, y_mean, we produce a total error. The model produces an error of Σ(y_true - y_pred)². R² measures how much better the model is than blindly guessing the mean.

      • R² = 1: a perfect model; predictions and actual values are identical.
      • R² = 0: the model is no better than blind guessing.
      • R² < 0: the model is worse than blind guessing and actively makes matters worse.

    • It provides an intuitive, unit-free percentage measure of model quality.

1.4 Ensemble-Learning Methods

Ensemble learning combines several models into one larger model in order to improve overall accuracy and robustness. The combination of several regression analyses into one grand “ana—fog—lysis” during the second internal competition was an example of the same idea.

Its principal forms are as follows.

Bagging

Bagging is a parallel ensemble method. It constructs several independent models and combines them by voting, averaging, or weighting to form a strong learner.

Random forests are a typical application. They build many decision trees and use voting or averaging to make the final prediction.

Boosting

Boosting is a sequential ensemble method in which base learners are arranged in series to construct a strong learner. It adjusts the weights of data points while training a sequence of weak learners, assigning greater weight to misclassified observations so that each later learner attempts to correct the errors of the preceding one. AdaBoost is a representative method.

Stacking

Stacking combines aspects of Bagging and Boosting. The outputs of first-layer models become the inputs of a second-layer model. Modelling this stack of predictions improves generalization.

Blending

Blending improves accuracy and stability by combining the predictions of several models. It has two main stages. First, several base models are trained; they may be homogeneous, using the same kind of algorithm, or heterogeneous, using different algorithms. Second, their outputs on a validation set become features for training a meta-model, usually linear regression, which then predicts the test set.

Its advantages include ease of understanding and high extensibility: base models can be added or replaced as required.

Its disadvantages are difficult implementation and heavy computation. At my present level, I do not think I would use it in the national competition.

2. Data Preparation and Exploratory Analysis

2.1 Introduction to Statistics

Definition: the science of collecting, analysing, presenting, and interpreting data.

The statistical research process consists of collecting, organizing, analysing, and interpreting data.

Basic concepts include the population, sample, parameter, and statistic.

2.2 Categories of Statistical Data

By level of measurement: nominal, ordinal, and interval data.

By collection method: observational and experimental data.

By temporal form: cross-sectional and time-series data.

2.3 Descriptive Statistics

Central tendency: mean, median, mode, and sum, together with their relationships and characteristics.

Dispersion: standard deviation, variance, minimum, maximum, range, and standard error of the mean.

Shape: skewness and kurtosis and their interpretation of a distribution.

The standard score and its uses.

2.4 Data Visualization

Visualization is the scientific study of visual representations of data. Its stages of development include scientific visualization, information visualization, data visualization, and visual analytics.

The DIKW hierarchy describes the transformation from data -> information -> knowledge -> wisdom.

Types of statistical chart:

Bar chart: shows the frequency distribution of categorical data.

Line chart: shows the changing trend of a variable and is suitable for continuous variables.

Box plot: displays the distribution of raw data—the maximum, minimum, median, and quartiles—and reveals its shape.

Scatter plot: displays the quantitative relationship and trend between two variables.

Histogram: displays the frequency distribution of grouped data.

P-P and Q-Q plots: test whether data follow a specified theoretical distribution, such as the normal distribution.

2.5 Exploratory Data Analysis, EDA

Introduction

EDA is a method of statistical analysis that uses visual charts and tables of statistics to explore the internal structure and patterns of data and extract key information without imposing many prior assumptions.

Purposes

  • Data understanding and preprocessing: clarify the meaning and structure of the data and discover outliers, missing values, and duplicates so that the dataset can be cleaned and organized.

  • Description and relationship analysis: understand important features, including the distributions of variables and the relationships among them.

  • Preparation for later analysis: decide whether transformations, non-parametric methods, or linear regression are needed, thereby translating a practical question into a feasible data-analysis problem.

Content

  1. Data screening: check for missing values, outliers, and duplicates; determine whether the sample is balanced; and decide whether sampling, new variables, or variable transformations are required.

  2. Description of data characteristics:

  • Continuous variables: use statistics such as the mean, median, and standard deviation and charts such as histograms and box plots.

  • Discrete variables, nominal or ordinal: use frequencies and proportions, together with frequency tables, bar charts, and pie charts.

  1. Relationships among variables:

Continuous versus continuous variables

This belongs to correlation analysis.

Charts: scatter plots, correlation matrices, and heat maps.

Measures: Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlation coefficients. See the related articles on this site for details.

Discrete versus discrete variables

Charts: pairwise cross-tabulations and grouped bar charts; grid charts for several discrete variables.

Ordinal discrete variables use correlation analysis and the correlation coefficients just mentioned.

Nominal discrete variables use contingency analysis, with the $\varphi$ coefficient, the $V$ coefficient, and the contingency coefficient as quantitative measures.

Discrete versus continuous variables

Charts: histograms, box plots, and violin plots.

Quantitative analysis: t-tests, analysis of variance, and similar methods.

Measures: the t statistic and corresponding p-value in an independent-samples t-test, and the statistics used in one-way and multifactor analysis of variance.

  1. Testing data for normality

Histogram: examine how closely its shape matches a bell curve.

Box plot: examine whether the distribution is symmetrical.

P-P plot: under normality, the cumulative proportion of the data remains broadly consistent with that of the normal distribution. Place the cumulative proportion of the data on the X-axis and the corresponding normal cumulative proportion on the Y-axis. If the points lie approximately along a straight line, the data follow the specified distribution.

Q-Q plot: compare the quantiles of the data with those of a theoretical distribution.

  1. Testing the type of distribution

The Shapiro–Wilk test.

The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test.

  1. Data transformation

The Box–Cox transformation.

Descriptive Statistics

  • Central tendency:

    • Mean: the most frequently used measure, but easily affected by extreme values.

    • Median: the middle value after ordering the data. It is not affected by extremes and is suitable for all distributions.

    • Mode: the most frequent value. It is not affected by extremes, and several modes may exist.

  • Dispersion:

    • Measures such as standard deviation, variance, and range describe how widely data are spread.

Visualization Charts

  • Bar chart: represents categorical frequencies by the length of bars and is suitable for discrete variables.

  • Line chart: uses rising and falling lines to show how a variable changes over time and is suitable for continuous variables.

  • Box plot: uses a box and line segments to display the maximum, minimum, median, and quartiles, making symmetry visible at a glance.

3. Principal Methods of Analysis

3.1 Hypothesis Testing

We may have a suspicion or claim, such as “this new drug is effective,” but cannot draw a conclusion directly. We must first establish a null hypothesis H0, which usually represents “no effect” or “no change,” and presume it innocent. We then collect sample data and ask whether the evidence is strong enough to overturn that innocent assumption beyond reasonable doubt—at a specified probability level.

The Steps of the Trial

  1. State the hypotheses

The null hypothesis, H0, represents the status quo or absence of an effect and always contains equality (=, ≤, or ≥). In court, it is the claim that the defendant is innocent. For example: H0: the mean effect of the new drug = the mean effect of the placebo.

The alternative hypothesis, H1 or Ha, is the opposing claim that we hope to establish and always contains an inequality (≠, <, or >). In court, it is the claim that the defendant is guilty. For example: H1: the mean effect of the new drug ≠ the mean effect of the placebo.

  1. Set the significance level α

Before the trial begins, we set a standard for conviction. This is the significance level α, commonly 0.05. It is the maximum risk of a mistaken judgement that we are willing to bear. An α of 0.05 means accepting a five-per-cent probability of condemning an innocent person—in statistical terms, wrongly rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true.

  1. Calculate the test statistic

This step reduces the evidence, or sample data, to a single numerical value. The statistic measures how far the sample result lies from what H0 predicts. Different problems require different statistics, including Z, t, χ², and F.

  1. Make the statistical decision

This is the final verdict. Two methods are available.

Critical-value method: compare the calculated statistic with a critical value obtained from a table according to α. If the statistic falls in the rejection region, reject H0.

P-value approach: this is the method most commonly used by modern statistical software. Calculate the p-value, which is the probability, if H0 is true, of observing the present sample result or one still more extreme. Compare it with α:

If p ≤ α, the observed event is unlikely under H0. We have reason to question H0 and therefore reject the null hypothesis.

If p > α, the sample result is ordinary under H0 and gives no cause for alarm. We do not have sufficient evidence to reject H0.

Two types of error:

A Type I error, or rejecting a true hypothesis, occurs when H0 is true but we reject it. Its probability is the chosen α.

A Type II error, or accepting a false hypothesis, occurs when H0 is false but the evidence is insufficient to reject it. Its probability is denoted by β.

Common Tests

1. Tests of Parameters in One Normal Population

Test of a mean with known σ: the Z-test

Question: “The national mean height of men is known to be 175 cm, with a standard deviation σ of 5 cm. A random sample of 100 men from our university has a mean height of 177 cm. Are men at our university taller than the national population?”

Test statistic:

$$ Z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} $$

Here, $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean, $\mu_0$ the hypothesized population mean, and $\sigma$ the population standard deviation; n is the sample size.

Test of a mean with unknown σ: the t-test

Question: this is the more common situation. “I want to know whether the mean lifetime of a new batch of light bulbs is 800 hours. I sample 25 bulbs and obtain a mean lifetime of 790 hours and a sample standard deviation s of 30 hours.”

Test statistic:

$$ t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}} $$

The sample standard deviation s is used here. The t distribution has heavier tails than the Z distribution because it allows for the additional uncertainty introduced when s estimates σ.

Test of a variance: the chi-squared test

Question: “A manufacturing standard requires that the variance in the length of a component not exceed 0.01 mm². A sample of 30 components has a variance of 0.015 mm². Is the production line insufficiently stable?”

Test statistic:

$$ \chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2} $$

Here, $s^2$ is the sample variance and $\sigma_0^2$ is the hypothesized population variance.

Test of a proportion: the Z-test

Question: “Our product had a market share of 20 per cent last year. After a promotional campaign this year, 230 of 1,000 new users chose it. Has the market share increased significantly?”

Test statistic:

$$ Z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}} $$

Here, $\hat{p}$ is the sample proportion and p₀ is the hypothesized population proportion.

2. Tests of Parameters in Two Normal Populations

The independent-samples t-test for means

Question: “Which of two teaching methods, A and B, is more effective? Students are randomly divided into two groups, one taught with A and the other with B, and their mean final-examination scores are compared.”

Test statistic, assuming equal variances:

$$ t = \frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)_0}{\sqrt{s_p^2 (\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2})}} \quad , \quad s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2} $$

Here, $s_p^2$ is the pooled variance.

The F-test for two independent-sample variances

Question: “Before carrying out the preceding t-test, I need to decide whether the variances of the two groups are equal. Group A has a score variance of 100 and Group B one of 120. Do the variances differ significantly?”

Test statistic:

$$ F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2} $$

By convention, the larger sample variance is placed in the numerator.

The paired-samples t-test

Question: “I want to know whether a weight-loss drug works. I record the weight of a group of people before they take it and again after one month, then compare the two sets of measurements.”

Approach: these are not independent samples because the observations occur in pairs, comparing the same person before and after treatment. First calculate each person’s weight difference d. The problem then becomes a one-sample t-test on these differences, asking whether their mean $\bar{d}$ differs significantly from zero.

Test statistic:

$$ t = \frac{\bar{d} - D_0}{s_d / \sqrt{n}} $$

Here, D₀ is normally 0, and s_d is the standard deviation of the differences d.

3.2 Contingency Analysis

Purpose: to determine whether qualitative, or categorical, variables are associated.

  • Approach—the chi-squared test:

    • Its central idea is a comparison between expectation and reality.

    1. State H0: first assume that the two variables are completely independent and unrelated.

    2. Calculate expected frequencies: under independence, calculate how many observations should theoretically appear in each cell of the contingency table.

      • Formula: expected frequency in a cell = (total of its row × total of its column) / total number of observations

    3. Calculate the chi-squared statistic: compare expectation with reality, meaning the observed frequency. The chi-squared value measures their overall difference.

      • Formula:
        $$ \chi^2 = \sum \frac{(\text{观测频数} - \text{期望频数})^2}{\text{期望频数}} $$

      • Interpretation: if reality differs greatly from expectation, χ² becomes large, suggesting that independence may be untenable.

    4. Make the statistical decision: compare χ² with a critical value, or inspect the p-value. If p is below α, reject the null and conclude that a significant association exists.

  • Measures of association in a contingency table:

    • The chi-squared test tells us whether an association exists but not how strong it is. The following coefficients measure its strength.

    • The φ, or Phi, coefficient is designed for a 2x2 contingency table.

      • Formula: $\phi = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2}{n}}$ (n is the total sample size)

      • Interpretation: values range from 0 to 1, and a value closer to 1 indicates a stronger association.

    • Cramér’s V is more general and can be applied to a contingency table of any size.

      • Formula: $V = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2}{n \cdot (\min(r, c) - 1)}}$ (r is the number of rows and c the number of columns)

      • Interpretation: it likewise ranges from 0 to 1, with values nearer 1 indicating stronger association. Because it can be compared across tables of different sizes, it is one of the most common measures in practice.

3.3 Correlation Analysis

  • Purpose: to determine whether quantitative data, or continuous variables, are associated and to measure the strength and direction of that association.

  • How does correlation differ from a functional relationship?

    • A functional relationship is deterministic: one value of X corresponds exactly to one value of Y. In y = 2x + 1, once x is fixed, y is fixed with no deviation, and the graph is a perfect line.

    • A correlation is non-deterministic and random. Variables follow a general tendency but not a strict rule. Taller people, for example, tend to weigh more, but not without exception. Their observations form a cloud of points around a trend line. Regression finds the average trend line behind that cloud, whereas correlation measures how tightly the points gather around it.

  • Measuring correlation:

    • The scatter plot is the most intuitive tool. Its pattern reveals:

      • direction—from lower left to upper right for positive correlation and from upper left to lower right for negative correlation;

      • form—a straight line or a curve;

      • strength—the more tightly points cluster around a line, the stronger the relationship.

    • A correlation coefficient turns the visual relationship into a number.

      • Pearson’s simple correlation coefficient, r:

        • Use: the most common coefficient, measuring the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two continuous variables.

        • Formula:
          $$ r = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}} $$

        • Interpretation:

          • Values range from -1 to +1.

          • r > 0 indicates positive correlation; r < 0 indicates negative correlation.

          • The larger the absolute value |r|, the stronger the linear relationship. |r| = 1 means perfect linear correlation, with every point on one line. r = 0 means no linear relationship.
