  • stayor/git-gui-zh
  • Chinese Localisation of Git—Zhihu
  • Git

entry.title: CMake, Static Libraries, and Dynamic Libraries
entry.content:
CMake

This post originated in the time I spent not paying attention during Signals and Systems.

Basic Concepts

CMake automatically generates build files for different platforms from CMakeLists.txt; it is therefore a tool for generating build systems.

It sits slightly above manual configuration at the basic level, defining project structure, dependencies, and compilation options without requiring each tool to be configured manually.

Configuration

  • CMakeLists.txt
  • A build directory created with mkdir build, which keeps the source tree clean.

(Perhaps the next post could discuss PATH. And the registry?)

CMakeLists.txt Syntax

  • CMake Tutorial — RUNOOB

(And what, exactly, are static and dynamic libraries?)

Workflow

  • Create the build directory → generate the build files (.../build # Cmake...).
  • Compile and build (make ...).
  • Clean the build files (make clean or delete Cmakecache.txt).

As one layer of the compilation process, CMake has build tools such as Make, Ninja, and Visual Studio beneath it. These deserve further study.

Static and Dynamic Libraries

The basic material comes from a RUNOOB blog post.

  • C++ Static and Dynamic Libraries — RUNOOB

As before, this note does not discuss their underlying formats or memory layouts.

What Is a Library?

A library is a toolkit of lower-level components that saves later programmers from reinventing the wheel. At bottom, it is a binary form of visible source code that can be loaded into memory and used.

  • Static libraries (.a, .lib)
  • Dynamic libraries (.so, .dll)

Source file → compilation → linking → execution

Both static and dynamic libraries enter during linking. The distinction lies in how that linking is handled.

Static Libraries

A static library is compiled into the program.

Advantages

  • Convenient when moving the program to another computer, because no environment needs to be configured
  • Convenient to update

Disadvantages

  • Occupies more space
  • Inconvenient to update

Building

  • On Linux, use the ar tool
  • On Windows, use lib.exe

Dynamic Libraries

Advantages

  • Loaded when the program runs
  • Convenient to update

Disadvantages

  • DLL Hell: the environment must repeatedly be configured

entry.title: Interstellar
entry.content:
Let me once again thank my partner for completing this programme with me. What follows is the part I wrote.

Introduction and Background

Interstellar is an original science-fiction adventure directed by Christopher Nolan. It was released on 5 November 2014 and has a Douban rating of 9.4.

Nolan explained his original impulse in roughly these terms: when he was a child, becoming an astronaut represented the noblest dream and the highest ambition. He missed the determination to keep exploring and to advance into the furthest reaches of the galaxy, and hoped that the film might begin a new age of outward expansion. Interstellar is both a tribute to the classic space film and a continuation of that childhood dream. As usual, Nolan favoured physical sets and IMAX film over complete dependence on computer-generated imagery, seeking a stronger sense of reality and immersion.

To keep the scientific theories in the film credible, Nolan invited Nobel laureate and theoretical physicist Kip Thorne to serve as scientific adviser, giving the wormholes, black holes, and other astrophysical phenomena a rigorous foundation. Thorne’s team used thousands of computers to solve simulations based on Einstein’s equations. The resulting image of the black hole also contributed positively to astrophysical research. Thorne later examined the principles behind the film one by one in his book The Science of Interstellar.

Reflections After Watching

The narrative structure of Interstellar is carefully designed and can broadly be understood as containing one visible line and one concealed line. In the visible story, Cooper saves his daughter and the human race by transmitting information from within the tesseract. Gravity is the medium of the message, while love is the motive for his action. Beneath it lies another story: humanity in higher dimensions saves its present-day ancestors by creating the wormhole and the tesseract.

The film’s foreshadowing is as rigorous and precise as a formula. At the beginning, books fall mysteriously from the study shelves, Murph speaks of a “ghost,” and patterns in the dust conceal the coordinates of the NASA base. What appear to be supernatural signs are all recovered at the end, when Cooper moves the world lines along the surface of the tesseract and Murph deciphers the trembling hands of the watch. The circuit closes. Nolan makes the five-dimensional bookshelf both a carrier of paternal love and a time capsule buried by humanity for its own rescue. In the spirit of Murphy’s law, every accident drawn together by gravity eventually becomes a necessary point of starlight.

The film also deserves attention for its handling of detail and its secondary characters. Consider Cooper’s two children. Murph is the pioneer who looks toward the stars and eventually receives the admiration of millions. His son, by contrast, is the guardian whose feet remain in the soil—indispensable, yet easily forgotten. Even his name is the thoroughly ordinary Tom. When their father leaves him the promise of “protecting the home,” this sole ordinary figure in the story carries humanity upon his back. His trust in his father is unconditional. Cooper asks only that he look after the family, and Tom remains with the old house and the fields for decades. Because of that persistence, Murph can return home and still find the watch her father gave her many years before, then decode his hidden message. The father’s spacesuit and the son’s plough shine with equal force: one brings data out of the black hole, while the other preserves the bridge across which that information can pass. Humanity cannot be saved by a handful of extraordinary heroes alone. It also depends upon countless ordinary people who stay at their posts, as Tom does.

After the film ended, I found myself returning to another question: why are people so fascinated by science fiction? Perhaps it is because such works act as prisms, refracting the deepest contradiction in the human soul. We are products of immense clouds of stardust, children of reason; yet among that dust, we are also the only beings moved to tears by starlight. In The Three-Body Problem, the Singer flattens the Solar System with a dual-vector foil and turns it into a flowing galaxy that might have come from Van Gogh. Cold reason and burning compassion meet for an instant in a brilliant final song. In Foundation, people living beneath the structure of psychohistory compose, through their own lives, an epic of faith and betrayal, power and feeling. Science fiction is never merely a fantasy about the future. It examines the reason and emotion within us. Reflected in its mirror, somewhere between the operation of a formula and the radiance of human character, we can finally see ourselves more clearly.

I think Interstellar is so powerful precisely because it sees that contradiction and writes it as an epic beneath the stars. Cooper floats against the surface of the tesseract and moves the world lines of the books with his fingers; suddenly, the cold formulas and the data from a black-hole singularity acquire bodily warmth. Every ray from the accretion disk becomes an echo of longing that crosses dimensions. Through this story, Nolan and Thorne show that science and technology, our strongest weapons in confronting nature, can also carve the shape of love when they turn toward humanity itself. As Carl Sagan wrote in Cosmos, the nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, and the iron in our blood were all formed from ancient stars. Technology and human feeling have never been opposites. Like the wave–particle duality of light, they are projections of the same substance in different dimensions.

As the credits rise into darkness with the roar of the organ, we beyond the screen remain trapped in the predicament called “humanity.” We are dust among the stars, yet also the only gods within that dust who attempt to understand it. Nolan tells us that when ripples of gravity spread through spacetime, only love can turn noise into a messenger; when molecules wander without direction through the void, only fingers interlocked beside a fire can define the temperature of existence. Perhaps the universe does not care how humanity opens a path for its species through a wormhole, or how line after line of equations and symbols is written upon a blackboard. Yet this romance, futile in the eyes of the universe, is exactly what enables us to cultivate an oasis called civilization in the desert of endless entropy. Let us raise our heads and look into the night. Every ancient patch of light seems to whisper: calculate the light-years, laugh, weep, and become the gentlest stardust in the universe.

Do not go gentle into that good night.

Old age should burn and rave at close of day.

Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

entry.title: 05-28 Twenty
entry.content:
Today is the second day of the fifth lunar month, three days before the Dragon Boat Festival, and my twentieth birthday.

That sentence alone is probably enough for my imagined readers to understand the title. Yes: the twentieth year of my life is about to arrive, and so is its twentieth summer.

On a day like this, I have begun tapping at the keyboard again, perhaps in order to pretend that I am writing something down, as anyone might who wishes to lend life a little ceremony.

Where should the account begin? With my frantic rush to the General Teaching Building for Signals and Systems this morning, or with finishing the homework last night? Perhaps it should begin with lying in bed, scrolling through my phone until four before I finally fell asleep. I have indeed been busy lately. The preliminary round of the Integrated Circuit Innovation Competition ended last week, immediately followed by the China Electrical Engineering Cup mathematical-modelling contest and work at the audiovisual event. I thought this week might offer a little room to breathe. Instead, my teacher began pressing us for progress in the circuit competition; I still had to edit and complete post-production on the Light and Shadow Group’s final programme; and both the municipal and university innovation projects had reached their mid-term deadlines.

Is this work I enjoy? It seems to be. Then why does finishing it leave me so tired? Is this truly the life I want? Am I willing to support myself through these things? Am I even capable of supporting myself through them? Or, pushing the question further, why should I remain alive, and what is remaining alive for? I do not know. I cannot find a reason to go on living; I merely have reasons why I cannot delete my account on Earth Online. Thus, even after reviewing the Z-transform late at night, even beneath a waning moon hanging over sparse paulownia branches, cheap little videos on an electronic screen remain beside me until the rooster announces dawn and the red sun rises.

The phoenix flute stirs the air, yet no graceful brow appears where the lights grow dim; the jade lantern turns, but for whom do fish and dragons dance?

There it is again—that awful habit from high school. Why am I still composing these sour little lines?

In ordinary language: perhaps I genuinely cannot find comfort elsewhere. Or perhaps Douyin offers me at least one guarantee—as long as I have electricity and an internet connection, it will continue recommending videos I may find interesting. And so, on the first day of my twentieth year, entertainment kept me awake until dawn.

Then I slept for three hours and went to Signals and Systems. The lecture concerned the Z-transform, and the course will finish in two weeks before the examination. To be honest, I do find the subject interesting. At the very least, it has taught me what signals and systems are, and how different transforms and analyses in the time and frequency domains can be used to process them. It creates the false yet strangely convincing sensation that, once I finish the course, I will be able to handle signals with ease—as though I had acquired some command over the fate of a thing.

Here I should thank my friend SC, who reminded me during the lecture that today was my birthday. Deeply moving, darling. I had almost forgotten it myself.

Perhaps this is also a place to say something about the meaning of anniversaries. I used to dismiss birthdays, graduations, and other supposedly special days; only holidays capable of giving me time off attracted much attention. Today, however, I might offer this apparently pointless observation: if you pay no attention to a commemorative day and assign it no meaning, then it truly has none. If you do attend to it and find it meaningful, then it becomes meaningful to you. Such a date resembles a mile marker in a marathon. You can ignore it and keep running without difficulty. Yet if you notice it, you realise how far you have already travelled, look back over what was gained and lost along the way, adjust your state of mind, and—whether the judgment is good or bad—continue forward.

The afternoon consisted of the thoroughly absurd classroom component of our social-practice course. The teacher was mostly filling time; I listened to the arrangements, signed in, and left. Nothing more needs to be said.

After dinner, I went to the engineering-training building to work on the drone. The situation was fairly abstract: “Your ministers have only just taken one city—why does Your Majesty press the army onward? How could we dare settle down? Three victories in a month!” When we finished, the senior student left to eat barbecue. The restaurant was decent. Then the two of us suddenly decided to fly the drone on our own; the moment we reached the field and tried, we packed up again. In truth, Brother Ding is usually reliable. This time, I was the unreliable one.

Afterward, Brother Ding and I rode our bicycles along the tree-lined central road of the south campus. The summer evening breeze carried not the slightest trace of coolness, while shouts from the men playing football on the field reached us from the side. Why, in memory, do the stadium lights still seem to have been on? The moment felt inexplicably youthful. On the first day of being twenty—twenty already exhausted, like an office worker or an old man—I felt, for a little while after ten at night, the freedom and vigour of youth from the seat of a bicycle. Perhaps that was the finest twentieth-birthday present the world could have given me.

Do not say the twilight comes too late; the evening sky is still filled with glowing clouds. I should catch the tail of youth and try to form, somewhere in the brain, a few synaptic connections worth remembering.

May we both take courage from this.

entry.title: The Pursuit of Happyness
entry.content:
(Piano version of A Father’s Way)

【Plot Summary】

Hello, listeners. Welcome to today’s edition of The Age of Light and Shadow on the Voice of BIT. I am your host, xxx.

Today, I would like to talk about an old film released in 2006: The Pursuit of Happyness, starring Will Smith.

The story takes place in San Francisco in 1981. Its protagonist, Chris Gardner, is a medical-equipment salesman who has invested all his savings in a portable bone-density scanner. The device is slightly more accurate than an X-ray machine, but it costs twice as much. The doctors’ response is simple: unnecessary and too expensive.

He therefore has no choice but to carry the forty-pound machine around every day, facing rejection again and again while continuing to try. His wife works two jobs to support the family, but eventually she can bear the situation no longer and leaves. Three months behind on the rent, he is evicted by his landlord. He and his son sleep in a toilet at a subway station, wait in long queues outside shelters, and even sell blood.

During that period, his only opportunity is an unpaid internship as a stockbroker. He works at the firm during the day and rushes to a shelter at night, while using whatever spare time remains to sell the scanners and obtain money for daily life.

In the end, he is hired and later establishes his own company. To be honest, when I watched this film in the past, I regarded it as a standard inspirational story: a poor man reverses his fate; a father’s love is as firm as a mountain; relentless effort finally carries him to Wall Street. Watching it now, however, I am most deeply impressed not by that “success,” but by the hands with which he covers his son’s ears in the toilet, and by the moment when he walks out of the office building, his eyes red, and applauds himself.

【Artistic Techniques】

The film’s director, Gabriele Muccino, is Italian and previously directed The Last Kiss. He brings traces of Italian neorealism into this film. Handheld cameras are used extensively, giving the images a slightly unsteady quality. The film was shot directly on the streets of San Francisco, and Will Smith was even asked to interact with homeless people there.

The young actor who plays the son is Jaden Smith, Will Smith’s own son. Many of the looks and physical gestures between them are not so much “acted” as genuine responses between father and son. This approach to casting is typical of the neorealist desire to “move life onto the screen”: the suffering in the film appears less like a performance and more like a record of reality.

【Thematic Analysis】

Why has this film remained popular for so long? I think it is because the film does not beautify suffering. It is not a bowl of chicken soup telling us that “effort always leads to success.” Instead, it presents the living and truthful story of a man who repeatedly fails, repeatedly loses what he has, and is repeatedly forced back into his original condition by life.

Chris loses a scanner, a shoe, and a place to live; he nearly loses custody of his son. To reach the queue outside the shelter, he runs wildly through the streets with the machine in his arms. To meet his targets, he gives up his breaks and spends two more hours on the telephone than everyone else each day.

Even the film’s title contains a hidden point: the word Happyness in The Pursuit of Happyness is misspelled; the correct spelling is Happiness. The error is said to come from a piece of graffiti mentioned in the real protagonist’s memoir. It seems to suggest that the “happiness” we pursue is itself imperfect. It is not a standard answer, but the trail of footprints left behind as we make mistakes and continue moving forward.

In other words, happiness is not the sound of a knock for which we wait. It is the road we see behind us when, after running until we are breathless, we finally turn around.

In the eyes of others, Chris is also a man of almost complete “disrepute”: a “deadbeat” who cannot pay his rent, an “incompetent husband” abandoned by his wife, a “madman” who chases swindlers and scanner thieves through the streets, and a person “not worth knowing well.”

Nor does the film give him a single person who is truly his “friend.” He does not even have the chance to ruin a friendship, because he does not qualify to be judged by friends in the first place.

Yet at the moment when his reputation is at its worst, he does not stop and beg anyone to change their view of him. Silently and stubbornly, he simply continues knocking on that door and fulfilling his responsibility as a father.

Perhaps we do not need to be declared “innocent” before we are allowed to live. Perhaps, when the entire world attaches the label “unworthy” to us, the only thing left for us to do is stop begging the world for a judgement that calls us “worthy.” We must move forward with all the charges laid upon us and all those labels marked “unworthy.” Only after we have travelled far enough can the labels be blown away by the wind.

【Reading the Details】

There is a shot in the film which many people have discussed, but which is worth mentioning again.

Chris cannot afford a hotel, so he hides with his son in a subway-station toilet. He holds the boy in his arms and braces the door with his foot while someone outside pounds upon it. He reaches out, covers his son’s ears, and cries without making a sound.

He could have broken down. He could have put his son aside, opened the door, and argued with the person outside, or simply walked out by himself. But he does not. He covers his son’s ears not because the boy might hear the abuse outside, but because he does not want his son to hear his fear. He must still fulfil a father’s responsibility.

At that moment, no one will applaud him. No one will tell him, “You are a good father.” No one even knows. He does all this simply because he is a father. In that toilet, he decides to reserve the last of his dignity for his son.

Many of our decisions are made in order to be seen. We lose weight so that we will look good in photographs, revise so that we will not be mocked, and apologise so that we will be forgiven. But what if no one sees? If nobody sympathises with you after you are rejected; if your friends remain distant even after you have corrected your mistakes and begun again; if you cry alone in a toilet while the people outside merely demand that you hurry up and leave—will you still make the right choice?

Chris’s answer is yes, because some things are not done for the sake of being seen. Even without an audience, Chris still chooses to be a person with dignity.

I also particularly like one detail at the end of the film. After Chris is hired, he leaves the building and enters the crowd. He does not laugh or shout, and his eyes are red. Then he raises his hands and slowly applauds himself a few times.

Many people interpret this as “he has finally succeeded.” Yet if we look more closely, those few claps are not powerful; they are even slightly hesitant. This is not the cheer of a victor, but a man who has just run out of a shelter, with the smell of the toilet still on his body, confirming that he remains alive. He is not applauding fate, God, or any audience. He is applauding himself.

At this moment, he still remembers that night in the subway-station toilet. He remembers the self who braced the door with one foot, covered his son’s ears, and wept in silence. Those memories will not disappear because of one letter of employment. Success is not an eraser. It cannot rub suffering away. It merely gives you the right to carry that suffering and continue along the road.

The real person upon whom the film is based later established a company and sold it for several million dollars. But all that happened later. In the subway-station toilet, he did not know what came later. He knew only that he had to survive that night.

In the film, Chris tells his son, “Don’t ever let somebody tell you you can’t do something. Not even me.” At the time, he himself is at the moment when he seems least capable of doing anything. Yet he does not stop. We do not know what he said to himself on the hardest nights. We know only that the next morning he put on that shirt, tied his tie, and continued towards the next door.

Thank you for listening to today’s edition of The Age of Light and Shadow on the Voice of BIT. See you next time.

What follows is the revised version—the broadcasting script.

(Piano version of A Father’s Way)

【Introduction】

Hello, listeners. Welcome to today’s edition of The Age of Light and Shadow on the Voice of BIT. I am your host, Zhang Hengwei. And I am your host, Hao Mingkai.

Today, we would like to talk about an old film released in 2006: The Pursuit of Happyness, starring Will Smith.

In most inspirational films, “success” tends to be a clearly defined destination: a reversal, a comeback, applause, and control over one’s own life.

What makes The Pursuit of Happyness truly distinctive, however, is that it spends almost its entire running time telling us that the normal condition of life is not success, but continuous failure and hope whose fulfilment is repeatedly delayed. The film is not explaining “how to succeed.” It is asking a heavier question: when a person remains unable to see any certain future, in what manner can he continue living?

【Plot Summary】

The film is adapted from a true story. Its protagonist, Chris Gardner, was originally a medical-equipment salesman. He invested all his savings in bone-density scanners, but weak market demand quickly drove him into financial collapse. His wife left, the rent went unpaid, and his life fell out of control. With his son, he struggled to survive in the cracks of the city of San Francisco.

At the hardest point, he received the opportunity to serve as an intern at a securities firm. The internship, however, was unpaid, and only one person out of twenty would be allowed to remain. During the day, therefore, he wore a shirt and tie and worked at the firm. At night, he queued with his son for admission to a shelter. In his spare time, he still had to sell the remaining scanners to obtain money for daily expenses.

In the end, he succeeded in staying. Later, he founded his own company and truly changed his fate.

Yet what I remember most clearly is not “success” itself, but the moments of embarrassment and distress: Chris running through the crowd with a machine in his arms; the silent tears he sheds as he covers his son’s ears in the toilet; and the sight of him leaving the office building, his eyes red, slowly applauding himself.

【Thematic Analysis】

What makes the film genuinely distinctive is that it treats failure not as an occasional event, but as a normal condition of life.

Chris repeatedly loses things, arrives late, and faces rejection. He must hurry to sell the machines, hurry to collect his son, and hurry to join the queue outside the shelter. The film contains hardly any truly relaxed moments. Yet he does not suffer frequent emotional explosions. He simply continues in silence: he continues selling the scanners, attending interviews, queuing for the shelter, and caring for his child. He seldom explains himself and rarely seeks understanding from other people.

This silence is not the result of a defect in his character. It is closer to a practical strategy for survival: when a person has neither the resources nor the opportunity to prove his worth, his only choice is not to waste himself upon explanations.

His condition does not follow the conventional inspirational logic of “persisting because one can see hope.” It is closer to the logic of reality: even when hope cannot be seen, life must still continue.

As Romain Rolland wrote, “There is only one heroism in the world: to see the world as it is and to love it.” People do not necessarily persist because they “see hope.” They persist because, even when they cannot see hope, they still wish to keep life from collapsing.

【Artistic Techniques】

The director of The Pursuit of Happyness is the Italian filmmaker Gabriele Muccino. The film displays a distinctly realist visual style. It makes extensive use of handheld photography, for example. The camera is not stable; when the characters run, the image sometimes shakes visibly. In the sequences involving the pursuit of a bus or taxi in particular, the camera remains close to Chris as he moves, and the audience is given almost no “safe distance.” The images are always urgent, crowded, and even slightly disordered.

This method does not turn running into a passionate moment of inspiration. Instead, it produces the hurried sensation of being driven by life. The characters are not running towards success; they are trying to avoid being left behind by reality altogether.

The film contains few of the bright and uplifting shots common in traditional inspirational cinema. Many scenes take place in narrow spaces such as rented rooms, subway stations, and shelters, and even the light is generally grey. This sense of reality is close to the spirit of Italian neorealist film: it places little emphasis upon “legends” and directs attention instead towards the struggles of ordinary people under the pressure of life.

Jaden Smith, who plays the son, is Will Smith’s son in real life. Many of the subtle looks and movements exchanged between father and son possess an effortless authenticity, reducing the traces of “performance” throughout the film.

【Reading the Details】

There is one shot in the film that many people remember.

Unable to afford a hotel, Chris can only hide with his son in a subway-station toilet for the night. He braces the door with his foot while someone outside knocks repeatedly. Holding the boy, he gently covers his ears, but cannot prevent his own tears.

The sequence contains almost no music. The narrow and enclosed space, the uninterrupted knocking, and Chris’s consistently restrained movements give the scene an almost suffocating reality. The director does not allow the character to collapse into loud sobbing, and the camera remains restrained as well. Yet the greater the restraint, the more strongly the audience feels a despair from which there is nowhere left to retreat.

More importantly, even in this condition, he still does one thing: he lets the child fall asleep first and refuses to collapse himself. At its centre, the scene is not really about “suffering.” It is about the attempt to preserve a minimum degree of order and dignity within a life that has fallen completely out of order. What moves us may not be how brightly a person shines after success, but his willingness to remain dignified when no one is watching.

【Reading the Ending】

At the end of the film, Chris is formally employed. He walks out of the office building and across the street. There is no exaggerated celebration; he merely applauds himself softly. The gesture is not grand and is even rather restrained, but its significance lies precisely in the idea of “confirmation”: it confirms that he has truly passed through a period from which there was no way back.

In the film, Chris once tells his son, “Don’t ever let somebody tell you you can’t do something. Not even me.” The sentence appears full of strength when heard by itself, but within the context of the entire film it is closer to a reminder he has struggled to recover from failure. Perhaps what truly matters is not the certainty that “success will come,” but whether, amid every uncertainty and failure, a person remains willing to move forward.

【Conclusion】

Thank you for listening to today’s edition of The Age of Light and Shadow on the Voice of BIT. See you next time.

entry.title: 05-07 Random Thoughts Late at Night
entry.content:
I just finished copying out the homework for Chapter Six of Signals and Systems, and then I flipped through the lecture slides, since there’s another quiz tomorrow. It all looked manageable—at least I could still make sense of it on my own. And then I just lost the will to keep looking. Somehow I found myself opening a new file, wanting to write something.

But write about what, exactly? I could try some sentimental lines—something about the endless night, the pitch-black outskirts of the city—but there’s no real point to that. After all, who would ever come here specifically to read this? No recommendation algorithm is going to funnel traffic my way, and if I think about the people around me, none of them would bother to check in on me for no reason.

Out of nowhere, I remembered a news story I saw today. It was about a man from Hunan who was about to jump into the Xiang River to end his life. Before he did, though, he ordered a cup of milk tea, and even left a note saying he was going to die. What followed was the shop owner, the delivery guy, and the police all teaming up to pull him back. By the time they got there, the guy’s head was all that was still visible above the water—anyone looking would have thought there was a rubber ball bobbing along the river. What a mess, honestly.

If you ask me, that man didn’t really want to die. If he were truly set on ending his life, he wouldn’t have broadcast his own death to the world beforehand. The guy was just too lonely. He got a bit of warmth from strangers, and that was enough to make him willing to keep living. Take the shop assistant’s line, for instance: “If I add an extra scoop of jelly for you, will you please not die?” Honestly, reading that, I felt an inexplicable urge to laugh. It was like coaxing a child—a pat on the head, a smile, and the crying stops. But there’s no denying that this guy was truly missing just that little bit. At the same time, it stirred a certain feeling in me. From my perspective as the dregs of society, here was a man using his own life as leverage to extort a bit of concern from strangers he didn’t even know, and putting the shop assistant and the police to all that trouble. When he finally comes to his senses, won’t he feel an even deeper loneliness, or shame, at having bargained for sympathy with his own life?

My imagined reader, you might think I’m being too cruel here, accusing me of being a cold-blooded social parasite. And perhaps that’s exactly what I am. I accept your criticism, because I myself don’t know whether my way of thinking is right or wrong. I don’t even know why I’m up at three in the morning, tapping away at my keyboard. All I know is that, like that guy, being human makes it hard to find a kindred companion. Whether of the same sex or the opposite, every person is an island, not a part of some vast continent.

But how does one ease the loneliness that underlies fate? I don’t know. If I did, I wouldn’t still be here, aimlessly hitting keys.

Time to sleep.

entry.title: 05-04 Pavlov's 80/20 Dog
entry.content:
Forgive me for giving an essay written on Youth Day such a peculiar title. I was thinking in the shower about my recent condition and realised that I can rarely summon much interest in serious study or work. More precisely, I seem to take considerably longer than other people would under normal circumstances. The radio programme I worked on is one example; mathematical modelling is another, where something that took my roommate a day took me three. Whatever the explanation, the problem is real.

If I want to solve my habit of procrastinating instead of working—and this very essay is being written while several urgent deadlines burn behind me—I should begin by imagining myself as Pavlov’s dog. Leaving aside the original biological conclusions and all the surrounding complications, what interests me is the logic through which Pavlov’s dog learned a behaviour: roughly speaking, the construction of a positive feedback loop for learning.

flowchart TD
 A[初始的动力打开学习开关]-->B[进行相关知识的学习]
 B-->C[学习得到好结果]
 C-->D[转化为进行下去的动力]
 D-->B

The reason I could compete so desperately in high school was that this logic really did operate in me. Admission to a good university became the principal objective, while frequent examinations quantified the results of my work and converted them into further motivation. Beginning in middle school, that positive cycle supported me all the way to university.

Since entering university, however, the cycle has plainly broken. Studying often feels pointless, and the act of studying itself seems to produce very little. Nearly two years have passed, and most of the time I am still in roughly the same state.

One requirement is to find the motivation with which learning begins. That is admittedly vague, and it is precisely what I need most; I have not yet worked it out. Another is to find a way of converting visible progress into a strategy for the next step, which is also something I lack. There may be a further technique, but it belongs with what follows.

Then there is the question of why my work always takes longer than other people’s. I see two reasons. First, some things genuinely do not need to be made as good as possible. My roommates aim simply to finish, because completion is enough to qualify, and so they finish quickly. My partners in broadcasting would complete the voice recording without repeatedly recording and revising it. The first take already displayed eighty per cent of what they could do; why invest so much more time merely to extract the remaining twenty?

I remember an example from a microeconomic analysis of Japan’s bubble era. To cut costs, firms focused on making workers save the final scraps of material, only to waste an enormous quantity of labour in the attempt. How is what I do different from a Japanese company spending a fortune to save its scraps? And how different is it from a teacher, after inserting another routine waste of time into a lesson, consoling us that “learning a little more can do no harm”? Perfection is easy to praise, but in many situations I have no need to pursue it. The return on making one thing perfect may be far lower than the return on spending the same time elsewhere.

That leads back to the Pareto principle: eighty per cent of the benefit is produced in twenty per cent of the time. Before spending the remaining eighty per cent of the time to obtain the remaining twenty per cent, I need to weigh the decision—to ask whether the result is worth it, whether it can provide the achievement I need, and whether that achievement will supply enough motivation for the next stage of learning.

Of course, writing this essay has delayed my other work and therefore contradicts everything I have just said.)

Back to the point. The second reason is my inability to enter a state of flow. In middle school I had far less contact with phones and similar distractions than I do now. Today, whatever work I begin, I tend eventually to abandon it. Starting this essay halfway through writing code is one example. I think the response has two parts: reduce the attraction of entertainment, and return to the Pavlovian mechanism above, using positive feedback to make study and investigation more attractive in their own right.

All right, that is probably enough. If I extract two actions from the argument, they are these:

  • Work out what reward mechanism sustains my learning; treat myself as Pavlov’s dog.
  • Make trade-offs. Use the 80/20 rule to decide how far a task should be taken, and refuse perfectionism.

That will do. Now I am going to put the advice above into practice. La—

entry.title: ARCH and GARCH Models
entry.content:
ARCH and GARCH Models

I. Why Are Models of Conditional Heteroskedasticity Needed?

1. Typical features of financial data

Financial time series, including stock returns and exchange-rate movements, often exhibit volatility clustering:

  • A period of violent fluctuation is likely to be followed by further violent fluctuation, as during a market crash.
  • A calm period is likewise likely to be followed by calm, as when a market is moving sideways.

A classic example:
During the global financial crisis of 2008, the S&P 500 repeatedly moved by more than 5 percent in a single day, whereas its daily movement in quiet periods was often below 1 percent.

2. Limitations of conventional models

An ARMA model assumes that the variance of its residuals remains constant. It therefore fails to capture volatility clustering, which may lead to:

  • biased risk forecasts;
  • ineffective portfolio optimisation; and
  • inaccurate pricing of derivatives.

II. The ARCH Model: Autoregression of Volatility

1. Definition of ARCH(1)

For a return series ( r_t ), define its conditional variance as:
$$
\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2
$$
where ( \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t v_t ) and ( v_t \sim N(0,1) ).

Key constraints:

  • ( \alpha_0 > 0 )
  • ( 0 \leq \alpha_1 < 1 )

2. The ARCH(q) model

Extending the model to q lags gives:
$$
\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^q \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2
$$
The condition ( \sum \alpha_i < 1 ) is required for stationarity.

III. The GARCH Model: Introducing a Memory Effect

1. The GARCH(p,q) model

Bollerslev (1986) added lagged variance terms to the ARCH model:
$$
\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^q \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2
$$
Constraints:

  • ( \alpha_0 > 0 )
  • ( \alpha_i, \beta_j \geq 0 )
  • ( \sum (\alpha_i + \beta_j) < 1 )

2. Why is GARCH generally preferable?

  • Long memory: conditional variance is affected by earlier variances, enabling the model to represent persistent volatility more effectively.
  • Parsimony: GARCH(1,1) can often replace a high-order ARCH model with far fewer parameters.

IV. A Complete Modeling Procedure

1. Preparing and testing the data

(1) Calculating returns

$$
r_t = \frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}} \times 100%
$$

(2) Testing for stationarity

2. Modeling the ARMA mean equation

Determine the order of the ARMA model from ACF and PACF plots:

3. Testing for ARCH effects

(1) Testing the autocorrelation of squared residuals

(2) The LM test

Null hypothesis: no ARCH effect.
The test statistic must be calculated manually in Python, or the arch package may be used for automatic detection.

4. Estimating the GARCH model

5. Model diagnosis

  • Test of standardized residuals: they should follow a standard normal distribution.
  • Parameter significance: the coefficients of the ARCH and GARCH terms should be significant.
  • Information criteria: select the model with the smallest AIC or BIC.

V. Case Study: Forecasting the Volatility of the Shenzhen B-Share Index

1. Data

  • Period: 2 January 2014 to 15 May 2018
  • Frequency: daily
  • Principal variables: closing price and return

2. Key steps

(1) Verifying the stationarity of returns

The ADF test gives a P-value of 0.0000, so the unit-root hypothesis is rejected.

(2) The ARMA(3,3) mean equation

$$
r_t = 0.014 + 0.388r_{t-1} + 0.118r_{t-2} - 0.871r_{t-3} + \varepsilon_t
$$

(3) The GARCH(1,1) variance equation

$$
\sigma_t^2 = 0.105 + 0.238\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + 0.786\sigma_{t-1}^2
$$

(4) Forecast results

Date Actual return Forecast return
2018-05-14 1.46% 1.89%
2018-05-15 1.48% 1.73%

VI. Common Pitfalls

1. What if the data are not stationary?

  • Difference the series first and construct a combined ARIMA–GARCH model.

2. What if the model does not converge?

  • Check whether all constraints are satisfied.
  • Try another optimisation algorithm, such as BFGS or NM.

3. How should p and q be selected?

  • Begin with GARCH(1,1) and increase the orders gradually.
  • Compare the AIC and BIC values of the candidate models.

VII. Comparison and Extensions

Model Advantage Limitation
ARCH Simple and intuitive May require many lagged terms
GARCH Parsimonious and captures persistence Assumes a symmetric response to shocks
EGARCH Represents the leverage effect Computationally complicated
TGARCH Distinguishes positive and negative shocks Requires more data

entry.title: Ridge and Lasso Regression
entry.content:
A Complete Introduction to Ridge and Lasso Regression

I. Why Is Regularized Regression Necessary?

1. The difficulty faced by OLS

Ordinary least squares is a fundamental method of modeling. When the data contain multicollinearity or simply too many variables, however, OLS faces two major problems:

  • Unstable coefficient estimates: a minor change in the data may cause a dramatic change in the coefficients.
  • Risk of overfitting: the model performs well on its training set but generalizes poorly.

2. The introduction of regularization

A penalty term is added to the loss function in order to restrict the complexity of the model:

  • Ridge regression: L2 regularization
  • Lasso regression: L1 regularization

II. Mathematical Principles: From OLS to Regularization

1. OLS regression

The loss function is:
$$
\min_{\beta} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j x_{ij})^2
$$

2. Ridge regression

An L2-norm, or Euclidean-norm, penalty is added, with λ controlling the strength of the penalty:
$$
\min_{\beta} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j x_{ij})^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2 \right]
$$

Features:

  • All coefficients are shrunk proportionally, but none is reduced exactly to zero.
  • Multicollinearity is alleviated, and model stability improves.
  • Ridge regression addresses an ill-conditioned matrix at the cost of unbiasedness and some precision.

3. Lasso regression

An L1, or Manhattan-norm, penalty is added:
$$
\min_{\beta} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j x_{ij})^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j| \right]
$$

Features:

  • The coefficients of unimportant variables may be reduced to zero, thereby performing variable selection.
  • The method is suitable for high-dimensional data, including cases in which there are more variables than observations.

III. The Central Operation: Selecting the Regularization Parameter λ

1. K-fold cross-validation

  • Procedure: divide the data into K parts. In turn, use K−1 parts for training and one part for validation, and then calculate the average error.
  • Objective: select the value of λ that minimizes validation error.

2. The regularization path

  • Ridge regression: as λ increases, the coefficients gradually approach zero.
  • Lasso: as λ increases, some coefficients abruptly become zero.

Python example for visualizing the path:

IV. Case Study: Predicting Cotton Yield

1. Data

  • Independent variables: expenditure on seed, fertilizer, pesticide, machinery, and irrigation
  • Dependent variable: cotton yield per unit area, based on data from 1990 to 2007

2. Procedure in Python

(1) Standardizing the data

(2) Constructing the Lasso model

(3) Interpreting the results

  • Conclusion: expenditure on machinery and fertilizer is removed, leaving three principal variables in the model.

V. Points Requiring Attention

1. The data must be standardized

  • Reason: regularization is sensitive to scale, so a variable with a large numerical range may dominate the penalty.
  • Method: use StandardScaler to give each variable a mean of 0 and a variance of 1.

2. How should the coefficients be interpreted?

  • Ridge regression: the sign of a coefficient indicates the direction of a variable’s influence on the target, but its magnitude is affected by λ.
  • Lasso: a nonzero coefficient indicates an important variable, but absolute magnitudes are not directly comparable.

3. Traps in selecting λ

  • Too small: the model approaches OLS and loses the effect of regularization.
  • Too large: all coefficients are excessively compressed, and the model underfits.

VI. Comparing and Selecting Models

Criterion Ridge regression Lasso regression
Type of regularization L2 L1
Coefficient behaviour Continuous shrinkage, without zero Sparse, with some coefficients zero
Suitable situation Severe multicollinearity High-dimensional data or selection
Computational cost Closed-form solution and fast Iterative optimisation and slower
Implementation RidgeCV in Python LassoCV in Python

VII. Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: When should ridge be used, and when should Lasso be used?

  • Ridge regression: when all variables are important but collinearity is present, as in the analysis of economic indicators.
  • Lasso: when there are many variables and the principal factors must be selected, as in genetic-data modeling.

Q2: What is Elastic Net?

  • Mixed regularization: L1+L2, balancing variable selection against stability.
  • Formula:
    $$\text{损失函数} + \lambda (\alpha \sum |\beta_j| + (1-\alpha) \sum \beta_j^2)$$

Q3: How should λ=0 be interpreted?

  • When λ=0, the model reduces to ordinary OLS regression.

entry.title: Multiple Linear Regression
entry.content:
Multiple Linear Regression

Regression analysis is a central instrument of data analysis. By examining the relation between independent variables X and a dependent variable Y, it seeks to reveal how Y is produced and to make predictions. Multiple linear regression explains an outcome through a linear combination of variables and quantifies the weight of each factor. It is therefore widely applied in economics, management, engineering, and related fields.

I. Purposes

  1. Identify important variables: select the values of X that are significantly related to Y, through stepwise regression, for example.
  2. Determine direction: establish whether X has a positive or negative influence on Y.
  3. Estimate weights: use regression coefficients to represent the relative importance of the variables.

II. Construction

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \cdots + \beta_k X_{ki} + \mu_i
$$
Here, $\beta_0$ is the intercept, $\beta_j$ is a partial regression coefficient, and $\mu_i$ is the disturbance term.

  • Holding the other variables constant, $\beta_j$ means that each one-unit increase in $X_j$ is associated with an average change in $Y$ of $\beta_j$ units.
  • The data may first be standardized with a $Z-Score$. The larger the absolute regression coefficient, the more substantial the contribution.

III. Model Testing and Optimisation

1. Goodness of fit

  • Coefficient of determination $R^2$: represents the proportion of variation explained by the model. Since $R^2 \in [0,1]$, a higher value generally indicates a better fit.
  • Adjusted $R^2$: guards against an artificially high fit caused merely by adding too many independent variables.

2. Dealing with heteroskedasticity

  • Symptom: the residuals spread out as the predicted value increases.
  • Diagnosis: the Breusch–Pagan test or White test.
  • Solution: use OLS + robust standard errors or generalized least squares (GLS).

3. Multicollinearity

  • Symptoms: coefficient signs appear abnormal, or individual $t$ tests are insignificant even though $R^2$ is high.
  • Diagnosis: the variance inflation factor, with VIF > 10 commonly treated as severe.
  • Solutions: remove highly correlated variables, enlarge the sample, or reduce dimensionality through principal component analysis.
  • The subject itself deserves another blog post.

IV. Stata Examples

1. Basic regression

2. Stepwise regression

V. Applications and Extensions

1. Limitations

  • Endogeneity: omitted variables or measurement errors may bias the coefficients. More precisely, a model is exogenous when the error term $μ$ is unrelated to all independent variables. If they are related, endogeneity is present, and the estimates of the regression coefficients are neither unbiased nor consistent. Instrumental variables must then be introduced.
  • Overfitting: when there are too many variables, the model should be improved through cross-validation or regularisation such as LASSO or Ridge.
  • Misrepresenting nonlinear relations: variable transformations, such as logarithms, or interaction terms may be introduced.

2. Possible extensions

  • Combine regression with principal component analysis: reduce the dimensionality of high-dimensional data before regression so as to address multicollinearity.

  • Mixed-effects models: handle individual and temporal effects in panel data.

  • Combine it with machine learning: use a random forest to select important variables and then construct the regression model.

  • Take logarithms: a logarithmic form expresses the elasticity of the original dependent variable with respect to an explanatory variable—that is, percentage rather than numerical change. Its advantages include: (1) weakening heteroskedasticity; (2) allowing a variable that is not normally distributed to become approximately normal after transformation; and (3) giving the model a form with economic meaning.

  • Standardize in advance for easier interpretation: the data may first be processed with a $Z-Score$, after which a larger absolute coefficient indicates a greater contribution.

  • Introduce dummy variables:

    Qualitative variables such as sex and region must be converted into 0–1 dummy variables. For example:
    $$
    \text{工资} = \beta_0 + \delta_0 \text{Female}_i + \beta_1 \text{教育年限}_i + \mu_i
    $$
    $\delta_0$ represents the wage difference between women and men at the same level of education, while $ \text{Female}_i$ uses 0 and 1 to distinguish the two groups.

VI. Case Studies

Both examples come from Qingfeng’s mathematical-modeling materials.

Case 1: Factors influencing the number of product reviews in e-commerce

  • Objective: examine how price, brand, place of origin, and other factors affect sales.
  • Method: standardized regression coefficients and dummy variables.
  • Conclusion: price has a significant negative effect, while imported brands enjoy a clear premium.

Case 2: Population prediction

  • Data: historical population and economic indicators.
  • Model: introduce a Logistic curve to fit the growth trend.
  • Extension: combine the model with ARIMA forecasts of economic variables.

entry.title: Grey Prediction Models: GM(n,m)
entry.content:
Grey Prediction Models: GM(n,m)

I did not need this model in the mathematical-modeling contest for which these notes were prepared. The detailed derivation below was generated by AI and has not yet been checked by me.

I. Background

1. The shortage of data

Mathematical-modeling problems often provide very few observations, perhaps four to ten periods, or incomplete information. Examples include:

  • a city’s GDP over the past five years;
  • three years of experimental records for a new material; and
  • the number of infections during the first seven days of an epidemic.

Conventional forecasting methods, including regression and time-series analysis, generally require substantial amounts of data. Grey prediction attempts to identify regularities when both the sample and the available information are limited.

2. Grey system theory

  • White system: information is completely known, as in a circuit system.
  • Grey system: some information is known and some remains unknown, as in an economic system.
  • Black system: information is entirely unknown, as with dark matter in the universe.

Grey prediction is designed precisely for a grey system. Its central idea is to process disordered raw data into a sequence with stronger regularity and then construct a differential equation to forecast its future development.

3. Suitable situations

The following view comes from Qingfeng’s mathematical-modeling course.

The choice of a forecasting model is open to reasonable disagreement:

  1. The observations should be nonnegative annual data. Monthly or quarterly data should instead be handled with the time-series models discussed in the preceding lesson.
  2. The data should pass a test for a quasi-exponential pattern. Apart from the first two periods, the smoothness ratio should be below 0.5 in at least 90 percent of the remaining periods.
  3. The series should be short and not strongly associated with other data. Ten periods or fewer are suitable, although a series can also be too short—for example, only three observations. A conventional time-series model is generally preferable when many periods are available.

II. The GM(1,1) Model in Detail

1. Data preprocessing

(1) Converting the direction of indicators

See the corresponding benefit-type transformations in the notes on evaluation models.

(2) Testing the data

  • Level-ratio test: determine whether the observations are suitable for a GM model.
    $$
    \sigma(k) = \frac{x^{(0)}(k)}{x^{(0)}(k-1)} \quad (k=2,3,…,n)
    $$
    Every ratio must lie within $(e^{-\frac{2}{n+1}}, e^{\frac{2}{n+1}})$.

2. Constructing the model in four steps

Step 1: First-order accumulated generating operation (1-AGO)

Purpose: transform fluctuating data into a monotonically increasing sequence.
$$
x^{(1)}(k) = \sum_{i=1}^k x^{(0)}(i) \quad (k=1,2,…,n)
$$

Example:

Sequence 1 2 3 4 5
Original data 2.87 3.28 3.34 3.39 3.68
Accumulated data 2.87 6.15 9.49 12.88 16.56

Step 2: Generate the adjacent-mean sequence Z

Purpose: construct a discrete approximation to the differential equation.
$$
z^{(1)}(k) = 0.5x^{(1)}(k) + 0.5x^{(1)}(k-1) \quad (k=2,3,…,n)
$$

Continuing the example:

| Z sequence | - | (2.87+6.15)/2=4.51 | (6.15+9.49)/2=7.82 | … |

Step 3: Establish the grey differential equation

$$
x^{(0)}(k) + a z^{(1)}(k) = b
$$
The parameters are estimated by least squares:
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
a \
b
\end{bmatrix} = (B^T B)^{-1} B^T Y
$$
where:
$$
B = \begin{bmatrix}
-z^{(1)}(2) & 1 \
-z^{(1)}(3) & 1 \
\vdots & \vdots \
-z^{(1)}(n) & 1
\end{bmatrix}, \quad
Y = \begin{bmatrix}
x^{(0)}(2) \
x^{(0)}(3) \
\vdots \
x^{(0)}(n)
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Step 4: Solve the whitenization equation

The corresponding continuous differential equation is:
$$
\frac{dx^{(1)}}{dt} + a x^{(1)} = b
$$
Its solution is:
$$
\hat{x}^{(1)}(t) = \left(x^{(0)}(1) - \frac{b}{a}\right)e^{-a(t-1)} + \frac{b}{a}
$$

Restore the predicted values:
$$
\hat{x}^{(0)}(k) = \hat{x}^{(1)}(k) - \hat{x}^{(1)}(k-1)
$$

3. Testing the model

(1) Test for a quasi-exponential pattern—the crucial test

  • Smoothness ratio: (\rho(k) = \frac{x^{(0)}(k)}{x^{(1)}(k-1)})
  • Passing criterion:
    • the first two periods may be treated more leniently;
    • (\rho(k)<0.5) in the final 80 percent of the periods.

(2) Test of the development coefficient

Development coefficient (-a) Suitable forecasting horizon
<0.3 Medium or long term, 5–10 periods
0.3–0.5 Short term, 1–3 periods
>0.5 Residual correction or another model is required

(3) Residual test

$$
\text{平均相对误差} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{k=2}^n \left|\frac{x^{(0)}(k)-\hat{x}^{(0)}(k)}{x^{(0)}(k)}\right|
$$

  • Below 10 percent: high precision
  • 10–20 percent: acceptable
  • Above 20 percent: the model is not credible

III. MATLAB Example: Predicting Pollution in the Yangtze River

1. Preparing the data

2. Complete implementation

3. Output

IV. Common Pitfalls

1. Fewer than four periods of data

  • Possible response: average the results of three GM variants—the conventional, new-information, and metabolic models.

2. Negative predicted values

  • Cause: the data were not transformed into a suitable positive direction.
  • Solution: examine the preprocessing stage and translate the observations with (x’ = x - \min(x) + 1).

3. Distorted long-term forecasts

  • Response: use rolling forecasts, updating the model after each newly predicted period.

4. Improving precision

  • Residual correction: construct another GM(1,1) model for the forecast residuals.
  • Combined forecasting: form a weighted combination with ARIMA, exponential smoothing, or another model.

V. Recommended Applications

Situation Suitability Examples
Forecasting economic indicators ★★★★★ GDP and population growth
Engineering forecasts ★★★★☆ Material fatigue life and equipment failure rates
Ecological and environmental forecasts ★★★★☆ Pollutant concentration and carbon-emission trends
Forecasting emergencies ★★☆☆☆ Epidemic spread and disaster losses

entry.title: Curve-Fitting Algorithms
entry.content:
Curve-Fitting Algorithms

Unlike interpolation, curve fitting does not require a curve to pass through every data point. Instead, it seeks a function, or curve, that minimizes the overall error between itself and all the observations under a specified criterion. Its central purpose is to construct the most suitable mathematical model by fitting the features of existing data. It is widely used for trend prediction, parameter estimation, and similar tasks.

I. The Difference from Interpolation

Method Principal feature Suitable situation
Interpolation The curve must pass through every sample point and may be affected by Runge’s phenomenon. Precise data and a small sample
Curve fitting The curve need not pass through every point; the global optimum minimizes squared errors. Noisy data and the analysis of trends

When there are too many sample points, a high-order interpolation polynomial may oscillate severely. A fitting algorithm based on a low-order function, such as a linear or exponential function, can reflect the trend of the data more steadily.

II. Principles

1. Mathematical model

Suppose the sample points are $(x_i, y_i), i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ and the fitted curve is $y = kx + b$. The aim is to minimize the sum of squared errors:
$$
\min_{k,b} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \quad \text{其中} \quad \hat{y}_i = kx_i + b
$$

2. Solving for the parameters

Taking partial derivatives and setting them equal to zero yields the closed-form solution:
$$
k = \frac{n \sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i}{n \sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2}, \quad
b = \frac{\sum x_i^2 \sum y_i - \sum x_i \sum x_i y_i}{n \sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2}
$$

3. Extension

The model may remain linear in its parameters even when it is polynomial in x, as in a quadratic function:
$$
\quad \hat{y}_i = kx_i + kx_i^2 + b
$$

III. Evaluating Goodness of Fit

1. The coefficient of determination $R^2$

  • Total sum of squares (SST): represents the total variation in the data.
    $$ SST = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \overline{y})^2 $$
  • Sum of squared errors (SSE): represents fitting error.
    $$ SSE = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 $$
  • Regression sum of squares (SSR): represents the variation explained by the model.
    $$ SSR = \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y}_i - \overline{y})^2 $$

The goodness of fit is:
$$ R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SST} = 1 - \frac{SSE}{SST} $$

  • Since $ R^2 \in [0, 1] $, a value closer to 1 indicates a better fit.
  • Note: $ R^2 $ applies only to models that are linear in their parameters. Thus, $ y = a + bx^2 $ is linear for this purpose because it is linear with respect to the parameters (a,b).

IV. Implementation in MATLAB

1. Code example

2. Curve Fitting Toolbox (cftool)

Enter cftool to open MATLAB’s Curve Fitting Toolbox. It supports several kinds of functions, including polynomials, exponentials, and custom equations, and automatically calculates both the parameters and the goodness of fit.

V. Applications

Case 1: Predicting the population of the United States

A Logistic model is used to fit historical data:
$$
x(t) = \frac{x_m}{1 + \left( \frac{x_m}{3.9} - 1 \right) e^{-r(t-1790)}}
$$
Nonlinear least squares are then used to estimate $x_m$ and $r$ and to predict the population trend over the next thirty years.

Case 2: A model of fish growth

Exponential and trigonometric functions are fitted to data on shark length and weight, and the best model is selected by comparing SSE:
$$
\text{体长增长方程：} \quad y = 69.32e^{-0.004x} \quad (R^2 = 0.9704)
$$

VI. Summary

  1. Suitable situations: prefer fitting when the data contain noise, the overall trend must be extracted, or the relation between variables is complicated.
  2. Model selection: give priority to models linear in their parameters so that $R^2$ can be used; for nonlinear models, compare SSE directly.
  3. Recommended tool: MATLAB’s cftool provides a quick way to fit and visualize several kinds of functions.

entry.title: Outlier Detection
entry.content:
I have once again encountered the problem of dealing with outliers. This post therefore gathers the relevant algorithms in one place, as comprehensively as I can manage.

1. Statistical Methods

(1) The modified Z-score

  • Suitable situation: univariate data whose distribution departs slightly from normality or contains a small number of disturbing outliers.
  • Procedure:
    1. Calculate the median and the median absolute deviation (MAD).
    2. Apply the modified Z-score: $ \text{修正Z} = \frac{|x - \text{Median}|}{\text{MAD} \times 1.4826} $.
    3. Choose a threshold, such as an absolute modified Z-score greater than 3, and regard values beyond it as outliers.
  • Underlying idea: replace the mean and standard deviation with the median and MAD, thereby reducing the influence of outliers upon the statistics themselves.
  • Limitation: the method is restricted to a single variable and may be insensitive to extremely skewed distributions.
  • Advantage: it is less easily distorted than the conventional Z-score and is suitable for contaminated data.

(2) The Grubbs test

  • Suitable situation: strictly normal univariate data in which a single outlier must be detected.
  • Procedure:
    1. Assume normality and calculate the Grubbs statistic for the maximum or minimum observation.
    2. Compare it with a critical-value table determined by the sample size and significance level α, and decide whether to reject the null hypothesis that no outlier exists.
  • Underlying idea: identify one outlier through hypothesis testing.
  • Limitation: strict normality is required, and observations can be tested only one at a time.
  • Advantage: its statistical meaning is explicit, which makes it suitable for scientific research.

2. Quantile-Based Methods

(1) The IQR or box-plot method

  • Suitable situation: univariate data following any distribution, especially a skewed one.
  • Procedure:
    1. Calculate Q1, the 25th percentile; Q3, the 75th percentile; and IQR = Q3 − Q1.
    2. Define the limits as $ \text{下限} = Q1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}, \quad \text{上限} = Q3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR} $.
  • Underlying idea: use quantiles to define the “normal range” of the data, with relatively low sensitivity to the tails.
  • Limitation: anomalies that arise only from combinations of variables may be missed, and the multiplier of 1.5 is fixed.
  • Advantage: the method is simple, efficient, and free of distributional assumptions.

(2) Percentile trimming

  • Suitable situation: the empirical distribution is unknown and extreme values must be removed quickly, as in financial risk control.
  • Procedure: directly remove the lowest α percent and the highest β percent of the observations—for example, α=1% and β=1%.
  • Underlying idea: impose a hard cut at empirical quantiles, relying on domain knowledge to select the thresholds.
  • Limitation: normal data may be deleted, and the thresholds are subjective.
  • Advantage: it is fast and direct in noisy settings. Basically, it amounts to using a rather blunt instrument.

3. Distance-Based Methods

(1) Mahalanobis distance

  • Suitable situation: multivariate data whose variables are correlated, such as an unusual combination of height and weight.
  • Procedure:
    1. Calculate the covariance matrix Σ and its inverse.
    2. Calculate the Mahalanobis distance of every observation: $ D = \sqrt{(x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)} $.
    3. Set a threshold from the χ² distribution, using a confidence level such as 95 percent.
  • Underlying idea: use a generalized distance that accounts for correlations among variables and identifies outliers in a multidimensional space.
  • Limitation: the method depends on estimating the covariance matrix and becomes unstable in high dimensions; the sample size should exceed the number of dimensions.
  • Advantage: it can capture multivariate anomalies comprehensively.

(2) K-nearest-neighbour distance

  • Suitable situation: unstructured data or the detection of local anomalies in images, text, and similar material.
  • Procedure:
    1. Calculate the average distance from each point to its K nearest neighbours.
    2. Treat a point whose distance exceeds the threshold as an outlier.
  • Underlying idea: detect anomalies through differences in local density; a point in a sparse region is more likely to be abnormal.
  • Limitation: computation is expensive, and K must be selected.
  • Advantage: no distributional assumption is required, making the method suitable for complicated data structures.

4. Density-Based Methods

(1) Local outlier factor (LOF)

  • Suitable situation: multivariate data in which samples with unusual local density must be detected—for example, an isolated point within an otherwise dense region.
  • Procedure:
    1. Estimate the local density of each point from the observations in its K-neighbourhood.
    2. The LOF value is the average ratio between the density around the point and those around its neighbours. A value far greater than 1 indicates an outlier.
  • Underlying idea: judge abnormality through relative density, addressing local patterns that a global method may overlook.
  • Limitation: computation is expensive, and the result is sensitive to K.
  • Advantage: local anomalies in non-uniformly distributed data can be identified.

5. Machine-Learning Methods

(1) Isolation Forest

  • Suitable situation: high-dimensional or unstructured data, including logs and time series.
  • Procedure:
    1. Construct several random trees and isolate samples by repeatedly dividing the feature space at random.
    2. Outliers tend to be isolated through shorter paths, from which an anomaly score is calculated.
  • Underlying idea: an outlier is easier to “isolate” in feature space.
  • Limitation: the method may be insensitive to local anomalies and requires parameters such as the number and depth of trees.
  • Advantage: linear time complexity makes it suitable for large datasets.

(2) DBSCAN clustering

  • Suitable situation: density-based clustering in which noise points are automatically identified as outliers.
  • Procedure:
    1. Set the neighbourhood radius ε and the minimum number of observations, min_samples.
    2. Mark as noise, and therefore as outliers, points that cannot form part of a core cluster.
  • Underlying idea: points in low-density regions are treated as abnormal.
  • Limitation: the result is sensitive to ε and min_samples, and performance is poor in high dimensions.
  • Advantage: the proportion of outliers need not be specified in advance, and the method suits data with an unknown distribution.

Summary: Points to Note and Selecting a Method

Points to note

  1. Do not delete blindly: an outlier may be the very signal that matters, such as fraud or equipment failure. Domain judgment remains necessary.
  2. Analyse variables jointly: a univariate method may miss an anomalous combination, such as normal height accompanied by extremely low weight.
  3. Adjust thresholds dynamically: when streaming data or distribution drift is present, update the statistics through a rolling procedure such as a moving-window IQR.
  4. Verify visually: box plots, scatter-plot matrices, and t-SNE projections can assist the decision.

Guide to selecting a method

Feature of the problem Recommended methods
One variable, approximately normal Modified Z-score and the three-sigma rule
One variable, skewed distribution IQR and percentile trimming
Several correlated variables Mahalanobis distance and LOF
High-dimensional data with a demand for efficiency Isolation Forest
Local anomaly detection LOF and K-NN distance
No distributional assumption and a need for automation DBSCAN and percentile trimming

Central principles

  • Prefer simplicity: begin with IQR or a Z-score for univariate data.
  • Match the domain: percentile trimming may suit financial risk control, while LOF or Isolation Forest may suit industrial inspection.
  • Cross-check: combine statistical tests, such as a normality test, with feedback from the actual application when tuning thresholds.
  • Simple settings: IQR for resistance to extreme observations; Z-score under normality.
  • Complicated settings: LOF for local anomalies; Isolation Forest for high-dimensional data.
  • Use domain knowledge: select the method according to the actual context.
  • Validate the strategy: combine statistical testing with subject knowledge.

Of course, the decision in a real modeling contest still depends on which problem you chose, how much time remains, and how much of that time can reasonably be spent on outliers.

entry.title: Notes from a Mathematical Modeling Workshop
entry.content:
An Overview of Mathematical Modeling

Mathematical modeling is, in my view, a category of competition well worth entering. It teaches the basic process and techniques of academic writing, traditional methods of modeling and analysis—which matter all the more in an age dominated by machine learning—and the use of scientific reasoning to examine real problems. That last part can make one’s thinking more rational. From a more practical perspective, the competition may also contribute to comprehensive assessment, postgraduate recommendation, and interview performance. Our university has developed a fairly mature sequence: three rounds of campus competition introduce the basic models, after which students alternate between the Mathematical Contest in Modeling and China’s national contest. I would recommend it to first-year BIT students. Programming, advanced mathematics, and mathematical analysis are studied in the first semester, and the contest arrives in the second. The timing is rather good.

This article organizes the subject according to my own way of thinking. I am an engineering student, so the account may lean toward familiar engineering procedures. Deriving models from differential equations and similar work is left aside.

I also omit machine-learning methods. Many are black boxes that cannot readily be explained, and such contests were not originally designed as machine-learning exercises. Some competitions simply ban those methods.

This post follows a 2025 mathematical-modeling workshop held by the Network Association, and much of it is copied directly. My thanks go to the speaker, Guo Wentao.

Modeling and Programming

The following broad categories can guide model selection. Beginners may as well start from nothing and learn while competing—“learn warfare through warfare,” as Chairman Mao put it.

My recommended route is to enter a campus contest, use CSDN, Zhihu, and Bilibili to find methods, verify them in SPSS, and ask GPT, DeepSeek, or whatever AI is currently popular to explain them. Understanding grows gradually through use.


flowchart LR
  B[AI及搜索了解可用模型]
  B --> C[SPSS验证方法可行性]
  C --> D[写代码]

The prerequisite, of course, is knowing which methods exist. For each major direction, understand the available models, their inputs and outputs, their central ideas, and the situations and characteristics for which they are suitable.

Optimization

Optimization seeks a maximum or minimum. More precisely, it consists of variables, constraints, and an objective function. Anyone familiar with the basic idea of a neural network will notice a resemblance to placing an objective function before the model and training toward it. I tell you which variables exist and what final quantity I want—the shortest path, for example—and you construct a model that produces it.

Points to note include:

  • Linear route-finding and similar problems may have a unique optimal solution.
  • Simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, and particle-swarm optimization produce simulated results and may become trapped in local optima. Run them several times.
  • Differential and difference equations often appear in biological or population problems, with competition and other conditions added over repeated simulations. They are common in Problem A of the MCM.
  • The speaker did not know much graph theory, and neither do I. It is rather theoretical.

flowchart LR
  A[优化模型] --> B[数学规划]
  B --> B1[dp]
  A --> C[微分、差分方程]
  C --> C1[传染病模型SIR]
  C --> C2[Lotka-Volterra]
  C --> C3[Leslie种群模型]
  A --> D[图论与网络]
  D --> D1[最短路]
  D --> D2[网络最大流]
  D --> D3[旅行商问题TSP]
  A --> E[优化算法]
  E --> E1[退火算法]
  E --> E2[遗传算法]
  E --> E3[粒子群算法]

Classification

Classification assigns existing objects to classes and may involve large amounts of data. It seldom forms an entire problem by itself, but often appears inside an evaluation task.

K-means, SVM, and XGBoost are particularly important.


flowchart LR
  A[分类模型] --> B1[判别分析]
  B1 --> B11[距离判别法]
  B1 --> B12[Fisher判别法]
  B1 --> B13[Bayes判别法]

  A --> B2[聚类分析]
  B2 --> B21[K-means聚类]


  A --> B3[神经网络分类]
  B3 --> B22[CNN]
  B3 --> B23[yolo]
  B3 --> B31[随机森林]
  B3 --> B32[SVM]
  B3 --> B33[XGBoost]

Evaluation

Evaluation compares the quality of alternatives through an appropriate judgment method. Problem B in the first round of the 2025 campus contest belonged to this category. Entropy weighting combined with TOPSIS worked well, while PCA first removed several variables and also made it possible to draw attractive heat maps. If nothing else comes to mind, a purely subjective method such as AHP can at least produce a complete answer.

The danger is that these highly conventional procedures produce homogeneous papers. The final choice still deserves careful thought.


flowchart LR
  A[评价模型] --> B1[层次分析法（AHP）]
  A --> B2[灰色关联度分析]
  A --> B3[BP神经网络]
  A --> B4[数据包络法DEA]
  A --> B5[组合评价法]
  A --> B6[熵权法+TOPSIS]

Forecasting

Forecasting estimates future changes.

  • Input: variables arranged over time
  • Output: future values of variables arranged over time
  • Principal methods: linear regression and ARIMA\GM
  • Several variables: LSTM may be attempted, or a non-temporal model may make judgments from specified factors

flowchart LR
  A[预测模型] --> B1[回归分析]
  B1 --> B11[线性回归]
  B1 --> B12[岭回归]

  A --> B2[时间序列分析]
  B2 --> B21[ARIMA]

  A --> B3[灰色预测]
  B3 --> B31["GM(1,1)"]

  A --> B4["支持向量机 SVM"]

  A --> B5[机器学习]
  B5 --> B51[BP神经网络]
  B5 --> B52[LSTM]
  B5 --> B53[GRU]
  B5 --> B54[随机森林]
  B5 --> B55[梯度提升机 GBDT]
  B5 --> B56[XGBoost 回归]
  B5 --> B57[LightGBM]
  B5 --> B58[SVR 回归]

  A --> B6[组合预测]

Overall Procedure


flowchart LR
  B[AI及搜索了解可用模型]
  B --> C[SPSS验证方法可行性]
  C --> D[写代码]
  D --> E[优化图表]
  E --> F[结果验证，评估]

Evaluation is sometimes optional. When several models are available, compare them; when an indicator looks good—for example, an excellent fit—mention it. When the result is poor, perhaps do not. But let me repeat: always verify feasibility before investing effort in a method.

The Paper

Document Structure

  1. Abstract
  2. Contents
  3. Introduction to the problem
    • Background
    • Restatement
    • Analysis
  4. List of symbols
  5. Basic assumptions
  6. Model construction and solution
    • Parts one, two, and three
  7. Strengths and weaknesses, evaluation, and sensitivity analysis

Main Body

Introduce the method + present formulas + use figures + give results.

  • Explain why it is used: identify the category of model and the purpose it serves.
  • Explain how it is used: provide the formulas and, where useful, a process diagram.
  • Explain the result: show the result graph and analyse the error.

Points to Note

  • Pay attention to the position of each task. The first may be handled more lightly; the third usually demands much more work.
  • Always verify feasibility and avoid wasted effort.
  • Polish every graph. In practice, many teams use similar models, so attractive figures matter enormously.
  • The abstract is also important. The modeler should revise it after all other work is complete.
  • Remember to add the list of symbols.
  • Whatever the detail or completeness of the modeling, address every requested task and figure and fill every part of the template.
  • The writer should begin on the first day, working on background research and similar material.
  • Figures need patient refinement. A slide from the workshop appears below.

  • The modeler and writer must communicate properly.
  • The modeler should assess strengths and weaknesses and design a sensitivity analysis. According to the workshop, SHAP may be useful for this? I have never used it anyway.
