entry.title: An Introduction to the Fundamentals of Cameras
entry.content:
A Complete Explanation of Camera Fundamentals: From Beginner to Expert

1. Preface

Photography is not only an art for recording life, but also a product of the encounter between technology and creativity. From the earliest black-and-white film cameras to today’s powerful digital equipment, continuous technological innovation has given us unlimited possibilities. Understanding the basic structure and operation of a camera is an important first step towards professional practice for every photography enthusiast. This article examines the fundamentals of cameras from several levels, helping readers understand both the principles behind equipment specifications and their flexible use in the creative process. (Thanks to ChatGPT and DeepSeek for their summaries, as well as to the summaries produced by earlier writers.)

2. Classification and Basic Knowledge

2.1 Types of Camera

  • Digital Single-Lens Reflex Camera (DSLR):

    A digital single-lens reflex camera. The term single lens is used in contrast with twin-lens reflex cameras: the same lens on a DSLR is used both to compose and to capture the image. A mirror system makes viewing and image formation possible. More specifically, while the photographer is composing the image, light entering through the lens strikes the mirror, is reflected towards the pentaprism, and is then refracted by the pentaprism so that the photographer can observe it through the optical viewfinder. When the shutter is pressed to expose the image, the mirror rises and the light travels directly to the image sensor. Once the exposure is complete, the mirror falls again. DSLRs respond quickly and offer stronger manual control, making them suitable for professional photographers and serious enthusiasts. They are now gradually being replaced by mirrorless cameras.

  • Mirrorless Camera:

    A mirrorless camera removes the reflex-mirror design and uses an electronic viewfinder directly. The advantages are the absence of vibration caused by the mirror opening and closing, as well as a smaller body and lower weight. At the same time, it preserves most of a DSLR’s performance—whatever a DSLR has, it generally has too—and has become increasingly popular in recent years.

  • Compact Digital Camera (DC):

    In other words, a point-and-shoot camera. Its lens cannot be changed, but it is simple to operate and convenient to carry, making it suitable for ordinary people’s daily records and travel photography.
    At this point, CCD cameras within this category deserve a brief mention. They basically replace the CMOS sensor found in an ordinary camera with a CCD. I shall not pass judgement: buy one if you want. From my personal perspective, however, CCD cameras can sit at the same table as Pop Mart products and other inexplicably fashionable objects. For details, see the explanation by the Zhihu expert listed in the references.

  • Smartphone Camera:

    Omitted.

2.2 Types of Image Sensor

The image sensor is the heart of a camera, and its performance directly influences image quality. There are two principal types:

  • CCD (Charge-Coupled Device):

    CCD is short for charge-coupled device. It can convert light into electric charge, store and transfer that charge, and retrieve the stored charge so that a voltage changes. The photoelectric effect produces charge upon the device’s surface, thereby creating a digital image.
    CCDs produce delicate images and reproduce colour accurately, but their manufacturing cost and energy consumption are relatively high. In practice, CMOS has already surpassed them, and they have gradually disappeared from public view. Recently, however, a trend has begun to speculate upon them again.

  • CMOS (Complementary Metal-Oxide Semiconductor):

    CMOS sensors are relatively inexpensive and consume less power. Most mainstream cameras now employ the technology, while technical progress continues to improve its image quality.

The larger the image sensor, or format—for example, full frame or APS-C—the more light it can generally capture. It therefore performs better in low-light environments, while also offering a relatively wider dynamic range and better control of noise.

2.3 Sensor Formats

  • Full Frame:

    A full-frame sensor is the same size as traditional 35 mm film, approximately 36 × 24 mm. It offers outstanding image quality, limited noise in weak light, a wide dynamic range, and flexible control of depth of field. It is the first choice for professional photography and high-end video production. Its disadvantages are the larger bodies and lenses, together with higher prices.

  • APS-C (Crop Sensor):

    An APS-C sensor is approximately half the size of full frame, around 23.6 × 15.7 mm. Because it is cheaper and more portable, it is widely used in entry-level DSLR and mirrorless cameras. It should be noted that the focal length of the lens must be multiplied by a crop factor, such as 1.5 or 1.6. The format is suitable for daily photography, travel, and enthusiast projects. Its image quality is weaker than that of full frame, but its cost-performance ratio is excellent.

  • Medium Format:

    Medium-format sensors are considerably larger than full frame—for example, 44 × 33 mm or more—and provide exceptional resolution, colour depth, and dynamic range. They are designed for commercial advertising, high-end portraiture, and artistic photography. Traditional medium-format cameras are bulky and expensive, although recent models have gradually become more portable, as demonstrated by Fujifilm’s GFX series.

  • Micro Four Thirds (M4/3):

    Measuring approximately 17.3 × 13 mm, this format emphasises a lightweight design. Both bodies and lenses are compact, making the system suitable for video, vlogs, and mobile outdoor applications such as drones and action cameras. Its image quality is weaker than full frame and APS-C, but its video performance is generally well optimised.

  • One Inch and Below (for example, 1 inch or 1/1.8 inch):

    These sensors are common in compact cameras, action cameras, and smartphones. Their extremely compact size limits their ability to collect light, so they depend upon algorithms such as multi-frame composition and AI noise reduction to improve image quality. They are suitable for casual daily records and sharing on social media.

2.4 Lenses and Imaging Systems

The following parameters deserve the greatest attention:

  • Focal Length:
    Focal length determines both the field of view and the degree of visual compression. Wide-angle lenses are suitable for landscapes and street photography, while telephoto lenses are often used for portraits and wildlife.

  • Aperture:
    The size of the aperture determines the quantity of incoming light and the resulting depth of field, and is commonly expressed as an f-number. A smaller f-number represents a wider aperture, which performs better in weak light and can also produce a softly blurred background.

  • Image Stabilisation:
    Some lenses or cameras contain image-stabilisation systems that reduce the effect of hand movement at slow shutter speeds. This is useful for indoor and night photography.

2.5 Understanding the Controls

Before using a camera, one should at least know what its buttons do. The information below comes from a post on Xiaoheihe. I have not reproduced its detailed illustrations; consult the original article instead:

  • Practical Knowledge: An Introduction to Cameras - Xiaoheihe

  • Basic Control Area

    • Power switch: Usually marked ON/OFF; on some cameras it is integrated into the mode dial.
    • Shutter button: Half-press to focus and press fully to take the photograph. A beep indicates that focusing is complete.
    • Mode dial: Selects a shooting mode, such as AUTO (fully automatic), P (programmed auto), S/Tv (shutter priority), A/Av (aperture priority), or M (fully manual).
    • Hot shoe: The metal slot on top of the camera, used to attach an external flash or microphone.

  • Function Shortcuts

    • ISO button: Quickly adjusts sensitivity. A higher value produces a brighter image but also more noise.
    • Exposure-compensation button (±): Raises or lowers image brightness in automatic modes. Follow the principle of adding for white and subtracting for black.
    • AF/MF selector: Switches between autofocus (AF) and manual focus (MF).
    • Q/Menu button: Opens the settings menu or a quick-control interface.
    • Directional buttons/control wheel: Adjust parameters or change the focus point.

  • Other Important Buttons

    • INFO/DISP: Changes the information displayed on screen, such as the histogram or electronic level.
    • Delete button (bin icon): Deletes photographs or videos.
    • Playback button (▶️ icon): Displays captured material.

2.6 Understanding the Interface and Its Parameters

The following key parameters can be seen through the viewfinder or upon the LCD screen, although their presentation varies slightly among models:

  • ⚡️ Flash status
  • 📷 + number: number of exposures remaining
  • 1/125: shutter speed; the larger the denominator, the faster the shutter
  • F5.6: aperture value; the smaller the number, the wider the aperture and the stronger the background blur
  • ISO 100: sensitivity
  • ◼️▪️▪️▪️ Exposure scale; exposure is normal when the pointer is centred
  • AFS: single autofocus
  • ⭕️●⭕️ Position of the focus point

3. The Three Elements of Exposure

3.1 Aperture

Aperture controls not only the quantity of incoming light, but also depth of field:

  • Wide Aperture (small f-number):
    Allows more light to enter and is therefore suitable for weak-light conditions. It also produces a shallow depth of field, keeping the subject clear while blurring the background.

  • Narrow Aperture (large f-number):
    Reduces the amount of incoming light but increases depth of field. It is appropriate for landscapes and other scenes in which detail should remain balanced throughout the image.

3.2 Shutter Speed

  • Slow Shutter Speed:

    The exposure lasts longer, making it suitable for night scenes, flowing water, and light trails. A tripod is required to prevent blur.

  • Fast Shutter Speed:

    Freezes movement and is appropriate for sport, wildlife, and other rapidly moving subjects. It may, however, cause underexposure and leave you with a great dark lump of an image.

In creative photography, deliberately choosing a slow shutter can produce motion blur and add a dynamic rhythm to the image. Photographing star trails requires a different method: set an interval between individual exposures and combine the resulting images in post-production.

3.3 ISO Sensitivity

  • Low ISO:

    Produces less noise and better image quality, and is suitable for well-lit scenes.

  • High ISO:

    Increases sensitivity and is useful in weak light, but introduces more noise.

4. Metering and Exposure Compensation

4.1 Metering Modes

  • Spot Metering:

    Measures only a small area of the image and is suitable when the subject needs to be emphasised.

  • Centre-Weighted Metering:

    Gives priority to the centre of the frame while taking the surrounding light into account. It is suitable for most ordinary photographs.

  • Matrix/Evaluative Metering:

    Analyses the light across the complete frame and uses an algorithm to calculate the best exposure value. It is appropriate for general use.

  • Partial Metering:

    Meters the central portion of the frame. Use it when the subject occupies a relatively small local area and contrasts strongly with the background.

4.2 Exposure Compensation

In automatic modes, the camera may sometimes fail to measure complicated light accurately. Exposure compensation can then be used:

  • Positive Compensation:
    Increases exposure when insufficient detail is visible in dark areas.

  • Negative Compensation:
    Reduces exposure to prevent highlights from being overexposed and preserve more detail.

Understanding these settings makes it easier to respond flexibly to complicated lighting conditions and obtain more accurate exposures.

5. Shooting Modes

  • M Mode (Fully Manual):

    Gives the user complete manual control over aperture, shutter speed, and ISO, requiring the three elements of exposure to be balanced independently. It is suitable for experienced photographers dealing with complicated lighting, such as night scenes or studio work, and for precise forms of creation such as long exposures and astrophotography. It is demanding to operate, and the exposure scale must be observed in real time. Then again, you can take pictures perfectly well without it. There is no need to force yourself to use manual mode; enjoying the process is enough.

  • P Mode (Programmed Auto):

    The camera sets the aperture and shutter speed automatically, while offering slightly more manual adjustment than A mode.

  • Av/A Mode (Aperture Priority):

    The photographer sets the aperture manually and the camera chooses a matching shutter speed. Control of the aperture adjusts depth of field: a wide aperture can blur the background, while a narrow aperture extends the region in focus. It is suitable for portraits, landscapes, still life, and other subjects in which visual layers should be emphasised.

  • Tv/S Mode (Shutter Priority):

    The photographer sets the shutter speed manually and the camera selects the aperture. Control of the shutter speed can freeze movement with a fast shutter or create motion blur with a slow one, making the mode suitable for sport, traffic, and flowing water.

  • Auto Mode (Fully Automatic):

    The camera takes complete control of every parameter, including the flash, and the user needs only to compose the image and press the shutter. It is useful for urgent snapshots and complete beginners, but offers very little creative freedom and can easily be affected by an incorrect judgement from the algorithm.

  • Bulb Mode:

    Allows the shutter’s open time to be controlled manually: press the shutter to begin the exposure and release it to end. It is used for extremely long exposures, including star trails, light painting, and fireworks. A tripod and cable release are required to prevent camera shake.

  • Scene Modes (such as portrait, landscape, and night scene):

    The camera optimises a combination of parameters for a preset scene. Portrait mode, for example, automatically opens the aperture, while night mode raises the ISO. These modes are convenient for quickly photographing a particular subject, but are less flexible than semi-automatic modes such as P, Av, and Tv.

The essential difference among these modes is the distribution of “control over parameters.” From Auto to M, the user gradually takes control of more parameters. The cost is greater operational complexity, but the space for creative choice expands at the same time.

6. White Balance and Colour Management

The basic idea of white balance is that “under any light source, a white object should be restored to white.” In other words, it attempts to reproduce white as white under light of different colour temperatures.

Automatic white balance is sufficient in most situations. When the lighting is complicated, or when a particular tone is required, different Kelvin values can be selected to influence the image, producing a warmer or cooler appearance.

  • A lower K value → bluer, or cooler → suitable for snow scenes and ice sculptures;
  • A higher K value → yellower, or warmer → suitable for cafés and candlelit dinners.

6.1 Foundations of White Balance

White balance is primarily used to correct differences in colour temperature among light sources:

  • Automatic White Balance (AWB):

    The camera judges the colour temperature of the environment automatically, but complicated sources of light may produce a colour cast.

  • Manual Settings:

    The photographer adjusts the setting according to the source on location, such as daylight, tungsten lamps, or fluorescent light, ensuring that the colours in the image are accurate.

In practice, none of this is necessary. Just shoot RAW and throw the file into post-production for correction.

7. Focusing Systems and Focus Control

1. Manual Focus (MF): turn the ring yourself.

  • When to use it:

    • Macro photography, such as small insects or details of flower petals;
    • Stars at night or extremely dark scenes;
    • Situations in which autofocus repeatedly misses, such as animals behind cage bars or subjects behind glass.

  • Disadvantage: It is slow. You must turn the focusing ring yourself, and beginners can easily shake the camera and produce a blurred image.

2. Single Autofocus (AF-S): half-press the shutter to focus once; suitable for stationary subjects.

  • When to use it:

    • Landscapes, identification photographs, and arranged still life;
    • Focusing first and then moving the frame to compose—for example, focus upon a face before placing the person on the left side of the image;
    • It is less suitable for children or pets running around, or for sporting events.

3. Continuous Autofocus (AF-C): select the appropriate mode and hold the shutter for a burst, capturing moving subjects.

  • When to use it:

    • While the shutter is half-pressed, the focus follows a moving subject, such as a runner, bird, or car;
    • It works well with burst shooting.

  • Note: A complicated background may cause the system to lose the subject, so choose a clean background where possible.

4. Automatic Autofocus (AF-A): switches between AF-S and AF-C by itself. For example, it may first focus upon a stationary person and then follow automatically if the person suddenly starts running.

8. File Formats and Colour Spaces

  • RAW Format: An uncompressed file of original data, similar to a film negative, which records all the information captured by the sensor, including unprocessed colour, dynamic range, and detail.

    • Advantages:

      • Preserves the greatest possible room for post-production, allowing non-destructive correction of exposure, white balance, and colour deviation;
      • A high dynamic range reduces the risk of blown highlights and completely black shadows;
      • Suitable for professional photography, commercial work, and situations requiring careful retouching.

    • Disadvantages:

      • Large files, with high storage and transmission costs;
      • Requires specialised software such as Lightroom or Capture One and cannot be shared directly;
      • Straight-out-of-camera results appear relatively flat and depend upon post-processing skill.

  • JPEG Format: An image file compressed and processed inside the camera, directly producing a finished picture that can be shared.

    • Advantages:

      • Small files with strong compatibility; phones and computers require no special decoding;
      • In-camera algorithms optimise the output colours, including skin tones in portraits and saturation in landscapes;
      • Suitable for rapid delivery, social-media sharing, and non-professional requirements.

    • Disadvantages:

      • Compression loses detail, while reductions in dynamic range and colour information are irreversible;
      • Leaves very little room for post-production and easily produces tonal banding or noise.

Anyway, when taking photographs, just use RAW. JPEG is what you export after editing. As for the colour space, simply choose sRGB. Colour spaces are somewhat similar to the colour gamuts discussed in the article on monitors, which you can read if interested.

entry.title: Your Lie in April
entry.content:
Your Lie in April: A Programme by the Light and Shadow Group

—The April when I met you is coming. The April without you is coming.

Let me once again thank my partner for this programme. She recommended the anime to me, and she also worked with me to complete both the script and the broadcast. In fact, it would be more accurate to say that, as a senior member, she guided a newcomer like me—boo-hoo. Her contribution to the programme was far greater than mine.

Dramatic Excerpt I

Source: Your Lie in April (Chinese Dub)

Kousei: A melodica? Not bad. (The tone is slightly questioning; pause between the two sentences.)

Tsubaki: (Background voice; a sound effect can be added in post-production.) Miwa told me that the moment she met him, her life changed. (Speak with a smile; let the final sentence fade.) Everything she saw, heard, and felt—everything within her sight—began to fill with brilliant colours. (Pause after “everything within her sight”; strengthen the second half.) The whole world began to shine. (Strengthen the second half.)

(The sound of the melodica continues…)

Main Programme

Hello, everyone. Welcome to today’s edition of The Age of Light and Shadow on the Voice of BIT. I am your host, Zhang Hengwei, and I am your host, Wang Yiru. (Introduction.) At a time when the animation market is crowded with adaptations of light novels and fast-food series appear one after another, there is an anime that was released eleven years ago but still ranks second in an online Japanese poll of the most moving animated works. It has also become, for countless viewers, a masterpiece that every newcomer to anime ought to watch. More than ten years after its release, many people still commemorate it in their own ways every April. || If you are interested in stories of pure love and curious about a classic anime with such an enduring reputation, Your Lie in April may be exactly the work you have been expecting. In today’s edition of The Age of Light and Shadow, let us enter that April of falling cherry blossoms and listen to the symphony of music and love within Your Lie in April.

This story of music and love begins with an unexpected encounter. The protagonist, Kousei Arima, has studied the piano since childhood under his mother’s strict instruction and has repeatedly won first prize in competitions large and small. An unquestionably gifted young pianist, Kousei is, in almost everyone’s eyes, closely associated with the title of a rising star in the world of piano. Yet an unforeseen change destroys those hopes and breaks apart the musical dream he has always pursued. His mother, severe in her teaching and seldom given to smiles, dies suddenly after suffering from cancer. Faced with this disaster and overwhelmed by grief, Kousei becomes unable to hear the sound of his own piano, and his life loses all light. Then another unexpected encounter completely transforms that dim existence. While waiting for a friend, Kousei happens to meet Kaori Miyazono beneath a cherry tree, playing a melodica. He is drawn towards Kaori, a free and uninhibited violinist, and through a series of accidents the two become friends. Beneath Kaori’s bright and cheerful appearance, however, lies a shadow unknown to others. As an accomplished violinist, she began learning the instrument as a child because she wished to perform with the gifted Kousei Arima. To fulfil that childhood promise, Kaori creates their meeting through the lie that she “likes their mutual friend,” concealing the cruel fact that she is terminally ill. Yet this unexpected encounter not only restores music to Kousei’s world, in which only monotonous black and white keys remained, but also allows Kaori’s meteor-bright life to release its fiercest light during its final countdown. In the time left to her, Kaori uses her music and love to teach Kousei that music is not a chain, but a language through which he can speak to the world. She also teaches him how to face loss. Finally, in the spring when Kaori Miyazono departs, he performs the eternal composition that belongs to them both.

Dramatic Excerpt II

Source: Your Lie in April — Excerpt 2 — Bilibili

Kaori: Are you still playing the piano?

Kousei: I don’t play any more.

I knew it. You are sinking into despair alone again.

Kousei: I can’t do it any more. Everyone important to me has left before my eyes. Music took the people who truly mattered away, until I was the only one left.

Kaori: But you still have me, don’t you? Arima, I am going to have an operation on 18 February. I will give everything I have and struggle until the final moment. It is your fault—all of it. The reason I am struggling so awkwardly and chasing the hope of staying alive is you. The time I spent with you made me unwilling to leave. Won’t you try once more? Aren’t we best at fighting with everything we have? Aren’t we performers who struggle as if our lives depend upon it?

Kousei: But I haven’t touched the piano for a week.

Kaori: You hadn’t touched it when you accompanied me either.

Kousei: I occasionally played while working part-time then. There is no way I can perform well now. It would take a miracle to play in this condition…

Kaori: You are looking down again.

(Kaori plays the violin.)

Kaori: You wanted a miracle? There it is.

Main Programme

As a classic of Japanese animation, Your Lie in April is not merely a story of youth. It is also an anime about music, a classic whose flesh and blood are musical. From Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata in the first episode to Chopin’s Ballade No. 1 in G Minor in the last; from Saint-Saëns’s Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso, with which the two protagonists first perform together, to Kreisler’s Liebesleid, which they never manage to complete together, every piece of classical music corresponds precisely with the plot and becomes a bridge along which emotion can flow. As Kousei breaks free from his mother’s shadow amid the torrent of the Revolutionary Étude, and as Kaori interprets the final blaze of life through the wild freedom of Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso, the notes and the narrative have already become one, producing an almost fated resonance.

The film allows music and narrative to grow together, going far beyond the simple use of “music as background.” With notes as its bricks and tiles, it constructs a city that remains forever in April. As Kaori says, “Music is freedom!” The creators weave that freedom together with the solemnity of classical music, arranging a magnificent concert for the transience of youth. When, ten years later, we still hear news of this concert being performed again and again in the words of so many people, we know that the concert of that April has long since been engraved upon their hearts and entered eternity.

Zhu Guangqian once wrote that, although the contents of tragedy mostly appear frightening on the surface, tragedy is by no means limited to terror. Terror merely causes pain and finally leaves people gloomy and discouraged, whereas tragedy inspires and strengthens them. Your Lie in April is a fine work that carries this principle through. It takes a tragedy in April as its foundation, yet releases an astonishing vitality that urges people to grow and move forward.

The so-called “lie” of the plot is the most beautiful lie woven by a girl who, as her life enters its final countdown, wants to save the person she loves. With the lie that she “likes Watari,” Kaori Miyazono enters the life of Kousei, the former child prodigy, knocks upon the door of his heart, and helps him overcome his inner demon. Through this apparently light and conventional device, the author offers a delicate interpretation of the Japanese aesthetics of mono no aware. In The Tale of Genji, the evening face blooms in the morning and withers by evening; similarly, behind Kaori’s gentle “lie” lies endless sorrow. In the last part of her life, she chooses to build a bridge towards their meeting out of a lie, solely so that, before she disappears, she can use the final vitality within her to save the gifted performer she loves. Like a cherry blossom whose fall is already determined at the instant of its full flowering, this countdown narrative casts a reflected sorrow over every warm scene, producing a tragic aesthetic space with a profoundly Eastern quality.

Just as every cherry blossom that opens in April must return to dust, and just as every performance must eventually end, Kaori—who brings hope and vitality to Kousei—still falls before that April of cherry blossoms arrives. The ending reveals the existential nature of life as “being towards death”: every apparently eternal beauty is, in essence, merely a suspension granted by death. Such recognition of life’s meaninglessness ought to lead towards nihilism. In this work, however, the author completes the turn from nothingness to existence through the characters’ devotion to and love for music. In the last days of her life, Kaori continues her final struggle so that she might perform on the same stage as the person she loves. Even after both his mother and his beloved have left him, Arima continues to play Bach and Chopin for the world, still carrying hope for life. These moments of earnest living constitute defiance against an absurd world. Like Camus’s Sisyphus, who knows the boulder will roll down again but continues climbing, Kousei defies his fate. Likewise, in that final April, Kaori smiles and says, “Even if grief is impossible to restrain, even if we lie wounded at the bottom of the valley, we must not stop playing. Only in this way are we truly alive.” This is her defiance against her terminal illness. Only now do we suddenly understand: life conceals the essence of disappearance beneath the appearance of existence, while human beings, fully aware of the ending, still choose to live with passion. As Romain Rolland wrote, “There is only one heroism in the world: to see the world as it is and to love it.” Yes—the most magnificent heroism of life does not lie in avoiding the inevitability of disappearance, but in turning the final scene into a splendid movement in full bloom. Even if I am to disappear tomorrow, today I will still straighten my tie and go out to greet the final evening glow and the rising sun.

Today, ten years later, Japan’s cherry-blossom front still moves northwards at seventeen kilometres per day. Petals still fall at five centimetres per second, and a pink glow once again rises upon Tokyo Tower. When real visitors lift their heads towards that fleeting splendour on the branches and reach out to catch petals falling at five centimetres per second, perhaps they do not know that Chopin’s Ballade No. 1 in G Minor from ten years ago remains condensed within those blossoms. Perhaps they do not know that the cherry blossoms once contained the harmonics of the young girl’s violin. Yet perhaps, as people already understand, the greatest beauty of cherry blossoms lies in the rain of petals that fills the sky as they fall. This happens to echo the final lie Kaori leaves to the world: although the words written upon it are “farewell forever,” what we hear is “I will wait for you in the future.”

The April when I met you is coming. The April without you is coming.

Closing Song

光るなら

entry.title: An Introduction to Batch Files (.bat)
entry.content:
An Introduction to Batch Files (.bat)

A batch file, whose extension is .bat, is a script file used in Windows to execute a sequence of commands automatically. By writing such a file, one can automate routine tasks, administer the system, and perform file operations with relatively little effort.

How to Write and Use a .bat File

Writing one

Create a new file in Notepad or another text editor, enter the required commands and script logic, save it, and finally change its filename extension.

Running one

  • Double-click the .bat file to run it directly.
  • Alternatively, enter the path to the file at the Command Prompt.
  • A batch file may also be combined with Windows Task Scheduler so that it runs automatically at a specified time.

Common Syntax

  • Comments: explain the script without being executed.

  • Turn off command echoing: prevent commands themselves from being displayed during execution.

  • Display information: print text on the screen.

  • Pause the script: wait for the user to press a key before continuing.

  • Conditional statements: execute different commands according to whether a condition is satisfied.

  • Loops: iterate over files or a list of variables.

  • Variables: define and refer to variables; command-line arguments can also be received through %1, %2, and so forth.

  • Labels and jumps: use goto to control the flow of the script, loosely imitating a function.

Example

The following script checks whether a file exists and prints the corresponding message:

Other Points to Note

  • Debugging: add pause to the script when you need to inspect its output or debug it step by step.

  • Compatibility: batch files are designed specifically for Windows. Other systems, such as Linux, usually employ shell scripts with the .sh extension.

  • Security: do not store sensitive information in a script, and exercise particular care with dangerous commands involving deletion or formatting.

  • Extended use: batch files can work together with PowerShell, VBScript, and other automation tools to handle more complicated tasks.

References:
An Introduction to Windows Office Batch Files
A CSDN Tutorial on Batch Files
Baidu Baike: bat

entry.title: Building and Optimising a Hexo + Fluid + Obsidian Blog
entry.content:
1. Preface

The immediate reason I built this blog was that, while having dinner with a senior student some time ago, I saw the personal site he had made. I already knew that the relevant open-source projects were mature, so a thought struck me and I simply started working—not quite as dramatic as that, perhaps.

It also solved a problem that had troubled me for a long time: I had nowhere suitable to share things. I genuinely wanted to write more—to record the curious little projects I had experimented with, the works of art I had appreciated, and my own thoughts and feelings. While I still had time, I wanted to write longer essays that might protect my ability to think and express myself, rather than letting it disappear in the storm of short videos. But where could I write? Posting on Tieba, Zhihu, or Xiaohongshu did not appeal to me: I disliked the atmosphere of those platforms and had no desire to cover every statement in defensive disclaimers merely to suit it. QQ Space and WeChat Moments were not designed for long arguments; a short paragraph could neither satisfy my wish to express myself nor explain what I meant, and my WeChat contacts might not want to read it anyway. Making videos would be even worse: it would consume still more time and bring the culture of another online community into the calculation.

A personal blog meets these needs rather well. Here I can say whatever I want, describe what I think, and record what I wish to remember. After all, I am largely writing for myself, and almost nobody visits this site to read these articles. Besides, it is an amusing small project, is it not? The underlying software may be open source, but that does not prevent me from using the opportunity to learn something about front-end development.

The final paragraph of this preface is for any reader who happens to arrive. If you also want to build a personal blog of this kind, read on: I will record part of the construction process and the writing workflow I currently recommend.

2. Construction

Tools Used

  • Hexo: the blog framework, which may be understood as the skeleton of the site.
  • Fluid: the site’s theme. Its official documentation is detailed, so the configuration can simply follow that guide and needs no repetition here.
  • GitHub Pages: a convenient, free service for hosting static websites; one GitHub account can have one such site.
  • Obsidian: a text editor that becomes extremely convenient once configured. Its rich plugin system supports such tasks as importing templates and organising files through a directory structure.
  • Typora: a lightweight Markdown editor that adds rendering and keyboard shortcuts to what would otherwise be little more than Notepad.

Installation

Prerequisites

  • Node.js: a program capable of executing JavaScript code; more precisely, it is a JavaScript runtime.
  • Git: the well-known open-source distributed version-control system, designed to handle projects of any size efficiently. It is the Git underlying GitHub and can be regarded as a steward of file versions, supporting the storage, rollback, and upload of different revisions.

Installing Hexo

All the following steps should be carried out from Git Bash in the folder where the blog is to be stored.

The site can then be previewed locally at http://localhost:4000

Changing the Theme

This site uses Fluid:

3. Writing

At first, I used Typora. Yet every image insertion and every item of note metadata had to be handled manually, which felt like a disgrace to the entire business of writing code. I therefore moved to Obsidian, and this article became the first one I wrote with it.

Installing Obsidian needs no explanation here; consult its official site and the relevant articles:

  • Home—Obsidian Help
  • Obsidian Chinese Forum—Knowledge Management and Notes

If you do not yet know how to write Markdown, learn that first. It is useful, and anyone in an information-related field is unlikely to avoid it:

  • Basic Markdown Syntax—Markdown Tutorial

In practice, the syntax works best when combined with keyboard shortcuts.

4. Publishing

First configure hexo-deployer-git:

Then edit the _config.yml file:

5. Workflow, for Now

  • Create a new post with the new command:
  • Open Obsidian and begin writing.
  • After writing, preview the site locally from the terminal:
  • If the preview looks correct, publish it:

6. Optimisation

Folder-Based Category Trees through Automatic Classification

No project is perfect, and the workflow described above still felt awkward in several places. Categories were one example. Logically, when posts are written locally, their categories ought to follow the containment relationships among folders. Hexo’s native approach, however, requires the following metadata at the beginning of every post:

How am I supposed to manage this? Must I remember exactly where every file belongs in the directory tree, without getting a single character wrong? That merely creates more work. Categories are meant to make management easier; this reverses the whole purpose.

I therefore searched for another solution and found an open-source project:

  • xu-song/hexo-auto-category: Generate Categories Automatically for Each Post in Hexo

Installation and configuration can follow its official documentation. One point deserves attention: peculiar things may happen when a file has no category group—or so it appears.

Automatic Git Pushes

After writing the first few posts, I had to enter Git Bash and run hexo clean, hexo g, and hexo d manually every time. This soon became tiresome, which raised an obvious question: why not use an automation plugin?

The original documentation for the method is:

  • Maintaining a Hexo Blog Perfectly with Obsidian + Git—Zhihu

Importing Templates

Obsidian supports templates natively. Configure the path in Settings and create a template file; that is essentially all that is required.

7. Postscript

Image insertion while writing on this site still needs further improvement. For more detail, consult the following expert’s blog, from which much of this article was drawn:

  • My Process for Deploying a Personal Blog with Obsidian and Hexo—SagiRastar’s Blog
  • Obsidian2Hexo—Zhipeng’s Personal Blog
